units.title: Thinking in Compose
units.summary: Compose describes UI from the current state rather than updating a tree of View objects through setters. A composable body supplies a description that the runtime may execute again, skip, or discard. State flows down to the components that display it, and events flow back to the owner that changes it. These ideas provide the foundation for understanding state ownership, recomposition, effects, and performance in Compose.

lessons.title: Declarative UI and Why Compose Exists
lessons.summary: How describing a screen from its current state changes the way UI updates are expressed, and how it helps prevent application state and displayed values from drifting apart.

blocks.text: If you have built Android screens with Views, you already carry a mental model of how UI works. You create a tree of widget objects, usually by inflating an XML layout, you keep references to the ones you care about, and when something changes you call setters on them. Each widget is a long-lived object that holds its own state and exposes getters and setters for it, and your code's job is to keep the properties of those objects matching the application state they are supposed to be showing.

Compose asks you to work the other way round. You do not hold a widget and change it; in fact Compose does not hand you the emitted UI as objects to mutate at all. You write a function that says what the screen should look like for a given set of inputs, and when those inputs change the runtime calls the same function again with the new values and works out what to change on screen. That is the whole of what declarative means here: you supply the description, the runtime performs the update.

rows: Creating the UI
Instantiate or inflate a tree of widget objects and keep references to the ones that will change.
Call a composable function that describes the UI for the current inputs.
Updating the UI
Call setters on the widgets you kept references to.
Call the same function again with new inputs and let the runtime apply the difference.
Where the displayed state lives
Inside each widget, which owns and exposes its own mutable properties.
In the application state the description is derived from; the emitted UI is not exposed for mutation.
What you have to get right
Every code path that changes application state must also update every widget affected by it.
One description that is correct for any state the screen can be in.

blocks.text:
The last row describes a difference in what you need to keep consistent. In imperative code, each update path must change every widget affected by the new state. As a screen gains more update paths, there are more places where an update can be missed. In declarative code, the description maps the current state to the UI, so each state change uses the same mapping.

This helps with maintenance, but it does not make state bugs impossible. The state you compute can still be wrong. It reduces the risk of application state and displayed values drifting apart because one update path remembered a widget and another did not.

Writing layouts in Kotlin rather than XML does not by itself make them declarative. An imperative widget tree can also be built entirely in Kotlin. The distinction is how you express an update: with Views, you mutate widget properties; with Compose, you describe the UI for the current state and let the runtime apply the update.

Take a small profile screen that can be loading, can be showing content, can be showing an error, and has a submit button that is only enabled when the form is valid. In the View version the widgets already exist, so every state change is expressed as a set of mutations against them.

The `render` function maps the state to all the widgets shown here. `onSubmitFailed` adds a separate update path for one case, but updates only the progress bar and error view. If the content group was hidden and the submit button disabled during submission, this handler leaves them that way. The error is visible, but the screen has not returned to a state in which the user can act on it.

Nothing in these two functions ensures that their updates agree. As separate handlers accumulate, each must account for the other widget properties its change affects.

`ProfileScreen` now describes the UI from `ProfileUiState`. A failed submission can be represented by a state value with `loading` false, an error message present, and `canSubmit` true. The same composable then produces the corresponding screen without a separate set of widget mutations.

The state still needs to represent the screen correctly. A single immutable state type gives you one place to review the relationships between loading, errors, and submission, but it does not automatically prevent invalid combinations. Those relationships need to be expressed in the state model and in the code that creates each value.

When explaining declarative and imperative UI, describe how each expresses an update. Imperative code names the widgets and properties to change. Declarative code describes the intended UI for the current state and leaves the update to the runtime. In Compose, that state-driven description fits naturally with observable state and unidirectional data flow: an owner produces the state, and the UI displays it and reports events back.

lessons.title: What a Composable Is and How It Executes
lessons.summary: A composable contributes a description of UI to the Composition. The runtime can execute its body again, skip it, or discard its work, so the body must be fast, idempotent, and free of side effects.

blocks.text: The `@Composable` annotation marks a function that can participate in Compose's runtime. A UI-emitting composable contributes a description of UI to the Composition, the structure maintained by that runtime. It does not return widget objects for you to update or draw the UI itself. Instead, it calls other composables to describe the UI it needs. Such a function normally returns `Unit`, and calls to composable functions belong in a composable context.
Three terms need precise meanings, because Compose's behaviour is described in them.

items: Composition: the tree of UI descriptions that exists because your composables ran. It is the runtime's record of what your UI currently is, and the only way to change it is by running composables again.
Initial composition: the first run, in which the composables you called are executed and enter the Composition.
Recomposition: a later re-execution, scheduled when state that a composable read has changed, which updates the existing Composition rather than rebuilding it from nothing.

blocks.text: The runtime can execute your composable body again when it needs to update the description, even without a new call from your application code. **Recomposition** explains how state reads are tracked, which scopes a change invalidates, and when a call can be skipped.

sections.title: What a composable is

blocks.text: An `onClick` callback runs in response to a click, and lifecycle callbacks such as `onCreate` and `onResume` run in response to their lifecycle events. Their bodies perform the work associated with those events. A composable body describes UI, and the runtime decides when to execute it to keep the Composition current. You cannot rely on the following assumptions about a composable body.

items: That the body runs once. It runs during initial composition and again on every recomposition that is not skipped.
That the body runs a predictable number of times. How many times depends on what state changed and on what the runtime chose to skip, and that is not part of any contract you can rely on.
That calls to other composables happen in the order they are written, or that a sibling has already run. Compose may execute them in another order, for instance to produce higher-priority UI first.

That every execution reaches the screen. Recomposition is optimistic: Compose expects the inputs to hold still, and if they change again first it can cancel the recomposition and discard the UI it had produced.

blocks.text: With the same inputs, repeated execution should describe the same UI without also repeating an external action. This is the idempotence Compose requires: describing the UI again should not send another request or increment a shared counter. Together with fast execution and freedom from side effects, it lets the runtime update the Composition safely.

Code placed directly in a composable body runs when the runtime needs the description, which is not necessarily once when the screen appears. Sending analytics there can count repeated executions as repeated views; starting a request there can send it again as the UI recomposes. Work that responds to a user action belongs in its callback. Work owned by the Composition needs an effect API with an appropriate lifetime.

sections.title: The execution contract

blocks.text: A side effect changes something observable outside the composable's description of UI. In the following example, executing the body also sends an analytics event.

The problem is the event's trigger. `ProfileScreen` can execute because the runtime needs an updated description, including during recomposition or work that is later discarded. An execution does not necessarily mean the user has viewed the profile again. Calling `trackProfileViewed` from the body makes the analytics count depend on execution rather than on the event you intended to measure.

The counter below has the same problem. It counts executions of `ProfileTitle`, not profile openings. Such a count may describe runtime activity, but it cannot reliably stand in for the number of times the user opened the profile.

Choose the trigger and owner for the work. If a click causes it, put it in the click callback. If the Composition owns it, such as starting a screen load or registering a listener while a composable is present, use an effect API. These APIs give the work a defined lifetime instead of tying it to every execution of the body. **Effect Lifecycle and LaunchedEffect** explains how to choose and manage that lifetime.
In practice, these are the lines that should make you look twice when you find them written directly in a composable body.

items: Starting a network request, a database read, or any other work that should happen once per event.
Writing to SharedPreferences, DataStore, or a file.
Calling a function on a ViewModel that changes its state.
Sending an analytics or logging event intended to measure a user action or a business event.
Registering an observer, listener, or callback with anything outside Compose.
Mutating a variable, collection, or object that is shared with the rest of the app.

blocks.text: Calling functions from a composable body is normal. Reading parameters, formatting a string, mapping values into rows, and calling other composables can all be part of describing UI. The distinction is whether repeating the work only produces another description or also changes something outside it. Description work still takes time, so expensive computation needs separate attention even when it has no side effects.

Keeping composable bodies free of side effects gives the runtime freedom to manage UI updates. It can skip a call whose inputs are unchanged, because leaving the description in place does not omit an external action. It can execute a scope again without repeating a request or changing shared state.

The same reasoning applies to discarded work. If a recomposition is cancelled, no external action should already have depended on the description reaching the screen. And a composable should not rely on a sibling having run first to prepare shared state. These constraints let the runtime control execution without changing the application's intended behaviour.

The Android guidance distinguishes current execution from the contract your code should follow: composable functions are not currently run in parallel, but they should remain correct if execution becomes multithreaded. Do not rely on execution order or mutate shared objects from the body. The practical rule is to leave the number, timing, and relative order of executions to the runtime rather than using them to drive application behaviour.

A side-effect-free body lets the runtime skip, repeat, reorder, or discard a UI description without changing external application state. When an action is tied directly to body execution, those runtime decisions can accidentally omit or repeat the action.

Explain what a UI-emitting composable contributes to the Composition and why its body must be fast, idempotent, and free of side effects. The runtime can execute it again, skip it, change execution order, or discard its work. External actions belong in event callbacks or effect APIs with an appropriate lifetime. If parallel execution comes up, distinguish the current implementation described in Android's guidance from the requirement to write code that would remain correct under multithreaded execution.

lessons.title: State Down, Events Up
lessons.summary: How a state owner supplies values to a Compose screen, how children report user actions, and why this direction supports reuse, testing, and clear responsibility for state changes.

blocks.text: For a text field, the current text comes from its state owner. When the user types, the field reports the proposed change through a callback; the owner decides how to update the value. The field then displays the value it receives. This is the direction used by unidirectional data flow: state travels down from the owner to the composables that display it, and events travel back to the owner that handles them.

items: The owner holds the current state and passes it down as parameters.
The composable describes itself from those parameters and keeps no separate copy of them.
The user interacts, and the composable reports what happened by invoking a callback it was given.
The owner interprets that event and decides how the state changes.
The new state flows back down, and the description is produced again from it.

blocks.text: This is called unidirectional data flow: state is supplied to the UI, and events are reported to its owner. A piece of state has one owner responsible for changing it, so a wrong value can be traced through that owner's event handling and state updates. The UI does not need its own competing copy. Separating the state producer from the UI also lets you test those updates without rendering the screen.

The owner does not have to be a ViewModel. It is whoever is responsible for that piece of state: the parent composable, a plain state-holder class, or a ViewModel when the state is screen-level and has to outlive a configuration change. Choosing between them is a real decision, and the direction described here is the same whichever owner you pick.

An event parameter describes what happened or what the user requested. For a component that edits a single value, such as a text field, a current value and an `onValueChange` callback are a suitable pair. Other interactions describe actions: editing a profile or retrying a failed request, for example. Those components should expose callbacks for those actions, leaving the owner to decide what each action does.

`ProfileHeader` receives the name it displays and a callback for the edit button. You can preview or test it with a string and a lambda, and reuse it wherever the caller supplies those inputs. The caller decides what editing means. The next version moves that dependency into the child by giving it a `ProfileViewModel`.

The ViewModel-based version can render the same UI, but `ProfileHeader` now depends on `ProfileViewModel` and collects its state itself. A preview or component test needs that dependency, and reuse requires a caller able to supply it. The value-and-callback version exposes only what the header needs.

Passing a ViewModel does not by itself give state another owner: events can still be handled by that same ViewModel. The cost here is coupling the child to screen-level state and behaviour. Collecting state at the screen boundary and passing plain values and callbacks keeps that dependency out of reusable children and makes their inputs and actions explicit.

Concluding that unidirectional data flow means every piece of state belongs in a ViewModel. The direction says that each piece of state has one owner and that events travel to that owner. It says nothing about how far away the owner should be. Whether a checkbox, an expanded row, or a scroll position is owned by the composable showing it or by a screen-level holder depends on who else has to read or change it and on how long it needs to survive.

Unidirectional data flow also applies outside Compose. A ViewModel exposing state that a Fragment observes and renders can use the same loop. Compose fits this arrangement because a composable already describes UI from the state it receives.

The architectural benefits are consistency, testability, and maintainability. The UI derives its values from one source of truth. The state producer can be tested separately from rendering. Events are handled by an identifiable owner, so state changes can be traced through the code responsible for them.

The same principle scales into patterns you will be asked about by name: a single immutable state type per screen, user intent modelled as a type rather than a bag of lambdas, and a function that takes the current state plus an event and returns the next state, which is where reducer and MVI-style architectures come from. These architectural patterns are compared in **MVP, MVVM and MVI Responsibility Models**.

One term follows directly from all of this. When a child needs state that a higher-level owner should control, you move the state up into that owner and pass the current value down with an event callback going back up. That move is called state hoisting, and a child that no longer holds the state is called stateless. How far up to move it, which owner is the right one, and what it costs to hoist further than necessary make up a decision model of its own, covered in **State Hoisting and the Lowest Sensible Owner**.

Explain why the direction helps: each piece of state has an owner, children display supplied values and report user intent, and state updates can be tested separately from rendering. Use a specific example to justify whether its state belongs in a composable, a state holder, or a ViewModel. When discussing a child that receives a ViewModel, distinguish coupling to that dependency from introducing competing state ownership. The plain-data-and-callback boundary makes reusable children easier to preview, test, and reuse.

units.title: State and State Ownership
units.summary: Compose needs observable state to update the UI when values change. This unit separates four questions: how a change becomes observable, how a value survives recomposition, how it is restored after the UI is recreated, and who should own it. Collections bring these questions together: changing an ordinary list in place can leave the screen showing its previous contents.

lessons.title: Observable State: `mutableStateOf` and `State<T>`
lessons.summary: Why an ordinary variable can change without anything appearing on screen, what makes a value observable to Compose instead, and why it is the read rather than the write that decides which part of your UI depends on it.

blocks.text: A composable describes the UI from the values it reads. When one of those values changes, Compose needs a notification before it can produce an updated description. A value can change in memory while the screen continues to show its previous value if there is no observable connection between the two.

State, in this context, means any value that can change while the screen is alive and that the screen is described from: a counter, the text in a field, whether a row is expanded, the list of items loaded from the network. The question is what has to be true of such a value for Compose to notice when it changes.

Assigning to an ordinary Kotlin `var` changes its value without notifying Compose. `mutableStateOf` creates an observable `MutableState<T>`: a single-value holder whose reads and writes participate in the Compose runtime.

There are two types because there are two capabilities. `State<T>` is a value you can read and observe. `MutableState<T>` adds the ability to write. Handing a composable the read-only type is how you say that it displays this value but does not change it.

When a composable reads `value` during composition, the runtime records a dependency between that state object and the currently executing recomposition scope. A later change to `value` schedules recomposition of the scopes that read it. The location of the read therefore helps determine which part of the UI needs to execute again.

Reading `value` during composition creates the dependency. Creating a state object nearby or passing the holder as a parameter does not, by itself, subscribe the receiving scope. The scope becomes dependent when it reads the value.

The default mutation policy uses structural equality: assigning a value equal to the current one is not treated as a change.

A read made outside composition, such as in a click handler or coroutine, obtains the current value but does not subscribe a recomposition scope. Calling a plain helper function during composition is different: state reads inside that call are still part of the executing scope’s observation.

How the runtime records those reads and applies those writes is the snapshot system, which is also what makes state changes consistent rather than half-applied. The contract just described — reads record dependencies, writes invalidate them — is enough to reason about state without that machinery, which is covered in **Snapshot Fundamentals**.
In this counter, the click handler runs and increments the variable, but the displayed number does not update.

The debugger can confirm that `count` becomes 1 after a click. The increment works; the missing part is notification. `count` is an ordinary local `Int`, so reading it does not create an observable dependency and writing it does not schedule recomposition. The screen keeps the description produced by the last execution.
Making the value observable is the first correction. It is not yet the whole fix.

This version reads `count.value` in the body, so Compose records a dependency. The click changes that value and schedules recomposition. When the body executes again, however, it calls `mutableStateOf(0)` again and creates a new holder initialized to zero. The update was observed, but the next description uses the new holder rather than the one that received the increment.

Each execution that reaches `mutableStateOf(0)` creates a new holder initialized to zero. In this example the read is in the same body, so the write invalidates that body and the next execution resets the counter.

If the read moves into a child scope that can recompose independently, the counter may increase until the parent body executes for another reason. The parent then creates a new holder and the value resets. The underlying problem is the same in both cases. See **Recomposition Scopes and Selective Execution** for how read locations affect invalidation.

Being observable and surviving re-execution are two independent properties, and a working counter needs both. `remember` supplies the second (see **`remember`: Composition Memory**); with it in place, the observability half can be looked at on its own.

The `by` here is Kotlin's property delegation, not a Compose feature. A delegated property routes reads and writes to another object's `getValue` and `setValue` operators, and Compose defines those for `State` and `MutableState`. The effect is purely notational: `count` now behaves like an ordinary `Int` variable while still being a `MutableState<Int>` underneath, so `count` is a read of `value` and `count++` is a read followed by a write. It needs two imports that are easy to forget, `androidx.compose.runtime.getValue` and `androidx.compose.runtime.setValue`.

rows: Property delegate
`var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }`
`count`, `count++`
When direct value syntax makes the composable easier to read.
Explicit holder
`val count = remember { mutableStateOf(0) }`
`count.value`, `count.value++`
When the holder itself has to be passed somewhere, so the object rather than the value is the thing you need.
Destructured
`val (count, setCount) = remember { mutableStateOf(0) }`
`count`, `setCount(1)`
When a value and a setter are handed to something separately, which mirrors the value-plus-callback pair hoisting uses.

blocks.text:
These forms use the same kind of state holder; they differ in how you read and write its value. At a composable boundary, a value parameter such as `fun Badge(count: Int)` is often convenient because callers can supply a literal in a preview or test.

A `State<Int>` parameter moves the read into the child, which changes where the dependency is recorded and couples the child to Compose’s state API. That may be useful when the read location matters. A `MutableState<Int>` parameter also gives the child permission to write directly. A value-and-event callback pair makes it clearer that the parent owns the value and decides how to handle changes.

Writing to `value` records a state change; it does not draw the screen immediately. The runtime schedules work for the scopes that read the previous value and may combine several writes before updating the UI. Code on the next line should not assume that recomposition or drawing has already finished.

A composition read subscribes the recomposition scope executing at that moment. That scope may belong to a parent rather than to the function containing the read, so the function’s source-code boundary alone does not tell you which work a change will invalidate. `MutableState` schedules recomposition of its subscribed scopes when its value changes.

So the same state object read in two places produces two independent dependencies, and moving a read from a parent into a child moves the dependency with it. This is why "where do I read this?" turns out to be a design question rather than a matter of taste.

The equality behaviour matters for the same reason. `mutableStateOf` defaults to a structural-equality policy, so assigning a value equal to the current one is not treated as a change and schedules nothing. That is usually what you want and occasionally surprising: a state holding a mutable object can be assigned an instance that is `equals` to the old one and correctly produce no update, even though the object's contents differ from what is on screen. That failure and its fixes are covered in **Collections and Observable Mutation**.

For a counter that does not update, distinguish two causes. An ordinary `var` is not observable, so changing it does not schedule recomposition. A holder created with `mutableStateOf` is observable, but without `remember` it is recreated whenever execution reaches that call again.

Explain where the value is read as well: the read establishes the dependency, which helps determine whether an unremembered counter resets after its own update or later when its parent executes again.

lessons.title: `remember`: Composition Memory
lessons.summary: How `remember` retains a value across recomposition, how that differs from observing changes, and how keys determine when a cached value should be recalculated.

blocks.text: Calling `mutableStateOf(0)` directly in a composable body creates a new state object each time execution reaches that call. The object can notify Compose when its value changes, but that does not preserve it across executions. For a counter to keep its value, the next execution needs to use the same state object instead of creating another one initialized to zero.

`remember` lets the Composition retain that object. During initial composition, it runs the calculation you provide and stores the result. On recomposition, it returns the stored value without running the calculation again. The value is forgotten when the composable that called `remember` leaves the Composition.

The cached value belongs to a position in the Composition and lasts while that position remains present. It is not a global cache or a singleton. When a branch closes, a lazy-layout item leaves the Composition, or a screen is removed from the Composition, its remembered value is forgotten.

`remember` retains a value across executions. `mutableStateOf` makes changes to a value observable. Neither provides the other capability. A composable-owned counter needs both: the same holder must be retained, and changes to its value must be observed.

`remember` also takes keys. The value is stored with the keys it was computed from, and if any of them change, the next recomposition invalidates the cache and runs the calculation again. Compose compares keys with the class's `equals` implementation. Keys are how you say what the remembered value is a function of, which is the same as saying when it should be discarded.
Because the two properties are independent, there are four combinations, and each of them appears in real code.

rows: `var count = 0`
No
No

A variable nothing observes. The click really does change it, and it keeps changing — Kotlin's closure captures the variable itself, so repeated clicks accumulate in memory — but no dependency was recorded, so nothing is scheduled and the screen never changes. It returns to its initial value whenever this body executes again.
`val config = remember { loadConfig() }`
Yes
No
A cached object computed once while this position remains in the Composition. Useful for a formatter, a `Paint`, or a derived constant that does not need observable updates.
`var count by mutableStateOf(0)`
No
Yes

A write is seen and schedules recomposition, but the holder is recreated at its initial value every time this body executes. Looks like a counter frozen at zero when the read is in the same body; looks like a value that works and then silently resets when the read sits in a lambda that can recompose on its own.
`var count by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }`
Yes
Yes
Observable state owned by a composable: the holder persists while its position remains in the Composition, and changes to its value schedule updates for scopes that read it.

blocks.text: Not every retained object needs to be observable state. A formatter that is expensive to construct but never replaced can be cached with `remember` alone. Wrapping it in `mutableStateOf` adds a writable state holder even though this code has no updates to observe.
Keys can cause two different problems. If a key omits a dependency, `remember` can retain a value after the input used to create it has changed.

As long as `UserEditor` stays at the same position in the Composition, it keeps the remembered holder. Passing a different user therefore leaves the previous name, or the unfinished edit, in the field. Keying the holder by `user.id` resets the draft when editing switches to another user.

blocks.code: var draftName by remember(user.id) { mutableStateOf(user.name) }

blocks.text: A key that changes too often causes the opposite problem: the draft is discarded while the user is still editing. Keying this draft by the whole `user` value would reset it whenever an unrelated property changes and makes that value unequal. A fresh key object that compares unequal on each execution would reset it each time. A newly created but equal key does not invalidate `remember`; keys are compared with `equals`, not instance identity.

`remember` retains a value across recomposition but does not restore it after a configuration change recreates the UI. For that requirement, use a saved-state mechanism such as `rememberSaveable`, or an appropriately scoped owner that survives the recreation. See **`rememberSaveable` and State That Must Survive**.

A remembered value is identified by the call’s position in the Composition. The keys passed to `remember` control recalculation within that position; they do not give it a global name. Separate instances of the same call, such as calls in several list rows, can therefore retain separate values.

If closing the panel should discard its draft, keeping `remember` inside the branch gives it the intended lifetime. If the draft should remain when the panel reopens, move the remembered holder to a caller that stays in the Composition. This changes the owner and extends the value’s lifetime; see **State Hoisting and the Lowest Sensible Owner**.

There is a matching subtlety in what identifies a call site when the same one runs several times, as it does for the rows of a list. Compose has a mechanism for telling those instances apart, and getting it wrong makes remembered state stick to the wrong item after a reorder. That is composition identity, covered in **Composable Identity**; what matters here is that `remember` is attached to a position rather than to a name.

When explaining `remember` and `mutableStateOf`, distinguish retention from observation. `remember` keeps a value across executions; `mutableStateOf` makes changes observable. Their combination provides both capabilities.

For keys, explain the consequences for the user: omitting a dependency can leave stale data on screen, while a key that changes unnecessarily can discard an unfinished edit.

lessons.title: `rememberSaveable` and State That Must Survive
lessons.summary: Four things a piece of UI state might have to live through — re-execution, leaving the Composition, the screen being recreated, the process being killed — and how to pick a mechanism for a given piece of state without treating saved state as a database.

blocks.text: A value may need to survive recomposition, removal from the Composition, recreation of the UI, or recreation of the process. These events have different consequences for state. Choosing a mechanism starts with identifying which events the value must survive; saving it after UI recreation does not automatically retain it when a branch closes.

rows: Recomposition — the composable body running again
As needed when observed state or inputs change
`remember`, and anything stored in the Composition
The composable leaving the Composition and later being composed again — a branch closing and reopening, a screen going back on a navigation stack
Whenever a branch toggles or a destination changes

An owner that stays in the Composition, so hoisting the state to a caller that does not leave; or a `SaveableStateHolder` around the subtree, which is what navigation libraries use to give each destination its own saved state
The whole UI being recreated, as on an Android configuration change
Occasionally — a rotation, a theme change
A saved-state mechanism such as `rememberSaveable`, or an owner with a longer life such as a `ViewModel`
The process being killed by the system and recreated later with the user's task intact
Rarely, and never at a moment you control
A saved-state mechanism such as `rememberSaveable`, within the limits below; or durable storage. Not a `ViewModel` on its own

blocks.text: `remember` retains its value across recompositions while its position remains in the Composition. It does not restore that value after a configuration change recreates the UI and its Composition.

`rememberSaveable` alone does not retain a value when its call leaves the Composition. It unregisters from the saved-state registry on removal; toggling a branch is not the same event as saving the host’s state for recreation.

To retain the value, hoist it to a caller that remains present or put the subtree inside a `SaveableStateHolder`. The holder saves the subtree’s saveable state before disposal and restores it when the same key is composed again. Navigation libraries use this arrangement to restore destination state, such as scroll position, when a screen returns.

The third and fourth rows are where `rememberSaveable` earns its name. It behaves like `remember` in that it retains a value across recomposition, and additionally stores that value through the saved instance state mechanism, so it is restored across activity or process recreation. Using it is a one-word change at the call site.

`rememberSaveable` uses Android’s saved instance state mechanism to restore small values after system-initiated process death when the user’s task is retained. This depends on saved state being available and on the limits of the `Bundle` used to store it.

Use a database or file for durable data. Saved instance state is not retained after the user dismisses the activity, for example by swiping it away from Recents.

On Android, `rememberSaveable` registers with the Composition’s saveable-state registry. The host’s saved-state owner, such as an activity or navigation entry, connects that registry to the platform’s saved-state machinery. Values saved through this connection can be restored when the host is recreated. Keep the four events distinct: recomposition, removal from the Composition, UI recreation, and process recreation.

On Android, `rememberSaveable` automatically handles values that can be stored in a `Bundle`, including primitive values and strings. For a custom value that is not directly saveable, a `Saver` describes how to convert it to saveable values and restore it.

`listSaver` and `mapSaver` describe a value in terms of saveable list or map entries. On Android, a type can also implement `Parcelable` using `@Parcelize`, or you can implement a `Saver` directly. If a saver becomes complicated, check whether the whole object needs to be restored or whether a smaller identifier would be enough.

Saved instance state has a size limit, and the `Bundle` used by `rememberSaveable` is shared with other saved-state writers. Large objects can cause a `TransactionTooLargeException` when the state is transferred. In a single-activity app, state from several screens can contribute to the same limit.

The guidance that follows from that is to store the minimum: identifiers and keys rather than the objects they identify, and then use those to restore the richer state from somewhere that is built to hold it.

Typical saved UI values are small and transient: scroll position, an expanded section, an unfinished selection, or text not yet submitted. They let the user return to the same interaction after recreation. If losing a value would destroy important work or application data, store it durably rather than relying only on saved instance state.

Choose `rememberSaveable` when a value needs saved-state restoration. Each saved value must be representable in the shared, limited `Bundle` and requires work to save and restore. Values that can reasonably reset, be recalculated, or be reloaded may not need to be saved; retain only what is necessary to restore the user’s interaction.

`rememberSaveable`, `ViewModel`, `SavedStateHandle`, and durable storage serve different lifetimes and responsibilities. A screen can use several together: one mechanism retains an owner in memory, another restores small values, and durable storage holds application data.

blocks.text: The table covers recreation, but retaining a removed subtree is a separate requirement. Neither `remember` nor `rememberSaveable` alone keeps a value after its call leaves the Composition. An owner that remains present can retain it, and a `SaveableStateHolder` can save and restore the subtree’s saveable values. A `ViewModel` also retains values while its own scope remains alive, even if a consuming composable leaves.

A `ViewModel` instance is retained across configuration changes but does not survive system-initiated process death. `SavedStateHandle` restores small values needed to rebuild its state and uses the same limited saved-state mechanism. Store simple values such as selected identifiers there, then reproduce larger screen state from business rules and application data.

An article screen can save its scroll position as UI state, keep the selected article’s identifier in `SavedStateHandle`, and reload the article through a repository backed by a database. Each mechanism preserves a different part of the interaction or its data. Choose them by asking what each value must survive and where it can be reconstructed.

For a text field that should survive rotation, explain that `remember` retains a value across recomposition while `rememberSaveable` also participates in saved-state restoration. For a larger object, explain why saving its identifier and reloading the object is often preferable: the saved-state `Bundle` is limited and shared. A `ViewModel` retains its instance across configuration changes, but restoring after process death requires saved state or durable data.

lessons.title: State Hoisting and the Lowest Sensible Owner
lessons.summary: How to choose a state owner from the components that read and change the value, the logic that uses it, and its required lifetime. Hoisting gives callers control, but moving every value to the screen level adds costs.

blocks.text: Local state held with `remember` works well when a component can manage it independently. If a parent needs to read the value, a sibling needs to react to it, or a preview needs to supply a particular value, callers need control over that state. State hoisting moves the value to the caller: the caller passes the current value down and the component reports events back up.

A **stateful** composable retains state of its own. A **stateless** version receives the relevant state as parameters and reports user actions through callbacks. Hoisting separates the component’s rendering from ownership of that state, so callers can supply values for reuse, previews, and tests.
That value-plus-callback pair is state down, events up, applied to one component. The direction raises a question it does not answer: how far up the state should go.
The documentation gives three rules for choosing how far to hoist state:

items: State should be hoisted to at least the lowest common parent of all composables that read it.
State should be hoisted to at least the highest level at which it may be changed.
If two pieces of state change in response to the same events, they should be hoisted together.

blocks.text: The first two rules establish how high the owner must be to serve the readers and writers. The third keeps state together when the same events update it. If the owner is below a component that needs the value, the normal downward flow cannot supply that component. Moving the owner to their common parent provides a shared source of state.

Choose the lowest owner that can serve all readers and writers and support the required logic and lifetime. Keeping state near where it is used limits the number of components that need to know about it. Move it higher when a concrete requirement needs a broader owner.

A stateless implementation can be paired with a stateful convenience overload. Callers that need control supply the value and callback; other callers use the overload that retains default state. This preserves a convenient API while allowing the ownership decision to change later.

Consider a settings switch. If only the switch needs its `enabled` value, local ownership can be sufficient. If a summary elsewhere on the screen also reads it, their common parent can own the value and pass it to both. If a save action submits it, the form owner needs access as well.

Surviving rotation does not, by itself, require moving the state. A locally owned value can use `rememberSaveable` for restoration. Choose a broader owner when the readers, writers, or logic require it, and choose a persistence mechanism that supports the resulting lifetime.

Hoisting every local detail to the screen level adds responsibilities to the screen’s state type and requires values and callbacks to pass through intermediate components. A checkbox used by one component can then require changes across several layers.

It can also broaden invalidation if the screen reads the combined state before passing values down. Ownership alone does not determine recomposition: the location of the reads matters, and unaffected children may still be skipped. See **Recomposition Scopes and Selective Execution**.

When several related values and the UI logic coordinating them belong together, a plain state holder class can own them. Remembering that Kotlin object in the Composition keeps the logic within the UI layer while allowing it to be tested separately from rendering.

The `private set` properties prevent callers from assigning values directly. The named functions express the supported changes: editing the query and toggling a tag. Remembered in the Composition, this holder follows the owning composable’s lifetime and can work with UI types such as `LazyListState`. Business logic and application data normally belong to a screen-level or application owner with the dependencies and lifetime they need.

Hoisting means choosing an owner above the component that uses the state; it does not automatically mean using a `ViewModel`. A row’s expanded state can often remain in the component or a nearby UI owner. Business logic that reads or changes it may justify moving it to a screen-level owner.

Restoration is a related but separate choice. A composable can own state restored by `rememberSaveable` after rotation. If the value must remain when that composable leaves the Composition, a longer-lived owner or a saveable-state holder may be needed.
For each piece of state, choose the lowest owner that can meet its requirements. Check its readers, its writers, and the lifetime it needs.

items: Who reads it? The owner must be at or above the lowest common ancestor of every reader.
Who writes it? The owner must be at or above everything that can change it, including a save button, a retry, or a navigation event.

How long must it live? Configuration-change restoration can use `rememberSaveable` without moving local state. If the composable leaves the Composition, retaining the value requires an owner that remains or a `SaveableStateHolder` around the subtree. Surviving process death requires saved state or durable storage regardless of the owner.

blocks.text: The appropriate owner may sit outside the Composition. When business logic needs the value, a `ViewModel` can own it and expose state to the composables that display it. The common-ancestor principle still applies: the owner must be able to serve every consumer.

**UI element state** describes an element’s presentation, such as whether it is expanded, where it is scrolled, or whether it has focus. **Screen UI state** describes what the screen should display after business rules are applied to application data. A screen-level owner normally produces that screen state.

UI element state can remain local when only the component needs it. If business logic needs to read or change it, that same element state may need to be hoisted to the screen-level owner.

A single owner gives each value a clear source of truth. Events may arrive through several paths, but the owner coordinates the resulting changes, which makes incorrect state easier to trace. An overload pair also allows callers to take control when needed. Start with the lowest suitable owner and revisit the choice when a new reader, writer, or lifetime requirement appears.

Explain hoisting through both ownership and data flow: move state to an owner that can serve its readers and writers, pass values down, and report events up. This lets the child receive controlled values for reuse, previews, and tests.

A `ViewModel` is one possible owner when screen-level logic requires it. Hoisting farther than needed adds parameter passing and screen-state responsibilities; it can also broaden invalidation when reads move upward.

lessons.title: Collections and Observable Mutation
lessons.summary: Why mutating an ordinary list inside a state holder can leave the UI unchanged, how replacement and snapshot-aware collections make changes observable, and why a read-only `List` is not necessarily immutable.

blocks.text: An `Int` or `String` changes by replacing the value. A mutable collection can change in another way: its contents can be edited while the reference stays the same. If an ordinary list is held in `MutableState`, this internal mutation does not write to the holder, so it does not notify Compose.

The list grows after each click, but `add` changes the object referenced by `items.value` without assigning to `value`. The ordinary list does not notify Compose about that mutation, and the state holder still refers to the same object. The screen therefore has no state-change notification telling it to display the new item.

Compose observes the state holder, not arbitrary objects. `MutableState` reports a change when its `value` is written; it has no way to learn that something inside the object it holds was modified. Mutable objects that are not themselves observable — an `ArrayList`, a `mutableListOf`, a data class with `var` properties — do not trigger recomposition when they change.

One solution is to create a new list and assign it to `value`. Using a read-only `List<T>` at this boundary also prevents callers from invoking mutating methods through that reference. The following example combines replacement with an observable holder.

The value is now exposed as `List<String>`, so `add` is unavailable through this reference. The click produces a new list and assigns it to the state holder, which can observe the change. The read-only type helps enforce this update style, although it does not guarantee that no other reference can mutate the underlying object.
Kotlin’s collection operators support replacement when adding, removing, or updating elements:

The alternative is a collection that is itself observable. `mutableStateListOf` and `mutableStateMapOf` produce snapshot-aware collections where the mutating operations are the notification, so `add` and `remove` work the way the broken example expected them to.

Assign a new list to the holder
Call `add`, `remove`, `set` on the collection
Cost of a small edit
Copies the list
Supports observable mutation without replacing the collection reference
Crosses layers well
Yes — a plain `List` is what a repository or a `ViewModel` already exposes
No — it is a Compose runtime type, so it pulls Compose into wherever it is held
Fits it best
Screen state that arrives from elsewhere, and lists that are replaced wholesale
Frequently edited lists owned by the UI, when measurement shows replacement costs matter

blocks.text: Replacement is a useful default for screen state received from a repository or `ViewModel`, because the boundary can stay a plain `List`. A snapshot-aware collection can suit a locally owned list with frequent edits. Keep the ownership boundary in mind: exposing it from the data layer also introduces a dependency on the Compose runtime.
A nested mutable object can hide the same problem even when the outer holder is assigned a new instance.

In the assignment using `copy()`, the new `Filters` instance shares the original list because generated copies are shallow. Adding a tag changes that shared list in both instances, so the two instances still compare equal. The default policy treats the assignment as unchanged.

Replace the nested list as well, so the old value keeps its previous contents and the new value represents the update. In the next example, the `List` property is updated by constructing a replacement.

blocks.code:
data class Filters(val tags: List<String> = emptyList())

filters = filters.copy(tags = filters.tags + "kotlin")

blocks.text: When a collection change does not appear on screen, first check how it became observable. Was a new value assigned to the state holder, or was an operation performed on a snapshot-aware collection? Mutating an ordinary nested object provides neither notification. Investigate skipping and performance after verifying that the update can be observed.

Kotlin’s `List` is a read-only interface, not a guarantee of immutability. A `List<String>` reference has no mutating methods, but another reference may expose the same object as a `MutableList` and change its contents. Assigning that object to a read-only reference does not make a copy.

In this repository, `items` exposes the cache itself. A composable can hold that reference while `refresh()` changes its contents without an observable notification. To give the caller a separate snapshot of the list’s contents, copy the list or expose an immutable collection. A list copy is shallow: if the elements themselves are mutable and shared, their properties can still change.

This distinction also matters for stability. Compose treats standard `List`, `Set`, and `Map` parameter types as unstable because their read-only interfaces do not establish immutability. That classification does not mean a composable can never be skipped: with strong skipping, unstable parameters are compared by instance identity.

Read-only access restricts operations through a reference; immutability concerns whether the object’s contents can change. See **Stability and Skipping** for how these properties affect execution.

For a list that grows in memory but not on screen, explain whether the mutation writes to an observable holder or occurs on an observable collection. Replacing the list and using a snapshot-aware collection are two solutions; replacement keeps plain collection types at layer boundaries.

For nested data, also check shallow `copy()` behaviour and mutable aliases behind a read-only `List`. These can preserve the same notification problem after an outer assignment has been added.

units.title: Recomposition
units.summary: A user interaction can lead to a state write, invalidation of the scopes that read it, recomposition, and an updated frame. These are separate steps: a write does not immediately re-execute a composable or redraw the screen. Where state is read determines which work Compose needs to repeat. To assess performance, look at the cost of that work rather than the recomposition count alone.

lessons.title: Composition and Recomposition
lessons.summary: Follow a counter update from the button click through a state write, invalidation, and scheduled recomposition to the layout and drawing work needed to update the screen.

blocks.text: A composable describes UI when it executes. During composition, reading observable state records a dependency on that state. When the value changes, Compose can schedule the scope that read it to run again. Updating the screen involves several steps, so it helps to distinguish the state write, the scheduled execution, and the resulting frame.

During **initial composition**, Compose executes the composables you call and builds the Composition, its record of the UI they describe. During **recomposition**, it re-executes affected parts of that work and updates the existing Composition.

A composable enters the Composition, may be recomposed zero or more times, and eventually leaves it.
A composable does not need to recompose periodically to remain on screen. If its inputs and observed state stay unchanged, Compose can keep using the UI it already described.

Recomposition re-executes the composables that may need to describe different UI and updates the Composition with the result. It does not require every composable to run, and it is separate from the layout and drawing work that produces the visible screen.
Compose renders UI through three main phases. Composition describes what to show; layout and drawing use that description to produce the visible result.

rows: Composition
*What* to show
Runs composable functions and produces a description of the UI.
Layout
*Where* to put it
Measures each element and places it, in two steps, in 2D coordinates.
Drawing
*How* it renders
Draws the elements into a canvas — usually the device screen.

blocks.text:
Recomposition repeats work in the composition phase. Compose then performs the layout and drawing work required by the result, avoiding work whose inputs and output have not changed. It may not need to repeat either later phase.

Drawing can also happen without recomposition. If a changing value is read only during drawing, Compose can update the drawn content without re-running composition.

A state change does not always rebuild, remeasure, and redraw the whole UI. Recomposition updates the affected parts of the Composition. Compose repeats layout and drawing only where the change requires them.
This counter screen has a changing label and a static header. Follow what happens when the user taps Increment.

During initial composition, `CounterScreen`, `Header`, `CountLabel`, and `Button` describe their UI, and `remember` retains the counter’s state object.

The observable state read happens in `CounterScreen`, where `count` is evaluated to pass an argument to `CountLabel`. Inside `CountLabel`, the parameter named `count` is an ordinary `Int`; reading it does not read the state object again.
Now the user taps the button. Four distinct things happen, in this order.

items: **An event.** The button invokes `onClick`. This callback handles the click; it is not a composition pass.
**A write to observable state.** `count++` reads the current value and assigns a new one. Because the new value differs from the old under the default equality policy, this counts as a change.

**Invalidation.** The runtime marks the scopes that recorded a read of the state as needing recomposition. Here, that scope is `CounterScreen`. This records the need for execution; it does not immediately run the composable.

**Execution and application.** During a subsequent composition pass, `CounterScreen` runs with `count` equal to 1. Compose applies the resulting changes to the Composition, then performs the layout and drawing work they require.

blocks.text:
`CounterScreen` needs to re-execute because it read the changed state. It then calls `CountLabel` with a different `Int`, so the label can describe the new count. `Header` receives the same `String`, allowing Compose to skip its body if nothing else invalidated it. The button’s constant text does not depend on `count` and need not change.

The state change therefore requires an updated label, without requiring every composable on the screen to execute again.

Invalidation records that a scope needs updating; recomposition executes the code later. Multiple writes before that execution can be handled in one pass, using the latest values. Writes that occur across different passes may lead to further executions.

Assignment counts, composable execution counts, and drawn frame counts therefore measure different things. None gives a fixed conversion to the others.

A state write does not synchronously run the composable that reads it. Code immediately after `count++` cannot assume the visible UI already shows the new value. Handle the event by updating state; Compose schedules the UI work needed to reflect it.
An analytics call inside `CountLabel` would run when Compose executes the body, rather than when a defined user event occurs.

Calling `analytics.track` here does not reliably count how often the user saw the label. Compose may skip `CountLabel` when its inputs are unchanged, execute it for other reasons, or discard the result of an execution. The analytics call has already happened even if that result never reaches the screen.

Code in a composable body must not rely on a particular execution count or ordering relative to sibling composables. Work caused by a user action belongs in its event callback. Work tied to the Composition belongs in an appropriate effect API, which provides a defined lifecycle (see **Effect Lifecycle and LaunchedEffect**).
Recomposition may be cancelled, and a composable may execute frequently. Both behaviours affect what can safely go in its body.

Recomposition is **optimistic**: Compose starts with the current inputs and expects to finish before they change again. If they change during the pass, Compose may cancel that work and restart with the new values.

Compose can discard the UI result of a cancelled pass, but it cannot undo an analytics call, storage write, or other external effect that already happened inside the body. This is another reason to keep composable bodies free of side effects.

A composable may execute as often as every frame when, for example, it reads state that changes during an animation. Its body therefore needs to be fast enough for frequent execution as well as idempotent and free of side effects. The exact frequency depends on what changes and where those values are read.

Each phase tracks its own state reads. A change to state read during composition can schedule recomposition; a change read during layout can schedule layout; and a change read only during drawing can schedule drawing alone. Measurement and placement within layout also have separate restart scopes.

This lets the visible screen change without recomposition. When an API provides a suitable layout or drawing lambda, reading the value there can keep that dependency out of composition.

For a question about initial composition and recomposition, explain that initial composition builds the Composition, while recomposition updates it by re-executing affected scopes. Eligible composables with unchanged inputs may be skipped.

Distinguish both from layout and drawing: recomposition may require work in those phases, but does not always require it. A value read only during layout or drawing can change the visible UI without recomposition.

lessons.title: Recomposition Scopes and Selective Execution
lessons.summary: A recomposition scope is code Compose can restart independently. State reads determine which scopes a change invalidates. Compare a screen that reads a value in its body with one that passes the state holder to a child, and see why an inline layout wrapper does not create a new scope.

blocks.text: A state write invalidates the scopes that recorded a read of that state. If a screen reads a field’s value, a keystroke can cause the screen body to run again. If a child field reads the value instead, the change can be handled by that child’s scope.

A **recomposition scope** is a region of code Compose can restart independently. The compiler normally generates a scope for a non-inline composable that returns `Unit`. `@NonRestartableComposable` opts out of the generated restart and skip machinery.

Reading `State.value` during composition records a dependency in the currently executing scope. When the value changes, Compose schedules the scopes that recorded those reads for recomposition.

The dependency belongs to the scope executing the read, rather than to the code that created or wrote the state. Two independent scopes that read the same state can both be invalidated. A composable does not gain a dependency merely because it is close to the state declaration in the source.
These two versions render the same field and chart. They differ in where the field’s state value is read.

In version A the read happens in `ProfileScreenA`'s own body, because producing the argument `name = name` requires reading `value` there. That body is therefore the subscribed scope, and typing a character invalidates the whole of it. In version B `ProfileScreenB` passes the holder without reading it; the read happens inside `NameField`, so `NameField` is the subscribed scope and typing invalidates only that.

In both versions, the screen retains the state holder and the field’s change callback writes to it. Moving the read into `NameField` changes which scope is invalidated without changing where the state is stored.

Version A can still perform well. When `ProfileScreenA` runs again, `ExpensiveChart` receives the same data if the repository’s chart data has not changed. If the chart is eligible for skipping and its inputs compare unchanged, Compose can skip its body. Re-executing the screen does not necessarily repeat all of its children’s work.

If Compose cannot skip `ExpensiveChart`, version A may repeat its work on each keystroke. Skipping depends on the compiler’s rules, the parameter comparisons, and whether the chart itself was invalidated (see **Stability and Skipping**). In version B, typing into the field does not invalidate `ProfileScreenB`, so this state change does not make the screen call the chart again.

**Invalidation** marks a scope that read changed state as needing recomposition. **Skipping** allows Compose to avoid executing an eligible child call reached during recomposition when its inputs are unchanged and it has no independent reason to run. Read location determines invalidation; compiler rules and input comparisons govern skipping.
Adding a layout wrapper does not necessarily create a new recomposition scope. In this version, putting `TextField` inside another `Column` leaves the state read in `ProfileScreenC`’s scope.

`Column`, `Row`, and `Box` are inline composables. Their content executes within the caller’s scope rather than creating a separate restart scope. The read of `name` in the inner `Column` therefore still belongs to `ProfileScreenC`, so a change invalidates that screen scope.

Extracting code into a function creates a separate scope only if that function is restartable. A non-inline composable returning `Unit` normally gets one, unless it opts out with `@NonRestartableComposable`. An inline function does not establish that separate boundary.

A composable returning a value other than `Unit` is not eligible for skipping. The usual convention is for composables to emit UI through calls rather than return it.

headers: Effect on a read inside it
rows: A separate restartable `@Composable fun` returning `Unit`
Yes
The read is recorded against that function, so only it is invalidated.
A `Column`, `Row` or `Box` content lambda
No — these are `inline`
The read belongs to the enclosing composable, exactly as if the wrapper were not there.
A private helper function that is not `@Composable`
No
When called during composition, its state reads are recorded in the caller’s active scope.

blocks.text:
When `name` is a state holder, passing `name` passes the object without reading its value. Passing `name.value` reads the value in the caller. A lambda such as `() -> Int` can also defer a read: the dependency is recorded where that lambda is invoked.

Plain values are usually easier to understand, preview, and test. Pass a holder or defer a read with a lambda when controlling the read location has a useful purpose.

Extra layout wrappers do not necessarily narrow invalidation, and changing every parameter to `State` can make an API harder to use. Use the scope model to understand where a state change causes work, then adjust read locations when that work presents a measured problem. Keep plain value parameters where they serve the API well.

A state object can be used by several parts of the UI. The write alone does not identify which of them need updating. By recording reads, Compose learns which scopes depend on the value and can invalidate those scopes when it changes.

Reading `count` inside `onClick` gives the callback its current value without subscribing a recomposition scope. The callback runs outside composition, so no composition scope is observing that read. Reads during layout or drawing have their own tracking, as described below.

The same reasoning extends one phase further. Because layout and drawing track their own reads, a value read only where it is used for placement or painting can change the screen without invalidating any composition scope at all. Reading state inside a layout- or draw-phase lambda can move a dependency out of composition when that API is appropriate; it is the same principle — move the read to the code that depends on it — applied to a later phase.

Several writes can be handled in one execution, a recomposition can be cancelled and restarted, and eligible calls with unchanged inputs can be skipped. These behaviours prevent a fixed relationship between state changes and execution counts.

Use the scope model to identify which code a change can invalidate. Use measurements to find out how much work actually ran in a particular interaction.

For a question about state reads, explain that reading changing `State` during composition can schedule the reading scope for recomposition. Moving the read into a smaller restartable child can narrow invalidation. A read does not consume the state or remove its tracking, and a change does not require everything on screen to recompose.

Use `ProfileScreenB` to explain why read location matters more than storage or write location. Use `ProfileScreenC` to show why an inline `Column` does not create a separate scope.

lessons.title: Recomposition Is Not the Problem
lessons.summary: Recomposition updates the UI as state changes. To assess performance, examine what each execution costs and whether it causes a visible delay, rather than treating a low recomposition count as the goal.

blocks.text: A composable running often is not, by itself, evidence of a performance problem. Before adding stability annotations or memoization, identify work that is unnecessarily repeated and determine whether its cost matters for the interaction.

Recomposition is the normal way Compose updates its UI description. A composable that reads changing animation state may run as often as every frame. Frequent execution can be appropriate, provided the work in the body is fast enough.

A recomposition count tells you how often a composable executed. It does not tell you how long that work took, whether it caused a dropped frame, or whether its result reached the screen. Use the count alongside performance measurements and the user-visible behaviour.

A composable body usually reads parameters, makes decisions about the UI, and calls child composables. Those operations should stay small enough to repeat frequently. Sorting a large list, decoding data, allocating large objects, or performing blocking I/O can make each execution expensive.

Composition has a cost even when the body contains only UI code. The practical question is whether that cost fits the frame budget, and which unnecessary work contributes to it.

headers: Potentially expensive work to avoid repeating unnecessarily
rows: Reading parameters and formatting them into a string
Sorting or filtering a thousand-element list on every execution
Choosing between branches based on state
Parsing, decoding, or deserialising on every execution
Calling child composables and passing values down
Allocating large objects that a `remember` would have kept
Deciding a colour or a size from the current state
Blocking I/O, disk reads, or anything that waits

blocks.text: Repeating the operations on the right can make recomposition expensive. Similar work can also be costly in a `View` that binds repeatedly. If this work causes a performance problem, consider caching it for unchanged inputs or moving it out of composition (see **Keeping Work Out of Composition**).
Investigate the work performed during recomposition when assessing a performance problem. These three kinds of evidence help connect an execution count to something that needs changing.

items: **A symptom a user could notice.** Jank while scrolling, a laggy text field, an animation that stutters, or a screen that takes too long to appear. A high execution count alone does not establish any of these problems.
**Expensive work on the recomposing path.** Identify what the body repeatedly computes, allocates, or waits for. Frequent execution alone does not establish that this work is expensive.

**A causal link between the work and the symptom.** Check whether the expensive work runs during the affected interaction and whether reducing it improves that interaction. This helps avoid optimising code that was not causing the delay.

blocks.text: A composable that emits two `Text` elements on each animation frame may be inexpensive enough for that interaction. A composable that repeatedly sorts a large list on each keystroke may cause a noticeable delay. Reducing an unnecessary sort can help even if the recomposition count stays the same.

When `query` changes, `ContactList` needs to compute which contacts match it. The problem is that the filter and sort also run whenever the body executes for another reason. If both `contacts` and `query` are unchanged, the same inputs produce the same result, so recomputing it may be avoidable.

Choose the technique according to the repeated work. Cache a calculation using the inputs it depends on. Keep expensive non-UI work outside the UI layer. If a consumer needs updates less often than its source state changes, derived state can restrict updates to changes in the derived result.

Skipping can also avoid executing eligible composables whose inputs are unchanged. Stability affects how Compose compares parameters, but an annotation is a promise about a type’s behaviour, not a general performance switch. Use it only when that promise is accurate (see **Stability and Skipping**).

Avoid treating every recomposition as a bug, but do not assume recomposition is free. A body that runs every frame must do its work within the time available for that frame. Investigate unnecessary work and its measured cost before restructuring the code to reduce execution frequency.

When asked how to reduce unnecessary recomposition, connect the answer to the performance problem. Reading state close to where it is used can narrow invalidation; keeping expensive computation out of composable bodies can reduce the cost of execution. Explain which work you would avoid, then choose an appropriate tool such as memoization, skipping, or a later-phase state read.

units.title: Identity, Keys, Stability and Immutability
units.summary: Composition identity, observable changes and skipping answer different questions. Identity determines which composable instance owns remembered state. Observation determines which reads need an update after a change. Stability helps determine how arguments are compared when a call may be skipped. This unit separates those mechanisms, explains what Kotlin’s read-only and immutable types guarantee, and shows why `@Stable` and `@Immutable` must describe contracts your types actually satisfy.

lessons.title: Composable Identity
lessons.summary: Compose uses call sites and, for repeated calls, execution order or explicit keys to distinguish composable instances. Remembered state belongs to those instances. This lesson explains why a field can lose its draft when a branch changes, even if the screen still looks much the same.

blocks.text: Reading observable state during composition records a dependency; changing that state can invalidate the scope that read it. Compose also needs to track which composable instance is making the read. When execution reaches a call again, it must distinguish an existing instance with remembered state from a new instance that needs to be created.
Tracking an instance’s identity is separate from recording an observable change and deciding whether to skip a call. Each mechanism answers a different question:

rows: Is this the same composition identity?
The call site, execution order among repeated calls, and any explicit keys
It is not decided by comparing your data, and it is not decided by what appears on screen
Was an observable change recorded?
Whether an observable state holder recorded a change that affects a scope which read it
It is not decided by whether an object was modified
Can execution be skipped when this call is reached?
Whether the call is skippable, its arguments are unchanged, and no independent invalidation requires it to run
It is not a promise that the call never runs

blocks.text: This lesson follows composition identity. **Collections and Observable Mutation** explains observation, and **Stability and Skipping** explains the comparisons used for skipping.

A **call site** is the source-code location where a composable is called. The compiler distinguishes different call sites, so calling the same function from two places creates distinct instances in the Composition. Each instance has its own remembered state.

Typing in the display-name field does not change the email field. Both use the `LabelledField` function, but the two call sites create separate instances, each with its own `text` state. `remember` stores its value at that call’s position within the instance; you do not need to name a storage location yourself.

Remembered state belongs to a composable instance in the Composition. Its call site, execution order and any explicit keys determine its identity. Ordinary `remember` retains a value while that instance remains composed, provided its own keys do not change. Removing the instance also removes its remembered values.
A field can lose its draft when a change in screen structure replaces its composition instance. In this panel, switching between compact and expanded layouts does exactly that:

The two `NoteField` calls are different call sites, and only one is composed at a time. Changing `compact` removes the instance in the old branch and creates an instance in the new branch. The old instance’s remembered draft is forgotten.

The screen still shows a text field in roughly the same place, so its appearance alone does not reveal the change in identity.

An `if` does not automatically discard remembered state. The draft is lost here because the call site that owns it leaves the Composition. The following version changes the layout while keeping `NoteField` at one call site:

Changing `compact` now changes the width modifier while `NoteField` stays at the same call site. Its instance remains in the Composition, so its draft survives. When diagnosing a reset, check whether the change removes the call that owns the state or only changes that call’s arguments.

A remembered token can help you observe the identity change. In the two-branch version, its value changes when `compact` flips; in the one-call-site version, it stays the same. The fields can look similar even though their remembered values have different lifetimes.

If the draft needs to survive a branch change, hoist it to a caller that remains composed and pass it to the field. **State Hoisting and the Lowest Sensible Owner** explains how to choose that owner. If changing the panel should clear the draft, keeping the state inside the branch gives that lifetime.

Inferring identity from appearance. A field that looks unchanged may have been replaced by a new composition instance, while an instance can keep its state as its layout changes. Inspect the call sites, surrounding structure and keys to determine what survives.

Recomposing an existing instance and removing an instance before adding it again have different effects on remembered state. Both can execute the same composable function, but only the first retains that instance’s ordinary `remember` values.

rows: Recomposition
The same identity executes again
Kept — `remember` returns the value it already stored
Leaving the Composition
The identity is removed
Forgotten, along with everything else in that subtree
Entering again at the same call site
A new identity is created
Computed from scratch, as if for the first time

blocks.text: If a value resets on every recomposition, check whether it was remembered and whether its `remember` keys change on each execution. If it resets when a drawer, tab or panel changes, check whether that action removes the instance that owns it.
