Adding another `remember` inside an instance that is removed will not extend the value’s lifetime.

Compose cannot infer which item in your domain should keep a draft simply by comparing item contents. Two items may have equal contents while representing different records; one record may also change its contents without becoming a different record. Matching those cases incorrectly could attach a draft to the wrong row.

Call sites and execution order provide a predictable default. For a list whose items move, supply a domain key so that the remembered state follows the item (see **key and Keys in Lazy Lists**).

Use positional identity when position matches the lifetime you want. Supply keys when an item’s identity needs to survive a change of position. In both cases, ordinary remembered state lasts only while its owning instance remains in the Composition.

For “Why did my state disappear?”, distinguish recomposition from removal. Check whether the value was remembered, whether its `remember` keys changed, and whether its owning instance left the Composition. Two branches that each call the same composable create distinct instances; one call whose arguments change can retain its instance and remembered state.

lessons.title: key and Keys in Lazy Lists
lessons.summary: When a call site runs once per list item, Compose uses execution order to distinguish the instances unless you supply keys. Stable item keys let state follow items through insertion and reordering. This lesson compares runtime keys, lazy item keys and the inputs to `remember`.

blocks.text: A loop calls the same composable from one source location for several items. Compose distinguishes these instances using the **execution order** as well as the call site, unless you supply explicit keys. The first call belongs to the first position, the second to the second position, and so on.
Positional identity works well while existing items keep their positions. Insertion, removal and reordering can instead leave remembered state attached to a position now occupied by another item:

rows: An item is appended at the end
Every existing item keeps its position, and one new position appears
Existing rows retain their unkeyed remembered state
An item is inserted at the top or middle
Every item after the insertion point shifts into the next slot
Rows keep the state of whichever row previously occupied their position
An item is removed
Every item after it shifts back one slot
The same shift, in the other direction
The list is reordered
Every moved item lands in a slot that belonged to a different item
State appears attached to the wrong rows

blocks.text: If you reverse three rows that each use an unkeyed `remember` for an expanded flag or a draft, those remembered values stay at their positions. The movie that moves from the first row to the third receives the state previously held at the third position.
To make state follow a movie rather than a position, use the runtime’s `key` function around that movie’s content:

The values passed to `key` identify the group containing that item’s composables. Keys use `equals` and `hashCode`, and need to be unique among the invocations at that point in the Composition. They do not need to be unique across the app: unrelated loops can reuse the same movie ids.

A key tells Compose which item should retain this composition instance when its position changes. Use an identifier that stays the same for that item. Compose does not infer domain identity by comparing the item’s contents.

Lazy layouts have their own key parameter rather than requiring you to wrap items yourself, and it carries the same idea with one extra job. By default each item's state is keyed against its position in the list; supplying a stable, unique key ties the state to the item instead, and the layout also uses the key to keep the scroll position anchored when items are added or removed above the visible range.
Using the index as a key still identifies a position rather than a movie:

An index key means “the item currently at position n”. It therefore preserves the same association as the default positional identity. When a movie moves because of insertion, deletion or reordering, its index changes and the key no longer follows it. The code comment’s “not a key” means that it does not provide an item identity; it is still a key argument.
Compose uses keys for three related tasks. The distinction is what each key controls and what happens when it changes:

rows: `key(value) { ... }` from the runtime
A composition instance among the invocations at one call site
Discards that instance and composes a new one, so everything remembered inside it is gone
The `key` argument of a lazy `item` or `items`
A list item across dataset changes, for the lazy layout's own bookkeeping as well as identity
Keeping the key unchanged lets state follow an item when it moves; assigning a different key identifies a different item
The key arguments of `remember(key)`
Nothing about identity — the inputs a remembered value is a function of
Recomputes that one remembered value in place; the surrounding identity is untouched

blocks.text: `remember(user.id) { ... }` controls the cached value, not the surrounding composable’s identity. When `user.id` changes, `remember` runs its calculation again at the same position. Other remembered values in that instance are unaffected unless their own inputs also change.

Using a key to fix an unobserved mutation. Keys control composition identity; they do not make an ordinary `MutableList` observable or determine whether a call is skippable. If a list changes without an observable state update, fix that update path before investigating identity.

The runtime’s `key` requires uniqueness among the invocations at that point in the Composition. A lazy layout requires item keys to be unique across its dataset because it indexes items by those keys. Duplicate keys prevent the layout from distinguishing the items reliably; do not reuse one key for several rows.
Choose a key according to what should count as the same item after an update:

items: **A stable domain identifier**, such as a database or server id, follows the record when its position or displayed contents change. This is usually the appropriate key.
**The index** preserves positional identity. It does not keep state with an item that moves to another position.

**A hash or a copy of the item’s contents** can change when the item is edited, replacing its identity and losing its local state. A hash also needs a uniqueness strategy; different items can have the same hash.
**A freshly generated value**, such as a UUID created inside the loop, changes on each execution. Compose then treats the row as a new instance and discards the previous instance’s remembered state.

blocks.text: On Android, a lazy item key must use a type that the saved-state mechanism can store in a `Bundle`. Examples include strings, primitive values, enums and `Parcelable` types. This constraint supports saving item state; it is separate from the general composition identity model.

A stable key lets state follow a retained item through insertion and reordering. It does not extend the lifetime of ordinary `remember` after that item leaves the Composition. Lazy layouts may dispose of content they no longer need; when an item is disposed of, its ordinary remembered values are forgotten.

For a reordered `LazyColumn` with unkeyed remembered row state, explain that state stays with the position. A moved item can therefore display a draft or expanded flag from the item previously at that position. A stable domain key lets state follow the item instead; an index key preserves the positional association. Lazy item keys must be unique across the list.

lessons.title: Immutability in Kotlin vs. What Compose Needs
lessons.summary: A `val`, a read-only collection and a shallow `copy()` each provide different guarantees. None alone ensures that nested data cannot change. This lesson follows three cart updates to show how mutation and equality affect observable state, then considers what makes a screen-state value safe to compare.

blocks.text: Mutating an ordinary collection stored inside state does not write a new value to the state holder. The holder therefore records no change from that mutation. Even an assignment can leave Compose without an update if the new value compares equal to the previous one.
Kotlin’s reference, collection and equality features make different guarantees. Keeping them separate helps explain what a state holder or parameter comparison can detect:

rows: `val x = ...`
The *reference* will not be reassigned
Nothing at all about the object it points to, which may be mutable and mutated
A `List`, `Set` or `Map` type
*This reference* offers no mutating operations
That the underlying object is immutable — the same object may be held as a `MutableList` elsewhere and changed
`data class` and its generated `copy()`
A new instance whose constructor properties are the same values
That nested objects were copied — a copied reference points at the same nested object
`==` returning `true`
`equals` said these two values are equal
That they are the same object, or that `equals` looked at everything the screen displays

blocks.text: A `val` prevents reassignment through that property. A read-only collection interface provides no mutation operations through that reference. A generated `copy()` creates a new outer instance but can retain the same nested objects. And equality reports only what `equals` compares. None of these, by itself, prevents nested data from changing.

A state holder that uses equality to detect changes can only see differences included in that comparison. If the old and new states share a list that was already mutated, or `equals` ignores a displayed property, the holder may report no change even though the UI needs different data.

Read-only describes the operations available through a reference. Immutable describes an object whose value cannot change. For UI state, either replace values without mutating previously published data, or make mutations observable. Read-only types alone do not establish either behaviour.
Consider a cart whose state contains an ordinary mutable list. The `val` prevents replacing the `lines` property on an existing `CartState`, but does not stop code from editing that list:
These are three alternative ways to add a line. Only the third records a change in this state holder:

Path 1 mutates the list without assigning to `cart`, so its state holder records no change.

Path 2 assigns a new `CartState`, but `copy()` is shallow: both the old and new states contain the same, already-mutated `lines` list. The generated `equals` therefore considers them equal. `mutableStateOf` uses structural equality by default and records no change for an equal assignment.

Path 3 creates a new list containing the added line and assigns a `CartState` that differs from the old one. The holder can record that change. This works because the update replaces the list without first mutating the list in the previous state; the `MutableList` type alone does not enforce that discipline.

A state holder’s equality check and a composable’s skipping check happen at different stages. `mutableStateOf` can treat an assignment as no change, so its readers are not invalidated by that assignment. Separately, a reached child call may be skipped if its arguments are unchanged and nothing else requires it to run. Path 2 fails at the state-holder stage, before a parameter comparison could help.
When a screen stays stale, trace the update in this order:

items: **Did an observable update happen?** Editing an ordinary nested list does not assign to its enclosing state holder. If no observable change was recorded, fix the update path first.
**Did the holder treat the new value as a change?** `mutableStateOf` uses structural equality by default, so assigning something that compares equal to what is already there records nothing.

**Was the child call reached, and did anything require it to run?** Once the holder records a change, check which scope read it and whether a child was skipped because its arguments were unchanged (see **Stability and Skipping**).

blocks.text: A read-only `List` property makes the replacement-based update API clearer. The following version assumes the list is never shared through a mutable reference and that `CartLine` values are not mutated after publication. Adding a line then creates a new list and a new state value. A shallow `copy()` without a changed property would still compare equal.

Investigating skipping before checking the state update. Stability annotations and compiler settings do not make ordinary list mutation observable or make an equal assignment count as a change. Check the update path and the holder’s equality policy before changing how child parameters are compared.

When an update mechanism uses `equals`, the type’s definition of equality determines which differences it can detect. Kotlin’s `==` uses `equals`; an ordinary class inherits referential equality from `Any` unless it overrides that method. Data classes and value classes generate equality implementations. Compose does not check whether your equality includes everything the screen displays.

Referential equality treats separate instances as different even if their displayed contents match. That can cause avoidable work. Equality that ignores a displayed property causes the opposite problem: an equality-based update mechanism may report no change when the UI needs an update.

`Playlist` defines equality by id, so two instances with the same id compare equal even if their tracks differ. That may suit entity identity, but it can hide a UI change when the playlist is assigned to an equality-based state holder.

There is also a separate observation problem: adding tracks to this ordinary `MutableList` records no state change. A composable that displayed the count is not invalidated by that mutation and can keep showing the old count. Whether a later call is skipped also depends on its parameter comparison and any independent invalidation.

For replacement-based screen state, model the displayed data as a value. A data class with `val` properties and read-only collections can serve this role if nested objects are also values and published collections are never mutated through another reference. Include the displayed properties in equality, and update them by creating replacements.

A domain entity with id-only equality has different semantics. Check those semantics before using it directly as the value held by an equality-based UI state mechanism.

The kotlinx immutable collections library provides collection types whose contents cannot be changed in place, and the Compose compiler recognizes those collection types. Persistent collection operations return new versions, so they support replacement-based state updates. They do not replace the need to publish the new value through an observable holder.

For “Is a Kotlin `List` immutable?”, explain that it is a read-only interface: it offers no mutation operations through that reference, but another reference may still mutate the underlying object. Connect that distinction to UI updates: ordinary mutation is unobserved, `copy()` is shallow, and `mutableStateOf` uses structural equality by default. Equality must include the displayed differences you expect that holder to detect.

lessons.title: Stability and Skipping
lessons.summary: Skipping lets Compose leave a child’s existing composition unchanged when that call does not need to execute. Stability determines how its arguments are compared. This lesson distinguishes stable mutable state from immutability, explains Strong Skipping, and states the conditions needed to predict a skipped call.

blocks.text: Invalidation marks a scope as needing an update. When an executing scope reaches a skippable child call, Compose compares the arguments with those from its previous execution. If they are unchanged and no independent invalidation requires the child to run, Compose can retain the child’s existing composition without executing its body.

Being **skippable** means a call is eligible to be skipped. Whether it is actually skipped is decided for that execution when the call is reached. A state update can still require a skippable composable to run.

**Stability** describes whether Compose can rely on a type’s equality and observe relevant changes. Immutable values can satisfy that contract, but mutable state holders can satisfy it too. Their public property changes must notify composition, their equality must remain consistent for the same two instances, and their public property types must be stable. `FormState` below uses observable state for its changing property.

The compiler can infer stability for primitive types, `String`, enums, function types and classes it can analyze whose public properties are `val`s of stable types. Ordinary mutable properties and collection interfaces such as `List`, `Set` and `Map` generally prevent that inference. A read-only collection interface cannot guarantee that the underlying object will never be mutated.

Stable types may be immutable or may notify composition of their changes. Skippable calls are eligible to skip execution when their arguments are unchanged and no independent invalidation requires them to run. Stability describes a type’s contract; skipping is a decision about a particular call.

The experiments reported in this lesson used Kotlin 2.4.10, its version-matched Compose compiler plugin, Compose runtime 1.11.2 and default compiler options. Those versions describe the reported observations; predictions for another build should use that build’s compiler settings.

Strong Skipping has been enabled by default since Kotlin 2.0.20. It therefore applies to the default compiler settings reported here. The Gradle plugin’s legacy enable flag is deprecated; that concerns the configuration option, not the distinction between Strong Skipping and the older skipping rules.

With Strong Skipping, restartable composables are generally skippable even when their parameters are unstable; non-restartable composables remain unskippable, and a function can explicitly opt out of skipping. The documented comparison uses instance equality (`===`) for unstable parameters and `equals` for stable parameters. Lambdas created inside composables are also automatically remembered by default, reducing the new lambda instances passed during recomposition.

Assuming an unstable parameter always forces a call to execute. That rule describes the older skipping mode. With Strong Skipping, a restartable composable can be skipped even with a `List` parameter. When reading older explanations or the lifecycle guide, check whether their conditions include Strong Skipping.
For a skippable call whose identity is retained, whose other arguments are unchanged, and whose child has no independent invalidation, the documented comparisons give these results:

rows: The same unstable instance it passed last time
By instance — it is the same object
The call is skipped
A fresh but structurally equal unstable instance
By instance — a new object is not the same object
The call executes, even though the values are equal
A stable value equal to the one it passed last time
With `equals` — the values are equal
The call is skipped

blocks.text: If a caller creates a new unstable object on each execution, instance comparison treats that argument as changed even when its contents are equal. Mapping a domain object into a fresh UI object inside a composable body can have this effect.

One option is to reuse the derived object: remember it using the inputs it depends on, or move the mapping outside composition. When those inputs are unchanged, the same instance can be passed again. This requires inputs whose changes are observable or represented by replacement values; remembering an unobserved mutable object does not detect its internal changes.

Another option is to use a type whose stability contract genuinely holds. Stable parameters use `equals`, so a fresh but equal value can count as unchanged. **@Stable and @Immutable as Contracts** explains what that claim requires.
Three conditions matter when applying those comparisons:

items: **The same composition identity is executing.** A new identity has nothing to compare against, so its first execution is not a skip candidate at all.
**The call is actually reached.** Skipping is decided when the runtime arrives at the call; a call inside a branch that is not taken is not skipped, it simply does not exist this time.
**Nothing invalidated the child independently.** Parameters are not the only reason a composable runs.

blocks.text:
Suppose a parent passes the same `FormState` instance to a child, and only the child reads `query`. Changing `query` invalidates that reader; the parent need not run, and the child can execute even though its parameter is the same instance.

If the parent later recomposes for an unrelated reason, with no new child invalidation and the same arguments, it can skip the child call. The difference is whether the child’s own state dependency requires an update.

A reported experiment can differ from the documented comparison rule without establishing a new general rule. The observations below concern the stated toolchain and call arrangement. Use the documented rules for the general explanation, and inspect generated code when a specific result needs explaining.

In the reported experiment, a composable receiving a fresh, structurally equal `List` did not execute again. Changing the list’s contents did cause execution. A class with a `var` property behaved as the documented unstable-parameter rule predicts: a fresh but equal instance caused execution, while reusing the instance allowed the child to skip.

The list result alone does not establish which comparison the compiler generated. That requires inspecting the generated comparison and the stability information reaching that call.

One mechanism to investigate is stability information propagated from the caller. Generated code can use a known comparison for a statically classified parameter, or select between equality and instance comparison using runtime stability information. If an equal list is skipped, the generated code and the caller’s information can help explain why. The observed skip alone is not enough to establish that this was the mechanism.

Do not make correctness depend on whether one compiler build skips a particular equal list. Publish observable changes, keep the displayed data’s equality meaningful, and avoid unnecessary instance recreation when measurements show it matters. Those choices remain useful even when a compiler’s treatment of a specific call differs from the reported experiment.

Optimize the work performed during composition when it contributes to a measured performance problem. A recomposition count can help locate that work, but does not by itself show that the work is expensive. Compiler metrics and reports show which functions were classified as skippable and which types as stable; enable them deliberately when those decisions matter to the investigation.

For “What is stability, and when does Compose skip a composable?”, explain the stable-type contract, including mutable types whose changes notify composition. Then describe Strong Skipping: restartable functions are generally skippable, unstable arguments use instance comparison, and stable arguments use `equals`. State the conditions for an actual skip: the existing call must be reached, its arguments must be unchanged, and no independent child invalidation may require execution.

lessons.title: @Stable and @Immutable as Contracts
lessons.summary: `@Stable` and `@Immutable` tell the compiler that a type satisfies a stability contract. They do not add observation or prevent mutation. This lesson contrasts a valid observable state holder with a mutable playlist, then explains what must be checked before annotating a class or interface.

blocks.text: The compiler infers stability from the types and implementations it can analyze. It may lack enough information for an interface, a library class or a class with unknown property types. `@Stable` and `@Immutable` let you declare a contract that the compiler can then trust.

For a class or interface, `@Stable` promises three things: `equals` gives a consistent result for the same two instances, changes to public properties notify composition, and public property types are stable.

`@Immutable` makes the stronger promise that publicly accessible properties and fields do not change after construction. That includes the data exposed through those properties: a `val` prevents reassignment through a setter, but does not prevent mutation of an object it returns.

The compiler uses these declarations for optimization but does not verify that their contracts hold. An annotation does not freeze an object or make its changes observable. If the actual behaviour contradicts the declaration, recomposition can break and the UI can remain stale. Only apply an annotation after checking the type’s contract.

rows: `@Immutable`
The public properties will not change after construction — stronger than `val`
It does not freeze the instance or objects exposed by its properties
`@Stable`
`equals` is consistent, property changes notify composition, and property types are stable
It does not create observation; mutable properties must already notify composition

blocks.text: The annotations describe behaviour your type must already provide. Because the compiler trusts them, a false declaration can cause it to skip an update the screen needs. Verify the behaviour rather than using the annotation to request fewer executions.
`FormState` is mutable and satisfies the stable contract through observable properties:

`query` and `showAdvanced` can change, but both use observable state. Their types, `String` and `Boolean`, are stable, and the inherited referential `equals` stays consistent for the same pair of instances.

A composable that reads `query` is invalidated when it changes. If a parent recomposes for an unrelated reason and passes the same `FormState` with unchanged other arguments, a skippable child that has no independent invalidation can be skipped. The mutable properties do not prevent that optimization because their reads already have an observable update path.
This playlist does not satisfy the immutable contract. It also defines equality by id rather than by the contents displayed:

`tracks` exposes a mutable list, so callers can change the data after construction despite the `@Immutable` declaration. If a composable displays the count and tracks are then added in place, that ordinary list mutation does not invalidate the reader.

If an unchanged-argument comparison later allows the annotated child to skip, the screen can continue showing the old count. The id-only `equals` can also hide differences between replacement playlists with the same id.

The reported experiment with Kotlin 2.4.10 and default compiler options still showed a stale count after the annotation was removed. Removing an annotation does not make a `MutableList` observable, so it is not a complete fix for this update path. The reported skip does not, by itself, establish how the unannotated parameter was classified or compared.

The annotation adds a separate incorrect promise: the compiler is allowed to rely on immutability that this type does not provide. Fix the data and update contracts rather than relying on a particular toolchain to execute the child anyway.
Two approaches address the data and update contracts:

items: **Use replacement values.** Model `Playlist` so equality includes the displayed tracks, use a read-only list that is never shared mutably, and replace the whole value when tracks change. Its elements must also behave as values. An ordinary `List` still does not establish compiler-inferred stability; immutability by construction and compiler classification are separate checks.

**Make in-place edits observable.** A snapshot-aware collection can notify composition of list changes. A mutable state holder may then satisfy `@Stable` instead of `@Immutable`, but check the complete contract, including consistent equality and stable public property types. Changing the annotation alone is insufficient.

blocks.text: Adding stability annotations solely to reduce a recomposition count. First establish which work is expensive and why the child runs. If the compiler already infers the type as stable, an annotation may add no benefit. If it does not, the annotation is justified only when the type actually satisfies the declared contract.

Unnecessary execution can cost performance; an incorrect stability promise can cost correctness. A stale screen may send you looking at repositories, caches or the ViewModel even when the right value reached the UI. Include the skipped call and its type contracts in that investigation.

The symptom can be intermittent: another invalidation may cause execution and display the changed data, while an execution that skips the child leaves the old result visible. Whether a missed skip matters should be measured; it does not automatically make a screen slow.
An annotation on an interface makes a promise about every implementation, including implementations the compiler cannot inspect:

This interface annotation needs more than notification when `query` or `results` changes. The contract also requires consistent equality and stable public property types. `String` is stable, but an ordinary `List<Result>` is not automatically classified as stable; nor does this declaration tell us whether `Result` is stable. Treat the example as a contract to check, not as proof that backing an implementation with observable state is sufficient.

Every implementation must preserve the promised behaviour of the results and their elements as well as notifying property changes. Keep such interfaces small and document those requirements where implementers will see them.

A **stability configuration file** lets you declare contracts for types you cannot annotate, such as types from another module or a library. It changes the compiler’s assumptions, so the same responsibility to check those assumptions applies.

The **kotlinx immutable collections** library provides collection types that prevent in-place mutation, and Compose recognizes them. These types can address a collection’s classification, but their elements must also satisfy the relevant stability requirements. Start by checking the data model and update path before choosing either mechanism.

Distinguish a screen-state value from an object that owns changing state. A value can be a data class with `val` properties and nested values, replaced when displayed data changes. A form controller or scroll-state owner can instead expose observable properties and satisfy the stable mutable contract. Choose the model that matches the object’s responsibilities before considering an annotation.

A data class with `val` properties of stable primitive types can be inferred stable without an annotation. A class containing an ordinary Kotlin `List` needs a separate check: the compiler cannot infer that the collection will never be mutated merely because your code currently treats it as a value.

Replacement-based values still help correctness by keeping previous published data unchanged and making equality reflect displayed differences. But `copy()` remains shallow, and using value-style updates does not alone settle the compiler’s stability classification.

If equality-based parameter comparison is needed for such a type, consider a recognized immutable collection, a carefully checked configuration entry, or an annotation whose contract holds. Inspect the compiler’s classification rather than assuming it. The reported equal-`List` skip with Kotlin 2.4.10 concerns one experiment; it does not establish a comparison guarantee for other calls or toolchains.

For “What do `@Stable` and `@Immutable` do?”, describe the contracts the compiler trusts without verifying. `@Immutable` promises that publicly exposed data will not change after construction. `@Stable` promises consistent equality, notified property changes and stable public property types. Explain the consequence of a false declaration: a needed update may be skipped, leaving stale UI. When the compiler can infer a valid type’s stability, an annotation is unnecessary.

units.title: Derived State and Expensive Work
units.summary: Choose between calculating a value directly, caching it with `remember`, using `derivedStateOf` to avoid unnecessary recomposition, and moving work out of composition. The choice depends on what changes, how expensive the work is, and who should own it.

lessons.title: `remember(key)` as Memoization
lessons.summary: Use `remember` keys to describe a calculation’s dependencies. Missing dependencies can leave a stale result; irrelevant keys cause unnecessary recalculation. Learn how keys are compared, why mutating a key object does not invalidate the cache, and how composition limits the cached result’s lifetime.

blocks.text: `remember` can retain the result of a calculation as well as user-edited state. On a later execution, it can return that result instead of calculating it again. This is **memoization**: caching a result until the inputs it depends on change. The key list tells `remember` which inputs to compare.

`remember` stores the calculation’s result in the Composition at its call site. On each later execution that reaches the call, it compares the supplied keys with their previous values using `==`, which invokes `equals`. If all keys compare equal, it returns the stored result. If any key differs, it runs the calculation and stores the new result.

`remember` keys and skipping use different comparison rules. A key determines whether to repeat a **calculation** and is compared with `==`. Skipping determines whether to execute a **composable call**; under Strong Skipping, unstable arguments are compared by instance with `===`. An argument can therefore satisfy one comparison and fail the other.

For a cached result to remain correct, the keys must represent the changing inputs used by the calculation. In the contact list below, filtering depends on `query`, and both filtering and sorting depend on `contacts`. Those two values belong in the key list.

Without `remember`, each execution of `ContactList` repeats the filter and sort, even when `contacts` and `query` are unchanged. With both values as keys, later executions can reuse the result. While this call remains in the Composition, filtering and sorting repeat only when a key compares unequal to its previous value.

Read a key list as a dependency list: include the changing inputs the calculation uses, and leave out unrelated values. Missing a dependency can return a stale result; adding an irrelevant key causes unnecessary recalculation.
The following examples show three ways a cached calculation can go wrong: omitting a dependency, adding an unrelated key, and mutating a key object in place.
**A missing dependency serves a stale answer.**

When the caller passes the updated query, `ContactList` executes again and reaches `remember(contacts)`. If `contacts` still compares equal, `remember` returns the previous list without running the filter. The screen continues to show results for the old query. The initial display can look correct, so checking what happens after editing the query is essential.
**An irrelevant key causes unnecessary recalculation.**

When `selectedId` changes, the filter and sort run again even if `contacts` and `query` are unchanged. The displayed result stays correct, but selecting a row now pays for work that cannot change that result. The cache can still help on other executions; this extra key reduces its usefulness.
**Mutating a key object in place does not invalidate the cache.**

`Filter` inherits identity-based equality, so the same instance compares equal after its `value` changes. Making it a mutable `data class` would not solve this: `remember` retains a reference to the previous key, not a copy of its old contents. Both sides of the comparison would still refer to the same mutated object.

Use a value such as `filter.value` as a key so that `remember` retains the previous string for comparison. This calculation also depends on `items`, so a complete key list is `remember(filter.value, items)`. Changing an ordinary mutable property does not itself schedule recomposition; the key comparison happens only when execution reaches `remember` again.
With a counter in each calculation and in the composable body, the four cases behave like this:

rows: No keys at all
The calculation ran once, on initial composition, and never again however often the body executed
A result computed from the first inputs and served for the lifetime of the call site
The one value the result depends on
Ran again when that value changed; did not run when an unrelated value changed
A correct result, recomputed when the dependency changed
One real dependency plus one irrelevant one
Ran again for the real dependency **and** again for the unrelated value
A correct result, computed more often than it needed to be, for no change in what is shown
A mutable object, then mutated in place
The body executed twice more; the calculation did not run again at all
A stale result, because the retained key still compares equal

blocks.text: `remember` avoids repeating a calculation; it does not make one execution faster or move it to another thread. The first execution still pays the full cost synchronously during composition. If that cost is already too high, decide where the work should run and how it should be scheduled (see **Keeping Work Out of Composition**).
Distinguish execution of the composable body from execution of its remembered calculation. A recomposition can repeat the first without repeating the second.

items: **The composable executed again.** It may receive changed inputs from a caller or recompose after state it read changes. Execution reaches the `remember` calls on the branch being evaluated.

**The remembered calculation ran again.** Reaching `remember` does not necessarily run its lambda. The lambda runs when the call first enters the Composition and, while it remains there, when a supplied key compares unequal.

blocks.text: A body can execute forty times while its remembered calculation runs once. A recomposition count records executions of the body, not how often the cached work ran. To understand the cost of the filter or sort, measure that calculation as well.

The cached result belongs to that call’s identity in the Composition and is forgotten when the call leaves it. Ten rows executing the same source line have ten separate caches. In a lazy layout, scrolling a row off screen may eventually remove its composition and discard its cache; `remember` does not guarantee retention for every off-screen row.

A result that must survive the removal of a screen or be shared by several screens needs an owner beyond that composable. `remember` only calculates when its call is reached and only retains the result while that call remains in the Composition. It cannot guarantee that application-wide work has already been completed when another consumer needs it.

When asked how to avoid repeating a calculation on every recomposition, explain `remember` with the calculation’s inputs as keys. Describe equality comparison and the cache’s composition-bound lifetime, then give the failure cases: a missing dependency returns stale data, an unrelated key repeats work unnecessarily, and mutating a key object in place leaves it comparing equal.

lessons.title: `derivedStateOf`
lessons.summary: Compare direct calculations, `remember`, and `derivedStateOf`. Use `derivedStateOf` when observed inputs change more often than the result the UI needs, and account for its calculation cost, captured inputs, and remembered lifetime.

blocks.text: These three approaches reduce different kinds of work. Comparing them helps you choose the one that addresses the repeated work in your screen.

items: **A direct calculation filters nothing.** The value is recomputed by every execution of the body, whatever caused that execution — the first composition, a caller passing a changed parameter, or a write to state the scope read.

**`remember(keys)` avoids repeated calculations.** When the body executes, the calculation runs only if the call is new or a key has changed. Reusing the result does not prevent execution of the body.

**`derivedStateOf` can avoid invalidating its readers.** A change to snapshot state read by the calculation makes the derived value need checking. The calculation runs when its value is needed, and Compose can leave a reading scope unchanged if the result still compares equal.

blocks.text:
`derivedStateOf` returns a `State` object whose value is calculated from other snapshot state. A composable reading that value observes the result. When an input changes, Compose can check the calculation and avoid invalidating that reading scope if the result is unchanged.

This does not prevent recomposition for other reasons. The scope can still execute if another state value it reads changes or its caller supplies changed inputs.

Use `derivedStateOf` when its inputs change more often than the result the UI needs. Android’s guide compares it to Flow’s `distinctUntilChanged`: changes can keep arriving, while the consumer only needs an update when the result differs.

As the list scrolls away from the top and back, `firstVisibleItemIndex` can move through 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and return to 0. Reading the index directly makes the scope depend on each index change. Reading `showButton` instead lets Compose avoid invalidating that scope for changes such as 1 → 2, because the Boolean remains `true`. It changes to `false` when the list returns to the top.
Use `derivedStateOf` when an input changes frequently but the result a consumer needs changes less often. A value being calculated from other state does not, by itself, make this API useful.
Compare when each approach recalculates the value and when it can cause the consumer to recompose.

rows: A calculation written directly in the body
Every time the enclosing scope executes
Every time the enclosing scope executes
Cheap presentation logic whose result is wanted as often as its inputs change
`remember(keys) { ... }`
When the call first enters the Composition, then when a key differs
Every time the enclosing scope executes
A calculation that should not be repeated needlessly, whose result the consumer wants whenever it changes
`remember { derivedStateOf { ... } }`
When first read; later, when a dependency has changed and the value is next read or checked
When the derived result changes; other observed state or changed inputs can also cause execution
An input that changes far more often than the result it feeds

blocks.text: `derivedStateOf` can reduce executions of the reader without reducing executions of its calculation. After a dependency changes, the calculation must run when the result is next needed so Compose can determine whether that result changed. The measurement below shows these two counts separately.

In a reported JVM measurement, a composable scope read a derived `showButton` while the index moved 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4, with the runtime allowed to settle after each write. The calculation ran five times: initially and after each change. The reading scope executed twice: initially and when the Boolean changed at 0 → 1. Later index changes did not invalidate that reader through the derived state. These counts describe this observation schedule; they are not API guarantees.
Combining state values does not always reduce update frequency. The full-name example has a result that needs to change whenever either name changes.

Changing either `firstName` or `lastName` changes the displayed `fullName`. There are no unchanged results for `derivedStateOf` to filter out, so building the string directly is sufficient. The number of inputs is not the test: what matters is how often the result changes compared with those inputs.

In another reported measurement, a label changed at every index step. Its consumer executed five times with `derivedStateOf` and five times without it. The wrapper reduced no executions but added the derived-state object, dependency tracking, and result comparisons. Those costs are worthwhile only when the avoided recomposition justifies them.

`derivedStateOf` does not make an expensive calculation cheaper or move it off the composition thread. After a dependency changes, the calculation may run again when its value is read or checked. Its benefit comes from avoiding reader invalidation when that result is unchanged.

The reader can still recompose when the result changes or for other reasons. If the calculation itself is costly, consider caching repeated inputs or moving the work to a suitable owner and execution context.

Name the inputs and the result the consumer needs, then compare how often each changes. A cheap calculation whose result changes with its inputs can usually run directly. If processing the inputs is costly and they change less often than the body executes, consider `remember` with keys. If the result changes much less often than its snapshot-state inputs, consider whether `derivedStateOf` can avoid enough recomposition to justify its cost.
The derived-state object retains its calculation and tracks the snapshot state that calculation reads. Its lifetime and captured inputs therefore affect both cost and correctness.

Use `remember` to retain a derived-state object across executions of a composable. Creating it directly in the body constructs a new object each time execution reaches that expression, rebuilding its cached result and dependency tracking. It can still filter subsequent dependency updates, but recreating it adds unnecessary work on those executions.

A remembered calculation retains the values and references it captures when the object is created. Capturing an ordinary parameter such as `threshold` retains that value; passing a different threshold later does not update the existing lambda. Capturing a state holder lets the calculation read its current snapshot-state properties, but replacing the holder does not replace the captured reference. The next example has both kinds of input.

In a reported JVM measurement, the threshold changed from 1 to 5 and the index then moved to 2, but `past` remained `true`: the remembered calculation was still comparing the index with its captured threshold of 1. Use `remember(listState, threshold)` so replacing either input creates a calculation with the new values.

Keying only on `threshold` would leave another problem: a caller could supply a different `LazyListState` while the calculation continued reading the previous list’s scroll position. Alternatively, inputs held in snapshot state can be read inside the calculation so their current values are observed.

A dependency change does not necessarily run the calculation immediately. The runtime recalculates when the value is next read or when it checks whether a reading scope needs invalidation.

In one reported JVM measurement, four writes made without allowing the runtime to settle produced one recalculation. In another, a remembered derived state whose value was never read ran its calculation zero times, across initial composition and four writes to a dependency. These observations show why a dependency-write count need not match a calculation count.

A dependency change means the derived result needs checking when it is next required. Calculation counts therefore depend on when the value is observed as well as on how often inputs change. `derivedStateOf` can avoid consumer invalidation for unchanged results, but it still pays for recalculations needed to establish that equality.

The runtime provides `derivedStateOf(calculation)` and `derivedStateOf(policy, calculation)`. An explicit policy defines when two calculated results count as equivalent. With no policy, the derived state signals dependency updates and the observer decides whether the result matters. Compose’s recomposition machinery compares the new result with the one a reading scope last saw, using structural equality when no policy was supplied.

This is why the plain overload can avoid recomposition for an unchanged result. The result type’s equality still matters: if each calculation returns a fresh object that compares unequal to the previous one, the reader has a changed result every time. **How Compose Observes State** explains how the snapshot system records these reads.

For the scroll-to-top example, explain the frequency mismatch: the index changes as rows move past the top, while the Boolean changes when the list leaves or returns to index 0. An unchanged Boolean can avoid invalidating its reader. Contrast that with a full name that changes whenever either name changes, where `derivedStateOf` adds overhead without avoiding those updates. Also distinguish the calculation from its reader: the calculation may still run after a dependency changes, when its value is needed.

lessons.title: Keeping Work Out of Composition
lessons.summary: Decide which work belongs in a composable, which belongs in a state holder or another layer, and which must run through a lifecycle-aware operation. Memoization reduces repetition; ownership determines lifetime and responsibility. Moving work to a `ViewModel` does not automatically move it off the main thread.

blocks.text: Caching a result does not decide who should own the work. `remember` can reduce repeated calculation, and `derivedStateOf` can reduce reader invalidation, while leaving both calculations inside composition. Choose where the work belongs before deciding whether either optimization is useful.

A composable body describes UI. It can run frequently, in an order you do not control, and a recomposition may be discarded. Work that must happen once, in order, or at a particular lifecycle point needs an explicit owner or effect rather than an ordinary call in that body.
Consider the work’s purpose as well as its cost:

rows: Formatting a label, choosing a colour, picking which of two branches to emit
In the composable, calculated directly
It is cheap presentation logic used by this screen; extracting it may add indirection without a useful separation
Filtering, sorting, grouping or mapping a substantial collection into what the screen shows
Memoized in the composable for local presentation, or produced by a state holder when the screen needs one shared result
Caching can avoid repeating unchanged work; shared consumers, required lifetime, and product rules help determine who should produce the result
Reading a file, calling a repository, writing to a database, applying a business rule
Outside ordinary execution of the composable body, with ownership and lifecycle chosen for the operation
An ordinary body call can block composition or repeat unexpectedly. Data operations and business rules need suitable owners; UI-related asynchronous work can use lifecycle-aware effects

blocks.text: Android’s performance guide recommends moving calculations outside the composable when possible. For example, a `ViewModel` can produce a sorted list and pass it to the screen, which then only displays that result.
Memoization reduces repetition. Ownership determines who produces the result and how long it must live. Consider both before caching work inside a composable.
Formatting an order label and deciding which orders to display have different responsibilities, even if both calculations are inexpensive.

`OrderRow` formats a label for its own display. The order filter produces a result needed by both the list and its summary count, and it applies the product’s visibility rules. Producing that result above the row gives those consumers one consistent answer. Cost still affects where and how the work runs, but it does not determine its responsibility.
A blocking data read inside `remember` has a different problem: it ties the operation to execution of the composable body.

`remember(userId)` avoids repeating the read while the call remains in the Composition and the key is unchanged. It still runs `loadUserBlocking` synchronously on the thread executing composition, and supplies no coroutine job that can cancel the read when the screen leaves.

This example also has no loading or error state: the body waits for a user before it can call `ProfileBody`. A composable can display those states, but this blocking call does not produce them. Leaving and re-entering the Composition creates a fresh cache and starts the read again.

Wrapping a blocking read in `remember` supplies a cache, not an operation lifecycle. Choose an owner that can expose loading and failure and manage cancellation. Its lifetime should match the work: some operations belong to a screen’s state holder, while UI-related work may appropriately stop when an effect leaves the Composition.

**Moving work to a `ViewModel` or use case changes ownership; it does not automatically change the thread.** Work called from there can still run on the main thread. Android’s coroutine guidance makes the class performing long-running blocking work responsible for providing a main-safe operation, regardless of its architectural layer.

Memoization does not provide background execution either. `remember` runs its calculation synchronously during composition. Moving expensive work off that path requires an execution decision as well as an ownership decision.

Choose the work’s owner and its execution context separately. **Effect Lifecycle and LaunchedEffect** covers how effect APIs manage suspending work from composition; **Coroutine Context, Dispatchers and Concurrent Work** covers where that work executes.

The UI layer consumes application data and presents it. A screen-level state holder, often a `ViewModel`, produces the state the screen needs and coordinates the logic that produces it. Business rules belong in the domain or data layer. Moving work out of a composable does not, by itself, mean adding a use case.

The domain layer is optional. Use cases can help manage complex business logic or reuse operations across several state holders. Adding pass-through use cases without such a responsibility introduces indirection with little benefit. To choose where a calculation belongs, consider four questions:

items: **Cost.** How expensive is one execution, and is it on a path that runs often? A cheap calculation on a screen that rarely recomposes has no problem to solve.
**Lifetime.** How long must the result outlive whatever produced it? Anything that has to survive longer than a composable's presence in the Composition cannot be owned by a composable.

**Reuse.** Does another consumer need the same answer? If several UI elements need it, a shared state holder can keep them consistent. If it is needed beyond this screen, consider an owner with that wider responsibility.

**Responsibility.** Does this format or organize data for display, or implement a product rule about the data? Business rules belong in the domain or data layer; presentation logic belongs with the UI or its state holder.

blocks.text: Keep performance findings separate from ownership decisions. To claim that moving work improves performance, identify a visible symptom, the expensive work on its path, and evidence linking the two. A responsibility or lifetime mismatch can justify changing ownership even without a slow screen. Recomposition counts alone establish neither kind of problem.

Cheap, local presentation does not need to leave composition. Formatting two fields or choosing a colour from a status can remain in the screen. Work that is expensive, shared, needed beyond that screen, or responsible for a product rule needs closer consideration; any one of those constraints may justify a different owner or execution context.

When asked about an expensive operation in a composable, first identify what it does. Cheap local presentation can be calculated directly. A repeated pure transformation may benefit from `remember` with keys. Data operations and business rules need suitable owners; UI-related asynchronous work needs an appropriate effect lifecycle. Then explain execution separately: moving work to a `ViewModel` does not move it off the main thread, and the code doing blocking work should provide main-safety.

sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

units.title: Snapshot Fundamentals
units.summary: Compose tracks which snapshot state an observing context reads, then uses reported changes to identify work that may need to run again. This explains why an ordinary variable or an in-place mutation of an ordinary list does not trigger a UI update, how moving a read changes which scope observes it, and how derived state can avoid unnecessary recomposition. The same observation mechanism supports `snapshotFlow`, which exposes snapshot state as a `Flow` for coroutine-based processing.

lessons.title: How Compose Observes State
lessons.summary: Compose observes state by recording reads made during composition and responding to changes in the state that was read. Learn how those dependencies are established, why some changes do not trigger UI updates, and what consistency a snapshot provides.

blocks.text: An ordinary `var` can change without triggering a UI update. The same is true of an ordinary mutable list held inside a state object. By contrast, moving a state read into a child composable can narrow which scope needs to recompose, and reading derived state can avoid recomposition when its result stays equal. Each behaviour depends on the same two questions: which state was observed, and what change was reported?

The **snapshot system** lets Compose track reads and changes to state. Objects created by `mutableStateOf`, `mutableStateListOf`, and `mutableStateMapOf` participate in that system, as does the state returned by `derivedStateOf`. When code reads snapshot state while an observing context is running, that context records a dependency on the state. A reported change then lets the runtime identify the contexts that may need to run again.
For a state change to trigger a UI update through this mechanism, four conditions matter:

items: **An observable state object.** Snapshot state reports its reads and changes. An ordinary `Int` field, `ArrayList`, or property on your own class does not report them merely because a composable uses it.

**A read that happens inside an observing context.** An observing context is code that is recording reads while it runs: a composable executing during composition, a `derivedStateOf` calculation, and a `snapshotFlow` block. Reading the same object from a click handler, or from an ordinary function running outside any observing context, returns the current value and records no dependency. An ordinary helper called during composition does participate in the caller's observing context.

**A change recognised by the state object.** By default, `mutableStateOf` uses structural equality to compare a new value with the current one. Assigning an equal value therefore does not report a change.
**Invalidation.** A reported change can mark a context that read the state as needing to run again. Invalidation does not itself execute that context or draw the screen.

blocks.text: Writing state does not immediately refresh the screen. The runtime must respond to the reported change and perform the necessary work; several changes may be coalesced into one pass. Composition, layout, and drawing are separate phases, so a state write and a visible update are different steps.

A dependency is established when state is read inside an observing context. Creating a state object, passing it to a function, or writing to it does not by itself establish a reading dependency. When a UI update is missing, check whether an observable change was reported and whether the intended scope actually read that state.

A read outside an observing context does not establish a dependency. Likewise, a write of an equal value under the default equality policy reports no change, and a change to state with no observing readers has no dependent context to invalidate.

These three examples all leave the UI unchanged, but for different reasons: the value is not observable, the state holder does not see the mutation, or an assignment is equal to the value already held.

`Cart.itemCount` is an ordinary property. Reading it inside a composable does not record a snapshot dependency, and assigning a new value does not notify Compose. In the reported JVM measurement, changing it from 0 to 1 did not cause the composable to execute again; reading the field afterwards confirmed that it held 1. The property changed, but no observable change was reported.

Here, `items.value` is an observable read, so the composable has a dependency on the state holder. Calling `add` changes the ordinary mutable list inside it without assigning a new value to the holder. The holder does not observe mutations inside that list.

In the reported JVM measurement, the list grew to two elements, but the composable did not execute again. To make this change observable, assign a replacement collection to the holder or use a snapshot-aware collection whose own mutations are observable. See **Collections and Observable Mutation**.

The state object is observed and the assignment reaches it, but the new value equals the current value. Under the default structural equality policy, assigning 0 to a state already holding 0 reports no change. In the reported measurement, that assignment caused no further execution; assigning 1 afterwards caused one.
