blocks.text:
These examples help answer whether a change was reported at all. Missing updates can also have other causes. A composable may lose remembered state when its identity changes, or `remember` may retain a result after an unkeyed captured input changes. A child receiving ordinary parameters can be skipped if they compare equal, even after an observed change causes its caller to recompose. Those cases are covered in **Composable Identity**, **`derivedStateOf`**, and **Stability and Skipping**.

Start by checking the observable write and the reading dependency. If both are correct, investigate the consumer’s identity, retained values, and parameters.

Invalidation means a scope needs to be reconsidered; it does not mean the scope has already executed. Changes can be coalesced, and child calls with unchanged inputs may be skipped. Use the recorded reads to understand which scopes a change can affect, rather than predicting an exact execution count from the number of writes.

`derivedStateOf` uses observation at two levels. A composable reading its value depends on the derived state, while the calculation depends on the snapshot state it reads. A plain value captured by the calculation creates no snapshot dependency of its own.

When an input changes, the runtime can compare the new derived result with the result the composable last observed. If those results are equal, the input change need not cause that composable to recompose. This is how derived state can reduce recomposition without hiding the state reads needed to calculate its value.

A **snapshot** provides a view of state values at a particular point in time. Reads inside a taken snapshot see the values visible when that snapshot was taken, except for changes made within that snapshot where writes are allowed. A write applied elsewhere does not replace those values partway through the reader’s work.

That consistency applies to snapshot state, not to every object reachable from it. A `mutableStateOf` holding an ordinary mutable object tracks the value held by the state object; it does not track changes to that object’s fields. Similarly, a snapshot does not make an ordinary `ArrayList` safe to share between threads or make your classes transactional. The list-mutation example above demonstrates this same boundary.

Code outside composition can also enter a snapshot to read a consistent set of snapshot state values. `snapshotFlow` does this by evaluating its block inside a read-only snapshot. Simply reading state outside composition does not, by itself, give a sequence of reads this guarantee.

Snapshot consistency does not automatically make several assignments one atomic application update. If two state holders are written separately, an observer that runs between the writes can see the first holder’s new value alongside the second holder’s old value.

In the reported JVM measurement, a reader saw `(1, 0)` between `(0, 0)` and `(1, 1)` when each write was applied before the next. When both writes occurred before either was applied, it saw only `(0, 0)` and `(1, 1)`. That second result depends on when changes are observed; writing values close together is not an atomicity guarantee.

When two values must satisfy one invariant, holding them in one state object lets you replace both in a single assignment. This follows the same approach as replacing nested data or a collection: publish one complete new value instead of relying on the timing of separate mutations.

A state write cannot tell the runtime which parts of the UI use that value. Reads establish that relationship: while a context runs, the runtime records the state it accesses and can later use those dependencies to identify affected work. This tracking also supports derived calculations, layout and drawing contexts, and `snapshotFlow` blocks. The mechanism depends on observed reads, so it can serve consumers beyond composition.

To explain how Compose knows when to recompose, connect observable state, recorded reads, and invalidation. A composable’s state reads establish dependencies; reported changes let the runtime identify scopes that may need to run again. Invalidation precedes execution and does not guarantee one execution per write.

Include the boundaries: reads outside an observing context establish no dependency, equal assignments under the default policy report no change, and ordinary mutations inside a held object are invisible to its state holder. A taken snapshot provides a consistent view of snapshot state; it does not make arbitrary objects snapshot-aware or combine separate assignments into one atomic update.

lessons.title: `snapshotFlow` and Crossing Into Flow
lessons.summary: `snapshotFlow` exposes observable Compose state as a cold `Flow` for work such as analytics or saving a draft. Learn how its block records dependencies, when results are emitted, how collection lifetime is controlled, and why the flow cannot serve as a record of every state transition.

blocks.text: Some work needs to react to UI state without describing UI. Analytics may record when the user scrolls past the first list item. A draft may be saved a second after typing stops, or a search request issued after the query settles. These actions need to observe changing values, but should run in a controlled effect or coroutine rather than directly in a composable body.
A `Flow` lets that work filter and transform values, wait between updates, and call suspending functions. `snapshotFlow` provides the connection from Compose snapshot state to a flow.
`snapshotFlow` returns a cold `Flow`; four facts matter here:

items: **A cold flow produces nothing until it is collected.** The code inside the builder does not run when the flow is created. It runs when a collector arrives, and each new collector starts an independent execution.

**Collection is what starts it.** `collect` is a suspending call, so it needs a coroutine, and it does not return until the flow completes or the coroutine is cancelled. A `snapshotFlow` never completes on its own.
**The collecting coroutine bounds collection’s lifetime.** Cancelling it ends collection. Collection can also finish earlier, for example when a Flow operator limits how many values are collected.
**Ending collection releases observation.** When collection ends, `snapshotFlow` stops watching the state it read. There is no subscription to dispose of by hand.

blocks.text: Collection lifetime is covered in **Flow Fundamentals**. The `snapshotFlow { }` block adds these observation rules:

items: when collection begins it runs the block once and emits the result, unconditionally — the first value does not wait for anything to change;
while the block runs, it records which snapshot state the block reads, which makes the block an observing context in the same sense as a composable executing during composition;
when a change is applied to any state the block read, it runs the block again and records the reads again;
it emits a later result only when that result differs from the last emitted result according to `equals`, similar to `distinctUntilChanged`.

blocks.text: The block reads `listState.firstVisibleItemIndex`, so it records a dependency on that snapshot state. After `snapshotFlow`, ordinary Flow operators transform the index into a Boolean, suppress repeated Boolean values, and keep only `true` results before calling analytics. If collection starts while a later item is visible, the initial result can produce a report. After that, an observed return to the first item followed by scrolling past it again can produce another report.

A `snapshotFlow` block records the snapshot state it reads. Applied changes to that state can cause the block to run again, and a changed result is emitted to the collector. This gives coroutine code access to the same read-based observation mechanism that Compose uses for UI work.

When collection should last while this UI is in the Composition, `LaunchedEffect` provides a suitable coroutine. It launches when the effect enters the Composition and cancels when the effect leaves. If a key changes, it cancels the existing coroutine and launches another. See **Effect Lifecycle and LaunchedEffect** for how to choose among effect APIs.

`LaunchedEffect(listState, analytics)` captures both objects. If `analytics` is replaced but is omitted from the keys, the existing coroutine continues using the object it captured. Keying on `analytics` restarts collection with the new object.

Here, `listState` comes from `rememberLazyListState()` and is retained while that call remains in the Composition. If the state is instead supplied by a caller and replaced, keying on it prevents the effect from continuing to observe the previous list state. Use keys for values whose changes should restart the effect; values that should update without a restart need a different approach, covered in **Effect Lifecycle and LaunchedEffect**.
The snapshot state must also be read inside the `snapshotFlow` block. Reading it beforehand gives the block a plain captured value:

The block reads the captured `Int`, not `listState.firstVisibleItemIndex`, so it records no snapshot dependency. It emits an initial Boolean and then waits without observing changes to the list state. Recomposition may calculate a new local `index`, but the existing effect retains its captured value while its key stays the same.

In the reported JVM measurement, a block returning a captured plain value evaluated and emitted once, then did neither again after the underlying state changed. Reading `firstVisibleItemIndex` in the composable also makes that composable depend on it, so changes to the index can invalidate composition even though the effect does not receive them.
For a snapshot-aware collection, returning its reference is different from reading its contents:

The first block returns the `SnapshotStateList` reference without reading its contents, so it records no dependency on list changes. It also returns the same object each time; even if it were evaluated again, that object would compare equal to the previous result. In the reported JVM measurement, adding an element caused no further evaluation or emission.

The second block calls `toList()`. This reads the list’s snapshot contents and returns an immutable list representing them, so an added element can produce a result that differs from the previous one. The same measurement produced two evaluations and two emissions. `SnapshotStateList.toList()` is documented as an O(1) operation that returns its internal immutable list without copying it, and is recommended when exposing list contents through `snapshotFlow`.
`derivedStateOf` and `snapshotFlow` both observe snapshot state, but they provide results for different consumers:

rows: Who consumes the result
Composition — a composable reads it
A coroutine — a collector receives it
What it produces
A `State<T>`
A cold `Flow<T>`
What it is for
Keeping a reading scope from being invalidated while the answer is unchanged
Applying stream processing — `map`, `filter`, `debounce`, suspend calls — to a changing value
What starts it
Reading the value
Collecting the flow
Where it lives
Typically remembered in the Composition
Collected in a coroutine

blocks.text:
Choose based on how the result will be used. A composable can read derived state, which can avoid recomposition when the derived answer stays equal. Coroutine code can collect a `snapshotFlow` and process its values with Flow operators or suspending calls.

Neither API persists data or moves work to another thread automatically. In these examples, remembered derived state is retained in the Composition and collection lasts with the effect’s coroutine. A collector runs in its coroutine’s context; if its work is not safe on the main thread, that work needs an appropriate dispatcher.

`snapshotFlow` observes state rather than recording every event that changed it. Rapid changes can be conflated: if a value passes through 0, 1, 2, and 3 before the observer can process each change, seeing only 0 and 3 is valid. Its block may also run more than once for the same inputs, although equal consecutive results are not emitted again. An undo history, audit trail, or keystroke log that must preserve every transition needs to record those events where they occur.

State writes, block evaluations, and collector emissions are separate counts. A change can cause the block to run without producing an emission, and several rapid changes can be observed in one evaluation.

Measured on a JVM target, with the collector already running before any change was made and each change allowed to be applied and the scheduler allowed to settle before the next one, unless a row says otherwise:

items: A block returning an `Int` state: one evaluation and one emission when collection began, then one evaluation and one emission for the change that followed.
The same block, then assigned the value the state already held: no evaluation and no emission at all. An equal write is not a change, so nothing was ever reported.

A block returning `index > 2`, with the index driven through 1, 2, 3 and 4: five evaluations and two emissions. Every reported change re-ran the block; only the two results that differed from the previous one were emitted.

The `Int` block of the first row again, with 1, 2, and 3 written without time for collection to settle between them: two evaluations and two emissions, with 3 in the second emission. The block did not observe the intermediate values 1 and 2.

blocks.text: The first and last measurements use the same block but allow different amounts of time between writes for changes to be applied and collection to run. That timing affects whether the block observes intermediate values or only the latest one. These counts describe the reported runs, not guarantees: the API permits repeated evaluations for unchanged inputs and a single evaluation after several rapid changes.

Because evaluations do not correspond one-to-one with changes, the block must be idempotent and free of side effects: evaluating it again with the same inputs should give the same result without performing additional actions. It runs inside a read-only snapshot, so writing snapshot state from the block fails collection with an `IllegalStateException`. The reported JVM run produced `Cannot modify a state object in a read-only snapshot`.

This also rules out counting evaluations by incrementing snapshot state inside the block. Keep the block focused on calculating a value, and perform actions in downstream Flow processing or the collector. The runtime rejects snapshot writes, but that does not enforce the absence of every other kind of side effect.

State preserves the current value, which may not reveal all the events that produced it. A consumer of current state must be able to observe the latest value without relying on every intermediate transition. By contrast, an event record may need to preserve each action separately.

`snapshotFlow` can emit results as snapshot state changes, but those results cannot reconstruct transitions that were never observed. Use it to react to current state, and record events at their source when their individual history matters.

When explaining `snapshotFlow`, describe how the block, emission rule, and collecting coroutine fit together. The block reads snapshot state and records dependencies; applied changes can lead to another evaluation, and only a result unequal to the last emitted result is emitted. Read the state inside the block, rather than passing in a plain value captured earlier.

Explain the coroutine’s lifetime as well. In the example, `LaunchedEffect` cancels collection when it leaves the Composition and restarts it when a key changes. Finally, distinguish observing current state from recording every event: conflation makes `snapshotFlow` unsuitable as a complete transition log.

units.title: Production Screen State and Unidirectional Data Flow
units.summary: A production screen can have several state owners: an element owns its local interactions, a Compose parent coordinates shared UI state, and a screen-level owner supplies application data. A question-library screen shows how to choose each owner from the value's readers, writers and required lifetime, then connect those values to stateless content through an immutable screen value and intent callbacks. Moving state outside the Composition gives it the new owner's lifetime; persistence requires a separate mechanism.

lessons.title: Three Classes of State on One Screen
lessons.summary: A question-library screen needs local menu state, a filter shared by sibling composables, and data supplied by a screen-level owner. Choose each value's owner by who reads it, who writes it and how long it must live. Keeping a shared value inside one child prevents coordination; moving local details to a screen-level owner adds responsibilities and retains them longer than needed.

blocks.text: A production screen often contains several values with different responsibilities and lifetimes. A menu may need to remember whether it is open, sibling composables may share a selected filter, and the whole screen may display data from a repository. These values can belong to different owners. Keeping them all in one child can prevent coordination; moving them all to a screen-level owner can give that owner responsibility for every menu and visual toggle.

For each value, ask who reads it, who writes it, and how long it must live. Choose the lowest owner that can support all those readers and writers for the required lifetime, whether that is a composable or an object outside the Composition. See **State Hoisting and the Lowest Sensible Owner** for the reasoning behind this rule.

Consider a question-library screen with a difficulty menu, a result count, interview questions, saved-question markers, and a retry action when loading fails. Its menu expansion, selected filter and loaded data have different ownership requirements.

rows: Whether the difficulty menu is expanded
Only `DifficultyMenu` reads it and its button and dismissal callback write it
While `DifficultyMenu` remains in the Composition; the expanded flag can reset when that element leaves and is recreated
Local to `DifficultyMenu`
The selected difficulty filter
The filter control writes it; the result count and question list both read it
While this screen's Compose subtree remains in the Composition; no application rule depends on this filter
Hoisted to the lowest composable above those siblings
Loaded questions, saved markers and load failure
The whole screen reads them; retry and save intents start changes whose source is outside the UI
For the lifetime promised by the screen-level owner, including times when this destination is retained but not composed
A screen-level owner outside the Composition

blocks.text: The menu's expanded flag changes what the user sees, but only `DifficultyMenu` needs to read and change it. No sibling needs to coordinate through that value, and no longer-lived owner needs to retain it. Local state is therefore sufficient. A production screen can leave this interaction in the menu while using a ViewModel or another state holder for values with wider responsibilities.

One screen can combine local UI-element state, state hoisted to coordinate a subtree, and screen state supplied by an owner outside the Composition. Choose the lowest sensible owner that supports each value's readers, writers and required lifetime.

If `DifficultyMenu` owns the selected filter as well as its expanded flag, the result count and list have no shared selection to read. Giving each child its own copy requires keeping those copies synchronized; passing updates between siblings spreads the coordination across them. Their common Compose parent can own one selection, pass it to each reader, and handle the menu's selection callback.

Moving every UI detail into the outside owner creates a different problem. If that owner stores menu expansion, help-text expansion and press interactions alongside question data, its state and callbacks might look like this:

blocks.code:
data class QuestionLibraryState(
    val questions: List<QuestionItem>,
    val savedIds: Set<QuestionId>,
    val selectedLevel: QuestionLevel,
    val isDifficultyMenuExpanded: Boolean,
    val isHelpTextExpanded: Boolean,
    val pressedQuestionId: QuestionId?,
)

@Composable
fun DifficultyMenu(
    selectedLevel: QuestionLevel,
    expanded: Boolean,
    onExpandedChange: (Boolean) -> Unit,
    onLevelSelected: (QuestionLevel) -> Unit,
) { /* ... */ }

items: The screen state now includes menu, help-text and press details that are unrelated to producing question data.
Purely local interactions require owner methods and callbacks, so the parameter list grows with implementation details rather than screen intent.
Changing which menu details are exposed can require changes to the outside owner's contract and the callers that connect it to the UI.
Updates to unrelated local details travel through the screen-level state and its consumers instead of staying inside the smallest affected subtree.
Those details inherit the owner's longer lifetime even though their readers and writers disappear with one element.

blocks.text:
Return `isDifficultyMenuExpanded`, `isHelpTextExpanded` and press interaction state to the elements that use them. Keep `selectedLevel` at the common Compose parent unless a product rule or required lifetime calls for an outside owner. Loaded questions and saved markers remain at screen level because their source and update logic are outside these UI elements.

The menu can then change without changing the screen-level data contract, and its temporary interaction state lasts only as long as the element needs it.

Hoist a value until all necessary readers and writers can share one owner and its required lifetime is met. Moving it farther adds dependencies between that owner and UI details it does not need to coordinate.

The selected difficulty belongs to the Compose parent here because only its UI subtree uses it and it need not outlive that subtree. If selecting a difficulty starts a server query, changes a persisted preference, or must be restored after the subtree is removed, those requirements change. Screen-level ownership may then be appropriate. The same field can have a different owner when its readers, writers or required lifetime change.

A value's type does not determine its owner. A `Boolean` can represent local menu expansion or a business decision; a data class can hold local UI state or screen-level state. Look at which components must coordinate through the value and how long it must remain available.

Classify each value on a screen independently. Explain which readers or writers would lose access if it stayed in a child, which UI details would become part of a broader owner's contract if it moved higher, and how long the chosen owner retains it. A menu's expanded flag can remain local when its readers, writers and required lifetime all belong to that element.

lessons.title: The Stateless Content Boundary
lessons.summary: A screen composable connects state owners and event handlers. A separate content composable renders supplied values and reports user intent through callbacks. This lets a preview, test or another host render the content without constructing the production owner or its dependencies.

blocks.text: Once a screen has several owners, it needs one place where their values and events meet. That place is the screen composable. Its job is wiring: obtain the current screen-level value, keep any Compose-owned coordination state such as the selected filter, and connect UI events to the owner that handles each one. The content composable has a different job: render the supplied value and report what the user asks to do.

`QuestionLibraryScreen` is stateful: it reads from the outside owner and remembers the selected filter for its subtree. `QuestionLibraryContent` exposes a stateless API, taking the current screen value and callbacks instead of reaching into an owner. The inputs can come from a ViewModel, a remembered plain state holder, a preview, or a test; the content does not need to know which.

A stateful/stateless overload pair serves a different purpose. For example, a text field can offer a stateless function that takes a value and change callback, plus a convenience overload that remembers the value internally. The caller chooses either version of the same component.

`QuestionLibraryScreen` and `QuestionLibraryContent` have separate jobs. The screen connects application state and event handlers; the content renders their supplied values. Separate names make those responsibilities visible.

The screen composable wires owners to content; the content composable renders values and reports intent. Keeping that distinction visible gives the screen one obvious place where owners, current values and event handlers are connected.

A preview can call `QuestionLibraryContent` with an empty state, a long list, an error state or an unusual saved selection. It does not need to construct the production owner, start dependency injection, or wait for data. The ordinary value parameters let the preview choose exactly what the screen displays.

An isolated UI test can supply a state, perform an interaction, and record which callback was invoked without setting up an owner or data source. A demo host, another platform shell, or a future owner can also reuse the content by supplying the same values and callbacks.

Without a screen/content boundary, one descendant might obtain the owner for retry, another might mutate the selected filter, and a third might read a separate saved-state source. The inputs and event handlers are then spread across the rendering tree.

Assembling them in `QuestionLibraryScreen` gives the screen one place to inspect those connections. Replacing the outside owner or changing how the filter is retained changes the wiring there, while content keeps its value-and-callback contract.

rows: Content accepts ordinary immutable values and callbacks
Any caller can render a chosen state and decide what each event means
Content accepts the production owner
A caller must supply that owner, including any setup needed to construct it
Descendants obtain their own owners or state sources
There is no single boundary where the screen's current inputs and event routes can be inspected

blocks.text: Inspect the content signature. Can a preview or UI test render a chosen state by supplying values and callbacks, or must it also construct a production owner, dependency graph or live data source? If it needs those dependencies, application wiring still reaches into the rendering function.

sources.title: Preview your UI with composable previews

lessons.title: One Screen State Value, Events Back Up
lessons.summary: A value-based content contract sends one immutable current screen value down, while callbacks describing retry, selection and save intent travel up. Passing writable state or an owner reference downward creates extra write paths, hides ownership and couples rendering to a particular mechanism.

blocks.text:
`QuestionLibraryScreenState` groups the questions, saved markers, load result and selected filter that the content needs to render. A single `loadFailed` flag keeps this example small; a real screen may model loading and errors more precisely (see **Modelling the Current UI State**).

Treat each instance as an immutable snapshot: its collections and the objects they contain must remain unchanged after it is supplied to content. Kotlin's `val`, `List` and `Set` declarations alone do not guarantee that; they prevent reassignment or mutation through those particular declarations, not through other references.

The screen value describes the inputs crossing from `QuestionLibraryScreen` into `QuestionLibraryContent`. The screen can assemble it from the outside owner's data and its own selected filter. Content receives one current snapshot, rather than access to writable state holders.

A child can still own interaction state that does not cross this boundary. `DifficultyMenu`, for example, can remember whether its popup is expanded.

The callbacks describe user intent, not storage operations. `onLevelSelected(level)` says what the user selected; `onRetry()` says they asked to retry; `onToggleSaved(id)` says which question they acted on. The caller decides whether each event changes Compose-owned state, asks the screen owner to do work, or is ignored because the current state no longer permits it. This is state down and events up applied to the complete screen contract.
The content renders one immutable current screen value and reports intent upward. It neither owns a second writable copy nor chooses the mechanism that will handle an event.

Passing writable state can remove a callback, but it also lets content make changes directly. In this version, content can assign the filter's `MutableState` and invoke methods on the production owner for retry and save actions.

items: Another write path now exists lower in the tree: any descendant that receives `selectedLevel` can assign it, whether or not that component should make the decision.
Ownership is no longer visible in the signature. The reader cannot tell which layer validates a selection or coordinates it with the rest of the screen.
The child is coupled to `MutableState` and to the particular production owner instead of to the value it renders and the intents it emits.
Preview and reuse require constructing or faking those mechanisms rather than supplying an arbitrary screen value and callbacks.
The content can no longer be reasoned about as rendering a supplied snapshot because it reaches through the owner for some values and can mutate another in place.

blocks.text: Use the value-and-callback signature shown above. Each time `QuestionLibraryScreen` renders the content, it assembles `QuestionLibraryScreenState` from the current inputs. Its `onLevelSelected` callback updates the Compose-owned filter, while retry and save callbacks invoke the outside owner. Each callback routes the change to the layer that owns the affected value; content does not need to know that these events have different destinations.

A mutable holder interface still allows direct writes if it exposes arbitrary setters to content. Give content the immutable value it needs to render and callbacks for the user intents it can report. The caller then decides how to handle each intent.

An immutable screen value gives a log, preview or failing test a record of what content received. If an ordinary mutable field or collection changes through the same reference, an earlier reference no longer represents the old screen value, and Compose does not automatically observe that mutation. Producing a new screen value preserves the distinction between before and after; publishing it through observable state makes the update available to the UI.

Comparing screen values is useful when each value remains unchanged after publication. Mutating the contents behind an existing reference can change both the supposed old value and the current value, leaving no reliable before-and-after comparison. `@Stable` and `@Immutable` do not make an object immutable; its implementation must satisfy that contract. For how Compose uses equality to skip work, see **Stability and Skipping**.

Unidirectional data flow (UDF) means state flows down to the UI and events flow back to the owner. At this Compose boundary, the screen value and callbacks provide that direction. Reducers, action types, state machines and MVI are possible ways to organize the owner's work, but this content contract does not require them.

When reviewing writable state passed to a child, identify what the child can now change and who is responsible for that decision. Check for extra write paths, unclear ownership, dependencies on a particular state holder, and difficulty rendering the content in isolation. A supplied immutable value with intent callbacks makes the child's inputs and permitted interactions explicit.

lessons.title: Moving State Outside the Composition: Owner vs Lifetime
lessons.summary: Moving screen state outside the Composition gives it the new owner's lifetime. An entry-scoped ViewModel in Navigation 3 can retain state while its destination remains on the back stack, but it is cleared when the entry is removed. Restoring state after the owner is gone requires saved state or another persistence mechanism.

blocks.text: The question library's loaded questions, saved markers and load failure can belong to a screen-level owner outside the Composition. Re-executing a composable then reads from that owner instead of recreating the state locally. How long the values remain available depends on how long the host retains the owner; moving them outside the Composition does not make them persistent.

A ViewModel is one example of an outside owner. The host supplies it from a `ViewModelStoreOwner`, whose store determines how long the ViewModel is retained. If the host keeps that store while a composable re-executes or temporarily leaves the Composition, the ViewModel's in-memory state remains available. Clearing the store ends that ViewModel's lifetime. Other outside state holders depend on their own retention arrangements.

rows: The composable recomposes or its body executes repeatedly
Yes
Recomposition does not clear the retained entry's `ViewModelStore`
The destination is composed again while the same entry remains
Yes
The existing entry still supplies the same owner
Android recreates the UI for a configuration change
Yes, with the Android host and retained entry-scoped ViewModel setup used here
The host retains the relevant `ViewModelStore` across configuration recreation
The user navigates forward and this destination remains on its back stack
Yes
The Navigation 3 entry remains, so its entry-scoped `ViewModelStore` remains
The destination is popped and its entry is removed
No
The entry's `ViewModelStore` is cleared, which ends that owner's lifetime

blocks.text: Process death destroys the ViewModel and its in-memory state. Saved state can retain small values needed to reconstruct the screen; durable application data belongs in storage that outlives the process. See **`rememberSaveable` and State That Must Survive** for the distinction. For any value, identify the event it must survive and whether its owner survives that event or the value must be restored.

For state outside the Composition, identify the owner that holds it, when that owner is released, and what must happen after release. If the value must be restored then, it needs saved state or another persistence mechanism.

Consider an Android application whose `NavDisplay` installs a saveable-state entry decorator followed by the lifecycle ViewModel entry decorator. Each relevant Navigation 3 back-stack entry therefore receives its own `ViewModelStore`. Screen ViewModels are obtained at that destination, remain while their entry remains on the back stack, and are cleared when the entry is removed.

With this setup, a retained entry keeps its `ViewModelStore`, and the store retains any ViewModel obtained for that entry. Popping the entry clears its store and ends the ViewModel's lifetime. Navigating forward while keeping the entry on the back stack retains that state, even when the question-library content leaves the Composition.

The scope chosen when obtaining the ViewModel determines which host retains it. An Activity-scoped ViewModel is retained across Android configuration recreation and remains until that Activity finishes. Removing the question-library entry does not clear the Activity's store.

With the entry-scoped setup above, the ViewModel is also retained across configuration recreation, but its lifetime ends when that entry is removed. Both scopes can preserve state through rotation; they differ when the user navigates away and pops the destination.

The screen/content contract does not change when the owner changes. `QuestionLibraryContent` still receives an immutable current value and sends retry, selection and save intent upward. Only `QuestionLibraryScreen` knows how the owner is reached and how its current value enters Compose, so changing the owner's lifetime or the way its observable state is collected leaves the rendering tree untouched.

When explaining whether a ViewModel survives, name both its scope and the event. An entry-scoped ViewModel can survive Android configuration recreation and remain on a retained back-stack entry, then be cleared when that entry is popped. Process death destroys the in-memory instance regardless of that scope.

Use an outside owner when the required coordination or lifetime extends beyond the Compose subtree. The question library's selected filter remains in its Compose parent because only that subtree uses it and it need not outlive the subtree. If its UI logic becomes more complicated, a remembered plain state holder can encapsulate that logic while keeping the same Composition lifetime.

A ViewModel can coordinate screen data and retain the current in-memory value for its scope. Restoring that data after the instance is lost requires another mechanism. Ownership identifies who holds the state and handles changes, lifetime identifies when that owner is released, and persistence provides a way to reconstruct the value afterwards.

An entry-scoped ViewModel establishes who holds the screen state and when that instance is cleared. Saved state or durable storage can support restoration after process death without giving content another write path. The owner's construction, repository dependencies and UI-state model are further design decisions. Content can keep the same supplied value and callbacks as those decisions change.

For each event, trace the real lifetime: recomposition leaves the outside owner untouched; Android configuration recreation can retain a ViewModel through its store; a retained back-stack entry retains its entry owner; removing that entry clears it; process death destroys in-memory state unless another mechanism reconstructs it. Then state which fact is general and which is a guarantee of the Android owner in question.

sources.title: Apply logic or wrappers to destinations

units.title: Observable State Collection and Lifecycle
units.summary: A screen owner can expose a Flow or StateFlow, but Compose needs that stream collected into its own State to observe changes. Collection also has a lifetime and a cost. Choosing a collection API means deciding when the UI should subscribe and how the screen’s lifecycle affects that subscription.

lessons.title: What a Composable Can and Cannot Observe
lessons.summary: Reading `StateFlow.value` gives a composable the current value, but later stream updates do not trigger recomposition. Collecting the stream into Compose State connects StateFlow’s collector notifications to Compose’s state observation.

blocks.text: Suppose a screen owner outside the Composition exposes `val state: StateFlow<QuestionScreenState>`. `StateFlow` notifies its collectors when the value changes. Compose tracks reads of its own snapshot-aware state and invalidates the scopes that read that state when it changes. Reading a StateFlow property does not automatically connect these two observation systems.

At this execution, `owner.state.value` returns the StateFlow's current value and `QuestionContent` can render it. If the StateFlow later emits another value, however, that update does not itself invalidate this composition. The body did not read a Compose `State.value`; it performed an ordinary Kotlin property read on a type whose notification mechanism is collection.

An unrelated observed state change may cause `QuestionScreen` to recompose and read a newer `StateFlow.value`. That can make this code appear to work. The stream update itself still does not trigger recomposition, so the screen depends on another state change to display it.

Collect the external stream into Compose `State<T>`, then read that state while rendering. When a composition reads Compose state, snapshot observation records which scopes depend on it. A later change to that state invalidates those scopes so they can recompose and read the updated value.

Collection supplies the connection: values from the stream are assigned to Compose State, and the screen uses the same observation mechanism described in **How Compose Observes State**.
StateFlow notifies collectors; Compose observes reads of snapshot state. Collecting a StateFlow into Compose State lets stream updates trigger recomposition where the returned state is read.

Collecting state does not change who owns it. The screen owner still manages loaded questions, saved markers and load failures. The wiring composable collects that state for Compose, then passes the current immutable screen value and callbacks to `QuestionContent`.

rows: `composeState.value`
Compose snapshot observation records the read
A recorded state change invalidates the reading composition
`stateFlow.value`
No StateFlow collector is established by this property read
A later StateFlow update does not itself invalidate the composition
An arbitrary mutable Kotlin property
No observation mechanism unless its type supplies one and the caller subscribes
Assignment alone gives Compose no notification

blocks.text: StateFlow's retained current value still matters: it gives the conversion a synchronous value to expose immediately (see **`StateFlow`: One Current Value**). `snapshotFlow` travels in the opposite direction - Compose snapshot State into a Flow - and is covered in **`snapshotFlow` and Crossing Into Flow**.

The conversion belongs at the stateful screen wiring boundary. `QuestionContent` should not know about Flow or the owner. It continues to accept the current `QuestionScreenState`, so it stays previewable and reusable with any caller that can supply a value.

When asked why reading `StateFlow.value` is insufficient in a composable, identify the missing notification path. The read can return useful data now, but it neither starts collection nor records a snapshot-state dependency. A later emission therefore has no direct route to invalidate the composition.

lessons.title: `collectAsState`: Converting a Stream into Compose State
lessons.summary: `collectAsState` collects a Flow into Compose State. StateFlow supplies the initial value; a plain Flow requires one from the caller. Stream and context changes can restart collection, while the returned State exposes the latest collected value for recomposition.

blocks.text: `collectAsState` collects a stream and returns Compose `State<T>`. As values arrive, the collector assigns them to that state. Reading its `value`, directly or through `by` delegation, establishes the Compose-observed dependency that reading `StateFlow.value` alone does not.

For `StateFlow<T>`, Compose runtime 1.11.2 provides `StateFlow<T>.collectAsState(context)`. The returned Compose State is initialized from `StateFlow.value`, because StateFlow always holds a current value. On first composition, `QuestionScreen` can therefore render the owner’s current state without supplying a loading placeholder for collection.

A plain `Flow<T>` uses `Flow<T>.collectAsState(initial, context)`. An arbitrary Flow need not expose a current value before collection begins, so the caller supplies the initial Compose State value. `SearchResult.Loading` below describes the screen until a collected value replaces it.

This initial value belongs to the Compose state holder. Supplying it does not give the Flow a cache or replay buffer, turn it into StateFlow, or save it across recreation or process death.

When the collector assigns a changed value to the returned State, Compose invalidates the scopes that read it. Recomposition then reads the latest value. Equal assignments are conflated, and several rapid updates may be represented by one recomposition; collecting state does not promise a rendered frame for every emission.

`collectAsState` is state conversion. StateFlow supplies its own current value as the initial Compose value; plain Flow requires the caller to supply what should be rendered until the first collected value arrives.

In this example, `map` creates a new Flow object whenever `QuestionScreen` executes, even if `observeQuestions()` returns the same stream. In Compose runtime 1.11.2, the Flow and collection context are keys for the producer used by `collectAsState`. A changed key cancels the previous collection and starts another. The `initial` argument initializes the remembered State; it is not a restart key.

Changing the supplied stream restarts collection. That is useful when a question id selects a different source, but constructing another equivalent stream on recomposition can restart cold upstream work unnecessarily. Keep the stream in a stable owner, or use `remember` with the inputs that should select a new stream.

The optional `context` parameter controls the coroutine context used for collection. With the default empty context, collection uses the state producer's existing context; with a supplied context, collection runs inside that context. It does not replace `flowOn`, the Flow operator that changes the context of upstream work while leaving the collector's context alone.

A remembered `MutableState` and an effect that collects a Flow into it can provide the same conversion. For ordinary ongoing UI state, `collectAsState` expresses that requirement directly and manages the collector’s lifetime. Manual collection is useful when receiving a value should perform an effect, such as showing a message or navigating.

Compose runtime 1.11.2 implements the Flow overload with `produceState(initial, this, context)`. Here, `initial` initializes the remembered State; `this` (the Flow) and `context` are producer keys. Changes to those keys restart collection without resetting the state holder to `initial`. Equal assignments to the returned State are conflated. For the producer’s lifetime and state retention, see **`produceState`: a Composition-Scoped Producer**.

Choose an initial value that describes what the screen knows before collection supplies data. An empty list can briefly show “there are no questions” when a cold Flow has simply not emitted yet; a loading state represents that wait. StateFlow already supplies a current value, but that value still needs to model the screen’s state accurately.

Name both overloads and where each gets its initial value, then follow one emission all the way to invalidation. Treat the Flow object supplied to the composable as a lifetime input: a deliberately changed stream should replace collection; an accidentally fresh equivalent stream should not.

lessons.title: Collection Has a Lifetime and a Cost
lessons.summary: Ordinary collectAsState keeps a collector active while its state producer remains in Composition. That lifetime has concrete costs in database observation and transformation work, and cancelling the UI collector is a separate question from who owns a cold or shared upstream producer.

blocks.text: Ordinary `collectAsState` runs a collector while its call remains in Composition. Recomposition keeps that collection when its keys are unchanged. Leaving Composition cancels the producer coroutine and its collection.

A destination can be invisible while its content remains in Composition, depending on how navigation is implemented. Ordinary `collectAsState` continues collecting in that case. It cancels collection when the call leaves Composition, so screen visibility alone does not tell you whether the collector has stopped.

rows: The composable recomposes with unchanged Flow and context keys
The existing conversion remains; recomposition alone does not create a second collector
The Flow instance supplied to the call changes
The previous producer is cancelled and collection restarts for the replacement stream
The call site actually leaves Composition
Its producer is cancelled and this UI collection ends

blocks.text: Cancelling the composition-owned collector requests cancellation of its coroutine. Upstream work responds at a cancellable suspension point or an explicit cancellation check; arbitrary blocking or CPU-bound work is not interrupted immediately. The same cooperative cancellation rules apply here as in **Cancellation Is Cooperative**.
Ordinary collection continues while the call remains in Composition and the Flow and context keys are unchanged. Leaving Composition cancels it; changing a key replaces the collection.

Suppose the question library observes a Room query, maps rows into display models, combines saved markers, and records the result in screen state. Keeping its UI collector active may keep these operations running even while the user is looking elsewhere. Depending on how the stream is produced and shared, the costs can include:

items: The collector itself occupies a coroutine and remains ready for values.
Mapping, combining, filtering or other upstream work may still execute for each value.
A cold source collected only here may keep its database observer, polling loop or callback subscription alive.
A shared source may stay active because another scope and sharing policy own its production.
The conversion can write new UI state even while the host is not active enough for those updates to matter.

blocks.text: A quiet in-memory StateFlow may cost very little to collect, and continuous collection can be intentional. Extra work becomes a problem when collection lasts longer than the screen requires, particularly for database observation, network subscriptions or frequent transformations. Choose the lifetime according to the work and the UI’s needs.

After navigating away, check whether the destination’s collection call left Composition. If it did, its collector is cancelled. If its content remains composed, ordinary `collectAsState` continues collecting because it has no lifecycle or visibility condition.

Stopping the UI collector does not by itself prove that upstream production stopped. For a cold Flow whose producer runs only in this collecting coroutine, ending collection normally ends that production too, subject to cooperative cancellation. For a hot or shared stream, production can belong to an owner scope that outlives this screen. The upstream owner's lifetime and sharing policy decide whether it continues.

Collection policy decides whether this UI subscribes. A sharing policy, such as the `SharingStarted` strategy passed to `stateIn` or `shareIn`, decides when a shared producer runs as subscribers appear and disappear. Review both policies to understand what stops when the screen stops collecting. The sharing operators and their timers are covered in **Sharing Cold Flows with `stateIn` and `shareIn`**.

Lifecycle-aware collection removes this UI subscriber and its downstream processing while the lifecycle is inactive. An eagerly started shared producer can continue in its owner’s scope. A cold database Flow with only this collector may instead release its observer when collection ends. To assess the resource savings, measure the upstream work as well as the UI collection.

Trace both sides of the boundary. First say when the Compose collector ends. Then identify whether the upstream is cold and owned by that collection or hot/shared and owned elsewhere. Only the second answer tells you whether production stopped.

lessons.title: Lifecycle-Aware Collection and the Screen’s Lifecycle
lessons.summary: `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` collects while the call remains in Composition and its lifecycle owner meets the active-state threshold. The default is `STARTED`. A paused or unfocused screen can still meet that threshold, so collection follows the owner’s lifecycle state rather than visibility or focus alone.

blocks.text: A screen can remain in Composition after the app moves to the background. Ordinary `collectAsState` continues collecting while its call remains composed, which may keep database observation, polling or transformations running. `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` adds a lifecycle condition: it pauses this collection below the chosen active state, even if the composition remains.

rows: `collectAsState`
While the Compose state producer remains in Composition, subject to replacement when its inputs change
`collectAsStateWithLifecycle`
While the state producer remains in Composition and the relevant lifecycle is at least the configured active state

blocks.text: In lifecycle-runtime-compose 2.11.0-beta01, `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` defaults to `LocalLifecycleOwner.current` and `minActiveState = Lifecycle.State.STARTED`. At or above that state, it collects upstream. Below it, collection stops; when the lifecycle reaches the threshold again, collection restarts. `INITIALIZED` is not a valid threshold and the API rejects it with `IllegalArgumentException`.

The StateFlow overload initializes Compose State from the stream’s current `value`; the plain Flow overload requires `initialValue`. You can also pass an explicit `LifecycleOwner` or `Lifecycle`. By default, collection uses the owner provided at the call site: usually the Activity at the composition root, or a destination’s owner inside navigation content.

Lifecycle-aware collection has two independent gates: is this conversion still in Composition, and is its lifecycle at least the chosen active state? Upstream is collected only when both answers are yes.

At an Android composition root, `LocalLifecycleOwner` usually refers to the Activity. Inside a Navigation 3 destination, `NavDisplay` provides an owner for the entry. To determine whether collection continues, follow the event to that owner’s lifecycle state and compare it with `STARTED`:

rows: The user presses Home, or another Activity covers the whole screen
`ON_STOP`: the Activity is no longer visible and falls to `CREATED`
Below the threshold: collection stops, and restarts at `ON_START` when the Activity is visible again
A semi-transparent Activity, such as one styled as a dialog, opens on top
`ON_PAUSE`: the covered Activity is still partly visible and falls from `RESUMED` to `STARTED`
Still at the threshold: collection continues
Another app gains focus in multi-window mode

On Android 10 and higher, ordinary focus changes between multi-window Activities can leave both `RESUMED`. On Android 9 and lower, unfocused visible Activities normally fall to `STARTED`; some Android 9 devices support opting into multi-resume.
At or above the threshold either way: collection continues
A configuration change, such as rotation, recreates the Activity
The old Activity reaches `DESTROYED` and its composition is disposed; a new Activity and composition replace them
The old collection ends with its composition and the new one starts collecting; a `StateFlow` held by a retained ViewModel supplies its current value at once
A Navigation 3 entry remains on the back stack while its scene transitions or is covered by an overlay
The scene caps the entry at `STARTED`, subject to the host lifecycle
Collection continues if the host lifecycle also allows the entry to remain at least `STARTED`
A Navigation 3 entry is popped and is still animating out
The entry's lifecycle is capped at `CREATED`
Below the threshold: collection stops before the destination leaves Composition

blocks.text:
A partly visible Activity can be paused and still collect: `ON_PAUSE` lowers its state from `RESUMED` to `STARTED`, which meets the default threshold.

With multi-resume on Android 10 and higher, switching focus to another window can leave the Activity `RESUMED`. Losing the top-resumed position is reported through `onTopResumedActivityChanged`, so choosing `minActiveState = RESUMED` does not necessarily pause collection on a focus change. If collection continues while another app has focus, inspect the relevant owner’s state.

Use lifecycle-aware collection when this UI subscription should pause below a lifecycle threshold. Use plain `collectAsState` when collection should follow Composition lifetime throughout. Continuous collection can be intentional, particularly for a cheap source; choose the policy that matches the screen’s needs.

In lifecycle-runtime-compose 2.11.0-beta01, `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` uses `produceState` and `repeatOnLifecycle`. Compose cancels the state producer when the call leaves Composition. Within that producer, `repeatOnLifecycle` starts collection at the active-state threshold and cancels it below the threshold. Collection therefore requires both an active producer in Composition and an active lifecycle.

When the lifecycle falls below `STARTED`, the UI collector is cancelled; collection restarts when the owner reaches the threshold again. A cold source tied only to this collection normally stops and starts with it. A shared source follows its own scope and `SharingStarted` policy. Review those lifetimes together when resource use matters (see **Sharing Cold Flows with `stateIn` and `shareIn`**).

The overloads and defaults described here are those of lifecycle-runtime-compose 2.11.0-beta01 with Compose runtime 1.11.2. The lifecycle artifact is beta, so its API may change in later releases. The Activity transitions in the comparison are Android platform behaviour, and the entry caps are the ones Navigation 3 documents for its destinations.

Given an Android event and a collection API, answer in order: is the call still in Composition; which LifecycleOwner is relevant — the Activity or a navigation entry; what lifecycle state does the event produce; is that state at least the threshold; and who owns upstream production after this collector stops?
