units.title: Effect Lifecycle and LaunchedEffect
units.summary: A composable body describes UI, but executing it does not establish when imperative work should start or stop. `LaunchedEffect` ties suspend work to a place in the Composition. It launches on entry, continues through recomposition with equal keys, and is cancelled when its keys change or its call site leaves. Re-entry begins a new lifetime.

lessons.title: Why Compose Needs an Effect API
lessons.summary: Imperative work started directly in a composable body can run repeatedly, fail to run when the body is skipped, or change external state during a composition attempt that is later abandoned. Effect APIs give that work explicit start, cancellation and cleanup rules tied to the intended UI lifetime.

blocks.text: A composable body describes UI for its current inputs. Unlike an `onCreate` callback, its execution does not mark a single creation event. Compose decides whether and when to execute the body, so a statement inside it cannot by itself define when an operation should start, how long it should continue, or when it should stop.

Whenever this body executes, it records a screen opening and starts `questionWork`. Nothing here connects that operation to the screen's lifetime: there is no cancellation or cleanup when the screen leaves, and another execution can start another operation. If Compose abandons the composition attempt, the work may already have started even though the UI from that attempt is never applied.

Compose may execute a body repeatedly, skip it, execute composables in an order the caller must not depend on, or discard the result of an optimistic composition attempt. Application code cannot rely on a particular execution count or timing. These possibilities do not imply that Compose currently executes composables in parallel.

Work needs rules for when it starts, when it ends, and how it is cancelled or cleaned up. Those rules should match the UI lifetime it serves. Starting work directly in a composable body does not establish them.

If the body executes again, `screenOpened` records another opening and `questionWork.start` starts another operation. This can duplicate analytics, registrations or requests, leaving several operations running for one screen. Not every recomposition executes every composable, but whenever this body does execute, these statements execute with it.

Compose may skip a composable whose UI does not need to be recalculated. A statement in that body therefore cannot reliably represent an application event that must trigger an action. If a screen event requires work to begin, its trigger needs to be explicit rather than inferred from whether Compose executes the body.

Compose may begin calculating an updated UI and discard the result before applying it. An analytics event, request or registration started during that calculation may still have changed external state; discarding the UI does not undo it. Controlled effects defer such work until composition has succeeded, so an abandoned attempt does not start it.

headers: What direct body work gets wrong
rows: The body executes again
The statement runs again even when the logical work should still have one owner
The body is skipped
The statement cannot stand for a guaranteed application event
The composition attempt is abandoned
External mutation may survive even though the calculated UI is discarded

blocks.text: A `Boolean` that suppresses repeated calls still needs a lifetime: when should it be set, forgotten or reset as the screen leaves and re-enters? It also does not provide cancellation or cleanup for work already started. Defining those rules requires more than recording whether the body has run.

Different kinds of work need different lifecycle rules. Suspend work may last while a call site remains in the Composition. An external registration may need matching cleanup. Work triggered by a user event should start in response to its callback. A long-lived operation may need updated values without restarting. The effect APIs support these different requirements.

When reviewing an effect, identify what starts the work, what bounds its lifetime, and what cancels or cleans it up. If the work must continue after this UI position leaves the Composition, it needs a longer-lived owner, such as a screen-level state holder. A composition-owned effect would end too soon.

Explain why work started directly in a composable can fail: repeated execution can duplicate it, skipping makes body execution an unreliable event signal, and an abandoned composition can discard the UI without undoing external mutation. Then identify what should own the work and when it should end.

lessons.title: `LaunchedEffect`: Work a Composition Owns
lessons.summary: LaunchedEffect launches suspend work when its remembered position enters the Composition and bounds that coroutine by the position's lifetime. Equal keys preserve the running effect across ordinary recomposition; a changed key cancels and replaces it; removal cancels it; re-entry begins a new lifetime.

blocks.text: When `LaunchedEffect` enters the Composition, Compose launches its block in a coroutine. That coroutine is tied to the effect's remembered position and call-site identity in the Composition. Compose uses this identity and the effect's keys to decide whether the existing coroutine should continue or be cancelled and replaced.

headers: What happens to the call site
What happens to the effect coroutine
rows: It enters Composition
The block is launched and one effect lifetime begins
The body executes again and `questionId` still compares equal
The existing coroutine keeps running; ordinary recomposition does not restart it
`questionId` changes according to key comparison
The old coroutine is cancelled and a replacement is launched for the new id
The call site leaves Composition
Its coroutine is cancelled
The call site later re-enters Composition
A new effect instance and coroutine lifetime begin

blocks.text: Executing the composable body again does not necessarily restart its effect coroutine. If the effect keeps the same composition identity and all its keys still compare equal, the existing effect is retained. A changed key causes cancellation and replacement; leaving and later re-entering the Composition begins a new effect lifetime.

An effect's lifetime begins when it enters Composition, not whenever the composable is called. LaunchedEffect owns one coroutine lifetime at one remembered position. Ordinary re-execution with equal keys keeps that lifetime; changed identity or keys end it.

If `questionId` changes from `q1` to `q2` while prefetching is in progress, Compose cancels the `q1` coroutine and launches the block for `q2`. It does not update the old coroutine's captured ID. The old operation is asked to stop, and the replacement starts with the new ID.

Coroutine cancellation is cooperative. A suspending operation that supports cancellation observes it and unwinds. Blocking or CPU-bound code that neither suspends nor checks for cancellation cannot be forcibly stopped by Compose. Leaving the Composition requests cancellation of the effect; it does not instantly terminate arbitrary code. For the underlying rules, see **Cancellation Is Cooperative**.

When `question` becomes null, the branch and its `LaunchedEffect` call site leave the Composition. The pulse coroutine is cancelled even though the surrounding screen remains. If a question later becomes non-null, the call site enters again and launches a new effect. Here the pulse lasts only while the question branch remains composed. For how Compose assigns that identity, see **Composable Identity**.

Recomposition does not rerun LaunchedEffect on its own. It can execute the call again while the remembered effect and its coroutine continue unchanged. Whether the effect restarts depends on whether the position remained in Composition and whether its keys still compare equal.

In Compose runtime 1.11.2, the effect's coroutine context comes from the Composition's applying context. The runtime uses that context to launch and cancel the remembered effect.

On Android, a composition hosted in a window gets its Recomposer from Compose UI. Recomposition and composition effects run on `AndroidUiDispatcher.CurrentThread` for the window's UI thread, which is the main thread for an Activity. In that arrangement, effect code starts on the main thread; blocking or CPU-heavy work needs an appropriate dispatcher, for example through `withContext`.

Cancellation does not roll back an external action that has already completed. If an effect has sent analytics or written a remote record, cancelling its coroutine does not undo that change. Idempotency or an application-level consistency design may still be needed when repeated or partially completed external actions would matter.

Trace five moments precisely: entry launches; recomposition with equal keys preserves; key change cancels and replaces; removal cancels cooperatively; re-entry launches a new lifetime. Then state which call-site identity owns the effect and why body execution is not itself a restart event.

lessons.title: What an Effect's Keys Declare
lessons.summary: An effect key declares a lifetime dependency: a change means the current work is no longer the right work and should end. Keys use the same equality comparison as remember keys, not the instance comparison used for unstable parameters in strong-skipping decisions, and a constant key claims the call site's whole composition lifetime.

blocks.text: An effect's keys identify changes that should end its current work and start a replacement. A value belongs among the keys when changing it makes the current operation unsuitable. If the operation should continue and merely use the latest value, restarting it may discard valid progress; that value needs to be updated without redefining the effect's lifetime.

A changed `questionId` means the current hint sequence is for the wrong question. Cancelling it and starting a sequence for the new question is the intended behaviour, so `questionId` is a lifetime dependency. Other values may need to stay current while the same operation continues. `rememberUpdatedState` supports that case; see **Reading the Current Value Without Restarting**.

Android guidance recommends checking the variables used inside an effect when choosing its keys. Changes to captured inputs often require a restart. When a changing input should not restart the work, use `rememberUpdatedState` so the effect can read its latest value. The requirement is to keep inputs current while restarting only when the operation needs to change.
A key change tells Compose to cancel the current effect and launch a replacement. Choose keys for the changes that require new work; use an updated value when the same work should continue.

In AndroidX Compose runtime 1.11.2, `LaunchedEffect(key)` uses `remember(key)`. `remember` retains its value when the new key compares equal to the previous key using `==`/`equals`. Effect keys use this equality comparison as well.

Each body execution can allocate a fresh `QuestionKey("same")`. Fresh allocation alone does not restart the effect: two data-class values with the same `id` compare equal, so the remembered key is unchanged. A newly allocated value restarts an effect only when the supplied key stops comparing equal to the previous key.

rows: Should this effect restart?
Effect/remember-key equality: `==` / `equals`
Can this composable invocation be skipped under strong skipping?
Stable parameters use object equality; unstable parameters use instance equality `===`

blocks.text: Effect restarts and composable skipping use different comparisons. A newly allocated object can compare structurally equal and preserve an effect, yet prevent skipping if its type is unstable and its instance has changed. The strong-skipping comparison does not determine whether an effect key has changed.

Lambda keys use the same equality comparison as other effect keys. Whether a later execution supplies an equal lambda depends on the instances produced by the compiler.

A probe using Kotlin/Compose compiler 2.4.10 and runtime 1.11.2 reported one effect start for a non-capturing lambda, one for a lambda capturing unchanged data, and one for an explicitly remembered lambda. A lambda capturing changing data supplied a different instance and produced four starts across four passes.

Those probe results describe a particular toolchain. Strong skipping memoizes lambdas using their captures, and compiler transformations can change which instances are supplied. Lambda syntax alone therefore does not predict an effect restart. Check whether the supplied key stopped comparing equal, then whether that change should require the work to restart.

A constant key such as `Unit` keeps the effect through recomposition while this call site remains in the Composition. Leaving cancels the effect, and re-entry starts a new one, so it does not mean once for the whole application or screen history. Use it when changes to other values should not restart the work. If a changed input makes the current operation invalid, that input needs to be a key.

For each key candidate, answer two independent questions: does it compare equal to the previous supplied key, and should a real change end the current work? Comparison predicts what Compose does; the lifetime requirement decides whether the declaration is correct.

lessons.title: Two Ways to Get Effect Keys Wrong
lessons.summary: Omitting a lifetime dependency lets stale work continue. A key that changes unnecessarily cancels valid work, discards progress and may cause the replacement to repeat an external action. Diagnose both cases by comparing the work's intended lifetime with the key changes that actually restart it.

blocks.text: An effect can restart too rarely or too often. Omitting a required dependency preserves work after it has become stale. A key that changes while the operation is still valid cancels useful work and starts it again. To diagnose either case, compare when the operation should restart with when its keys actually change.

If this call site remains in the Composition while `questionId` changes, `Unit` still compares equal. The effect does not restart, so the old hint sequence may continue for the previous question while the screen shows another one. Here the sequence should change with the question, but the constant key does not express that dependency.

Using `questionId` as the key makes a changed question cancel the stale sequence and launch the appropriate one. A constant key is suitable only when this work should continue despite changes to the question.
When a changing input makes the current work invalid, include it among the keys. Otherwise the effect can continue using an input that no longer matches the screen.

The two fresh keys do not behave alike. `ValueKey` is a data class, so a new value with the same `id` is structurally equal and does not restart its effect. `IdentityKey` inherits default identity equality, so recreating it supplies a value unequal to the previous instance. If the body executes again while `questionId` is unchanged, the second effect is cancelled and replaced even though its logical work is still valid.

A restart cancels the current coroutine and launches a replacement. A delay or timer can begin again, animation progress can be lost, partial UI work can be abandoned, and a request can be issued again. If a key keeps becoming unequal on successive passes, the work may never reach completion.

rows: The screen changes item but work continues for the previous id
Too few dependencies: a change that should end the effect was omitted
Valid progress repeatedly resets while the logical item is unchanged
A supplied key keeps becoming unequal even though it should not define a new lifetime
The composable executes again and the effect keeps running
Not a bug by itself: equal keys correctly preserve the current effect

blocks.text: A fresh object alone does not explain a restart. Fresh, structurally equal data-class keys preserve the effect; a restart requires a supplied key that actually stops comparing equal, such as a newly created identity-equality wrapper.

The lambda measurements in **What an Effect's Keys Declare** illustrate the same distinction. Non-capturing lambdas and lambdas with unchanged captures were retained in the reported cases, so their effects did not restart. A lambda capturing changing data supplied a different instance and restarted its effect on every measured pass. These outcomes depend on the compiler's treatment of the lambdas; the effect itself still checks key equality.

Cancellation does not undo an external action that already completed. If an effect sent an analytics event before a needless restart, cancellation cannot retract it, and the replacement may send another. Unnecessary key changes can therefore waste work in progress and duplicate completed actions.

Sometimes an effect should keep running while an input changes. Making that input a key restarts the work, but simply leaving it out can retain an old captured value. `rememberUpdatedState` lets the effect read the current value when needed while keeping its existing lifetime; see **Reading the Current Value Without Restarting**.

Distinguish recomposition from effect restart: the body can execute again while equal keys preserve the existing effect. When debugging stale work or repeated restarts, identify which input changes should begin a new operation and check whether the supplied keys express those changes.

units.title: Latest-Value Effects and Event-Driven Coroutine Work
units.summary: Some running work needs a current value without restarting. Other work should begin only when a user event occurs. rememberUpdatedState lets an existing effect read an updated value while keeping its lifetime; rememberCoroutineScope gives event callbacks a scope whose lifetime is bounded by the Composition. These address separate decisions: which value running work should read, when new work should start, and how long it should live.

lessons.title: Reading the Current Value Without Restarting
lessons.summary: A value can matter to long-lived work without defining that work's lifetime. rememberUpdatedState keeps a remembered State holder current across recompositions so an existing effect can read the latest value when it needs it, while keying the effect remains correct when a changed value should cancel and replace the work.

blocks.text: An effect key should change when the current work needs to end and replacement work needs to begin. Sometimes, though, a running coroutine still needs to finish its work even when one of its inputs changes. Restarting would discard useful progress, but continuing with the value captured at launch could use stale data.

Suppose this call site should start one 30-second timer when the question enters the Composition and keep that timer running across recompositions. `Unit` expresses that lifetime: the timer does not restart when its inputs change, but leaving and re-entering the Composition starts a new timer.

If recomposition supplies a different `onTimeout`, the existing coroutine still holds the callback captured at launch. When the delay ends, it may invoke a callback that the screen no longer intends to use.

`rememberUpdatedState` lets the timer keep running while making the updated callback available. It remembers a `State` holder and updates that holder’s value when this call recomposes. The coroutine continues without being relaunched. When it reaches `currentOnTimeout()`, the delegated property reads the holder and returns the callback current at that moment.
Effect keys determine when running work is cancelled and replaced. rememberUpdatedState lets work that should continue read an updated value.

Reading time matters. If the coroutine first copies `val captured = currentOnTimeout`, then delays and invokes `captured()`, that local still refers to the callback read before the delay. If it delays first and then invokes `currentOnTimeout()`, the State read happens after the delay and can observe a callback supplied by a later recomposition. State makes a current value available when read; it does not retroactively rewrite ordinary local variables.

rows: A changed callback makes the old timer obsolete
LaunchedEffect(onTimeout) { delay(...); onTimeout() }
The old timer is cancelled and a full new timer starts
The original timer remains valid, but completion must use the current callback
rememberUpdatedState(onTimeout) plus LaunchedEffect(Unit)
The timer continues; its later State read obtains the current callback

blocks.text: Use `LaunchedEffect(onTimeout)` when a different callback means the existing timer should be replaced. Whenever the key stops comparing equal, Compose cancels the in-flight delay and starts the whole block again, including a fresh delay. Use `rememberUpdatedState` when the timer should continue and only the callback invoked at the end needs to change.

rememberUpdatedState does not prevent, reduce or optimize recomposition. It is Compose State. If composable code reads the returned State during composition, ordinary state-read invalidation rules apply. The timer survives here because the changing callback is read inside the running coroutine and is not a changing effect key.

The public runtime contract describes a remembered State whose value is updated on recomposition so a long-lived lambda, object or operation can persist without cancellation and restart. In Compose runtime 1.11.2, the implementation is equivalent to `remember { mutableStateOf(newValue) }.apply { value = newValue }`. That implementation confirms the model, but the public contract is what to rely on: preserve the long-lived operation and change which value it reads.

Before using a callback as an effect key, decide whether a changed callback should end the running work. If the work should continue, use `rememberUpdatedState` to supply the callback it will read later.

If restarting is appropriate, whether the effect actually restarts depends on key equality and the compiler’s memoization of lambdas (see **What an Effect's Keys Declare**). Callback syntax alone does not tell you whether the key will change.

Explain both valid models. Key on a value when its change makes old work obsolete. Use rememberUpdatedState when old work remains valid and only the value read later must be current. Neither choice is a recomposition optimization.

lessons.title: `rememberCoroutineScope`: Launching From an Event
lessons.summary: rememberCoroutineScope returns a remembered CoroutineScope and starts no work. A click or other callback chooses whether and when to call launch, while the Composition still owns the scope's lifetime and cancels it when the call leaves Composition.

blocks.text: A screen may need suspend work that starts in response to an event: showing a snackbar after a tap, scrolling after a button press, or running a transient animation. The event determines when the work starts; the Composition can still determine how long it is allowed to run.

`rememberCoroutineScope()` returns the same remembered scope across recompositions of this call site. It does not start a coroutine. In this example, the coroutine starts when `onClick` calls `scope.launch`. Each click can launch another coroutine unless the handler explicitly limits or coordinates that work.

rows: Composition creates and remembers the scope
Composition owns the scope lifetime
The user taps Save and the callback calls launch
The event/caller owns the trigger
The call site leaves Composition
Composition cancels the remembered scope

blocks.text: The event starts the coroutine. The Composition owns the remembered scope and cancels it when this call site leaves.

Suppose the user taps Save and `showSnackbar` is still suspended when navigation removes this screen from the Composition. Compose cancels the remembered scope, and cancellation propagates to its child coroutines. Cancellation-aware suspending work responds to that request, but arbitrary blocking code is not forcibly stopped as soon as the screen disappears.

Calling `launch` directly in the composable body starts work whenever execution reaches that call. The body may run repeatedly, be skipped, or run as part of a composition that is later abandoned, so this does not tie the launch to a user event.

For event-driven work, call `launch` inside the event callback. If entering the Composition or changing an effect key should start the work, use a composition-triggered effect.

`scope.launch` returns a `Job` that the handler can retain if it needs to cancel or coordinate the work. Without such a policy, another click can start another child coroutine. The handler must decide whether repeated clicks should run in parallel, be ignored, or cancel earlier work; `rememberCoroutineScope` does not make that decision.
rememberCoroutineScope provides a scope whose lifetime ends when its call site leaves the Composition. You still choose where to call launch and how to handle repeated events.

In Compose runtime 1.11.2, the KDoc describes a scope bound to this point in the Composition. It is cancelled when the call leaves the Composition and uses the Recomposer’s applying dispatcher unless you supply a dispatcher. The optional context cannot contain a parent `Job`: the scope is already a child of the Composition.

The KDoc also describes what happens if the supplied context violates this restriction: the composable call does not throw directly. In the 1.11.2 implementation, the returned scope contains a failed `Job`, so attempts to launch children cannot run their work. The failed scope reports the invalid context; it does not give the caller a different lifetime owner.

Describe the sequence precisely: composition remembers a scope; an event calls launch; a child coroutine starts; leaving that composition point cancels the scope and requests cooperative cancellation of its children.

lessons.title: Composition-Driven or Event-Driven?
lessons.summary: Use LaunchedEffect when entering the Composition or changing an effect key should start work. Use rememberCoroutineScope when an event should choose when to launch. Both bind the work’s lifetime to the Composition; work that must continue after the screen leaves needs a different owner.

blocks.text: Two coroutines can both be cancelled when a call site leaves the Composition but need to start for different reasons. A timer for the active question should begin when that question’s effect enters the Composition and restart when its question key changes. A snackbar requested by a tap should begin in response to that tap. In each case, the trigger is the occurrence that should start the work.

rows: LaunchedEffect
Effect enters Composition or its keys change
Composition
rememberCoroutineScope plus launch
Event or callback
Composition

blocks.text: When this effect enters the Composition, it starts the delay for `questionId`. If the id changes, the old question’s timer is no longer needed: Compose cancels it and starts a timer for the new question. No click is required. Starting this timer only from a click callback would miss the case where the active question appears without a click.
Use LaunchedEffect when entering the Composition or changing an effect key should start or restart work. Use rememberCoroutineScope when an event should decide when to launch.

Suppose the requirement is to show one confirmation snackbar for each Save tap. In the version below, `showSavedMessage` remains true after the tap. The effect starts when the branch enters the Composition; the flag does not record a separate occurrence for each tap.

If this branch leaves and later re-enters the Composition while the flag is still true, the effect starts again and can show the same snackbar again. The persistent flag therefore does not express this one-snackbar-per-tap requirement.

Here, the click callback calls `saveAnswer()` and then launches the snackbar work in the remembered scope. Each callback invocation supplies the trigger, while the Composition still owns the scope’s lifetime.

This example shows where the snackbar is launched. It does not establish that an asynchronous save has completed successfully: that depends on the contract of `saveAnswer()`.

A persistent UI condition can remain true across several taps or across leaving and re-entering the Composition. A tap is one occurrence. Decide which of these should trigger the work before choosing LaunchedEffect or a launch from an event callback.

If an operation must continue after this screen leaves the Composition, launch it through an owner whose lifetime meets that requirement. Neither a composition-owned effect nor a remembered scope provides that lifetime. This matters for an upload, save, payment submission, or background synchronization that must continue after navigation.

Leaving a LaunchedEffect call site cancels its coroutine; changing its keys cancels and replaces that coroutine. Leaving a rememberCoroutineScope call site cancels its scope and the work launched in it. Cancellation-aware suspension responds cooperatively; blocking or non-cooperative work may continue until it can observe cancellation. Cancellation also does not undo an external action that has already completed. These limits apply whether an effect or an event started the work.

`rememberUpdatedState` lets an existing object or effect read an updated value without being recreated. `rememberCoroutineScope` gives an event handler a scope in which to launch new work. You may need both: the handler chooses when work starts, and the running work may later need a current value. Updating a State holder makes a value available to read; it does not deliver an event.

Give a three-part answer: name the trigger owner, name the lifetime owner, and test whether that lifetime is long enough. Composition state can trigger LaunchedEffect; an event can launch into a remembered scope; work that must survive the screen needs a different owner.

units.title: Cleanup, External Synchronization and State Producers
units.summary: A screen may register with an external object, publish composed state to it, or receive data from it. These needs call for different kinds of ownership: releasing a registration when its effect ends, publishing only after composition succeeds, or giving a state producer a composition lifetime. Whether a source adapter belongs at the Compose boundary or below the UI depends on ownership and reuse.

lessons.title: Registration and Release as One Decision
lessons.summary: Some screen work involves registering a listener or observer with an object outside Compose. `DisposableEffect` pairs that registration with an `onDispose` cleanup, which runs when a key changes or the effect leaves the Composition. The registration and its release can use the same objects captured by the effect block.

blocks.text: A screen may register a listener with a session, an observer with a lifecycle, or a callback with a platform service. Registration usually returns immediately, but the external object continues to hold the listener or callback. The screen therefore needs a way to remove that registration when it no longer needs it.

This is a resource ownership problem: which effect lifetime owns the registration, and when should it release it? Unlike a suspend operation, the registration does not finish by returning a result. It remains active until it is removed.

`DisposableEffect` is built for that problem. Its block runs when the effect enters the Composition for a given key, and it must end with an `onDispose` clause. The block acquires; `onDispose` releases. The Compose runtime 1.11.2 documentation states the guarantee plainly: there is one call to `onDispose` for every call to the effect block, and both run on the composition's apply dispatcher.

The effect registers for key K when it enters the Composition. That registration remains active for the effect’s lifetime. When K changes or the call site leaves the Composition, `onDispose` runs to release it.
Keep registration and release together in `DisposableEffect`. The cleanup should remove the same listener from the same object that the effect registered with.

Suppose the `onDispose` body is removed. A user opens a session and moves through three questions. Each question creates a separate `QuestionSessionStatus` composition instance, which leaves when the next question arrives. The session now holds three listeners. When the next answer is graded, all three receive it; two write into state that the UI no longer reads.

Each listener retains the state it updates. If the session outlives those composition instances and keeps the listeners, that state cannot be collected.
Without release, stale listeners accumulate each time this call site re-enters. In this scenario, the cost is duplicated callback work and retained state from questions that are no longer composed.

The block runs once and registers for K

Nothing. The existing registration stays; the block does not run again
K changes to L
`onDispose` for K runs first, then the block runs and registers for L

blocks.text:
A key change releases the old registration and establishes a new one. Leaving the Composition only releases it. Recomposition with equal keys keeps the existing registration.

The Compose documentation specifies cleanup of the old effect before initialization of its replacement. The reported Compose runtime 1.11.2 probe observed setup for A, dispose for A, then setup for B; the registrations did not overlap in that sequence.

In this example, setup and cleanup are defined by the same execution of the effect block. `onDispose` captures the listener created there and the session it was registered with, so it can remove that exact registration. This pairing makes the cleanup easier to keep correct; the API does not verify that the cleanup body releases the right object. The key list has a separate responsibility: it must identify changes that require a new registration.

With a constant key, the registration lasts for this call site’s composition lifetime. Changing `session` does not restart it: the screen continues listening to the first session while displaying the new one. The eventual `onDispose` removes the first session’s listener, but the new session has had no listener during that interval.

If `onDispose` has an empty body, check whether the effect acquired anything that needs releasing. A publication of composed state to an external object usually belongs in `SideEffect`; suspend work belongs in `LaunchedEffect`. If the block registered a listener or acquired a resource, its cleanup needs to release it.

`LaunchedEffect` can also clean up resources, using a `finally` block as its coroutine unwinds. Cleanup that suspends needs additional care; see **Cleanup, `NonCancellable` and Timeouts**. The useful distinction is what the Composition owns: a coroutine operation or a registration with an external object.

rows: A suspend operation that should run while this position is composed
`LaunchedEffect`
Cooperative cancellation of the coroutine; any release happens as the coroutine unwinds
A registration or resource held by an object outside Compose
`DisposableEffect`
A synchronous `onDispose` call at a defined moment on the apply dispatcher

blocks.text: For an in-flight suspend operation, ending the effect means cancelling its coroutine; cleanup runs as that coroutine unwinds. For an external registration, ending the effect means making a specific release call, such as `session.removeListener(listener)`. `DisposableEffect` provides that synchronous release point without requiring a coroutine.

A registration can remain valid while the callback it invokes changes with recomposition. Keying the effect on that callback would remove and re-add the observer even though the session has not changed. `rememberUpdatedState` lets the existing listener invoke the latest callback without restarting the registration.

Use `rememberUpdatedState` for a changing callback when the existing registration should remain active. A value that changes where the observer belongs, such as the session or lifecycle owner, still belongs in the key list. Here, changing `session` must move the listener to the new session.

Explain the registration the Composition owns, then identify both release paths: a key change and leaving the Composition. Give a concrete consequence of missing cleanup, such as three listeners on one session delivering each result three times.

lessons.title: `SideEffect`: Publishing to Non-Compose Code
lessons.summary: An object Compose does not manage sometimes has to hold the value the UI is currently built from. SideEffect schedules that publication to run when a composition completes successfully and applies its changes, which is what separates it from the same assignment written directly in a composable body.

blocks.text: An analytics client may hold a user property that it attaches to later events. A logging context may hold the current screen identifier. These external objects do not participate in composition or automatically observe the screen’s Compose state; code has to update their properties.

The external property should match the state used by a successfully applied composition. Publishing a value from a discarded composition attempt could leave the external object describing an update that never took effect.

`SideEffect` schedules its block rather than running it. Compose runtime 1.11.2 documents it as scheduling the effect to run when the current composition completes successfully and applies changes, so that objects managed outside the Composition are not left in an inconsistent state if the composition operation fails. The block runs on the composition's apply dispatcher and always after `RememberObserver` callbacks, and the documentation states the resulting guarantee as executing after every successful recomposition.

Compare it with the same assignment written in the body. That version publishes while the composable is executing — which is before anything has decided whether this composition attempt will become the applied UI.
`SideEffect` publishes state after composition succeeds. Assigning an external property directly in the composable body changes it immediately, even if Compose later discards that attempt.

Compose may calculate an update and discard it before applying it. A direct assignment has already changed `analytics.userType`, so the external property can describe a composition that never took effect. A `SideEffect` recorded by that abandoned attempt does not run.

Successful application is the timing boundary here. It does not guarantee that a frame has been drawn or shown to the user.

If the composable containing `SideEffect` is skipped, its body does not execute in that pass and schedules no effect. The previously published property remains. In the unchanged-input example below, there is no new value from that call to publish.

headers: What happened to this composition pass
rows: The call executed and the composition was applied successfully
The scheduled block runs on the apply dispatcher, after remember callbacks
The composable was skipped in this pass
This call scheduled nothing in that pass; the previously published value still stands
The composition attempt was abandoned instead of applied
Nothing that attempt scheduled publishes the state it attempted

blocks.text: A probe with Compose runtime 1.11.2 showed this: a parent that recomposed twice published twice, while a child composable whose parameter had not changed was skipped on the second pass and published once. The child published once because its call did not execute on the second pass, not because `SideEffect` watches for state changes.

The skipping row does not mean "SideEffect only runs when state changes". The contract is about successful composition passes in which this call participates, not about which state changed. A pass that executes this call and is applied publishes, whatever caused the pass.
Use `SideEffect` to publish composed state, rather than to handle an event such as submitting a payment.

`SideEffect` runs after each successful composition in which its call executes. A later recomposition can therefore submit the payment again. The API provides no once-only event boundary, so it cannot determine how many payments should be submitted.

Choosing the right mechanism instead starts from the trigger. If a click should start suspend work, the click owns the trigger and a remembered scope launches it. If entering or changing a composition state should start work, `LaunchedEffect` owns it. If an object outside Compose must be handed something back later, `DisposableEffect` owns it. `SideEffect` answers only the remaining case: composed state must be pushed synchronously into a non-Compose object once that composition has succeeded.

The block is synchronous and cannot call suspend functions directly. Use the appropriate coroutine effect or event scope for asynchronous work. `SideEffect` runs on the composition’s apply dispatcher, so expensive work there occupies the same serialized application work and can delay UI updates. Keep publication brief, such as a simple property assignment.

Describe when the block runs: after its composition completes successfully and applies its changes. Explain why an assignment in the composable body is unsafe if that attempt is abandoned. Then connect the timing to the use case: synchronizing an external object with composed state, rather than handling an event or starting coroutine work.

lessons.title: `produceState`: a Composition-Scoped Producer
lessons.summary: produceState turns an asynchronous or external source into a Compose State the UI can read, with a producer the Composition launches on entry, cancels on exit and restarts on a key change. Its returned State is remembered independently of those keys, which decides what the screen displays in the interval after a key change and before the new producer writes.

blocks.text: When a screen already has a `Flow`, `collectAsState` converts its collected values into Compose `State`. Other sources need an adapter first: a one-shot suspend load returns a result, while a platform object may deliver updates through callbacks. Neither exposes Compose `State` for the UI to read.
`produceState` is the composition-scoped answer: a producer whose output is a Compose `State<T>`. The composable gets something it can read; the producer gets a lifetime the Composition owns.

The producer follows `LaunchedEffect`’s lifetime rules. It launches when `produceState` enters the Composition and is cancelled when the call leaves. A changed key cancels a running producer and launches a replacement. The producer assigns its results to `value`, and the composable reads them from the returned `State`.

`initialValue` initializes the returned `State` when that holder is first created. The holder keeps that value until the producer assigns another one. Restarting the producer does not automatically reapply `initialValue`, and this state is neither persisted across removal from the Composition nor a cache or replay mechanism.

`produceState` is a producer with a composition lifetime and a `State` output. Everything about when it starts, stops and restarts follows `LaunchedEffect`'s lifetime; what is new is that the result is a value the UI can read.
Suppose `questionId` changes from `q1` to `q2`. The running `q1` producer is cancelled and a `q2` producer is launched. While the new load is pending, the returned `State` keeps its existing value.

If `q1` had already produced a preview, that preview remains until the `q2` producer writes a replacement. The screen can therefore display the previous question’s preview under the new question’s id.

The implementation cited for Compose runtime 1.11.2 uses `remember { mutableStateOf(initialValue) }` and a `LaunchedEffect(key)` that writes into that state. The holder’s `remember` has no keys; the key restarts the producer while retaining the holder and its current value.

The reported probe observed the same separation: key A produced `A-result`; switching to B restarted the producer while the `State` still contained `A-result`; the B producer’s assignment then changed it.

To set the state to Loading on each producer restart, assign `PreviewState.Loading` at the start of the producer block. That assignment runs for each new producer, followed by the load. It happens when the coroutine starts executing, so it does not reset the holder synchronously at the moment the key changes.

The returned `State` also conflates. The runtime states it directly: no change is observable if a value equal to the current one is assigned, and observers may only see the latest value if several values are set in rapid succession. A probe with Compose runtime 1.11.2 matched that — a producer that assigned the same loaded value three times produced exactly one observable change, and the reading composable executed twice in total, once for the initial value and once for the loaded one.

A changed producer key does not reset the remembered holder to `initialValue` in the implementation described here. If the UI should clear the previous item’s data while loading the next one, make that state transition explicit.
The two forms below use the same arrangement: a remembered state holder and a launched producer. `produceState` packages them into one call.

Both forms retain the old value when `questionId` changes because their state holder is remembered without keys. This lets you reason about `produceState` using the same state-and-coroutine model as the explicit version.

Using `remember(questionId) { mutableStateOf(PreviewState.Loading) }` in the explicit version would create a new holder when the key changes. The `produceState` key restarts its producer instead. The forms are therefore equivalent only when the explicit holder is also unkeyed; choose the arrangement that gives the screen the state transition it needs.

If the source already exposes a `Flow` and the screen only needs its collected value, use `collectAsState` or the lifecycle-aware variant when lifecycle state should control collection. A collect call can be written inside `produceState`, but the dedicated collection API expresses that purpose more directly. **A Flow Below the UI, or a Producer at the Boundary?** explains where a source adapter belongs.

Explain three properties: the producer starts, restarts and stops with its composition lifetime and keys; the returned `State` is remembered independently of those keys; and equal assignments or rapid updates need not each produce an observable change. The output is a current value, rather than a queue of assignments.

lessons.title: A Flow Below the UI, or a Producer at the Boundary?
lessons.summary: A callback-based source can be adapted into a reusable Flow below the UI or into a Compose-local state producer at the boundary. awaitDispose is what keeps a non-suspending subscription alive inside produceState and unregisters it on disposal, and the placement decision itself is answered from ownership and reuse rather than from API preference.

blocks.text: A one-shot producer calls a suspend load, assigns its result and finishes. A callback subscription is different: registering the listener returns immediately, but the source keeps sending updates. If the producer returns at that point, its coroutine has finished without arranging to unregister the listener when the composition lifetime ends.

`awaitDispose` suspends the producer without resuming normally; its return type is `Nothing`. Once execution reaches this call, its cleanup runs as the coroutine exits, including cancellation caused by a key change or leaving the Composition. It cannot clean up a registration if an earlier error prevents execution from reaching the call.

The block registers a listener, then suspends in `awaitDispose`. While the producer remains active, callbacks assign to `value` so readers can observe the updated state. When the producer is cancelled, cleanup removes that listener from the monitor.
For this callback subscription, `awaitDispose` keeps the producer suspended and gives it a cleanup that unregisters the listener when the producer ends.
Both `DisposableEffect` and a producer with `awaitDispose` can own a callback registration and release it. Choose between them by the output the composable needs.

`DisposableEffect`
The registration itself
A callback source must become a `State<T>` the UI reads
`produceState` with `awaitDispose`
The subscription that was feeding `value`

blocks.text: If a `DisposableEffect` only feeds a nearby remembered `MutableState`, `produceState` can express the producer and its `State` output together. If the registration instead reports lifecycle events to analytics or tells a service that the screen is present, it needs cleanup but no state output; `DisposableEffect` fits that responsibility.

The trigger still matters. A listener registration begins when its effect enters the Composition and ends when that effect is disposed. A button click begins work because the user acted. Choose the mechanism from who owns the work, what starts it, how long it should last and whether it requires a release.

If a `produceState` block registers a listener and then returns without cleanup, its coroutine completes while the source can still hold the listener. Suspending in `awaitDispose` ties unregistration to the producer’s end.

The same callback source can also be adapted below the UI with `callbackFlow`. Its `awaitClose` keeps the callback adapter active and provides cleanup when collection ends. The placement decision depends on who needs the source and who should own the subscription.

Stream operators and composition are part of the source contract

The producer's lifetime belongs below the UI
Extracting a reusable stream would add an abstraction nothing reuses
A platform or domain layer should expose the observation API
The value is read by one screen and has no meaning elsewhere

blocks.text:
A connection monitor used by three features, or combined with a retry policy below the UI, can expose a reusable Flow adapter. `callbackFlow` builds that adapter; see **Flow Builders and Adapting Callback APIs**. Its Flow is cold: each collection starts the adapter and owns that subscription’s lifetime. The monitor itself may have an application lifetime independently of those subscriptions.

If one screen only needs a Compose `State` and the Composition should own its subscription, a local producer may be sufficient. Extracting a reusable stream needs a responsibility beyond merely adding another layer.
For a value used only by one composable, a repository, mapper and state holder may add no behavior. Before introducing them, identify what each would own or what reuse it would support.

A Flow adapter below the UI still needs collection at the Compose boundary. `collectAsState` or its lifecycle-aware variant provides the `State` the UI reads. Moving the adapter makes it usable by other consumers; it does not remove that final conversion. For a comparison of the Compose mechanisms against a stated requirement, see **Choosing the Smallest Sufficient Mechanism**.

Answer the placement question with ownership and reuse, and give a concrete threshold: more than one consumer, or meaning outside Compose, or a lifetime that is not a composition's, argues for a Flow below the UI. One screen, a Compose-only lifetime and a `State` output argue for the producer at the boundary. Then name `awaitDispose` and `awaitClose` as the same registration-and-cleanup idea on the two sides of that line.

units.title: Production UI Effects and Mechanism Selection
units.summary: Choose a Compose mechanism by identifying who owns the state, what triggers the work, how long it must live, and what needs cleanup. Rendering a current condition differs from performing a one-off action. For that action, also decide what must happen if no UI is available to handle it; an effect API alone does not provide a delivery guarantee.

lessons.title: Choosing the Smallest Sufficient Mechanism
lessons.summary: Identify the state owner, trigger, required lifetime and cleanup before choosing a mechanism. Ordinary rendering may be enough. If work must outlive the Composition, it needs another owner.

blocks.text: A screen requirement arrives in product terms: this screen has to show something, remember something, start something, register something, or hand something outward. The engineering question is which Compose mechanism that requirement needs, and why.

An effect adds a lifetime, a set of keys and work that later readers must understand before changing the screen. Use one when the requirement needs work to run, rather than adding one merely because it could implement the behaviour. A value the screen already has can often be rendered directly.
For each scenario, identify four facts:

items: Who owns the state — nobody, because nothing needs remembering; this composable; the closest common ancestor of the composables that use it; or an owner that lives outside the Composition.
Who owns the trigger — whether there is any work to start, and if there is, whether entering or changing a composition state starts it or an event does.
What lifetime the requirement needs — one composition, one value of one key, the screen, or longer than the screen.
What has to be released — nothing; a coroutine that ends by cancellation; or a registration that has to be handed back to an object Compose does not manage.

blocks.text: Use those facts to decide which parts of the requirement need rendering, collection or work with a managed lifetime. A screen may need more than one mechanism for different responsibilities.

items: Is there state to render? If there is none, do not invent some so that an effect has something to watch. If there is, ask who should own it — an ordinary parameter, local Compose state, hoisted state, or the screen's one current value.

Is an external observable value driving the UI? Collect it into Compose `State` so changes can update the rendering. Use lifecycle-aware collection when collection should also stop below the selected lifecycle’s active-state threshold. Whether the upstream producer stops depends on its ownership and sharing policy.

What starts imperative or suspend work? If entering or changing a composition state starts it, the Composition owns the trigger and `LaunchedEffect` is the mechanism. If a click or another callback starts it, the event owns the trigger and a remembered scope is.
Does ongoing work need the latest value of something whose changes should not restart it? Use `rememberUpdatedState` to make that value available without making it a restart key.
Does the Composition acquire something that has to be given back? A registration paired with its release is `DisposableEffect`.
Does code outside Compose need the value the composed UI was actually built from? That is `SideEffect`.

Does an external producer have to become Compose `State`? Decide from ownership and reuse — a stream that already exists below the UI is simply collected, a source worth reusing is adapted into a Flow there, and a source that exists only for this boundary can be a Compose-local `produceState`, with `awaitDispose` when its subscription does not suspend.
Must the work continue after this screen leaves the Composition? It needs an owner outside the Composition; none of these composition-owned mechanisms provides that lifetime.

blocks.text: Choose from the state owner, trigger, lifetime and cleanup the requirement needs. Use the smallest mechanism that satisfies them. Ordinary rendering may need no effect, while work that outlives the Composition needs another owner.
These three practice-question examples need different mechanisms because they have different triggers and lifetimes. The first only changes what is rendered.

`QuestionExplanation` owns `expanded` because no other composable reads or changes it. The tap updates that value; rendering the expanded or collapsed panel needs no coroutine or effect. Nothing requires cleanup.

`remember` retains the local state while this call remains in the Composition. In this example, reopening with the panel collapsed is acceptable. Preserving it through screen recreation would be a saved-state requirement. The `explanation` parameter can be rendered directly because this composable does not own or change that text.
The countdown needs one mechanism to manage its coroutine and another to keep its callback current.

The active question belongs to the screen’s state; the countdown has no additional screen state to own. Its trigger is entering the Composition with a question, and its required lifetime is one value of `questionId`. A different question makes the old countdown obsolete. `LaunchedEffect(questionId)` cancels its coroutine when that key changes or the effect leaves the Composition.

When the delay finishes, the countdown must call the latest `onTimeout`. A callback change should not restart the timer. `rememberUpdatedState` keeps the callback current without making it a restart key; adding `onTimeout` as a key would begin the delay again whenever that callback changes.
The hint action starts from a tap rather than from entering the Composition.

The tap starts the scroll and snackbar. This composable adds no state to own: it uses the supplied list and snackbar state objects. `rememberCoroutineScope` provides a scope for launching from the callback, and cancels that scope when its call leaves the Composition. If navigating away removes this screen, the work stops with it. No flag or effect is needed to turn the tap into a trigger.

Converting a click into a `Boolean` so that a `LaunchedEffect` has something to key on. The click is already the trigger. The flag adds state nobody renders, a second thing that has to be reset, and a lifetime that no longer matches the occurrence it was meant to represent.
Apply the four facts to the rest of a practice-question screen. For the submitted-assessment upload, the answer is no Compose mechanism at all.
