blocks.text:
Some rows describe two responsibilities in the same code. The countdown uses `LaunchedEffect` to control when the timer starts and ends, and `rememberUpdatedState` to supply its current callback.

The callback-source rows differ in who needs the data. A source used only at this Compose boundary can be adapted locally; one also needed by another screen and code below the UI benefits from an adapter in the layer that owns it. Choose by ownership and reuse, then check the trigger, lifetime and cleanup.
The smallest sufficient mechanism adds only the ownership and lifetime the requirement needs. These substitutions add responsibilities that may be unnecessary:

items: Writing a value the screen already has into state from inside a `LaunchedEffect`. If rendering the value is sufficient, there is nothing to run and nothing to keep consistent.
Introducing a screen-level owner for a value one composable reads and writes. Keep it local if no other requirement needs a wider owner; hoist it when shared use or a longer lifetime requires one.

Collecting a stream by hand in a `LaunchedEffect` and assigning into a `mutableStateOf`. That is an ongoing conversion written as an effect, and the conversion already has mechanisms with the right contract.
Turning an event into persistent state so an effect can observe it. The event owns the trigger; giving the trigger to the Composition changes when the work starts and how often.

Reaching for `produceState` because a callback is involved. Its purpose is producing a `State`; a listener whose job is to notify something else produces none, and the registration mechanism is the smaller answer.
Adding a restart key only to keep a value current. A changed key ends and restarts the work. Use `rememberUpdatedState` when the value must be current but its changes should not restart that work.

blocks.text: `LaunchedEffect`, `DisposableEffect`, `SideEffect` and the state-producing APIs manage different responsibilities. Choose by the work and lifetime needed. The Compose side-effects guidance also recommends keeping effect work UI-related and preserving unidirectional data flow.

A committed submission, durable save, upload or payment may need to continue after the screen leaves the Composition. A remembered scope or launched effect cannot supply that lifetime: its work is cancelled when its call leaves. Such work needs an owner that remains available for the required duration, rather than a different composition-owned API.
That result still states a requirement: the work needs an owner whose lifetime matches it. The required lifetime exceeds the Composition's, so the Composition cannot be the owner.

When asked which effect API you would use, name the facts before the API: who owns the state, who owns the trigger, how long the work must live, and what has to be released. Then name the smallest mechanism those facts allow — and be willing to answer that the requirement needs no mechanism, or that it needs an owner the Composition cannot provide.

lessons.title: Rendering State and Running a Transient Effect
lessons.summary: A screen can render a current condition and also perform a one-off action. Re-rendering a disabled save button preserves the same UI; running a save-confirmation snackbar again produces another confirmation. A persistent flag alone does not say whether that confirmation has already been handled.

blocks.text: Two requirements on one screen can read almost identically and behave nothing alike. "The save button is disabled while a save is in flight" describes what the screen currently is. "Confirm the save with a snackbar" describes something the UI should do once. The first is rendered, as often as Compose needs to, and rendering it again changes nothing anybody can see. The second is executed, and executing it again is immediately visible.

The selected question, loading status, active filter and a validation message that remains while input is invalid are current state. Compose can render them whenever it needs to update the UI. Describing those values does not require an effect.

Showing a snackbar, requesting focus, starting a scroll animation or requesting navigation performs an action rather than merely describing the UI. Run that work from an event callback or an effect with the appropriate lifetime. The relevant distinction is between rendering a condition and executing an action.

The widget alone does not decide the contract. “The unsaved-changes dialog remains visible while an unsaved edit exists” describes a condition that can be modelled as state. “Open the image chooser once because the user just asked for it” describes an action. Choose from what the UI must do and whether that behaviour should repeat after the screen is rebuilt.

A current condition can be rendered repeatedly without repeating an action. If the UI must perform an action once, its representation and handling need to distinguish that occurrence from a condition that remains true.
The common failure is an occurrence given the contract of a condition. Here is a screen state carrying a flag for a completed save.

blocks.code:
data class EditorScreenState(
    val draft: String,
    val saved: Boolean,
)

blocks.text:
`saved` records that a save succeeded. Nothing in this type records whether the confirmation has already been shown, and the flag can remain true.

The effect starts when the `saved == true` branch enters the Composition. If the branch later leaves and re-enters with the flag still true, a new effect starts and shows the snackbar again. Screen recreation or returning to a removed screen can therefore produce another confirmation of the same save.

An unchanged key prevents a restart during recomposition of the same effect. It does not prevent a new effect from starting after the old one left the Composition.

In this example, `saved` answers “has a successful save been recorded?” The snackbar requirement also needs to establish whether that save should still be announced. Changing the effect keys cannot supply the missing handling information.

headers: What the screen should do with it
rows: A save is currently in flight
The same disabled button is described again — nothing changes for the user
Render it
A validation message is currently set
The same message is described again — nothing changes for the user
Render it
A save succeeded at some point
The snackbar runs again — the user sees a second confirmation of one save
Establish what the occurrence actually requires before rendering or executing it

blocks.text:
If the requirement is simply “confirm the user’s Save tap,” a callback can launch the snackbar through a remembered scope without adding a flag. **Composition-Driven or Event-Driven?** works through that case.

That does not replace every state-driven confirmation. A fact that must remain available after the screen is absent still needs an owner and a representation. Decide what the value means before removing it or moving its trigger.

Once a requirement really is an occurrence, the trigger still decides which mechanism runs it. A tap that should scroll, move focus or confirm is event-owned, and a remembered scope launches it from the callback. A composition state that genuinely means "this screen now represents something that should be announced" is composition-owned, and an effect keyed on whatever identifies that occurrence runs it. Neither is a default.

Choosing an API solely because the action is transient. A tap-owned action can start from its callback; a composition-owned action can use an effect. First establish what the action represents and when it should run.

A request to show the result screen also needs a trigger and a rule for repetition. If performing the request twice adds the same destination twice, the duplicate is visible to the user. This decision applies regardless of how routes and the back stack are implemented.

Some facts must remain available because the screen may miss the moment they become true. A completed payment is one example: if reopening the app must show it, retain the payment result and render that state.

State-driven actions can also be legitimate. The editor example fails because `saved` retains a fact without establishing whether another confirmation is needed. It does not show that one-off actions can never be represented in state.

Before treating an occurrence as transient UI work, decide what must happen if no UI is available to handle it. An effect can act only while its Composition lifetime exists; receiving or retaining the occurrence depends on the surrounding design. **What Delivery Guarantee Does This Occurrence Need?** examines those requirements.

Whether such an occurrence is carried in the screen's state, recorded somewhere as handled, or delivered in some other way is an application-architecture decision with real trade-offs. The Compose-side diagnosis is narrower and can be stated exactly: an execution mechanism was given a value whose contract does not say "once", and no effect key repairs that.

Distinguish a condition that can be rendered repeatedly from an action whose repetition may be a defect. Use the saved flag to explain the failure: re-entering the Composition creates another effect lifetime, so the snackbar runs again. Then establish what should happen if the UI is absent when the save completes.

lessons.title: What Delivery Guarantee Does This Occurrence Need?
lessons.summary: Decide what must happen if no UI can receive a one-off occurrence. May it be dropped, should a later screen see it, is duplication acceptable, and must handling be recorded? Those requirements determine whether a transient UI mechanism is sufficient or another owner is needed.

blocks.text: The screen that should handle an occurrence may be absent when it is produced. Decide what must happen during that gap before choosing a SharedFlow, channel, state holder or Compose effect. Each offers different retention and delivery behaviour; none determines the product’s handling requirement for you.

A user starts a practice session and navigates away, removing its screen from the Composition. Work below the UI later finishes—a sync completes, a purchase is confirmed or a session is scored—and produces “show the result.” The screen may return afterwards.

Backgrounding can create a similar gap if lifecycle-aware collection stops, even when the screen remains in the Composition. In either case, no relevant UI collector is available at the moment of production.
Decide what the requirement allows in that situation:

items: Must the occurrence still happen when a screen finally appears, or was it only meaningful while somebody was watching?
May it simply be discarded because nobody was there?
May a screen that arrives later observe it?
May more than one observer act on it?
Is repeating it harmful, or merely untidy?
Does anything have to record that it was handled?

blocks.text: These questions describe the required behaviour, rather than a stream type. Replay can retain an occurrence for a later subscriber, but it can also expose that occurrence to a subscriber whose earlier instance already handled it. Retention and acceptable repetition must therefore be considered together.

Decide whether an absent UI may miss the occurrence, whether a later UI should receive it, whether it may run twice, and whether handling must be recorded. Choose a design that satisfies all of those requirements.
A producer completing an emission and the intended UI handling the occurrence are separate events. A SharedFlow’s emission result does not acknowledge the UI’s work.

blocks.code:
// Accepted by the flow under its current configuration — and nothing more than that.
val accepted = events.tryEmit(ShowSessionResult(sessionId))

blocks.text:
`tryEmit` returns `false` when emission would need to suspend for buffer space. That can happen only with `BufferOverflow.SUSPEND` and subscribers. A `true` result means the non-suspending call completed under the flow’s configuration; it can include dropping a value under an overflow policy. It does not establish that a collector received or handled the occurrence.

With no subscribers, only the replay cache retains values. On `MutableSharedFlow()`, `replay` is zero, so `tryEmit` returns `true` and the value is dropped. A later collector cannot recover it. A log written after the successful call therefore says nothing about whether a screen showed the result.

Replay retains a limited number of values for later subscribers. A recreated screen can therefore receive an occurrence produced while it was absent. It can also receive an occurrence that its previous instance already handled, if that value remains in the replay cache.

Replay provides retention within the flow’s lifetime and cache capacity. It does not record handling or guarantee exactly-once execution. Preventing loss and preventing duplicates are separate requirements.

Adding replay to fix a missed confirmation without deciding how repeated handling should work. A recreated screen may show the retained confirmation again. Whether that is acceptable depends on the action: a repeated navigation request can be more disruptive than a repeated toast.
The answers lead to three broad kinds of requirement:

headers: What the requirement says about the UI being absent
rows: If no relevant UI exists, nothing needs to happen
An ephemeral, UI-only occurrence
The Compose side is sufficient: whichever screen is present executes it
A screen arriving later must be able to see that this is currently true
A fact about current state, not an occurrence at all
A current value that somebody owns and a late collector reads at once — current-value semantics, as `StateFlow` provides
It must not disappear merely because nobody was watching, and somebody must have handled it
A retained occurrence whose handling must be tracked
An owner and handling record that outlive the absent UI; persistent storage if handling must survive process loss

blocks.text: A brief score animation, non-essential confirmation or focus request can be meaningful only while the relevant UI is present. If the requirement permits dropping it during absence, a remembered scope or keyed effect can run it without retaining it for a later screen.

“There is an unfinished practice session” and “the last submission failed” describe current facts, even though each became true at a particular moment. If a later screen must show the current situation, expose that state rather than relying only on an occurrence emitted earlier.

`StateFlow` holds a current value for new collectors. Its updates are conflated, so a slow collector can skip intermediate values. The state holder’s lifetime still determines how long the fact remains available. **Choosing a Stream Abstraction by Delivery Guarantees** compares this contract with other stream contracts.

If an occurrence must remain available until it is handled, an owner outside the absent UI needs to retain it and track the required handling. Queueing, acknowledgement and retrying can be arranged in memory for as long as that owner lives. If the requirement includes process death or a later app restart, the representation must also be durable.

A stream or Compose effect alone does not provide that end-to-end guarantee. Android’s UI-event guidance notes the delivery and processing gap when a producer outlives its consumer. Choose the owner and record according to the specific lifetime the requirement needs.

Current-value semantics make `StateFlow` useful for state. That does not make another stream type a complete solution for every event. A SharedFlow broadcasts according to its replay and buffering configuration; a channel distributes an element to one receiver. Neither contract by itself establishes that the receiver completed the required action.

Compare both delivery and handling. Does the UI need a current value? Will an observer be present when a value is produced? What is retained for a later observer? Is delivery broadcast or single-receiver? Then decide whether loss or duplication is acceptable and whether successful handling must be recorded.

The UI’s lifetime matters as much as the stream’s delivery contract. A flow may deliver according to its configuration while the relevant screen is not collecting, or the screen may leave before it finishes handling a value.

A successful emission is not acknowledgement that the UI handled it. Replay caches and buffered channel elements remain in memory; their retained values are lost when their holders disappear, including on process death.

Surviving only the UI’s absence can require a longer-lived in-memory owner and a handling record. Surviving process death or an app restart requires a durable representation. State which of those guarantees is needed before choosing the owner.

State the requirement before naming a type: what happens with no UI collector, whether a later screen should see the occurrence, whether duplication is acceptable, and whether handling must be recorded. Distinguish successful emission from handling, retention from exactly-once execution, and a longer-lived owner from durable storage.

units.title: Coroutine Fundamentals and Structured Concurrency
units.summary: Asynchronous work needs a clear lifetime: who starts it, who can cancel it, and how a caller knows it has finished. Suspension explains how a coroutine can wait without holding a thread. Builders start coroutines and return handles to their work; `Job` represents lifetime and parent-child relationships; `CoroutineScope` provides the context in which work is started. Structured concurrency connects these pieces so callers can rely on completion and cancellation boundaries.

lessons.title: Suspension Is Not Blocking
lessons.summary: A `suspend` function may pause without blocking its thread, but the keyword does not choose where the function runs. Its implementation determines whether it suspends, blocks, or performs CPU work. To decide whether a call is safe on the main thread, use its documented contract or inspect the implementation when that contract is unclear.

blocks.text: Programs often wait for a network response, a file, a timer, or user input. A coroutine can handle that wait by blocking its thread or by suspending and allowing the thread to run other work. The difference matters whenever several operations share a limited number of threads.

A **thread** is a unit of execution scheduled by the operating system. On the JVM, an ordinary platform thread has its own call stack and consumes memory and operating-system resources. Stack sizes and the number of threads a process can support depend on its configuration and environment, so creating a thread for every waiting operation can become expensive.

A **blocking** call keeps its thread occupied until the call returns. While the thread waits, it cannot run another coroutine. With **suspension**, the coroutine pauses without keeping that thread occupied. Another coroutine can use the thread while the first waits for data or a timer.

`suspend` marks a function as allowed to suspend. It may call other suspending functions, and it must itself be called from a suspending context, such as another suspending function or a coroutine builder’s block. A call to a suspending function does not necessarily suspend.

`suspend` does not select a thread or thread pool, move work into the background, or make a slow operation faster. A function can be marked `suspend` and still spend a second blocking its current thread without reaching a suspension point.

Both functions compile with `suspend`, but they wait differently. `delay(1_000)` suspends the coroutine without blocking its thread. `Thread.sleep(1_000)` blocks the thread for the wait. The signatures alone do not reveal that difference.

`Thread.sleep` is a JVM API, so this pair is a JVM and Android example. The underlying distinction applies more broadly: marking a function `suspend` does not change the behaviour of a blocking call inside it.

A suspended coroutine retains a **continuation**: the point to resume from and the local state needed to continue there. It does not need to keep a thread parked with a dedicated call stack while it waits. The retained state still uses memory, and its size depends on what the coroutine holds, but this usually permits many more waiting coroutines than dedicated platform threads.

`suspend` describes how a function is allowed to pause. It does not describe where the function runs, and it cannot change what the code inside it does. A suspending function full of blocking calls blocks exactly as much as the same code would without the keyword.
Reading asynchronous code well means keeping three questions apart, because they have three different answers and only the first one is visible in a signature.

items: **Is this function allowed to suspend?** The `suspend` modifier answers this, and only this.

**Does this call block?** Check the API’s contract or implementation. A blocking operation still occupies a thread inside a suspending function; awaiting an asynchronous operation can let the coroutine suspend instead.
**Where does this run?** The coroutine’s dispatcher and any context changes inside the function determine where its code executes. The `suspend` modifier does not.

blocks.text: The **dispatcher** controls how coroutine execution is assigned to threads. A coroutine normally inherits its dispatcher from its scope, although code can supply another dispatcher or change context for a block. The `suspend` keyword does not select one. Dispatcher choices are covered in **Dispatchers and Where Code Actually Runs**.
That leaves the question you actually have to answer in front of real code: is this call safe from the main thread? Two functions with the same signature can have opposite answers.

Android recommends that suspending functions be **main-safe**: safe for callers to invoke from the main thread. A function that performs long-running blocking work should move that work off the main thread itself, rather than require every caller to know which dispatcher it needs.

This is an API design responsibility, not something the `suspend` modifier enforces. `readSettings` above still performs its blocking file read on the caller’s thread. A documented main-safety contract can guide callers; when a function’s behaviour is unclear, inspect its implementation and the APIs it calls. For `fetchArticles`, the example assumes that the HTTP client handles the request without blocking the main thread and that any remaining processing is suitable for that thread.

The curriculum reports a JVM measurement on a dispatcher backed by a single thread: two coroutines each running `Thread.sleep(300)` took **607 ms** in total, while two coroutines each running `delay(300)` took **310 ms**. The sleeping calls could not overlap because the first occupied the only thread. The delays could overlap because each coroutine suspended while waiting. These timings illustrate the difference rather than guarantee exact durations. Blocking Android’s main thread similarly prevents it from handling UI work during the wait.

Adding `suspend` does not move a function off the main thread. If its body performs blocking work there, it still blocks there. Before calling an unfamiliar function from the main thread, check whether its contract guarantees main-safety. If that is unclear, inspect whether it uses a non-blocking API or moves expensive work to an appropriate dispatcher.

Suspension makes large numbers of waiting operations practical because each coroutine retains its continuation instead of occupying a dedicated platform thread. Kotlin’s comparison uses 50,000 tasks that each wait five seconds and gives approximate memory figures of 500 MB for coroutines and up to 100 GB for JVM threads. Those figures depend on the environment and what each task retains; the thread version may run out of resources before all tasks start. The useful comparison is the cost of retaining many waiting coroutines versus many dedicated thread stacks.

Keeping the word "blocking" precise matters here, because two different things get called by that name. A **blocking call** holds a thread that is doing nothing — waiting on a socket, a lock, a sleep. A **CPU-bound loop** holds a thread that is doing work as fast as it can. They share one consequence, that the thread is unavailable and the coroutine reaches no suspension point, and they need different answers, which is why they belong on different dispatchers.

The shared consequence can be measured the same way: on a single-thread dispatcher, a coroutine running a 250 ms busy loop finished entirely before a second coroutine launched onto the same dispatcher started at all. Nothing had gone wrong and nothing was misconfigured; there was simply no moment at which the first coroutine offered the thread back.

That points at a second consequence. Cancellation in Kotlin is **cooperative**: a coroutine finds out it has been cancelled where it suspends at a cancellable point, or where its own code deliberately looks. A coroutine that does neither runs to the end regardless of what anybody else has asked for — the request is recorded and simply never observed. Where those checks belong, what they cost, and what a cancelled coroutine may still do are covered in **Cancellation Is Cooperative**.

When asked what `suspend` does, explain that it permits a function to pause at suspension points without holding a thread. It can be called from a suspending context, including a coroutine builder’s block. The keyword selects no thread or dispatcher, and it does not make blocking operations main-safe. To explain why suspension is useful, describe the continuation a waiting coroutine retains instead of a dedicated thread stack.

sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

lessons.title: Starting Coroutines: `launch`, `async` and `runBlocking`
lessons.summary: Coroutine builders start a coroutine and determine what its caller receives. `launch` returns a `Job` for work without a result to hand back. `async` returns a `Deferred` whose result can be awaited. `runBlocking` blocks the calling thread until its block and children finish, providing a bridge from ordinary blocking code to suspending code.

blocks.text: A suspending function needs a suspending context in which to run. **Coroutine builders** provide an entry point by accepting a suspending block and running it as a coroutine. Inside that block, suspending functions can call one another.
`launch`, `async`, and `runBlocking` all run their block as a coroutine. Their main differences are what they return and whether the caller waits for the work before continuing.

rows: `launch`
the work has to happen and there is no result to return
`Job`
after the builder returns; it does not wait for coroutine completion
`async`
the work produces a value somebody is going to consume
`Deferred<T>`
after the builder returns; `await()` waits for the result, suspending if needed
`runBlocking`
non-coroutine code has to call suspending code and there is no scope to launch into
whatever the block returns
only once the coroutine and everything launched in it has finished

blocks.text: `launch` starts a coroutine and returns a `Job`, a handle to its lifetime. Use it when the work has no result to hand back. The caller does not wait for completion, although the coroutine may begin executing before the builder returns, depending on its dispatcher and start mode.

`async` starts a computation and returns a `Deferred`, which represents its eventual result. Calling `await()` retrieves that result, suspending the caller if it is not ready yet. Use `async` when code needs a handle to a computation whose result it will consume.

`runBlocking` blocks the current thread until its block and all its children finish. It bridges ordinary blocking code to suspending APIs, for example in a `main` function, a test, or a callback that must wait synchronously for a result. That makes it appropriate only where occupying the calling thread is acceptable; application code with a coroutine scope can usually launch work instead.

`launch` and `async` are extension functions on `CoroutineScope`, so their scope supplies the context used to start the coroutine. `runBlocking` creates its own scope and waits for it to finish.

The `{ }` after each call is an ordinary Kotlin trailing lambda. Because the last parameter is a function, the block can go outside the parentheses. `launch(dispatcher) { }` passes a dispatcher as well as that block.

Use `launch` for work with no result to return, and `async` for a computation whose result will be consumed through its `Deferred`. Use `runBlocking` when ordinary blocking code must wait for suspending work and blocking that thread is acceptable.
If code starts an `async` computation but discards its `Deferred`, there is no result handle left for that code to await. Compare these two ways of saving a draft.

Both versions run `save`. If the caller does not need a result, `launch` expresses that choice more clearly. `async` creates a `Deferred` that invites the reader to look for where its outcome is consumed; discarding it leaves that question unanswered. The distinction here is the intended use of the result, not a claim that one builder is faster.

A `Deferred` stores failure as well as success, so discarding it can leave the outcome unread. This does not mean failure is isolated: an `async` child of an ordinary, non-supervising parent still cancels that parent if it fails with a non-cancellation exception, even if nobody calls `await()`. See **How a Coroutine Failure Travels** for the propagation rules.

Calling `runBlocking` on Android’s main thread prevents that thread from handling frames, touch events, and lifecycle callbacks until the call finishes. A sufficiently long block can lead to an ANR. Suspension inside the block does not release the calling thread: the curriculum reports that `runBlocking { delay(300) }` returned after **306 ms** in a JVM measurement. The exact timing varies, but the caller still waits through the delay.

Inside a suspending function, call other suspending functions directly rather than wrap them in `runBlocking`. The wrapper adds a blocked thread where the caller could have suspended, and can contribute to thread starvation. At an application callback, use an appropriate coroutine scope when the callback does not need to wait synchronously for the result.

A `Job` lets code observe and control lifetime: whether work is active, whether it has completed, and when cancellation should be requested. A `Deferred` adds a result that code can retrieve with `await()`. When reviewing a builder choice, look for whether the caller needs that result. If nothing consumes it, `launch` usually expresses the operation more clearly.

`withContext` also returns a result, but it does so as part of the suspending call. It runs a block in a modified context and does not return until that block and its children finish. Unlike `launch` and `async`, it does not hand back a handle while the caller moves on to unrelated work.

Changing the dispatcher dispatches execution to the new context and then back to the caller’s context. Keeping the dispatcher unchanged avoids that dispatcher switch. See **`withContext` and Main-Safety** for the details.

`async` can support overlapping computations, but choosing it does not itself guarantee parallel execution. Whether work should overlap is a separate decision, covered in **Sequential by Default, Concurrent on Purpose**.

Both `launch` and `async` accept a `CoroutineStart`. With `CoroutineStart.LAZY`, the coroutine is created without being scheduled immediately. Calling `start()` or `join()` starts a lazy job; calling `await()` starts a lazy `Deferred` too. This changes when the work begins, while the result distinction between `launch` and `async` remains the same.

The blocking in `runBlocking` applies to the caller’s thread. Its coroutine can still suspend and resume, but the call keeps that thread occupied until the block and children finish. This is useful at a boundary where synchronous waiting is required, such as a blocking entry point. It is unsuitable for Android’s main thread, which needs to remain available for UI work.

When comparing `launch` and `async`, explain both the returned handle and how it will be used: `launch` returns a `Job` for lifetime control; `async` returns a `Deferred` whose result can be awaited. A discarded `Deferred` is a reason to ask whether the operation needs `async`. For `runBlocking`, explain that it blocks the calling thread until the work finishes, which can be appropriate at a blocking boundary but freezes main-thread UI work on Android.

sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

lessons.title: `Job`: the Handle That Carries Lifetime
lessons.summary: A `Job` represents a coroutine’s lifetime and its relationship to parents and children. Keep the handle when you need to wait for particular work, request its cancellation, or inspect its state. A parent’s `Job` does not complete until its children have completed, even if the parent’s own body has already finished.

blocks.text: The coroutines started by `launch` and `async` each have a `Job`. `launch` returns it directly; `async` returns a `Deferred`, which is a `Job` that also represents a result. The handle makes the coroutine’s lifetime available to other code.
Holding it lets you do three things, and they are the reasons the builders return it at all.

items: **Wait for it.** `join()` waits for completion, suspending if needed. Completion can be successful, cancelled, or failed; `join()` does not return the job’s result or rethrow its failure. The waiting coroutine can still be cancelled.
**Ask about it.** `isActive`, `isCompleted` and `isCancelled` report which part of the lifecycle the job is currently in.
**Locate it in the tree.** A job exposes its `parent` and its current `children`, making its parent-child relationships available to inspect.

blocks.text:
By default, a new coroutine uses the `Job` in its launching scope’s context as its parent. A nested `launch` using the coroutine’s own scope therefore creates its child. A scope with no `Job` creates a parentless coroutine.

Passing a different `Job` explicitly to a builder replaces the parent and breaks the relationship to the original scope. This is not a supported way to preserve structured concurrency; see **`CoroutineContext` and What Children Inherit**.

Discarding the returned `Job` is normal and usually right. It is returned for the cases that need it, not as something every call has to consume: you keep it when you have to wait for exactly this piece of work, when something else has to be able to stop it, or when you want to report on whether it is still going.
The `Job` is also an element of the coroutine's **context**, alongside things such as the dispatcher — that is how a new coroutine finds the right parent without anybody passing one around by hand.

A `Job` lets code observe a coroutine’s state, wait for completion, request cancellation, and inspect its parent-child relationships. Keeping the returned handle is useful when those operations are needed for this particular piece of work.
In this example, the parent’s block finishes before its child’s delay. Consider whether that means the parent’s `Job` is complete.

The parent's block has run to the end. It is nevertheless not complete, because it has a child that is not finished. Measured on a JVM target at the 100 ms mark: `isActive` was `true`, `isCompleted` was `false`, the job reported exactly one child, and printing the job itself gave `StandaloneCoroutine{Completing}`. After `parent.join()` returned, `isCompleted` was `true`.

A parent enters the **completing** state when its own body finishes but a child is still running. It waits there until all its children complete. Finishing the body and completing the `Job` are therefore separate events; `join()` waits for the latter.

The end of a `launch` block does not necessarily mean its `Job` has completed. If it started children that are still running, the parent waits for them. Use the parent’s `Job` to wait for that completion rather than assume the end of its body is the end of all the work.

`Deferred<T>` has the same lifecycle as a `Job`, with a result attached. It can have a parent and children, and code can wait for it with `join()`.

`await()` also retrieves the computation’s result, suspending if necessary while it waits. If the computation failed, it throws that failure; cancellation can also interrupt the wait. Joining a `Deferred` establishes that it has completed, but does not retrieve its outcome. See **How a Coroutine Failure Travels** for propagation beyond the awaiter.

Cancellation travels along these same parent-child edges, and the `Job` is the handle through which it is requested. Cancellation is cooperative: a request the cancelled code has to observe, not a forced stop (see **Cancellation Is Cooperative**).

The state table distinguishes a coroutine’s body running from its job waiting for children or completing cancellation. `New` is an optional initial state, used for lazy start; `Active` is the usual initial state.

rows: New (optional initial state)
false
false
false
Active (default initial state)
true
false
false
Completing (transient)
true
false
false
Cancelling (transient)
false
false
true
Cancelled (final)
false
true
true
Completed (final)
false
true

blocks.text:
**Completing and Active have the same public state flags.** A job waiting for its children still reports `isActive == true` and `isCompleted == false`; those flags do not reveal whether the body has ended.

**Both final states report `isCompleted == true`.** Completion therefore does not establish success: `isCancelled` distinguishes successful completion from cancellation or failure, although it does not by itself distinguish cancellation from failure.
`isActive` is read here strictly as a question about state. The same property also serves as a cancellation check — deciding whether a loop should keep going — and that use has rules of its own.

Use `join()` when subsequent code needs the job to have completed. Reading a state property only samples the state at that moment: for example, a job that is active during the check may complete before the next line runs. Once `join()` returns normally, that job is complete and cannot become active again.

Taken together, this is what makes the `Job` more than a receipt. The builder call tells you work started; the job tells you where that work sits in a hierarchy, whether the hierarchy is finished, and — because a parent waits — lets a single handle stand for an entire sub-tree of work you never named.

To explain why code would keep the `Job` returned by `launch`, describe waiting with `join()`, inspecting state, and requesting cancellation. Then explain the structural role: a parent’s `Job` completes only after its children have completed. The completing state provides a concrete example: the parent’s body has ended, a child is still running, and the parent’s job is not yet complete.

lessons.title: `CoroutineScope` and Who Owns a Coroutine's Lifetime
lessons.summary: A `CoroutineScope` supplies the context for coroutines started in it. When that context contains a `Job`, the job gives them a shared parent and cancellation boundary. Identify who owns the scope and what ends its lifetime. Without that boundary, work can continue after it is useful and retain the objects it captured.

blocks.text: A `CoroutineScope` provides the context in which coroutines are started. With a `Job` in that context, it lets an owner manage several coroutines together: cancelling the shared parent requests cancellation of all its children. The scope’s lifetime should match the lifetime of the work it owns.

The `CoroutineScope` interface has one property, `coroutineContext`; `launch` and `async` are extension functions. A scope therefore **holds** a context rather than being a context. For lifetime management, the relevant element is its `Job`. A coroutine launched with the scope’s default context uses that job as its parent while the parent-child relationship remains attached.

The identity check below illustrates that relationship, but its empty coroutine may finish before the check runs. A completed job can report `parent == null`, so this particular check is not guaranteed to succeed. Inspecting the relationship requires keeping the child unfinished until it has been checked.

For coroutines attached to the scope’s `Job`, two relationships follow. Cancelling the job requests cancellation of its descendants, and the job cannot complete until those descendants have completed. Cancellation is cooperative, so requesting it does not mean all work has already stopped.

The **owner** decides when that shared lifetime should end. A class that creates a scope typically cancels it during teardown. A lexical scope such as `coroutineScope` waits for its block and children before returning. If neither cancellation nor a completion boundary is defined, the scope does not provide a useful limit on work’s lifetime.
When reviewing asynchronous code, identify the scope’s owner and the event that ends the work’s lifetime.

**Who owns this coroutine, and what event ends its lifetime?** A screen, view model, session, or download can provide that boundary. If the work has no defined cancellation or completion boundary, check whether it could continue after its purpose has ended.
`SearchController` creates a scope for its searches, but has no teardown method that cancels it. Closing the screen therefore does not end work started through this scope.

`SupervisorJob()` prevents one child’s failure from cancelling that parent or its other children. It does not decide who ends the scope’s lifetime. The missing cancellation boundary remains with or without supervision; its failure rules are covered in **`SupervisorJob`, `supervisorScope` and the Limits of Isolation**.
Nothing cancels this scope when the controller is no longer needed. Its searches can therefore continue beyond that point. That can have several consequences:

items: Work can continue after the screen that requested it has closed, consuming network, parsing, or database resources for a result no longer needed.
A result can arrive after its target has been torn down. Separate overlapping searches can also deliver an older result after a newer one unless their ordering is controlled.
A running or suspended coroutine can retain captured objects, such as the controller, repository, or objects reachable through them, for as long as its continuation needs them.
Without a clear owner, diagnosing which screen or request a failure belongs to can be harder. How the failure is reported still depends on its builder, parent, and exception handling.
No caller can find out whether the work has finished, because nothing was returned and there is nothing to join.

blocks.text: The curriculum reports a JVM comparison in which a suspending function launched work into a separate scope. It returned after **5 ms**, while that work took **300 ms** and continued after the caller moved on. A structured version returned after **306 ms**. These reported timings illustrate different completion contracts: the first call starts work, while the second waits for it to finish.

A class can legitimately create a `CoroutineScope` for its own lifecycle. It must also define how that lifecycle ends. In this example, add a teardown method that cancels the scope and ensure the controller’s owner calls it when the controller is no longer needed.

Android supplies scopes with lifecycle boundaries already defined. Coroutines launched in `viewModelScope` are automatically cancelled when the `ViewModel` is cleared. This gives work a shared owner without requiring each operation to arrange its own teardown. It illustrates lifecycle ownership; deciding which responsibilities belong in a view model is a separate design question.

Some work should outlive the screen that started it, such as a bookmark write or an upload that should continue after navigation. Give that work an explicitly longer-lived owner. Injecting its scope records that lifetime choice as a dependency and allows tests to replace it.

A scope cannot preserve running work after the process is killed. If work must be scheduled durably across process death, use an appropriate scheduler such as WorkManager; the coroutine scope alone cannot provide that persistence.

Creating a `CoroutineScope` is appropriate when a class needs to own asynchronous work. Define its lifetime, cancel it at teardown, and make sure teardown is called. Framework scopes also need a known lifecycle boundary. The question is how the scope’s work ends, rather than whether the scope was created manually.

Choose an owner whose lifetime is long enough for the work and ends when that work is no longer needed. Screen-specific work often belongs to a screen or view model; a shared cache may need a longer-lived owner. Application-wide work needs an explicit reason to remain active across screens.

`GlobalScope` has no parent `Job`, so it provides no shared handle for cancelling or waiting for all the coroutines launched through it. Work started there can continue across screen lifetimes, which is a poor fit for a request needed only while one screen exists. Long-lived work can be valid, but its lifetime should be a deliberate choice.

For genuinely application-wide work, an injected scope with a documented lifetime is easier to control and replace in tests than a hard-coded `GlobalScope`. The returned `Job` of an individual `GlobalScope.launch` can still be cancelled or joined, but `GlobalScope` itself has no parent job that groups that work. An owned scope provides that shared control.

Ownership and exception propagation answer different questions. Ownership identifies which screen, request, or object the work serves and when it should end. The builder, parent job, and exception-handling arrangement determine how failures travel and how they are reported. A missing owner can make diagnosis harder, but does not by itself establish that every failure will become a crash or log message.

When screen-specific coroutines share an owned parent job, one cancellation request reaches them all. That gives the screen a reliable place to request shutdown; waiting for the parent job to complete establishes that its children have finished too.

For a code-review question about scope ownership, identify the scope, who owns it, and what cancels or completes its job. If no boundary is defined, describe the concrete risks: unnecessary work after navigation, results arriving after teardown, retained objects, and difficulty waiting for completion or diagnosing failure. Work that must outlive the screen needs a longer-lived owner; work that must persist across process death needs a durable scheduling mechanism.

sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android
Use Kotlin coroutines with lifecycle-aware components

lessons.title: Structured Concurrency and What It Guarantees
lessons.summary: Structured concurrency links parent and child jobs so a parent waits for its children and cancellation reaches its descendants. Failure follows defined propagation rules, with supervision changing the parent’s response to a child failure. These lifetime relationships do not decide execution order, parallelism, or how an application recovers from errors.

blocks.text: **Structured concurrency** connects coroutine lifetimes through parent and child jobs. Builders started in a scope normally attach work to its `Job`. That parent waits for its children to complete and can request their cancellation together, giving the owner a completion boundary for the group.

In a structured hierarchy, the parent’s own body can finish before its children, but the parent job does not complete until they do. Cancelling the parent, including cancellation caused by its failure, requests cancellation of its descendants too.

items: **A coroutine normally becomes a child of the launching scope’s job.** This requires a `Job` in the scope’s context and no replacement parent passed to the builder.

**A parent does not complete until its children do**, even when the parent's own body finished long beforehand — a `Job` in its *completing* state, with its body finished and its children still running, is this guarantee made observable.
**Cancellation travels down.** Cancelling a parent cancels its children recursively, so the request reaches every descendant rather than only the coroutine you named.
**Child failure follows defined rules.** With an ordinary parent job, a non-cancellation failure cancels the parent. A supervising parent isolates that child failure instead.

blocks.text:
A scope without a `Job` starts **root** coroutines with no parent. Each root can still have its own children, wait for them, and cancel them. What is missing is a shared parent above those roots to manage them as a group.

`GlobalScope` is an example: it has no `Job`, so it cannot collectively cancel or await the coroutines launched through it. Individual returned jobs remain available for cancellation and joining.

Passing another `Job` to a builder also changes the parent, severing the normal link to the launching scope. This breaks that scope’s structured lifetime and is not a supported pattern. See **`CoroutineContext` and What Children Inherit** for the details.

`coroutineScope` gives a suspending function a structured boundary for its internal work. It creates a job attached to the caller’s job, and children launched through the block’s scope attach to that new job. The call returns only after its block and those children have completed.

This new scope is the root of its own subtree, but it is not parentless: it remains attached to the caller. That connection carries cancellation into the function’s internal work.

When a structured suspending function returns, its block and the child work attached to its scope have completed. Cancelling its parent requests cancellation of that work; completion is the point at which all of it has finished.
The clearest way to see what the model gives you is to look at a function that quietly opts out of it.

`loadSomething` starts work in `someUnownedScope` without waiting for its completion. After the builder returns, the function returns too. The caller’s relationship to that work differs from an ordinary structured suspending call:

items: The return does not establish that the work has completed. The curriculum reports a JVM measurement in which this version returned in 5 ms for work lasting 300 ms; the actual ordering and timing depend on execution.
A failure in the launched coroutine is handled through its own parent and exception-handling arrangement, rather than rethrown from `loadSomething` to the caller’s `try`/`catch`.
Not the ability to stop it. Cancelling the caller cancels the caller's children, and this coroutine is not one of them.
The signature does not say that work may continue after the call returns or identify the scope that owns its lifetime.

blocks.text: The structured form differs by one line and changes every one of those answers.

The launched coroutine is now attached to the scope created by `coroutineScope`, so the function waits for it. A non-cancellation failure fails that scope and is rethrown to the caller; cancelling the caller requests cancellation of this child too.

The curriculum reports that this version returned after **306 ms** for the same 300 ms of work. The additional wait reflects the changed completion contract: the caller resumes after the work finishes, rather than merely after it has been started.

`coroutineScope` is also what lets a suspending function do several things at once without saying so in its signature. A function that launches three children inside its own scope is concurrent on the inside and an ordinary suspending call on the outside, because the scope re-imposes a single completion point at the boundary. Whether the work *should* overlap, and what overlapping actually buys, is a separate decision (see **Sequential by Default, Concurrent on Purpose**).

A function that starts detached work has a different contract from one that waits for its internal work. Make that difference explicit in its name, documentation, and API. Returning a `Job` can give the caller a handle for cancellation and completion, while a plain `suspend` signature alone does not reveal that work continues in another scope.
Keep the lifetime guarantees separate from scheduling and recovery decisions. The table compares what parent-child structure establishes with what still depends on dispatchers or application policy.

rows: Work attached to a scope’s job remains part of that parent’s lifetime
That anything runs in the background. Where code executes is the dispatcher's business, and a child inherits one rather than being given a new one
A parent completes only after its children have completed
That children run one at a time. Children launched together run concurrently and may finish in any order
Cancelling a parent cancels its children, recursively
That anything runs in parallel. Concurrency is about overlapping lifetimes; parallelism additionally depends on the dispatcher and the hardware
Failure follows defined parent and supervision rules
That a failure is handled, retried or recovered. The structure decides where it goes, never what to do about it

blocks.text: Children started in one scope can have overlapping lifetimes, run on different threads, and finish in different orders. The parent-child relationship does not decide those scheduling details. It establishes that the parent job waits for its attached children before completing. Wrapping `launch` calls in `coroutineScope` therefore changes the enclosing call’s completion boundary; it does not by itself guarantee a performance improvement.

A **supervising** parent does not let a child’s failure cancel it or its other children. That changes upward failure propagation while preserving the parent’s waiting and downward cancellation relationships.

`withContext` also waits for its block and children, but runs the block with a modified context, typically a different dispatcher. The examples here use dispatcher changes, not replacement jobs.

In structured code, a function’s completion boundary includes the child work attached to its internal scope. Once that call returns, those children have completed. Cancelling the scope’s job sends a request through its descendants; waiting for the job to complete establishes that they have finished. This lets callers coordinate through defined lifetime boundaries rather than search for every operation separately.

To explain structured concurrency, describe parent and child jobs with linked lifetimes. A parent waits for its children, cancellation reaches its descendants, and failures follow defined propagation and supervision rules. Then distinguish lifetime from scheduling: the structure does not guarantee parallel execution, child ordering, or error recovery. In a detached-work example, identify which parent link is missing and what that changes for the caller.

units.title: Coroutine Context, Dispatchers and Concurrent Work
units.summary: A coroutine's context determines its execution policy and Job parentage. Dispatchers serve different workloads: CPU computation, blocking calls and UI access. The implementation that knows the work should usually choose its dispatcher. Independent operations can also overlap, but concurrency and dispatcher choice are separate decisions within a structured lifetime.

lessons.title: `CoroutineContext` and What Children Inherit
lessons.summary: A child coroutine combines its scope's context with any supplied elements; matching keys are replaced. It then receives its own Job, with the Job selected from that combined context as its parent. Passing an explicit Job can therefore change its parentage.

blocks.text: A coroutine needs an execution policy and a connection to a lifetime. `CoroutineContext` carries both: a dispatcher controls execution, and a Job connects the work to its parent and children. A scope holds a context, but neither the scope nor the context is itself a running coroutine.

Think of the context as a small collection of named slots, formally called an indexed set. Each slot has a key, and at most one element occupies that key. A Job occupies the Job key; a dispatcher occupies the ContinuationInterceptor key; CoroutineName supplies a diagnostic label. CoroutineExceptionHandler is another context element; **How a Coroutine Failure Travels** explains when it is consulted.

Context composition uses `+`. Elements with different keys coexist. When both contexts contain an element with the same key, the element on the right replaces the one on the left. This produces a new context without changing the original or starting work. A name and a dispatcher can coexist, while `Main + IO` selects IO because both dispatchers occupy the same key.

blocks.code:
val base = Dispatchers.Default + CoroutineName("refresh")
val renamed = base + CoroutineName("profile")

check(base[CoroutineName]?.name == "refresh")
check(renamed[CoroutineName]?.name == "profile")
check(renamed[ContinuationInterceptor] === Dispatchers.Default)

blocks.text: The name changed, the execution policy did not, and the original value still says refresh. CoroutineName can make diagnostic output easier to connect to a task; it neither allocates a thread nor changes scheduling priority. Similarly, looking up `coroutineContext[Job]` inside a coroutine tells you about that coroutine's Job, not which worker happens to execute it.

A builder combines its receiver scope's context with the supplied context. It then creates a Job for the new coroutine and uses the Job selected from that combined context as its parent, if one is present. The child has its own completion handle; it does not reuse the parent's Job.

Read child creation in two steps: combine the starting context, then attach the new coroutine's own Job to the selected parent Job. Dispatcher inheritance and Job parentage answer different questions.

Suppose an Android UI owner already provides a scope whose context contains a parent Job P, Dispatchers.Main and the name screen. The following fragment requests a different dispatcher for one operation.

IO replaces Main under the dispatcher key. The screen name remains because the argument contains no CoroutineName. A fresh Job C represents refresh, with P as its parent because the argument supplies no replacement Job. Inside the block, ownJob is C, and the returned refresh handle refers to that same coroutine. The scope still holds Main and P; the launch has not changed it.

A sibling started later with `scope.launch { ... }` uses the scope's original dispatcher. An unqualified `launch { ... }` inside refresh instead uses refresh's receiver scope, so it inherits IO and has C as its parent. Writing `scope.launch` inside that block still uses the outer scope. To determine parentage, read the actual receiver and context arguments rather than relying on indentation.

C may finish before P, and cancelling P also cancels C. Choosing IO has changed where refresh runs without detaching it from the parent's lifetime. If processSmallResult becomes substantial CPU work, its execution policy still needs consideration: IO was selected for the blocking file read, not for an expensive transformation.

Reading `scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO)` as replacing the whole scope, or reading an inherited dispatcher as an inherited Job instance. Only the matching dispatcher element is replaced; the new coroutine still has a distinct completion handle.

Older code may pass a fresh SupervisorJob to a builder, as in this diagnostic example. Trace the Job key first; the supervision behavior is a separate issue. This pattern should not be copied into new code.

The supplied SupervisorJob S replaces P under the Job key, so S becomes the selected parent. launch still creates its own Job C: the relationship is S -> C, not P -> S -> C. Because S was constructed without a parent argument, it has no connection back to P.

The dispatcher and name can still be inherited from scope. Sharing that execution policy does not restore the missing parent-child relationship.

An explicit Job argument can re-parent work; the builder does not insert it beneath the scope's existing Job. The launch API describes this as unsupported behavior retained for compatibility, and its Job overload is deprecated. Use this rule to diagnose existing code while preserving the intended parent-child relationship in new code. **`SupervisorJob`, `supervisorScope` and the Limits of Isolation** explains how the position of a supervisor affects failure propagation.

P no longer owns C through the scope's original parent-child relationship; C's parent is S. A builder whose effective starting context contains no Job can instead create a root coroutine, which may have children of its own. Determine the parent from the selected Job rather than assuming it is always the coroutine containing the launch call.

When reviewing unfamiliar code, record the receiver context, the explicit overrides and the resulting child's Job parent. Two coroutines with the same name and dispatcher can have different parents; coroutines on different dispatchers can share a parent. These three pieces of information distinguish execution policy from ownership.

items: Find the builder's actual CoroutineScope receiver.
Resolve competing elements by key; the right-hand value wins.
Distinguish the selected parent Job from the newly created coroutine Job.
Treat an explicit Job argument as an ownership warning, not a dispatcher option.
Treat supervision as a property of the selected parent Job, not of any other element.

blocks.text: Which element wins, and whose child is this? Explain the ordinary Main-to-IO launch first, then the fresh-Job counterexample. Neither a thread name nor the position of the braces proves parentage.
