lessons.title: Dispatchers and Where Code Actually Runs
lessons.summary: A dispatcher is an execution policy chosen from the work: CPU computation, a blocking call, or UI access. On Android and the JVM, switching between IO and Default changes the policy but need not change the physical thread, and supplying the dispatcher from outside keeps the choice replaceable in tests.

blocks.text: A coroutine can freeze a screen if it performs a blocking file read on the UI thread. That thread remains occupied until the read returns. A dispatcher controls where coroutine code executes, including when it resumes after suspension. Calling a suspend function does not select IO, and starting a coroutine does not by itself move its body into the background.

Choose a dispatcher by examining the work. CPU computation, a call that holds a thread while waiting, and UI access impose different constraints. A dispatcher can place a blocking call on a thread intended for that workload, but it does not make the call non-blocking or reduce the computation an algorithm requires.

rows: Substantial parsing, image computation, large transformations
Dispatchers.Default
CPU work needs execution capacity; multiplying runnable workers beyond useful CPU capacity is not the goal.
Blocking filesystem, JDBC-style database or legacy network calls
Dispatchers.IO
The call holds a thread while waiting. The blocking-work policy can accommodate more occupied workers.
Android UI access and short UI coordination
Dispatchers.Main with the Android implementation
UI access is confined to the main thread. Keep that thread available for input and rendering.

blocks.text: Default is the general choice for CPU-intensive work. On the JVM its documented default thread maximum follows the CPU core count, with a minimum of two. A standard launch or async supplies Default when its combined context has no dispatcher or other ContinuationInterceptor. That fallback does not override a dispatcher already inherited from a scope. A child of a Main scope therefore does not silently receive Default.
On Android, Main serves UI-thread work. Short UI operations belong there, but a long uninterrupted computation delays rendering and input. Sufficiently prolonged unresponsiveness can lead to an ANR.
A dispatcher expresses an execution policy. Choose it from what the implementation does, not from the presence of `suspend` or from the broad label 'networking'.

Consider an Android/JVM import operation with two phases: an old filesystem API reads bytes synchronously, and an algorithm builds a substantial index from them. withContext runs each scoped phase under the requested policy and waits for it; where such a call belongs is covered in **`withContext` and Main-Safety**.

Running both phases on Default can occupy computation workers with blocking disk reads, delaying unrelated CPU work when enough imports run together. Running both on IO treats the expensive index computation as blocking work. Separate context blocks reflect the two substantial workloads; small operations do not each need a dispatcher switch.

The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0 JVM documentation explains that IO and Default share threads and resources. Switching between them does not guarantee a different physical thread; entering IO from Default typically keeps the current thread on a best-effort basis even though the execution policy changes.

JVM IO's default parallelism is the larger of 64 and the number of cores, configurable with `kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism`. This limits threads executing IO work in parallel, rather than defining a separate pool of exactly that size. Workers are created and shut down on demand, and additional workers can exist during startup or shutdown.

A log may show the same worker name before and inside the IO block even though the dispatcher changed. Inspect the effective context to identify the selected dispatcher, and use a trace to identify the thread that executed a particular segment. Neither an unchanged nor a changed worker name tells you whether the wrapper was useful.

For a concrete blocking resource, a reused `Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4)` view can restrict simultaneous blocking calls sent through that view. The view limits execution parallelism, not the number of suspended requests in flight; once a coroutine suspends, another may execute. It does not automatically limit calls made through some other dispatcher or another separately created view. Resource-wide admission and shared-state coordination are separate problems.
Explaining IO as 'a separate pool of exactly 64 threads'. That predicts both isolation and a thread-count guarantee the documented JVM behavior does not provide.

IO's JVM views are elastic: their parallelism limits are not constrained by IO's own limit, although they share underlying resources. A collection of generously sized views can therefore permit substantially more simultaneous blocking work than the base IO limit suggests. This is capacity for blocking workloads, not evidence that the application, disk or remote service can profitably handle that much work.

Suppose several screens each create an IO view for the same small connection pool. Each view may have a cautious limit, yet their combined demand can exceed the pool's capacity. Check which consumers share the resource and whether they also share an execution limit. IO accommodates blocking work; available database connections, memory and bandwidth still constrain how much work can progress.

On Android, `Dispatchers.Main` is the main-thread dispatcher supplied by kotlinx-coroutines-android. `Dispatchers.Main.immediate` avoids an extra dispatch when execution is already on the main thread. `Default` and `IO` use the JVM policies described above, including shared threads and elastic IO views.

Injecting a dispatcher keeps the implementation's execution policy replaceable. Production code can supply IO, while a test can supply a TestDispatcher so the work uses the test scheduler. Android's coroutine-testing guidance recommends this approach.

Some APIs, such as viewModelScope, use Main internally. Local JVM unit tests do not have Android's main thread, so these tests replace Main with `Dispatchers.setMain`.

Dispatchers.Unconfined is an advanced execution option rather than a general performance optimization. JVM custom executors and their asCoroutineDispatcher adapters are also available. Ordinary workloads usually fit Main, Default or IO; consider another option when an integration imposes a specific requirement.

items: Default fits substantial CPU computation.
IO fits blocking IO.
The UI dispatcher is for UI access and short coordination.
The effective dispatcher, the thread that ran a segment and the useful parallelism are three separate facts.
On Android, Main is the main-thread dispatcher; supplying IO and Default from outside keeps them replaceable in tests.

blocks.text: Does this call actually block, and is a physical thread switch guaranteed? Answer those separately. Then explain why a dispatcher that tolerates blocking still cannot make unlimited overlapping work a good idea.

lessons.title: `withContext` and Main-Safety
lessons.summary: The function that knows its implementation blocks or computes heavily should choose the execution context for that work, and withContext keeps the choice scoped while the caller still waits for the result. An IO wrapper around an already asynchronous call can add complexity without solving any blocking problem.

blocks.text: A function may need to return the result of a blocking read without occupying the UI thread. withContext lets it run that read under a different execution policy while keeping the ordinary suspending call relationship: the caller waits for the function's result.

withContext combines the current context with additional elements, runs a scoped suspending block, and returns its result after completion. It creates a lexical child scope, like coroutineScope, while allowing a different execution context. The caller waits suspendingly; the next statement does not proceed concurrently with the block. It is therefore not a builder in the launch/async sense of returning a Job or Deferred for independently progressing work.

Changing the dispatcher applies to the block, not to every coroutine in the surrounding scope. Afterwards the caller continues in its original context. Returning to that context is not necessarily returning to the same physical thread when its dispatcher uses a pool. The structured block also waits for its ordinary children; moving its own execution policy does not turn those children into fire-and-forget tasks.

coroutineScope gives a function's internal work a structured completion boundary without a context change. Use withContext when the block needs a modified context. Both preserve structured lifetime in ordinary use. These examples supply dispatchers, not replacement Jobs; passing another Job to withContext is not a supported way to preserve the caller's ownership.

Main-safety means an API can be called from the UI thread without making that thread perform long blocking or CPU-heavy work. A suspend signature does not enforce this: a suspend function can call a blocking API directly and still compile. Android guidance recommends placing the dispatcher decision in the function that knows about the expensive implementation, so callers do not each need to handle it.
withContext changes how a scoped block executes while the caller waits for its result. Main-safety comes from the implementation's execution choices, not from the `suspend` keyword.
Here is a common way to wrap a legacy blocking dependency in a repository. Both the dependency and the blocking dispatcher are supplied from outside, so tests can substitute them.

On Android/JVM, production code can supply IO and an adapter over a blocking file API. The read still occupies a worker until it returns, while the caller can wait without occupying the UI thread. readText returns its String only after the read completes. Its dispatcher choice stays with the repository implementation, and callers have no additional lifetime owner to manage.

Contrast that with a repository that merely adds suspend to `store.readText()` and expects each caller to remember an IO wrapper. One missed wrapper can freeze a screen. If the repository later replaces the store with an asynchronous integration, the wrappers distributed across callers also become obsolete. Keeping the decision with the implementation gives a single place to review the change.

An already main-safe suspending implementation may need no dispatcher wrapper. In the following example, assume the client's documented contract says it enqueues a request, suspends while waiting, and performs no substantial blocking or CPU work on the caller's thread. The method name alone does not establish that contract.

Under that contract, an IO wrapper does not make the server respond sooner or release a thread that the client was already releasing while waiting. It changes the caller-side context, which may matter for surrounding code, but the network call itself does not require the wrapper. A client that instead performs a blocking legacy call needs a different execution policy; check its actual contract or implementation.

Check the work after the call as well. A main-safe network wait followed by a large synchronous decode can still occupy Main. The function that owns that CPU-heavy decode should generally run it on an appropriate computation dispatcher. Waiting for bytes and computing over them have different execution needs; cheap field access and small transformations may need no switch.
Wrapping every suspend call in IO, or assuming no suspend call ever needs an execution decision. Both skip the same necessary step: finding out what the implementation does to the thread.

The cost of a redundant wrapper is conditional. With a different dispatcher, withContext schedules the block and the continuation back to the original dispatcher. With the same dispatcher, it can avoid those dispatches; simply changing a CoroutineName does not request a different execution resource. And JVM IO/Default scheduling can still use the same physical thread. A dispatch and a thread switch are not synonyms.

Suppose a main-safe repository already runs its blocking region on the supplied IO dispatcher, and the caller wraps the whole repository call in the same dispatcher. The inner block may keep the existing dispatcher, so each nested wrapper need not cause a thread switch.

The design concern is that the caller now handles an implementation detail the repository already owns. Keeping that decision in the repository makes it easier to identify which switch is needed.

Start with the contract at each boundary. Identify work before suspension and after resumption, separating blocking calls from computation. Names such as fetch or parse suggest what to inspect but do not establish cost. Trace the dispatcher through those regions, then place any needed switch in the function that knows about the expensive work.

The same distinction appears in **Keeping Work Out of Composition**: moving code into a state holder or repository changes responsibility but does not itself change execution. withContext is one way the responsible suspending function makes that second decision. It is not a way to call a suspend API from an ordinary composable body, and it does not decide which Compose effect or lifecycle owns the call.

Accepting a dispatcher makes the policy explicit and replaceable, including in tests. Whether the implementation is main-safe still depends on where its expensive work runs. A blocking call continues to block a thread; the supplied dispatcher must keep that work away from the UI thread when the function is called from Main.

items: withContext fits a result-producing block that needs a modified context.
coroutineScope fits when only a structured child scope is needed.
The function that knows the expensive work should generally own its execution decision.
A suspending API's contract, not its name, decides whether an IO wrapper is needed.
Dispatch overhead is conditional, and physical thread switching is a separate fact.

blocks.text: Who should own this dispatcher switch? Point to the blocking or substantial CPU work, then to the function that knows it exists. Explain how the caller still waits for a result and why an already asynchronous client may need no wrapper.

sources.title: withContext: structured scope and dispatching behavior
Best practices for coroutines in Android

lessons.title: Sequential by Default, Concurrent on Purpose
lessons.summary: Suspending code is sequential within a coroutine, and overlap exists only when independent work is started before it is awaited. Overlap is concurrency, not necessarily parallel execution, and its latency benefit has to outweigh the extra coordination and resource demand.

blocks.text: An account screen needs a profile and the user's display settings. Both requests use an account ID that is already known, neither needs the other's result, and the screen needs both to build its complete model. The requests are candidates for concurrent loading, provided the client, service and execution environment allow useful overlap.
Start with the direct version, in which loadProfile and loadSettings are main-safe suspending functions.

loadProfile must return before loadSettings is invoked. Suspension inside loadProfile allows other coroutines to run, but this coroutine resumes within that call's sequence rather than starting the next call early. This implementation uses one request at a time and may be sufficient for the screen.

Concurrency means tasks have overlapping lifetimes in which multiple tasks are in progress. Parallelism means work executes at the same instant on different execution resources. Concurrent requests can make progress while a single thread alternates between short pieces of code and the requests wait elsewhere. Parallel CPU execution additionally needs an execution environment with available parallel resources.

async creates a coroutine with a future result. Here it lets loadOverview start one independent operation and then start another before requesting either result. With the default start mode, async schedules work without waiting for await. The dispatcher decides when the body executes, so it may not have begun by the next line.

Suspending code is sequential within a coroutine unless you introduce overlap. Use async when having a result-producing child progress independently serves the problem, not merely because the function returns a value.
Keep the same inputs, result and loading functions, but give the function a structured scope and create both children before waiting for either result.

Both Deferred handles exist before the first await. While loadOverview waits for profile, the settings child can progress; its result may already be available when settings.await() is reached. Await order does not require the requests to finish in that order.

coroutineScope keeps both children within the function's completion boundary. The caller still receives one completed AccountOverview through an ordinary suspending call.

For an illustrative model, suppose profile waits 400 ms and settings waits 250 ms, with negligible computation and enough service capacity. Sequential loading needs about 650 ms; useful overlap can approach 400 ms plus coordination overhead. These are arithmetic predictions under stated assumptions, not measurements or latency guarantees. A client that serializes requests, server throttling or expensive local processing can erase that gain.
In this version, each async is followed immediately by await. Compare when the second child is created with the version above.

The settings child is created only after profile.await() returns. Whether that await suspends or returns immediately, loadProfile has completed before loadSettings starts. The loads are sequential, with extra Deferred handles and child lifetimes but no overlap. Direct sequential calls express the same loading order more clearly.

For a small collection of independent results of the same type, use `map { async { ... } }` to create the Deferreds, then `awaitAll()` to wait for them. Creating the children before waiting makes overlap possible; awaitAll waits for those children rather than starting the work. For an unbounded collection, decide how to limit demand before starting one child per item.

No example selects another dispatcher. Children inherit the effective dispatcher and rely on the load functions' main-safety contracts. Two asynchronous waits can overlap on one thread. Two blocking calls on that same thread cannot make it run a second block while the first occupies it. And two substantial CPU loops need actual parallel execution resources to run simultaneously. async does not replace the dispatcher and main-safety decisions.
Awaiting each async immediately and inferring concurrency from the builder name. Trace when the second task is created; that is the point at which overlap becomes possible.

Operations are independent only if both their inputs and the decision to run them are available. If loadSettings needs a region returned by loadProfile, it must wait for that result. If settings should be requested only for an enabled account, eagerly loading it may waste a request even when its inputs are available. Both result dependencies and conditional work can justify sequential loading.

The account example has neither dependency, but capacity still matters. Two requests from one screen may be inexpensive; many screens refreshing together can increase connection demand, server load and memory retained for unfinished results. Useful overlap depends on available resources. Contention at a bottleneck can reduce throughput or worsen tail latency.

Concurrency also requires local coordination: creating children and Deferreds, scheduling them, retaining state and collecting results. For two tiny in-memory lookups, this may cost more than the original operations.

Starting both operations means the second may already have performed a side effect when the first fails. Under coroutineScope, a child's failure with a non-cancellation exception cancels the scope and its sibling whether or not its result has been awaited; **How a Coroutine Failure Travels** explains this behavior.

Two independent network requests on the Android main thread, or another single-threaded dispatcher, can be concurrent without parallel Kotlin CPU execution. Each suspends while waiting, and the thread runs their short CPU segments in turn. Two substantial transformations executing simultaneously on different Default workers are both concurrent and parallel. The sequential overview function's two loads are neither, even if unrelated application work overlaps them.

Before adding async, check whether the operations are independent, whether their waits can overlap, whether substantial CPU work has resources to run in parallel, and whether earlier completion benefits the caller. Then measure user-visible latency and resource pressure. Concurrency cannot remove a dependency between operations.

items: The simplest correct form is usually sequential.
Data dependencies and conditionally needed work are both reasons to keep sequencing.
Overlap needs independent children created before any of them is awaited.
Concurrent waiting and parallel CPU execution are different things.
The cost includes coordination, downstream demand and failure reasoning.
With structured children, a function's completion still means its children are finished.

blocks.text: What does async buy in this example? Identify the interval of useful overlap, explain why the immediate-await version loses it, and name a condition under which the direct sequential version is the better choice.

units.title: Cancellation, Failure and Coordination
units.summary: Cancellation asks coroutine work to stop, but the code must observe the request. Cleanup and timeouts use the same mechanism. Failures propagate through parent-child relationships; supervision isolates failures at a particular boundary. Even when all the work succeeds, concurrent updates to shared state still need coordination.

lessons.title: Cancellation Is Cooperative
lessons.summary: Cancellation records a request on the Job. The coroutine reacts at cancellable suspension points or explicit checks; a busy loop can keep running, and a broad catch can swallow the CancellationException.

blocks.text: Calling cancel() requests cancellation, but it does not wait for the work to stop. The request travels down the coroutine hierarchy, and each coroutine must reach code that observes it.

When cancellation is requested, the Job enters its cancelling state. Running code continues until it observes cancellation. A cancellable suspension point or an explicit check can then throw CancellationException, allowing the coroutine to unwind. Cancellation does not forcibly interrupt arbitrary code.

Coroutine cancellation is cooperative: code inside the coroutine must suspend in a cancellable operation or check for cancellation explicitly. The coroutine hierarchy carries the request, but cannot make non-cooperative code respond to it.

Suspending functions in kotlinx.coroutines support cooperative cancellation. Custom suspending code built with plain suspendCoroutine does not gain cancellation support from that primitive; suspendCancellableCoroutine provides it for callback-based operations. Declaring a function suspend does not itself insert a cancellation check.

The loop never checks its Job and has no cancellable suspension point, so it keeps running after cancel(). Declaring performCpuWork as suspend would not change that unless its implementation cooperates. cancel() returns after requesting cancellation; the Job completes later, once its work and children have finished.
cancel() requests cancellation. To know whether the coroutine can stop, check whether its code reaches a cancellable suspension point or an explicit cancellation check.

Long-running code that does not otherwise suspend can cooperate in three ways. isActive returns false after cancellation, so it fits a loop condition. ensureActive() throws CancellationException, so it fits a point where the operation must stop and unwind. yield() checks cancellation and gives other coroutines a chance to run, making it useful when CPU work would otherwise monopolise a dispatcher thread.

rows: isActive
Reads false once cancellation has been requested; throws nothing.
The loop should end normally and the surrounding code should carry on.
ensureActive()
Throws CancellationException when cancellation has been requested.
Continuing past this point would be wrong, so unwinding is the correct outcome.
yield()
Releases the thread to other coroutines and throws CancellationException if cancelled.
The work is long and CPU-bound, and holding the thread would starve other coroutines.

blocks.text: Calling a suspend function does not guarantee that execution suspends. await() can return immediately for an already-completed Deferred, and a repository can return cached data without waiting. A loop whose only suspend call returns immediately may therefore keep running without observing cancellation. Add ensureActive() when each iteration must check, or yield() when other coroutines should also get a chance to run.

Cancelling a parent requests cancellation of its descendants too. Each descendant still has to observe the request, so some may continue their current step or run cleanup. join() waits until a Job completes; cancelAndJoin() combines the cancellation request with that wait.

Reading a cancelled scope as a stopped scope. After scope.cancel() returns, children may still be finishing their current step and running their cleanup. If a test or a shutdown path depends on the work being over, it has to wait for completion rather than for the request.

Forcibly stopping code could leave a mutation unfinished: two related fields might disagree, or a resource might be acquired before cleanup has been arranged. Cooperative cancellation lets code choose where to stop and unwind through finally blocks. The trade-off is that work can continue between the cancellation request and the next cooperative point.

The second consequence is that CancellationException is not an application error. It belongs to coroutine control flow: it is how a cancelled coroutine unwinds, and the machinery treats it differently from a failure. That makes a broad handler dangerous in a specific way.

The handler catches CancellationException along with other exceptions, then allows execution to continue. That can trigger another loop iteration, a retry, or a result for work that was cancelled. A broad catch is usable when it rethrows CancellationException and handles the remaining failures; the example below preserves cancellation in that way.

Ending with CancellationException does not fail a parent. Under ordinary parent-child rules, ending with another exception does. **How a Coroutine Failure Travels** follows that propagation; the supervision lesson explains the boundary where it is isolated.

items: Cancelling requests cancellation on a Job and returns; completion is a separate event.
A coroutine observes the request at a cancellable suspension point or at an explicit check.
Library suspension points support cancellation; the suspend keyword alone does not insert a check.
isActive, ensureActive() and yield() are the three checks, and they suit different kinds of loop.
A handler that swallows CancellationException lets cancelled work carry on.

blocks.text: For a CPU-bound coroutine, explain what cancel() requests and how isActive, ensureActive() and yield() let the code respond. Then show how a broad catch (e: Exception) can preserve cancellation while handling other failures.

lessons.title: Cleanup, `NonCancellable` and Timeouts
lessons.summary: A cancelled coroutine unwinds through its finally blocks, and a deadline is cancellation with a clock. Ordinary cleanup belongs in finally, suspending cleanup needs NonCancellable, and a timeout bounds only what is prepared to observe cancellation.

blocks.text: When a cancelled coroutine observes cancellation and unwinds, its finally blocks run. Ordinary non-suspending cleanup can go there: closing a handle, releasing a lock, restoring a flag, or removing an entry from a map.

Prompt cancellation means a coroutine cancelled while suspended can resume with CancellationException instead of receiving an available result. This prevents cancelled work from using a result that arrived too late, such as updating a closed screen. For a closeable resource, it creates a cleanup risk: the call may produce the resource without delivering it to the caller, so the caller never assigns the reference it intended to close.

The remedy is more specific than declaring the variable earlier: the capture has to happen inside the block, into a variable the finally block can already see. Then the reference exists whether or not the block's result is delivered.

When writing the suspending producer, arrange cleanup where the resource is passed to the continuation. The resume overload below accepts a cancellation handler that closes the resource if cancellation prevents the caller from receiving it. The caller cannot close a resource it never received.

Cleanup can itself require a cancellable suspending call. In an already-cancelled coroutine, that call can throw CancellationException before cleanup completes. withContext(NonCancellable) allows the cleanup block to run without reacting to the enclosing coroutine’s cancellation.
Put ordinary cleanup in finally. If cleanup needs cancellable suspending operations after cancellation, use withContext(NonCancellable) so those operations can finish.

Use NonCancellable for cleanup that must suspend after cancellation. The enclosing coroutine cannot stop that block through its usual cancellation request, so any lengthy work inside it delays completion. Keep the block focused on releasing resources rather than finishing the operation that was cancelled.

Keep the cleanup small and bounded: release a lease, flush a buffer, or send a close frame. Avoid continuing transactions or user-visible work inside it. A cleanup network call, such as session.abort() below, also needs a bounded completion policy.

Use NonCancellable with withContext. Passing it to launch breaks the parent-child relationship: the original parent neither waits for that coroutine nor receives its failure. After withContext(NonCancellable) returns, the enclosing coroutine may still be cancelled; call ensureActive() before continuing work that requires an active coroutine.

withTimeout requests cancellation of its block at the deadline using TimeoutCancellationException. withTimeoutOrNull uses the same mechanism but returns null for its own timeout. The block still has to observe cancellation.

Like coroutineScope, withTimeout creates a lexically scoped child and waits for its work to finish. Timeout cancellation can race with the block, including after the block finishes but before its result reaches the caller.

Treating withTimeout as a hard deadline for the caller. It is a request to cancel the block at a moment in time. If the block cannot observe cancellation, the deadline passes and the work continues, and because the block is a structured child the caller waits for it.

The cases below were reported from a JVM run using kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0, with withTimeoutOrNull and a 100 ms deadline. These are observations from one machine, not API guarantees. In the same run, a cooperative delay(1500) returned after 171–212 ms; that baseline shows timing overhead, but does not establish its cause or a fixed amount to subtract from every result.

rows: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(1500) }
null
about 1.7 s
A 1500 ms CPU loop with no suspension point and no check
the computed value, not null
about 1.5 s
join() on a Job belonging to a separate, non-child scope
null, and that job was still active afterwards
about 0.2 s
The same blocking call wrapped in runInterruptible
null
about 0.2 s

blocks.text: In the second row, the CPU loop ran for about fifteen times the deadline and returned its value. It never checked cancellation, so this run shows that non-cooperative work can outlive a timeout and still produce a result. The first row also outlived the deadline, but returned null after the blocking work finished. In both cases, structured completion kept the caller waiting for the timeout’s child work.

In the third row, cancellation stops the join() wait, and the caller returns near the deadline while the unrelated Job remains active. That Job belongs to another scope, so the timeout neither cancels it nor waits for its completion. The deadline applies to the wait, not to the independently owned work.

The fourth row uses runInterruptible, a JVM-specific bridge between coroutine cancellation and thread interruption. When cancellation interrupts the thread, a blocking API that supports interruption can throw InterruptedException; runInterruptible converts that into CancellationException. Coroutine dispatchers do not interrupt blocking calls on their own. Other targets need their own cancellation support for blocking operations.

A timeout becomes effective where the work observes cancellation, and structured ownership determines what the caller must wait for. Make the operation cooperative where possible. On the JVM, runInterruptible can help when a blocking API supports interruption. If the operation cannot be interrupted, account for its continued execution rather than relying on the timeout to stop it.

items: Ordinary cleanup in finally runs as the cancelled coroutine unwinds.
Prompt cancellation can discard an already-available value: capture resources inside the block, and release them at the resume site when you write the producer.
Suspending cleanup after cancellation needs withContext(NonCancellable), kept small and limited to cleanup.
A timeout is cancellation with a clock, and withTimeout's block is a lexically scoped child.
Non-cooperative work can outlive its deadline and even return a successful result.
runInterruptible is a JVM bridge to thread interruption, not universal coroutine behaviour.

blocks.text: Does withTimeout(100) guarantee that the call returns in about 100 ms? Answer with the mechanism: what the deadline requests, why the caller waits for a structured child, and what happens when the block never checks for cancellation.

lessons.title: How a Coroutine Failure Travels
lessons.summary: Under ordinary Job rules, a child’s unhandled non-cancellation exception cancels its parent, which cancels the other children. launch and async differ in how a failure can be observed, rather than whether it affects an ordinary parent. CoroutineExceptionHandler reports failures with no other propagation path.

blocks.text: CancellationException represents cancellation control flow and does not fail a parent. Under ordinary Job rules, an unhandled non-cancellation exception does fail the parent. The parent then requests cancellation of its other children. Supervision changes that failure relationship, as the next lesson explains.
From there the ordinary rules follow from the parent-child hierarchy. Take a parent with three regular children, where B throws.

blocks.code:
Parent
 |- Child A
 |- Child B   <-- throws IllegalStateException
 |- Child C

blocks.text:
B’s failure cancels Parent with that exception. Parent then requests cancellation of A and C. Their cancellation does not create a new failure to report, although their cleanup could itself fail.

Parent waits for all its children to finish unwinding before completing exceptionally. Where its exception goes next depends on Parent’s own parent and how Parent was created; the later section follows those paths.

launch and async differ in how a failure can be observed. async stores its outcome in a Deferred, and await() rethrows a stored failure to the caller. launch returns a Job rather than a result-bearing Deferred. Under ordinary parent-child rules, an unhandled failure from either builder still cancels the parent.

Under ordinary Job rules, an unhandled non-cancellation failure cancels the parent, which cancels its remaining children. CancellationException does not fail the parent. async additionally exposes its failure through Deferred.await().
An async child can fail its ordinary parent even when await() is never called. Storing the failure in Deferred does not remove the child’s parent-child relationship.

The async coroutine is an ordinary child of coroutineScope, so its failure cancels the scope even without await(). await() lets a caller observe the Deferred’s failure as a thrown exception. Catching that exception does not undo cancellation of an ordinary parent; a fallback requires an arrangement in which the failing operation has not already cancelled its caller, such as supervision.

Inside launch, catch an expected exception close to the operation that can throw it. Handling it there lets the coroutine provide a fallback or error state without ending in failure. CoroutineExceptionHandler serves a different purpose: reporting failures that escape the coroutine and have no other propagation path.

One detail matters when several children fail. The rule is that the first exception wins: it is the one that gets handled, and the ones that follow are attached to it as suppressed exceptions. On the JVM and Android they are reachable through `Throwable.suppressed`, so a log reporting only the first failure's message is telling a partial story, and the suppressed list holds the rest.
Believing an unawaited Deferred makes a failure irrelevant. It removes the place where the failure would have been observed, not the structural relationship that propagates it.

CoroutineExceptionHandler handles an unhandled exception when the coroutine has no other propagation path. It does not act like try/catch around every coroutine in a scope. Before invoking it, the runtime can handle an exception through the following paths.

items: The exception is caught by a try/catch inside the coroutine, so the machinery never learns about it.
The coroutine is lexically scoped, like coroutineScope or withContext, so the exception is rethrown to the caller.
The exception is transferred to a parent that processes child failures, through structured concurrency.
The builder returns a handle that allows querying the result, which is async and its Deferred.

blocks.text:
When none of those paths applies, the handler in the failing coroutine’s context is invoked. Common cases are launch on a scope with no Job, or launch directly in supervisorScope or under a SupervisorJob (see **`SupervisorJob`, `supervisorScope` and the Limits of Isolation**).

If no handler is present, the runtime uses its last-resort handling. On the JVM and Android, it invokes handlers registered through ServiceLoader and the current thread’s uncaught-exception handler. An unhandled exception can therefore crash an Android app.

The handler above is not invoked: the child’s failure cancels coroutineScope, and coroutineScope rethrows the exception to its caller. A handler on an ordinary child does not isolate that child. If the failure eventually reaches a root launch with no further propagation path, that root’s handler can run instead.

CoroutineExceptionHandler runs after the coroutine has failed, so it cannot resume or retry that coroutine. It can log, report, or initiate separate replacement work. It ignores CancellationException, which is treated as cancellation rather than an unhandled failure.

Expected outcomes, such as not-found responses or invalid input during parsing, can often be represented in the return type (see **Model and Error Boundaries: What May Cross**). Callers can then handle those outcomes explicitly. Unexpected exceptions still follow the coroutine propagation rules described here.

items: Under ordinary Job rules, a child’s non-cancellation failure cancels the parent and its remaining children.
launch propagates automatically; async represents the failure in its Deferred, where await() observes it.
A dropped Deferred still fails its parent under ordinary Job rules.
The first exception wins; the later ones arrive as suppressed exceptions on it.
CoroutineExceptionHandler applies only to a failure with no propagation path, never to async, and never to an ordinary child.

blocks.text: Draw a small tree, fail one child, and narrate the consequences: parent state, sibling cancellation, where the exception ends up, and when the parent is considered complete. Then say why a handler attached to that child would never run.

lessons.title: `SupervisorJob`, `supervisorScope` and the Limits of Isolation
lessons.summary: Supervision lets direct children fail independently: one child’s failure does not fail the supervisor or cancel its siblings. Cancellation of the supervisor still cancels its children, and each independent operation still needs appropriate error handling.

blocks.text: Under ordinary Job rules, a child’s failure cancels its parent and remaining siblings. SupervisorJob isolates the failures of its direct children: one child can fail or be cancelled without failing the supervisor or cancelling the other children.

Cancellation still travels downward: cancelling a supervisor cancels its children. If the SupervisorJob has a parent, that parent’s cancellation or failure also cancels the supervisor and its children. Supervision changes how a direct child’s failure affects its parent; it does not reverse downward cancellation.

supervisorScope is the lexically scoped form: it runs a block in a new scope containing a SupervisorJob, based on the caller's context. A child launched in it that fails does not affect the other children. The scope still waits — its lifecycle completes when both the block and all the coroutines launched in it complete — and if the block itself finishes with an exception, that does cancel the scope and all its children.

blocks.code:
supervisorScope
 |- Child A
 |- Child B
     |- Grandchild C   <-- fails

blocks.text: In the diagram, supervisorScope supervises its direct children, A and B. C is an ordinary child of B, so C’s failure cancels B. B’s failure does not cancel the supervisor or A, so A can keep running. B’s own Job has not become a supervisor.

Supervision isolates failure at one parent-child boundary. A direct child’s failure does not fail the supervisor or cancel its siblings. Nested children still follow their own parent’s rules, and cancellation of the supervisor still travels downward.

Supervision fits independent work presented together. Suppose three dashboard panels refresh from separate sources and one source is unavailable. Under a regular Job, an unhandled refresh failure cancels the parent and the other refreshes. A supervised parent lets the remaining panels finish.

Isolating sibling failures does not decide how the application handles an error. The supervisor does not process a direct child’s failure. That child still needs local handling, a CoroutineExceptionHandler for launch, or a caller that observes the outcome of async through its Deferred.

For a supervised launch, CoroutineExceptionHandler can report an unhandled failure because it is not propagated to the supervisor. For a supervised async, await() exposes the failure stored in Deferred. Local try/catch remains the option for handling an expected failure inside either child and providing a fallback.

Adding SupervisorJob does not handle an error. It isolates the failure from siblings, but an unhandled launch exception can still reach the runtime’s uncaught-exception handling. Arrange error reporting or an error state for each independent operation so a failed panel does not silently retain stale data.

Passing SupervisorJob() to launch replaces the scope’s Job as the parent for the newly launched coroutine (see **`CoroutineContext` and What Children Inherit**). It does not make that coroutine’s own Job a supervisor.

The fresh SupervisorJob becomes the parent of the coroutine created by launch. Because it replaces the scope’s Job, cancelling the original scope does not cancel this coroutine, and the scope does not wait for it.

The launched coroutine still has its own ordinary Job. A and B are its children, so A’s failure cancels that Job and B. The SupervisorJob isolates failure only at the boundary above the launched coroutine; it does not isolate A from B.

To isolate A and B, put them directly inside supervisorScope or launch them directly from an owning CoroutineScope with a SupervisorJob. Passing a Job to launch breaks the original structured parent-child relationship; the launch API discourages it, and the overload accepting a Job is deprecated.

rows: supervisorScope { }
The scope and the coroutines launched directly in it.
Does not reach nested children, and does not survive the block itself throwing.
CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + ...)
The scope's Job and everything launched from that scope.
Does not supervise coroutines those children launch in turn.
launch(SupervisorJob())
A boundary with one child: the coroutine launch created.
Does not supervise that coroutine's own children, and detaches it from the scope.

blocks.text: Before choosing supervision, decide whether the children can succeed or fail independently. Separate panels or uploads may support that relationship. Steps that jointly apply a change may not: allowing one to continue after another fails can leave a partial update or inconsistent screen data. Supervise the independent boundary, and handle each operation’s outcome there.

items: A supervised child's failure does not cancel the supervisor or its siblings.
Cancellation still travels down: cancelling a supervisor cancels its children.
supervisorScope supervises its direct children only, and still waits for all of them.
Supervision isolates propagation to the parent; each direct child still needs appropriate error handling or observation.
launch(SupervisorJob()) replaces the original parent and does not supervise the coroutines launched inside its block.

blocks.text: Given a nested launch inside a supervisorScope whose inner child fails, name every coroutine that is cancelled and say why. Then explain why launch(SupervisorJob()) does not isolate the siblings inside it, in terms of which Job became whose parent.

lessons.title: Shared Mutable State and Choosing a Coordination Mechanism
lessons.summary: Coroutines give no protection to state that two of them can touch at once. An atomic fits one independent value, confinement fits related state with one owner, and a Mutex fits a critical section that must stay consistent across several suspending steps.

blocks.text: Several coroutines can complete successfully and still corrupt state they update together. Coroutine lifetime and failure handling do not provide isolation for shared mutable state. Concurrent access needs its own coordination.

The reason is that counter++ is not one indivisible operation. It reads the current value, adds one, and writes the result back. Two coroutines running on different threads can read the same value before either writes, and one increment is lost. The Kotlin guide's version of this example makes the same point and notes that it is highly unlikely ever to print the expected total.

On Android and the JVM, Dispatchers.Default can execute coroutines on multiple threads, allowing the reads and writes above to overlap. If all these increments instead run on one thread, such as the Android main thread, they cannot interleave because counter++ contains no suspension point. Confinement relies on deliberately keeping every access on the same serial execution boundary.

A common first attempt does not work either. Marking the variable volatile on the JVM makes reads and writes individually atomic and visible to other threads, but it does not make a read-modify-write sequence atomic, so the lost update survives. Visibility and atomicity are different problems. The three answers that do work are a thread-safe or atomic operation, confining the state to a single execution owner, and mutual exclusion with a Mutex.

Concurrent unsynchronised updates to shared mutable state can race. Choose an atomic operation for a suitable value, confinement to one serial owner, or a Mutex around the critical section. The state’s consistency requirements determine which mechanism fits.

An atomic fits when the state is one value and the update can be expressed as a single atomic operation. On Android and the JVM there are two families: `java.util.concurrent.atomic`, such as `AtomicInteger`, and Kotlin's own `kotlin.concurrent.atomics`, whose `AtomicInt` is represented on the JVM by an `AtomicInteger`. The Kotlin API is still marked @ExperimentalAtomicApi on Kotlin 2.4.10, so a usage needs @OptIn or the matching compiler argument; the Java classes need no opt-in.

An atomic counter protects an individual increment. Two atomic fields do not automatically make an update to both fields atomic. If a balance and transaction log must change together, protecting each separately still lets another coroutine observe only half the change. Protect that relationship as one operation.

Confinement puts all access to mutable state on one serial execution owner, such as a single-threaded context or a dispatcher view with parallelism limited to one. Encapsulation alone does not provide that guarantee: two callers can enter a class’s suspending functions concurrently.

The granularity matters too. Switching context for every increment adds overhead for each small mutation. Keeping a whole chunk of work on the owner avoids those repeated switches while preserving serial access.

A serial dispatcher prevents simultaneous execution, but does not exclude another coroutine throughout a logical operation. If one coroutine suspends midway through an update, another can run before it resumes. limitedParallelism limits executing coroutines, not the number of operations in progress. Use a Mutex when the critical section must remain exclusive across suspension points.

A Mutex provides exclusive access to a critical section, including across suspending steps. When the lock is held, Mutex.lock() suspends the caller instead of blocking its thread. withLock releases the lock in finally, including when the protected block throws or is cancelled. Every access that depends on the protected invariant must use the same lock.

Protecting a line instead of an invariant. A lock taken around one statement, or an atomic per field, makes each individual write safe and still allows another coroutine to observe the state halfway through a change that was supposed to be one step.
Choose the mechanism according to what must remain consistent and whether the operation can suspend. Performance measurements can then help refine that choice.

rows: One independent value with a single-operation update
An atomic
A Mutex may add unnecessary contention; confinement may require a context switch for a small update.
Several related fields that must agree across a few steps
A Mutex around the critical section
Atomics protect each field and not the relationship; a serialised context does not hold across a suspension point inside the section.
A body of related state with a natural owner
Confinement to that owner
Locking requires every relevant access to use the same lock; confinement can centralise access with the owner.

blocks.text:
First establish where the state is shared, how it can change, and which relationships must remain consistent. Choose a mechanism that protects those relationships, then measure contention if the path affects performance. A Mutex serialises the protected work, so taking it unnecessarily can add cost.

Also consider whether the state needs to be shared. Computing independent values and returning them can remove the coordination problem instead of adding a lock.

A Channel can let one coroutine own the state while others send it values or commands. This replaces direct shared access with communication and can make ownership clearer when several coroutines need changes to the same structure. **Choosing a Stream Abstraction by Delivery Guarantees** compares Channel delivery with observing values through a stream.

items: A race needs concurrency and shared mutable state; removing either removes the race.
Read-modify-write is not atomic, and volatile fixes visibility rather than atomicity.
Atomics exist in java.util.concurrent.atomic and, behind an experimental opt-in, in kotlin.concurrent.atomics.
An atomic protects one value; a Mutex protects an invariant across several steps.
Confinement requires serial access, not just encapsulation. Coarser-grained work avoids repeated context switches.
Mutex.lock() suspends rather than blocking, and withLock releases through failure and cancellation.

blocks.text: Given a counter incremented from many coroutines on a multi-threaded dispatcher, explain the wrong total in terms of read-modify-write. Then justify a choice among an atomic, a single owner and a Mutex for a given shape of state, and say when communication would be a better design than sharing.

units.title: Flow Fundamentals
units.summary: A suspending function returns one result. A Flow lets a caller receive values over time, such as updates to a stored setting. Collecting a cold flow starts its producer under the collecting coroutine's lifetime; cancellation uses the same cooperative mechanism as other coroutine work.

lessons.title: One Value or Many: Why `Flow` Exists
lessons.summary: A suspending API returns one result; a Flow-returning API can deliver later updates. Choose according to the consumer's needs, with collection, coroutine lifetime and repeated delivery as part of the tradeoff.

blocks.text: A suspending function can perform work and return one result: loadUser(id) returns a User, and saveDraft(text) returns when the draft is saved. That contract suits a caller that needs one answer or wants to know when an action has completed. A caller that needs later updates requires a different contract.

Take a value that lives in local storage and can be written by more than one part of the app — the selected theme, say. A suspending read answers correctly at the moment it is called. Then something else writes a new theme: another screen, a sync job, a restore from backup. The suspending call has already returned. It has no way to say anything further, so the caller is now holding a value that used to be true.

Flow<T> represents a stream of values produced asynchronously and received by a consumer one at a time. readTheme() suspends until it can return an answer. observeTheme() is not suspending: it returns a Flow that the caller can collect to receive themes. In the cold-flow case used here, that object describes how to produce the values; returning it does not run the producer. **Cold Flows: Producer, Collector and Operators** explains when production starts.

Flow<T> does not specify how many values a consumer will receive. A flow may emit nothing, emit once and complete, or continue until cancellation. observeTheme() reports later themes because its API promises observation, not because Flow<T> requires repeated emissions. Document which values the API delivers and how current they are; callers cannot infer those guarantees from the return type.

Once readTheme() has returned, that call cannot deliver a later theme through its return value. The caller would have to read again, either when it learns about a change or by polling. An observation API provides a stream so the caller can receive updates without repeatedly requesting a new snapshot.

The question that chooses the return type is not “can this data change?”, because nearly all data can. It is “does this consumer need to be told when it changes?” A consumer that needs one answer now gets a suspending function. A consumer that must stay in step with a changing value gets a Flow.

Android's guidance recommends suspending functions for one-shot calls and Flow for notifying callers about data changes in the data and business layers. A repository can expose both: read or write a value for a single operation, and observe it for a consumer that needs updates.
Calling themeChanges() also gives the caller responsibilities that a one-shot read does not. The caller must arrange collection and decide how long it should continue.

items: It has to collect the cold flow to start this producer. Returning the Flow alone does not run its production block.
Collection is a suspending operation, so it needs a coroutine, and the caller has to decide which one.
The collecting coroutine bounds the collection's lifetime, so the caller must choose a scope appropriate to the consumer.
Values may arrive more than once. The API defines how many and for how long; downstream code must handle the deliveries it promises rather than assume a single result.
For an ordinary cold flow, every collector runs the producer again, so two collectors can mean two database reads.

blocks.text:
An observable API lets the consumer receive updates instead of continuing to use only the snapshot from an earlier read. That requires collection and a lifetime for it, and it does not by itself guarantee that every value is immediately current.

For a screen that must reflect later theme changes, those responsibilities are useful. For a one-time upload, validation or payment, a suspending function usually expresses the operation more directly. Wrapping one result in a Flow asks callers to manage a stream even when this operation needs only one answer.

Choose an observation API according to the consumer's needs, rather than only because the stored data can change. A screen that must update when another part of the app writes needs notifications. A use case that computes a total once for a report may need only a suspending read; a Flow adds collection, cancellation and possible repeated delivery to that caller's responsibilities.

A hot stream shares production among consumers instead of starting a new producer for each collection. Depending on its contract, it may produce without listeners and retain values for later subscribers. **Hot and Cold: When Production Happens** explains this distinction. The themeChanges() example here uses a cold flow, so each caller starts its own observation when it collects.

With a cold themeChanges() API, the repository describes how to observe storage and the caller starts that work by collecting. The caller can attach collection to the lifetime in which it needs theme updates. If the repository instead starts shared production, that work needs an explicitly owned scope and cancellation policy; returning a stream does not supply them automatically.

An observable view helps consumers stay in step with a single source of truth. When the theme store owns the value, each screen can observe that store instead of maintaining an unrelated copy that needs manual updates. Consumers may receive or process an update at different times, but they draw their values from the same authority.

When asked when to return Flow instead of using a suspending function, start with the consumer: does it need one answer, or later updates as well? A completed suspending call cannot deliver those later updates through its return value. Explain the cost of observation too: collection, a collecting coroutine, a suitable lifetime, possibly repeated emissions and, for a cold flow, another producer execution for each collector. Flow<T> permits zero or more values; the API must document its delivery and freshness guarantees.

sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

lessons.title: Cold Flows: Producer, Collector and Operators
lessons.summary: Constructing a cold flow or adding intermediate operators does not run its producer. A terminal operator starts collection, and each new collector runs a new producer execution. In a simple sequential chain, that work runs in the collecting coroutine.

blocks.text: A cold flow describes how to produce values when a caller collects it. Creating that description and running its producer are separate steps.

Creating updates does not execute the producer block: nothing is printed, loadFirst() is not called, and neither value has been emitted. In the reported JVM measurement, this construction ran the block zero times. The variable holds a Flow object that will run the block when collected.

A cold flow's builder block runs when collected, and each new collector starts a new execution. Kotlin's documentation compares this to a recipe: having the recipe does not produce a meal, and using it twice means doing the cooking twice.

collect is a suspending call. In this example, it runs the producer block in the collecting coroutine: “producer starting” is printed, both loads run, and their values reach the collector. The call returns when this flow finishes, unless collection ends with failure or cancellation.

The **producer** generates values, and work toward the producer is **upstream**. The **collector** receives values, and work toward it is **downstream**. An **emission** delivers one value from the producer. **Collection** runs the chain for one consumer.

Constructing a cold flow and adding intermediate operators do not run its producer. A terminal operator such as collect starts collection; in this simple sequential chain, the producer runs inside the collecting coroutine.
Each collector executes a cold flow's producer again, including any reads or requests in that producer.

blocks.code:
val articles = flow {
    executions++
    emit(loadFeatured())
    emit(loadRecent())
}

articles.collect { }   // executions is now 1, two values delivered
articles.collect { }   // executions is now 2, the same two values again

blocks.text:
In the reported JVM measurement, collecting a two-emission flow twice ran its producer twice and delivered 1, 2, 1, 2. The same repetition applies to work performed in the producer: opening a database cursor on each run gives each collector its own cursor; issuing a request on each run gives each collector its own request.

This cold-flow object does not expose a current value. Holding a reference to it gives you a way to collect its values, rather than a stored result you can read directly.

Flow operators form a pipeline. **Intermediate operators** return a downstream Flow that transforms or filters upstream values when collected. **Terminal operators** collect that pipeline and trigger its execution.

Adding map does not start processing values. In the reported JVM measurement, adding it without a terminal operator ran the producer zero times; collecting the resulting chain ran it once.

Terminal operators include collect and collectLatest; operators that produce a result, such as first, last, single, count, toList, toSet, fold and reduce; and launchIn, which starts collection in a supplied scope. Intermediate operators such as map return another Flow without collecting it at that point. Terminal operators perform collection, either through a suspending call or by launching a collecting coroutine.

**Flow Composition, Timing and Failure** explains how to choose intermediate operators, combine sources, handle timing and respond when a collector cannot keep up. For this model, the key distinction is that adding an intermediate operator does not start collection.

A property declared as Flow<Theme> provides a stream to collect, not a Theme value to read. For the cold flow shown here, production starts only on collection. Logging the Flow object or comparing two Flow references does not retrieve the themes they produce.

Cold flows and Kotlin sequences are both lazy. In a simple sequential pipeline, each element passes through the processing steps before the next element is produced, rather than creating a whole intermediate collection at each step. A sequential flow chain works the same way until an operator introduces concurrency or buffering.

The difference is suspension. A Sequence supplies its next value through an ordinary call, so that call holds the thread while it runs. Inside a flow builder, the producer can call suspending functions and wait for a database operation, socket or timer without blocking the thread, provided those operations themselves support suspension. Collection lifetime, cancellation and execution context therefore follow the coroutine model as well as the flow's laziness.

Cold describes a stream's behaviour, not the Flow type itself. Kotlin also provides hot streams whose production is shared independently of individual collectors; some retain values for later subscribers. The examples above are cold, so each collection starts the producer again. **Hot and Cold: When Production Happens** explains the alternative.

For a cold flow snippet, check three things: constructing it or adding intermediate operators does not run the producer; a new collector starts a new producer execution, including its reads or requests; and a terminal operator starts collection. In the simple sequential case, the producer runs in the collecting coroutine. These checks let you explain what the snippet will do before choosing more operators.

lessons.title: Collection Lifetime and Flow Cancellation
lessons.summary: A cold flow has no lifetime of its own: collect runs the producer under the collecting coroutine, so that coroutine's Job bounds the collection, and cancelling it is ordinary cooperative cancellation, not a Flow-specific mechanism.

blocks.text: To understand a collection's lifetime, identify the coroutine that collects and the conditions that end collection. A cold flow uses ordinary coroutine ownership and cancellation.

When a flow { } builder is collected directly, its producer runs in the collecting coroutine. Operators and builders can add coroutines: flowOn does so when it changes the dispatcher, and channelFlow can launch child producers. Those coroutines remain part of the structured collection, so collection does not finish while its owned work is still running. Cancelling the collecting coroutine requests cancellation of that work too.

The launch creates a coroutine under the scope's Job. In this simple cold-flow collection, the producer runs in that coroutine's context and under its Job. collect runs until completion, failure or cancellation. A storage-observation API that is designed to keep reporting updates usually ends through cancellation rather than normal completion.

The scope you choose determines who can cancel the collecting coroutine. A screen-owned scope cancels its collection when that owner ends. An application-lifetime scope can keep collecting after the screen leaves, even if no consumer still needs the values.

For a cold flow, each collection has a lifetime bounded by its collecting coroutine. Choose a scope that matches how long the consumer needs the values, and account for any earlier completion, failure or cancellation.
launchIn(scope) starts collection in a new coroutine in that scope. It is a terminal operator and is shorthand for scope.launch { flow.collect() }.

onEach adds work to perform for each value, but does not start collection. launchIn starts it and returns the collecting coroutine's Job. The reported JVM measurement returned a StandaloneCoroutine, a Job implementation; cancelling the scope ended that collection.

launchIn does not turn a cold source into a hot one. Each call starts a separate collection, so two calls can execute the producer twice. That is what the reported JVM measurement found for the same cold adapter.

The supplied scope owns cancellation of both collecting coroutines. You can also use the returned Job to cancel one collection earlier without cancelling the scope.

In a UI application, choose a collection lifetime that matches when the consumer needs updates. **Lifecycle-Aware Collection and the Lifecycle a Screen Actually Has** explains the lifecycle-aware arrangements. They start and cancel collecting coroutines according to the relevant lifecycle.

A collection can keep running after its consumer no longer needs it if the chosen scope remains active. The producer may continue observing storage or doing other work, and its callbacks can retain an obsolete consumer. Choose the scope and cancellation conditions to end that collection when its work is no longer needed.

Cancelling the collector requests cancellation of upstream production; it does not forcibly interrupt arbitrary code. As with other coroutine work, the Job records the request and running code stops when it observes it at a cooperative cancellation point.

In the reported JVM measurement, the producer began with a 600-millisecond blocking sleep. Cancellation was requested after 100 milliseconds, but the sleep continued. Joining the coroutine returned about 694 milliseconds after the start. This JVM-specific result illustrates that cancelling collection does not interrupt an ordinary blocking call.

The flow { } builder checks cancellation on each emission. Suspending operations between emissions can provide further cancellation points when their APIs support cancellation. In the reported JVM measurement, a tight producer loop with no delay or yield stopped after cancellation because emit was its cooperative check; the loop did not exit normally.

Production stops when it reaches a check that observes cancellation. A long blocking call or calculation between those checks can delay the end of collection, even when emit itself is cancellable.

A cold flow does not have an independently owned producer Job to cancel. The collecting coroutine owns the collection, including child coroutines introduced by operators. Cancellation follows that hierarchy, and the same cooperation requirements apply to the producer's code.

Identify which coroutine collects and what ends its work: cancellation usually comes from its owning scope. launchIn starts a collecting child coroutine and returns its Job; it does not change a cold source's per-collection production. Cancellation remains cooperative, so joining the cancelled coroutine waits for non-cooperative work already in progress to finish.

lessons.title: Context Preservation and `flowOn`
lessons.summary: A cold flow runs in the collector's context by default, an ordinary flow { } producer may not switch its own emission context, and flowOn exists precisely because of that rule — it moves the upstream and leaves the collector where it was.

blocks.text: By default, a flow { } producer executes in the collecting coroutine's context. To determine where a particular pipeline runs, read the collector's context and any operators that change upstream execution.
Writing flow { } does not select a dispatcher. By default, its producer runs in the collector's coroutine context; asynchronous values do not automatically move work off the caller's thread.

Suspension and execution context are separate decisions. A suspending function or a Flow does not automatically run in the background. In this example, collecting on the UI dispatcher also performs the file read there; a blocking read can delay the UI.

A flow's **context preservation** means upstream work does not change the downstream collector's context. You can determine where the collector runs from its coroutine context, while operators such as flowOn can give upstream work a different context.

A cold flow runs in the collector's context by default. Operators such as flowOn can give upstream work a different context without changing the collector's. To determine where each part runs, read the collector's context and the operators between it and the producer.

Use flowOn to run this file-reading producer on another dispatcher while leaving the collector in its own context. Changing the context around emit with withContext is not supported by the flow { } builder.

The flow { } builder requires emit to run in the builder's coroutine context. Emitting inside withContext(ioDispatcher) violates that requirement when it changes the context. The reported kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0 run produced this IllegalStateException:

blocks.code:
IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated:
	Flow was collected in [CoroutineId(1), "coroutine#1":BlockingCoroutine{Active}@..., BlockingEventLoop@...],
	but emission happened in [CoroutineId(1), "coroutine#1":DispatchedCoroutine{Active}@..., Dispatchers.IO].
	Please refer to 'flow' documentation or use 'flowOn' instead

blocks.text: The message shows the collection and emission contexts and points to flowOn. Keeping upstream context changes from leaking downstream lets the caller reason about where its collector runs. flowOn changes upstream execution while preserving that boundary.

blocks.code:
fileLines()                    // runs in ioDispatcher
    .map { parse(it) }         // runs in ioDispatcher
    .flowOn(ioDispatcher)
    .collect { render(it) }    // runs in the collector's context, untouched

blocks.text: flowOn affects preceding operators that do not already have their own context. In this chain, fileLines() and map use ioDispatcher, while collect continues in the collector's original context. The supplied context does not leak downstream.

Place flowOn after the upstream work that needs its context. Moving it changes which preceding operators it affects. A chain can contain more than one flowOn, so different upstream segments can use different contexts. If none of the upstream work needs a context change, there is no reason to add one.

flowOn(ioDispatcher) moves applicable upstream operators to IO; it does not move the collector or operators below it. In the example, parsing runs off the UI dispatcher and rendering stays in the collector's context. Place the operator according to which work needs the change.

When flowOn changes the dispatcher, upstream runs in a coroutine using the supplied context and downstream collects in the original context. A channel with a default buffer connects them, unless a nearby buffer operator specifies a different capacity. This lets upstream emit in its own context while the collector remains in its own.

Across that dispatcher boundary, upstream and downstream can run concurrently, and upstream can get ahead of the collector until the buffer fills. **When the Collector Cannot Keep Up** covers policies for that situation. A dispatcher-changing flowOn therefore affects execution overlap and buffering as well as execution context.

In the reported JVM measurement, a flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) upstream was collected from Dispatchers.Default. Upstream ran in a separate coroutine on DefaultDispatcher-worker-3; the collector ran on DefaultDispatcher-worker-1. Those names do not indicate separate IO and Default thread pools: on the JVM, IO shares threads with Default, and switching between them may reuse a physical thread.

flowOn selects an upstream context. The physical thread that executes it is a scheduling detail, so this observation should not be used to predict a particular worker for another run.

Context preservation and exception transparency both support local reasoning about a chain. Upstream context changes must not alter the collector's context, and upstream operators must not swallow failures from downstream code. **`catch`, `retry` and `onCompletion`** explains the operators for observing and handling failures while preserving that boundary.

Explain both what flowOn affects and why the emission rule exists. flowOn changes applicable upstream operators while preserving downstream context, including the collector's. emit inside a dispatcher-changing withContext in flow { } violates context preservation and can throw IllegalStateException. Use flowOn to change upstream execution without changing where the collector runs.

lessons.title: Flow Builders and Adapting Callback APIs
lessons.summary: Use flow for sequential suspending production, channelFlow for concurrent producers, and callbackFlow to adapt callback or listener APIs. In a long-lived listener adapter, awaitClose keeps collection active and unregisters the listener when the channel closes or collection is cancelled.

blocks.text: The flow { } builder fits one particular kind of producer: sequential work, done by suspending calls, emitting from the builder's own coroutine.

The flow { } builder can produce any number of values over any duration. Its restriction concerns emission: emit must run in the builder's coroutine context. Concurrent producers and external callbacks need a builder that allows values to arrive from elsewhere.

channelFlow allows multiple coroutines to send values, including from different contexts. Its ProducerScope supports thread-safe sending while preserving the downstream collector's context. Use send in these producers instead of emit.

channelFlow is cold: each collection executes its block again. The child producers can run concurrently, so launch order does not determine the combined stream's order. In the reported JVM measurement, two children, one delayed, delivered values according to their sends rather than their launch order. Choose this builder when production needs that concurrency, and do not rely on a fixed order between producers.

The builder follows from how the producer works rather than from preference. Sequential suspending production is flow. Production by several coroutines at once is channelFlow. A callback or listener belonging to something outside the coroutine world is callbackFlow.

Listener APIs deliver values through callbacks rather than suspending calls: location updates, sensors, connectivity, players and sockets are common examples. A flow adapter must register the listener for collection and unregister it when collection ends, or the source can keep delivering callbacks after the consumer has left.

Collection starts by registering the listener. Each callback uses trySend to offer a location to the channel, even if the source invokes it on another thread. A plain flow { } cannot emit directly from that callback because it is not running in the builder's coroutine context. After registration, awaitClose keeps the adapter active and supplies its cleanup boundary.

trySend does not suspend the callback. It returns a result indicating whether the value was accepted, and can fail when the buffer is full or the channel is closed. Ignoring that result can silently lose an update.

For a location that a later update will supersede, dropping may be acceptable, but the adapter should make that policy explicit. The example handles failure through onLocationDropped. Another adapter might count drops, report them or choose a different buffering policy according to its delivery needs.

After registration, the block needs to stay active while callbacks can arrive. awaitClose suspends for that purpose and arranges cleanup. If a callbackFlow block returns while its channel is still open, the builder throws IllegalStateException to warn that the callback registration may leak. In the reported JVM measurement, a block that sent one value and returned failed with:

blocks.code:
IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end
of callbackFlow block. Otherwise, a callback/listener may leak in case of external cancellation.
See callbackFlow API documentation for the details.
