blocks.text: A registered listener keeps being called and may retain everything it captured, including a screen the user has left. awaitClose waits until the channel is closed or cancelled and runs its cleanup block even if the wait ends through cancellation. In this adapter, unregister(listener) therefore releases the subscription when collection ends.

Keep this listener's registration and cleanup in the same collection. Registering in callbackFlow but unregistering only in an unrelated lifecycle or disposal callback can leave the listener attached after collection ends. awaitClose { unregister(listener) } ties cleanup to the subscription that created it.

Each callbackFlow collection runs the block again and registers its own listener. In the reported JVM measurement, two simultaneous collections registered twice, and scope cancellation unregistered both listeners. Each consumer therefore owned its subscription and cleanup.

Separate registrations can be costly, or incompatible with a source that permits only one listener. Sharing one collection among consumers addresses that case; **Sharing Cold Flows with `stateIn` and `shareIn`** explains how.
Choose the builder according to how values reach the flow:

rows: A sequence of suspending calls made by one coroutine
flow
The producer can emit sequentially in the builder's coroutine context; no channel-backed concurrent producer is needed.
Several coroutines producing values at the same time
channelFlow
The channel supports thread-safe sends from multiple coroutines. The combined order depends on their sends, not the order the coroutines were launched.
A callback or listener registered against an external source
callbackFlow
Callbacks send from outside the collecting coroutine. awaitClose keeps a listener subscription active and ties its cleanup to channel closure or cancellation.

blocks.text:
Both channelFlow and callbackFlow use a channel-backed ProducerScope, and both allow values from different contexts. channelFlow suits concurrent coroutine producers. callbackFlow expresses a callback subscription and adds a check against returning with an open channel, helping detect a missing lifetime or cleanup arrangement.

A listener can also be adapted with channelFlow and awaitClose, but then that callback-specific guard is absent. Channels used directly for coordination — including capacities, fan-out and pipelines — are covered separately.

Both builders use a channel with a default buffer, unless a buffer operator configures another capacity. That lets producers get ahead of the collector until the buffer fills; trySend can then fail, and it also fails after the channel closes. **When the Collector Cannot Keep Up** covers buffering, dropping and cancellation policies for producers that outpace their consumers.

For a listener adapter, explain why callbackFlow fits: callbacks can send values from outside the builder's coroutine context. awaitClose keeps the subscription active and unregisters the listener when collection is cancelled or the channel closes. Returning while the channel remains open triggers IllegalStateException; the guard does not replace cleanup. Because the adapter is cold, each collection creates a separate subscription.

units.title: Flow Composition, Timing and Failure
units.summary: Flow operators define how a pipeline handles values, timing and failure. Some filter by value or wait for a pause; others combine current state or pair corresponding emissions. Flattening operators decide whether inner work runs sequentially, overlaps or is cancelled by newer input. Buffering determines how a slower collector affects delivery, and failure handlers must sit where they can observe the failures they handle.

lessons.title: Transforming and Filtering: by Value and by Time
lessons.summary: map, filter and transform change or select values; distinctUntilChanged removes consecutive repetitions. debounce waits for a quiet interval, while sample emits the latest value at periodic ticks. Choosing between them depends on whether the decision concerns the value, previous values or timing.

blocks.text: An intermediate operator returns another Flow without starting collection. A terminal operation starts collecting the resulting pipeline. To choose an operator, identify what the decision depends on: the incoming value, previous values or the timing of arrivals.

A value-based transformation can inspect a query and trim its whitespace or reject it when it is too short. A time-based filter also needs to know when values arrive: a query that has settled after a pause may be worth searching even though the same query, midway through typing, is not.
map, filter and transform differ in how many outputs they can produce for each input:

map replaces each value with another. filter either passes the value through unchanged or drops it. transform can emit zero, one or several values, so it fits an input that should produce a loading placeholder followed by a result.

All three accept suspending lambdas. A mapping step can therefore call a suspending storage or network operation directly.

distinctUntilChanged compares a new value with the last value it emitted, using equals by default. Equal repetitions are suppressed, but a value can appear again after a different value has been emitted. It does not retain a history of every distinct value.

Choose an operator by the information its decision needs. map, filter and transform act on each input; distinctUntilChanged compares it with the last emitted value; debounce and sample use the timing of arrivals.
Compare debounce and sample using the same search-field timeline. The user types kotlin one character at a time, pausing after kot and again at the end.

blocks.code:
val typing = flow {
    emit("k");      delay(80)
    emit("ko");     delay(80)
    emit("kot");    delay(520)   // the user pauses
    emit("kotl");   delay(100)
    emit("kotli");  delay(200)   // a hesitation, but not a pause
    emit("kotlin"); delay(520)   // and stops
}

blocks.text: debounce emits a value after no newer value has arrived for the configured interval. Each arrival restarts the wait, so intermediate keystrokes are suppressed while typing continues. In the reported JVM run, typing.debounce(300) produced kot and kotlin. The 200-millisecond hesitation before the final keystroke was shorter than the timeout and produced no output.

sample checks for a new value on periodic ticks. At each tick it emits the most recent value received since the previous tick, or nothing if no new value arrived. It can emit while the user is still typing.

In the reported JVM run, typing.sample(300) produced kot, kotl and kotlin. The user did not pause at kotl; it was simply the latest value at a tick. Which intermediate value appears depends on how arrivals align with those ticks, so this exact sequence is not guaranteed.

Use debounce when the action should wait for input to settle, as with a search field. Use sample when updates should be processed at a periodic cadence, as with a telemetry feed reporting positions hundreds of times a second. A continuously changing feed may never have the quiet interval debounce needs.
The two search-field operators solve different problems and are commonly wanted together, in this order:

blocks.code:
queries
    .debounce(300)            // first: collapse the timing noise of typing
    .distinctUntilChanged()   // then: drop a query equal to the one already run

blocks.text: The operators remove different kinds of repetition. debounce suppresses intermediate keystrokes, but it can emit the same settled query again after another pause. distinctUntilChanged removes that consecutive repeat, but on its own would pass each different keystroke through. In the reported JVM run, the user typed kot, paused, added and deleted a character, then paused again: debounce alone emitted kot twice, while the pair emitted it once.

debounce waits for a quiet interval; it does not emit at a fixed rate. If values keep arriving faster than its timeout, it can remain silent until the stream ends or arrivals slow down. Use sample when the requirement is periodic updates while input continues.

In kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0, debounce and sample use @FlowPreview rather than @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi. FlowPreview provides no backward compatibility guarantees, including for semantics; ExperimentalCoroutinesApi allows a more limited range of future changes. Both annotations produce warning-level opt-in requirements. @OptIn acknowledges the API stability contract; it does not change the operator’s behaviour.

Completion also distinguishes the operators. When upstream completes normally, debounce emits its pending latest value without waiting for the timeout. sample does not flush a pending value at completion: a value received after the final sampling tick can be lost. This matters when a finite stream ends with a value the collector needs.

take(n) ends collection after n values, which can bound an otherwise endless stream. drop(n) skips the first n values. onStart runs an action before upstream collection begins, and onEach runs an action for each value. Both are intermediate operators, so onEach alone starts no collection. scan emits a running accumulation, including the intermediate totals rather than only the final result.

To compare debounce and distinctUntilChanged, explain what each observes. debounce waits for a quiet interval; distinctUntilChanged suppresses values equal to the last emitted value. They can be useful together, but neither replaces the other. A value can pass distinctUntilChanged again after a different value, and a continuous stream faster than the debounce timeout can produce no output while it continues.

lessons.title: `combine` and `zip`: Current Values or Paired Emissions
lessons.summary: combine builds results from the latest value of each source. zip pairs corresponding emissions in order. Independent screen state usually needs combine; zip fits sources whose values correspond one for one and completes when either source ends.

blocks.text: When two flows contribute to one result, decide whether you need their latest values together or their emissions paired in order.

A signed-in user and a settings snapshot change independently. The screen needs the latest user together with the latest settings. By contrast, request and response streams can be paired by position when each request has exactly one response and the responses arrive in request order. In that arrangement, the third response belongs with the third request.
combine builds a result from the latest value of every source. It must first wait until all sources have supplied a value:

items: Nothing is emitted until every source has emitted at least once. Without a value from each source, combine cannot construct the result.
After that, source updates can produce results using the latest value from each source. This does not guarantee one output for every upstream emission.

blocks.text: If a screen renders nothing even though each source appears to work, check whether every source has emitted its first value. A source that emits nothing for an empty table, or waits for a permission that has not been granted, prevents combine from producing a result. In the reported JVM run, combining a working source with one that completed without emitting produced no values.

combine means "the current combination of these inputs". Its startup rule follows from that: there is no current combination until each input has a current value, so combine emits nothing until every source has emitted once.
zip takes one unused value from each source and pairs them. A value waits until its partner arrives, so the faster source is limited by the slower one.

A3 has no partner. zip completes when either source completes and cancels the remaining source. In the reported JVM run with four values on one side and two on the other, the faster source produced three values, but only two pairs were emitted. The unmatched value was discarded at completion.

Independent UI state usually needs combine rather than zip. With zip, a settings update cannot reach the screen until the user source supplies its next value, and completion of either source ends the combined updates. Those behaviours follow from pairing emissions; they do not fit a screen that should update whenever either current value changes.

Use zip when the data has positional correspondence: walking two ordered sequences together, matching items with their computed keys, or pairing requests with responses when their counts and ordering correspond. Recency would pair the wrong values in these cases.
merge interleaves values from several flows of the same type into one flow. It does not build combinations or pairs.

merge is the answer when the sources are alternative origins of the same kind of value rather than components of one result — several event sources feeding one handler, for example. In kotlinx-coroutines 1.11.0 it carries no opt-in annotation, unlike the flattening operators (see **Flattening: Should New Input Cancel Old Work?**).

rows: What is the current state of all of these?
combine
Results built from the latest value of every source, once all have emitted; not necessarily one result per upstream emission
Which value of this corresponds to which value of that?
zip
Pairs of unused values; completes when either source can no longer supply one
Should values from these sources feed one handler?
merge
Values from every source, interleaved unchanged; no ordering guarantee across sources

blocks.text: Waiting for both sources to be ready does not require zip. combine already waits for every source’s first value, then updates from either source. Choose zip only when the emissions themselves should be paired.
combine uses the latest value from each source. It does not guarantee exactly one output for every upstream emission.

The current implementation processes pending updates in batches. It ends a batch when it encounters a second update from the same source, so waiting updates from different sources can contribute to a single result.

In the reported JVM runs, the two-source timeline emitted three results with emissions 200 milliseconds apart, but sometimes only two with emissions 100 milliseconds apart. An intermediate combination was skipped. The reported run of the documentation’s 10- and 15-millisecond example also produced one fewer result than its illustrated output. These observations describe particular runs, not a guaranteed output count.

combine fits current state because a later combination can supersede an intermediate one. If every change must be observed, use a stream contract that preserves those events, such as a single ordered source. zip is suitable when the sources’ values correspond one for one.

StateFlow always has a current value, which a new collector receives immediately (see **`StateFlow`: One Current Value**). Unlike a cold source that has not yet emitted, it can provide combine with an initial value without waiting for a new update.

Compare latest values with matched pairs. combine waits for every source’s first value, then uses their latest values without guaranteeing every intermediate combination. zip pairs emissions in order, limits the faster source to the slower source’s pace, and completes when either source completes, cancelling the other.

lessons.title: Flattening: Should New Input Cancel Old Work?
lessons.summary: When each input produces a Flow, flattening turns those inner flows into one stream of results. flatMapConcat collects them sequentially, flatMapMerge allows overlap, and flatMapLatest cancels the previous inner flow when a new input arrives. The choice depends on ordering and whether earlier work must finish.

blocks.text: Some values are not transformed into other values; they are transformed into more work. A query becomes a stream of search results, a selected identifier becomes a stream of updates for that record, an upload request becomes a stream of progress reports. The mapping function returns a Flow, and so mapping produces a flow of flows.

blocks.code:
val queries: Flow<String> = searchField()

val nested: Flow<Flow<Result>> = queries.map { query ->
    repository.search(query)   // returns Flow<Result>
}

blocks.text: The collector receives Flow objects rather than their results. Flattening turns Flow<Flow<Result>> into Flow<Result> by collecting the inner flows. The operator determines whether those collections follow upstream order, overlap or replace an earlier collection when a new input arrives.

rows: flatMapConcat
Yes — upstream order, exactly
No — one at a time
No — it runs to completion first
flatMapMerge
No — emissions interleave
Yes — up to a concurrency limit
No — every inner flow finishes
flatMapLatest
Within each inner flow; earlier flows may emit before cancellation
No
Yes — cancellation is requested when new input arrives

blocks.text: If every input’s work must finish, choose between sequential collection and overlapping collection. flatMapConcat preserves upstream order; flatMapMerge allows interleaved results. If newer input makes earlier work disposable, flatMapLatest cancels that earlier collection.

Choose flattening semantics to match the work: sequential collection for ordered operations, overlapping collection for independent operations, or replacement when newer input supersedes earlier work. Speed alone does not determine which contract is appropriate.
One timeline makes the three concrete. Two queries arrive fifty milliseconds apart; the first opens a slow inner flow and the second a fast one.

flatMapConcat finishes collecting one inner flow before beginning the next. Results therefore follow upstream order, and the fast second query waits behind the slow first one. This fits document edits or server requests that must be applied in the order they were submitted.

flatMapMerge collects inner flows concurrently, allowing B’s first result to arrive before A’s even though A started first. The transform function itself is still called sequentially; the overlap is in collecting the flows it returns.

The concurrency parameter bounds the number of inner flows collected at once. Its default is DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY, which is 16 in kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0 and can be overridden by a JVM system property. A bound prevents a long upstream from starting an unlimited number of inner collections.

Reach for flatMapMerge when the inner operations are genuinely independent and interleaved completion is acceptable — fanning out a list of identifiers into per-item requests, for instance. Concurrency here means overlapping coroutine lifetimes, not a promise of parallel execution on separate cores; whether those inner flows ever run at the same instant is the dispatcher's business.

The documentation for flatMapConcat and flatMapMerge recommends simpler linear transformations for ordinary application flows when they are sufficient. If each input needs one asynchronous result, a suspending map body can produce that result directly. Flattening is needed when the transformation returns a stream of results.

flatMapLatest cancels collection of the previous inner flow and starts the one for the new input. In the reported run, A had not emitted before B arrived, so only B’s results were received. This fits search-as-you-type when results for an earlier query are no longer needed.

blocks.code:
queries
    .debounce(300)
    .distinctUntilChanged()
    .flatMapLatest { query -> repository.search(query) }

blocks.text: flatMapMerge permits interleaved results; flatMapConcat preserves input order. Using merge for ordered work can produce a failure that appears only when one inner flow finishes before another. Choose according to the ordering requirement rather than treating the operators as faster and slower versions of the same behaviour.
flatMapLatest uses ordinary coroutine cancellation to stop a superseded inner collection. Whether it fits the operation depends on what that collection may already have done.

Cancellation stops work from continuing. It does not undo work already performed. Measured on a JVM target, two queries flattened with flatMapLatest started two inner flows and completed one — but both inner flows had already executed their first statement before either was cancelled. If that first statement had sent a request, charged a card, or written a row, the cancellation would have arrived afterwards and changed nothing about it.
Before choosing a latest-value operator, check both whether newer input supersedes older input and whether the older work is safe to abandon part-way through.

items: Usually safe to abandon: computing suggestions, loading results for a superseded query, rendering a preview or transforming transient input, provided no externally visible partial effect needs to finish. Discarding that work then costs only the effort already spent.

Needs further design: submitting a payment, performing a durable write, incrementing a persistent counter or sending a request with a lasting server effect. Cancellation can stop the caller before it learns whether that effect completed.

blocks.text: Latest semantics fit work that is safe to abandon. Idempotency, cancellation tokens and transactional boundaries may help design an operation around cancellation, but the operator supplies none of them. The inner flow responds through ordinary cooperative cancellation, and any effects already performed remain.

In kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0, flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge, flatMapLatest, transformLatest and mapLatest use @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi at warning level. merge requires no opt-in. The annotation concerns API stability rather than cancellation safety: @OptIn acknowledges that the annotated API may change in a future release.

Compare the operators by ordering, overlap and cancellation of earlier work. If asked what flatMapLatest does after a request has been sent, distinguish cancelling its collecting coroutine from reversing the request’s effect. It can stop waiting for a result; it cannot recall an effect that has already occurred.

lessons.title: When the Collector Cannot Keep Up
lessons.summary: When a producer outpaces its collector, decide which values and which work must be preserved. A simple unbuffered flow makes the producer wait. buffer allows a backlog, conflate replaces pending values with newer ones, and collectLatest cancels processing when a new value arrives.

blocks.text: In a simple unbuffered pipeline, the producer waits while the collector processes each value. Before adding buffer, conflate or collectLatest, decide whether that coordination fits the operation or whether production and processing should overlap.
In this example, the producer pauses for 100 milliseconds after each emission, and the collector spends 300 milliseconds on each value.

The collector receives all five values in order. Each emit waits for the collector’s processing to return before the producer reaches its own delay, so those delays occur sequentially rather than overlapping. The reported JVM run took 2,676 milliseconds. That measurement includes execution and scheduling time; it is not a duration guaranteed by the operators.

This coordination applies backpressure: the collector limits how quickly upstream can proceed. In this simple cold pipeline, no values are lost and no queue is introduced. If the producer reads data between emissions, it cannot continue those reads until emit returns; that does not necessarily stop activity inside the external source itself.

Other pipelines can contain buffers. flowOn introduces a channel when it changes dispatchers, channelFlow is buffered by default, and buffer adds one explicitly. Backpressure therefore depends on the pipeline and its overflow policy, not only on its Flow type.

First decide what must be preserved. An unbuffered pipeline delivers each value and waits for its processing. buffer allows production to run ahead using memory; conflate can discard pending values; collectLatest can abandon processing already started.
buffer gives the two ends room to run independently. It puts a channel between them, so the producer emits into the buffer and carries on rather than waiting for the collector to finish.

blocks.code:
producer.buffer().collect { value -> process(value); delay(300) }
// Measured on a JVM target: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in 1,870 ms

blocks.text:
Every value still arrives in order. The producer’s delays can now overlap the collector’s work instead of adding to it.

The buffer uses memory to let production run ahead temporarily. If the producer stays faster, a bounded buffer eventually fills and its default overflow policy suspends the emitter. An unbounded buffer avoids that suspension but can grow without limit when the mismatch persists.
conflate makes the opposite trade. Instead of retaining a backlog, it keeps only the most recent unconsumed value and discards the ones the collector never reached.

blocks.code:
producer.conflate().collect { value -> process(value); delay(300) }
// Measured on a JVM target: 1, 3, 5 in 1,101 ms

blocks.text: In the reported run, values 2 and 4 were never collected. Processing of 1 continued while 2 and 3 arrived; when the collector was ready, it received 3 instead of 2. conflate does not cancel processing already in progress. It uses a drop-oldest buffer so that a newer value replaces a pending older value without suspending the emitter.
collectLatest changes something else entirely. It does not drop queued values; it cancels the processing of the current one.

In the reported run, processing started for every value, but each new arrival cancelled the previous block; only the final block completed. The producer’s values were emitted, while the superseded downstream work was abandoned. Cancellation is cooperative, so a block that neither suspends nor checks for cancellation may finish before it responds.

rows: none
Every value, processed to completion
The producer runs at the collector's pace
buffer()
Every value, processed to completion
Memory for the backlog, and latency behind it
conflate()
1, 3, 5 — processed to completion
Values the collector never reached
collectLatest
All five started, only 5 finished
The partial work of every superseded value

blocks.text: A buffer can absorb a temporary burst, but it cannot make a permanently faster producer sustainable. With the default overflow policy, a bounded buffer eventually fills and the producer suspends, leaving queued values waiting for the collector. Those waiting values add latency even if overlapping work improves throughput.
conflate and collectLatest had similar measured durations, but they handle existing work differently. conflate lets current processing finish; collectLatest cancels it when a new value arrives.

Use conflate when current processing should finish but intermediate pending values may be skipped. Use collectLatest when a new value makes the current processing unnecessary and that processing is safe to abandon. Neither fits an operation that must process every value to completion.

A collectLatest block may be cancelled before it reaches its end. Preview rendering or transient formatting can fit when partial work has no effect that must finish. Durable writes need more care: cancellation can stop the next step without undoing a step that already succeeded.

If every value must finish processing, use a pipeline that preserves values, such as the unbuffered default or buffer with a suspending overflow policy. If the required production rate remains higher than the processing rate, the system needs a capacity or rate change beyond choosing a Flow operator.

When flowOn changes dispatchers, it collects upstream and downstream in separate coroutines connected by a channel with a default buffer. An adjacent buffer configures that channel rather than adding another one.

StateFlow already conflates values, so applying conflate() to it has no effect.

Explain the baseline for a simple unbuffered pipeline: emit waits for downstream processing, and values are preserved. Then distinguish the two forms of loss: conflate replaces pending values while letting current work finish; collectLatest abandons current work when a newer value arrives. A collectLatest block must therefore be safe to cancel part-way through.

lessons.title: `catch`, `retry` and `onCompletion`
lessons.summary: catch handles upstream failures, while retry re-collects upstream after an eligible failure. onCompletion observes successful completion, failure and cancellation, including downstream failures. A success side effect must therefore check that its cause is null.

blocks.text: The position of catch determines which failures it can handle. It observes exceptions from upstream code, so moving a potentially failing operation above or below it changes whether that operation is covered.
catch handles failures from the part of the chain above it. Failures from operators and collector code below it propagate to the caller.

blocks.code:
source                       // \
    .map { transform(it) }   //  |  catch sees failures from here
    .catch { cause -> ... }  // <-'  the boundary
    .map { render(it) }      //     and not from here
    .collect { display(it) } //     nor here

blocks.text: Here, the collector throws below catch, so catch does not handle the failure:

This is exception transparency: catch does not handle failures from downstream code. Conceptually, it wraps only the upstream portion in try/catch. The collector remains responsible for its own failure handling, rather than having an earlier operator silently absorb those failures.
Place catch below the upstream code whose failures it should handle. A failure in collect remains outside that boundary; cancellation also propagates rather than becoming a recoverable failure.
A failure produced by the collector can be handled locally, or the failing operation can move upstream if it belongs in the transformation pipeline.

items: Handle it where it happens. If the failing operation belongs to the collector — writing to the screen, updating a widget, running an effect — wrap it in an ordinary try/catch inside the collect block. The stream is not involved in that failure and should not be made to carry it.

Move it upstream. If the failing operation is really a transformation of the value and only happens to be written inside collect, move it into an operator and put catch after it. Now it is part of the pipeline and the pipeline's failure handling applies.

blocks.text: Keep collector-specific side effects in the collector rather than moving them upstream solely to reach catch. Moving them changes the pipeline’s responsibilities and can expose those effects to repetition if that part of the chain is retried.
A catch block can emit a value that represents the failure:

blocks.code:
productFlow
    .catch { cause ->
        log(cause)
        emit(Products.Unavailable)   // the failure becomes a value
    }

blocks.text: Products.Unavailable gives downstream an explicit failure state to display. Keep it distinct from a valid empty result: if both cases become an empty list, the collector cannot distinguish “no products” from “could not load products”. Decide whether the stream’s contract should represent an expected failure as data or let the exception propagate.
retry re-collects upstream after a matching failure. For a cold flow, that runs the producer again from the beginning; it does not resume at the line that threw.

The producer side effect ran three times, so retry is appropriate only when repeating upstream is safe. Values from earlier attempts had already reached the collector and remain delivered. If a retry emits those values again, a collector that accumulates results may receive duplicates.

retryWhen is the conditional form, and its predicate receives both the cause and a zero-based attempt index. Measured on a JVM target, a flow that failed every time and stopped retrying at attempt 2 saw the indexes 0, 1 and 2. Because the predicate is a suspending function, a delay between attempts belongs inside it.

retry() defaults to Long.MAX_VALUE attempts. A permanent failure, such as invalid credentials or a malformed request, can therefore trigger repeated attempts without a practical bound. Limit the retries and select failures that have a reason to succeed on another attempt.

onCompletion is similar to a finally block around collection: its action runs after successful completion, failure or cancellation. Unlike catch, it also observes downstream failures and cancellation exceptions. Its cause is null only when collection completes successfully.
Measured on a JVM target, across four endings of the same pipeline:

rows: The flow completed normally
null
The producer threw
IllegalStateException — the upstream failure
The collect block threw
IllegalStateException — a downstream failure, which catch would not have seen
The collecting coroutine was cancelled
JobCancellationException

blocks.text: This analytics event does not check how collection ended:

All four endings run the action, although only normal completion indicates a successful collection. A failed request or cancellation can therefore record “Successfully synced”. Check cause == null before recording the success event.

catch and retry do not handle exceptions used to cancel the flow. Cancellation tells the coroutine to stop; absorbing it as a recoverable error would interfere with that request. onCompletion can observe cancellation, but its action does not turn cancelled collection into successful collection.
Context preservation (see **Context Preservation and `flowOn`**) and exception transparency protect different boundaries in a pipeline:

blocks.code:
context transparency:
    an upstream operator cannot change the context the downstream runs in

exception transparency:
    an upstream operator cannot consume a failure the downstream produced

blocks.text: These boundaries help a reader reason about each part of a chain. Upstream code cannot silently change downstream execution context or absorb downstream failures. The comparison is a useful mental model, but the two contracts are separate and neither implies the other.

Explain three boundaries: catch handles upstream failures but leaves collector failures to the caller; retry repeats upstream collection, including a cold producer’s side effects; onCompletion observes success, failure and cancellation. Collector failures need local handling or a transformation moved above catch, repeated upstream work must be safe, and a success event in onCompletion must check cause == null.

units.title: StateFlow, SharedFlow and Hot Streams
units.summary: Hot streams separate three concerns: whether production runs per collector or is shared, what earlier values a subscriber can recover, and when a shared upstream starts and stops within its owning scope. Choose a stream abstraction by the delivery guarantee the problem requires, then configure retention and sharing policy to match.

lessons.title: Hot and Cold: When Production Happens
lessons.summary: A cold flow runs its producer separately for each collector. A hot stream has an instance shared by its subscribers. Retention determines what a late subscriber receives, while a sharing policy determines when a shared upstream runs.

blocks.text: A cold `Flow` describes how to produce values. Each collector runs that producer independently, so two collectors of the same cold flow share a definition but have separate executions.

A hot stream has an instance that exists independently of any individual collector. Subscribing joins that shared instance; it does not create a separate execution for the new collector. The instance can remain after all its subscribers leave.

The stream instance can exist even when its producer is not running. Some sharing policies start the upstream only when the first subscriber arrives.

In the reported JVM measurement with a lazily started shared stream, the object existed and its current value was readable before any subscriber arrived, but the upstream had not run. The first subscriber started it. Production was still shared rather than repeated for each collector.
An active collector of a hot flow is called a **subscriber**. It observes the shared stream, including when its arrival triggers the start of the upstream.

Hotness alone tells you neither what values are retained nor whether production is running. A hot stream may start eagerly or lazily, retain values or discard them, and stop its upstream when nobody is subscribed.
Cold means production runs separately for each collector. Hot means subscribers observe a shared stream instance. Retention and start-and-stop policy are separate choices.

Keep three concerns separate. The stream’s construction determines whether production runs per collector or through a shared instance. Retention determines what earlier values a subscriber can obtain from a current value or replay cache. A `SharingStarted` policy determines when a shared upstream is collected.

rows: Does each collector get its own execution of the producer?
Production lifetime — hot or cold
The builder, or sharing through `shareIn` or `stateIn`
What can a subscriber obtain that was emitted before it subscribed?
Retention — a current value, a replay cache, or nothing
A `StateFlow` current value, or a `SharedFlow` replay cache
When does the upstream of a shared stream actually run?
Start and stop policy
The `SharingStarted` policy

blocks.text: Consider a producer that emits A, B, C and D over time, and a subscriber that arrives between B and C. What it receives depends on both the production model and retention.

blocks.code:
producer:    A----B----C----D
                    ^
                 subscribe

blocks.text: For this cold flow, a new collector starts its own execution and receives A, B, C and D from the beginning. Those values belong to its execution; it has not joined the producer already shown in the timeline.

For a hot stream, the subscriber joins the existing production. With no retained values, it receives C and D. With the last value retained, it receives B first, then C and D. With the last two retained, it receives A and B before the live values. All three streams are hot; their retention differs.

Retention also determines what happens to values produced while nobody is subscribed. A cold flow’s producer does not run without a collector, but a hot stream’s producer can.

In the reported JVM measurement against kotlinx-coroutines-core 1.11.0, a shared stream with no retention produced six values before anyone subscribed. The subscriber first saw the seventh. Configuring retention of the last two values instead let the subscriber receive those two before continuing with live values.

A hot stream may discard values emitted without subscribers or retain them for later subscribers. Neither behaviour defines hotness. First identify whether production is per collector or shared, then check what values are retained.

A hot stream’s producer can also stop when nobody is subscribed. With the default `SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed()`, the upstream is stopped when the last subscriber leaves, while the shared stream remains hot (see **Sharing Cold Flows with `stateIn` and `shareIn`**).

A `callbackFlow` can wrap a hot external source such as a sensor, listener or socket while exposing a cold flow: each collector runs the builder and registers its own callback. Conversely, `shareIn` turns a cold repository flow into a hot stream by collecting the upstream in one shared coroutine. Classify the flow by how its production is organised, including when its external source behaves differently.

Observable state retains a result rather than the history that produced it. A field containing "abc" does not tell you whether the user made three edits or entered the text in one edit. A late observer can still learn the current field value, but cannot reconstruct those edits from it. The same distinction appears in **`snapshotFlow` and Crossing Into Flow**.

If a stream models current state, retaining the current value lets a late subscriber learn that state immediately. If it models occurrences whose history matters, retaining nothing means an occurrence emitted before subscription is lost to that subscriber. Choose retention from what subscribers need to know.

When only the current state matters, a new observer needs that value and conflation can skip intermediate states. When each occurrence matters, skipping values can lose required information. State the delivery requirement explicitly; **Choosing a Stream Abstraction by Delivery Guarantees** works through the choice.

Explain hot and cold in terms of shared or per-collector production, then distinguish retention. Be ready to show why a hot stream may replay earlier values or retain none, depending on its configuration.

lessons.title: `StateFlow`: One Current Value
lessons.summary: A `StateFlow` always has a current value. It requires an initial value, makes the latest value available to new subscribers, conflates updates using equality, and never completes normally.

blocks.text: `StateFlow` holds one observable current value. It is useful for UI state, but its contract applies wherever subscribers need to observe the latest state.

Constructing a `StateFlow` requires an initial value. You can read its current value synchronously through `value` without collecting it, and a new collector receives the latest value without waiting for another update.

The private `MutableStateFlow` lets the owner assign new values. Exposing it through the read-only `StateFlow` type gives callers observation without exposing the setter. This separates the public API from the owner’s mutation operations.
A `StateFlow` replays its most recent value to new subscribers and retains no additional values. It provides the current state, not a history or queue of changes.

A `StateFlow` never completes normally: `collect` does not return normally, and there is no `close` operation. Failure and completion are not terminal signals on the flow. If subscribers need to know that a load failed or finished, represent that information in the state type.

A `StateFlow` requires an initial value, exposes its current value synchronously, and replays the latest value to new subscribers. It never completes normally; errors needed by observers are represented as state values.

`StateFlow` uses **strong equality-based conflation**: it compares values with `Any.equals` and suppresses emissions of equal values. Assigning a value equal to the current value does not produce a new emission.

blocks.code:
val state = MutableStateFlow(User("Ada"))

state.value = User("Ada")   // data class: equal to the current value, nothing is emitted
state.value = User("Grace") // different: collectors are updated

blocks.text:
In the reported JVM measurement, a `MutableStateFlow` held a `data class` value. An attached collector received only the initial value despite three spaced assignments of equal values.

Repeating the experiment with a class that inherited identity equality produced four observations: the initial value and the three new instances. Their fields matched, but distinct instances compared unequal. The difference was the class’s `equals` behaviour.

rows: `data class` with the field in the primary constructor
Compares equal to the current value
Nothing — the assignment is suppressed
Ordinary class with no `equals` override
Compares unequal, being a different instance
A new unequal value can be observed; a slow collector may skip intermediate values
Class whose `equals` ignores a field that changed
Compares equal although the object differs
Nothing — the change is invisible

blocks.text: The state type’s equality semantics determine which updates are observable. If two states that should look different to the user compare equal, assigning the second will not notify the UI.

Mutating an object already held in a `StateFlow` does not assign a new value, so the flow does not emit that mutation. In the reported JVM measurement, the held object’s count changed in place from 1 to 99, followed by assignment of an equal instance. The collector received only the value at subscription, while a later read of `value.count` returned 99. Neither operation produced another emission.

Mutating an object inside a `StateFlow` does not produce an emission. Reassigning an equal value also produces none. Use state values whose equality captures the changes subscribers need to observe; behaviour is unspecified for classes that violate the `Any.equals` contract.

Equality is not the only reason an update may go unobserved. A slow collector can skip intermediate updates and receive the latest value when it is ready.

In the reported JVM measurement, values 1 through 10 were assigned at 20-millisecond intervals while the collector took 200 milliseconds per value. It observed 0, 7 and 10: eight intermediate states were skipped, and the final state was observed. That particular sequence is a measurement, not a timing guarantee.

This makes `StateFlow` suitable when observers need the latest state, but unsuitable for counting separate occurrences. Three "refresh finished" notices may collapse into fewer observations if the collector is slow. Equal notice values are suppressed even when the collector could otherwise keep up.

Assigning to `value` is thread-safe, but reading it and then assigning a computed result is not one atomic operation. Another coroutine can update the value between the read and write, causing a lost update (see **Shared Mutable State and Choosing a Coordination Mechanism**).

In the reported JVM measurement, eight coroutines each performed 2,000 increments. Using `value = value + 1` produced 5,998 instead of 16,000; using `update` produced 16,000.

`update` retries a compare-and-set operation if another update wins first. Its function may therefore run more than once under contention. Keep that function free of side effects: compute and return the new value, so a retry does not repeat unrelated work.

`compareAndSet` also uses `equals`. If both the expected value and the proposed value equal the current one, it returns `true` without replacing the stored reference. Callers that care about object identity cannot assume the flow now holds the instance they passed.

`StateFlow` already provides some behaviours that flow operators would otherwise add. Applying `flowOn`, `conflate`, `buffer` with conflated or rendezvous capacity, `distinctUntilChanged`, or `cancellable` has no effect on it.

`StateFlow` is also a specialised `SharedFlow`, optimised for sharing the latest state value.
`StateFlow` belongs to kotlinx.coroutines and does not itself manage a UI lifecycle or ViewModel lifetime.

Explain how `Any.equals` suppresses equal updates and how a slow collector can skip intermediate states. Distinguish a failed operation represented in state from failure or completion of the flow itself.

lessons.title: `SharedFlow`: Replay, Buffering and Subscribers
lessons.summary: A `SharedFlow` broadcasts values to its subscribers. Replay, buffer capacity and overflow policy determine what late or slow subscribers can receive and whether an emitter waits. With no subscribers, only the configured replay is retained.

blocks.text: `SharedFlow` is a hot flow that broadcasts values to subscribers. Each value is offered to every subscriber rather than assigned to one receiver. Whether a subscriber actually receives every offered value depends on buffering and overflow policy. `StateFlow` is the specialised form that retains one current state value.

Like `StateFlow` it never completes, and like `StateFlow` its active collectors are called subscribers. Unlike `StateFlow` it has no current value, no mandatory initial value, and no fixed retention — retention is something you configure.

Three parameters configure it, and they answer different questions. `replay` is how many of the most recent values a subscriber receives when it arrives. `extraBufferCapacity` is additional room beyond replay, so that an emitter is not held up by a subscriber that is behind. `onBufferOverflow` decides what happens when that room runs out: suspend the emitter, drop the oldest buffered value, or drop the value being emitted.

`replay` serves two purposes: retaining values for new subscribers and buffering values for existing subscribers that fall behind. `extraBufferCapacity` adds room only for existing subscribers; it is not replayed. With the default suspending overflow policy, the available buffering is `replay + extraBufferCapacity`, while a late subscriber can recover at most `replay` values.

headers: Room for a slow subscriber (`SUSPEND` policy)
rows: `replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 0`
None — the emitter waits for every value
Nothing
`replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 0`
One value
One value
`replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 1`
One value
Nothing
`replay = 2, extraBufferCapacity = 3`
Five values
Two values

blocks.text:
The reported JVM measurements tested both columns with the default suspending overflow policy. A subscriber taking 400 milliseconds per value could lag by `replay + extraBufferCapacity` before `tryEmit` returned `false`.

For late subscription, six values were emitted before anyone subscribed. With `replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 3`, the new subscriber received none: extra capacity buffers for existing subscribers, not future ones.

`SharedFlow` broadcasts to current subscribers. Replay both retains values for late subscribers and contributes buffering for slow subscribers. Extra capacity adds buffering without replay, and overflow policy determines whether a full buffer suspends the emitter or drops a value.
To see what replay changes, emit A before subscription and B afterwards. Compare a stream with no replay to one that retains its latest value.

blocks.code:
emit(A)          subscribe        emit(B)
   |                 |               |
   v                 v               v
replay = 0:  A is gone            B delivered
replay = 1:  A delivered on subscribe, then B

blocks.text: With `replay = 0`, a subscriber arriving after A cannot recover it from the flow. With replay enabled, a late subscriber receives A only if it is still in the replay cache. Later emissions continue to reach active subscribers according to the buffering and overflow configuration.

A default `MutableSharedFlow()` has neither replay nor extra buffer. Its `emit` suspends until all active subscribers receive the value.

In the reported JVM measurement, a subscriber took 300 milliseconds per value and three emissions returned roughly 109, 414 and 718 milliseconds after the start. The first handed a value to a waiting subscriber; later emissions waited for the subscriber to become ready again. These timings describe that run.

A dropping overflow policy avoids waiting when the buffer fills, allowing a slow subscriber to miss values. In the reported JVM measurement, six values were emitted 20 milliseconds apart while a subscriber took 300 milliseconds per value. The suspending strategy delivered all six; one extra buffer slot with `DROP_OLDEST` delivered 1 and 6.

The subscriber remained present in both runs. Broadcast describes who is offered values; overflow policy can still determine which values a slow subscriber receives.

With no subscribers, the default unbuffered flow behaves differently: `emit` returns immediately and the value is discarded because there is no replay cache. In the reported JVM measurement, a thousand such emissions completed in about 1 millisecond and left an empty replay cache. None waited for a subscriber or queued a value for later delivery.

An unbuffered `SharedFlow` with `replay = 0` discards values emitted while nobody is subscribed. It fits a notice intended only for current observers, but cannot retain a must-not-be-lost occurrence through a subscription gap. Choose from that delivery requirement rather than from the label "event".

Without subscribers, buffering retains only the most recent `replay` values. Extra capacity is unused and the overflow policy has no effect: overflow requires an existing subscriber that is not ready. In the reported JVM measurement, ten emissions to a flow with `replay = 2` left only the last two in its replay cache.

`tryEmit` does not suspend. It returns `false` only when the suspending overflow strategy would require waiting for subscribers; with no subscribers it returns `true`.

In the reported JVM measurement, an unbuffered flow with no subscribers returned `true` and kept an empty replay cache. The value was discarded. With a slow subscriber attached, the same call returned `false`. Success therefore does not establish that anyone received the value.

`tryEmit(value) == true` means the call completed without needing to suspend, not that a subscriber received the value. On a default unbuffered flow, it succeeds only when there are no subscribers, and the value is discarded.
Choose the configuration by what subscribers need to receive, including those that arrive late or cannot keep up.

rows: Must an observer arriving at any moment know the current truth?
`StateFlow` guarantees an initial and current value
Retention is optional
Should only observers present at emission receive the value?
`replay = 0`
Choose a replay size deliberately
Should a full buffer suspend the emitter for slow subscribers?
Use `SUSPEND` and choose buffer capacity
Configure a dropping overflow strategy
Must the occurrence eventually be handled by somebody, even if nobody is subscribed when it happens?
No shared flow configuration guarantees this
Loss may be acceptable; choose replay according to what late subscribers need.

blocks.text:
A fresh `MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1)` has an empty replay cache. A subscriber arriving before its first emission waits; replay capacity alone does not create a current value. In the reported JVM measurement, there was also no retained value for a new subscriber after `resetReplayCache()`. A `MutableStateFlow`, by contrast, supplied its initial value.

The `StateFlow` documentation describes equivalent behaviour using a shared flow configured with `replay = 1` and `DROP_OLDEST`, seeded with `tryEmit(initialValue)`, and observed through `distinctUntilChanged`. Replay is one part of that arrangement, alongside the initial value and equality-based conflation.

Replay can retain an occurrence through a subscription gap, provided it has not been displaced by later values. It does not track whether anyone completed the work that occurrence requests. If eventual handling is required, retention alone is insufficient; **Choosing a Stream Abstraction by Delivery Guarantees** examines that requirement.

The documented event-bus example deliberately uses an unbuffered shared flow: `emit` waits until every active subscriber has received the event. This is rendezvous delivery. The slowest subscriber can hold up the producer, so suspension supplies backpressure. With no subscribers, the same emitter does not wait.

`subscriptionCount` exposes the current number of subscribers as a `StateFlow<Int>` and supplies the count used by `SharingStarted` policies (see **Sharing Cold Flows with `stateIn` and `shareIn`**). `resetReplayCache` clears values retained for new subscribers by a `MutableSharedFlow`.

State the broadcast rule, then distinguish replay from extra buffer capacity in one sentence each. Be able to say what an unbuffered `emit` does with subscribers and without them, and be able to say why `tryEmit` returning `true` is not evidence of delivery.

lessons.title: Sharing Cold Flows with `stateIn` and `shareIn`
lessons.summary: `stateIn` and `shareIn` collect a cold upstream in a sharing coroutine owned by the supplied scope. `SharingStarted` controls when the upstream runs within that lifetime. Subscribers observe the resulting shared stream.

blocks.text: A cold repository flow runs separately for each collector. If its producer runs a query or opens a connection, two direct collectors perform that work independently. Sharing can avoid duplicating expensive production.

`shareIn` and `stateIn` launch a sharing coroutine in the supplied scope. It collects the upstream and distributes values to subscribers, so concurrent subscribers share one upstream collection.

That collection can restart during the shared stream’s lifetime. For example, `WhileSubscribed` stops and restarts the upstream as subscribers leave and return. Sharing removes per-subscriber production; it does not promise that production starts only once.

The `stateIn` overload shown here returns a hot `StateFlow` with the supplied initial value and current-value semantics. `shareIn` returns a hot `SharedFlow` with the configured replay size, including zero. Both broadcast to subscribers, but `StateFlow` guarantees a current value.

The supplied scope now owns upstream production. Individual subscribers no longer run their own upstream collections, so cancelling one subscriber does not itself cancel the sharing coroutine. The scope bounds the coroutine’s lifetime, while the sharing policy controls upstream activity.

Sharing relocates a cold upstream's lifetime from the collector to a supplied scope. The scope bounds how long the shared production can live; the `SharingStarted` policy decides when, inside that bound, it actually runs.

Cancelling the supplied scope cancels the sharing coroutine. A screen-lifetime scope bounds production to that screen; a process-lifetime scope can support production for as long as the app runs. Choose the scope from who should own that work and how long it should be able to continue.

Within the scope’s lifetime, `SharingStarted` controls when upstream collection starts and stops. The built-in policies make different trade-offs between work performed without subscribers and readiness when a subscriber arrives.
Measured on a JVM target, using a cold source that counts how many times it is started and stopped, with one subscriber that arrives and later leaves:

rows: `Eagerly`
Upstream already started and producing
Keeps running; nothing stopped
Joins the run already in progress
`Lazily`
Not started
Keeps running; nothing stopped
Joins the run already in progress
`WhileSubscribed()`
Not started
Stopped immediately; retained value kept
Upstream is started again from the beginning
`WhileSubscribed(500)`
Not started
Still running for a further 500 ms, then stopped
Started again if the grace period expired

blocks.text:
`Eagerly` starts the upstream before any subscriber arrives and does not stop it merely because subscribers leave. This spends work without observers in exchange for potentially having data ready sooner.

Without subscribers, `shareIn` retains only the configured replay. In the reported run with `replay = 0`, six values were produced before subscription and discarded; the subscriber first saw the seventh.

`Lazily` starts the upstream when the first subscriber arrives. With `shareIn`’s default buffering, that subscriber is guaranteed the emitted values; later subscribers recover only values still in replay before receiving live emissions. The upstream continues when all subscribers leave, subject to its own completion and the owning scope’s lifetime.
`WhileSubscribed` starts the upstream on the first subscriber and stops it after the last leaves. You can separately configure the delay before stopping and the delay before retained values expire.

blocks.code:
SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(
    stopTimeoutMillis = 0,                    // default: stop as soon as the last subscriber leaves
    replayExpirationMillis = Long.MAX_VALUE,  // default: keep the retained value forever
)

blocks.text: `stopTimeoutMillis` gives subscribers a grace period after the last one leaves. During that period the upstream keeps running. It does not set a polling or refresh interval, or delay values for a new subscriber.

`WhileSubscribed(5_000)` waits five seconds after the last subscriber leaves before stopping the upstream. It does not refresh every five seconds or delay a new subscriber.

A new subscriber can immediately receive what is retained: the current value from `stateIn` or replayed values from `shareIn`. With `shareIn` and `replay = 0`, it waits for a new upstream emission.

Five seconds is an application choice; the API default is zero. On Android, a configuration change can briefly remove and recreate a collector. A grace period longer than that gap avoids restarting an expensive query, while a longer absence still stops it. Choose the timeout from the gaps your application experiences and the cost of keeping or restarting the work.

Consider a state holder that derives a small value from shared history and exposes it to several screens through `stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, ...)`. Keeping the derivation running can make the result ready when a screen opens and keep it current between visits. The cost is continuing that work while nobody observes it.

A process-lifetime scope permits this lifetime, but does not require eager production. `WhileSubscribed` in the same scope would still stop upstream collection after subscribers leave. Choose the policy by the cost of ongoing work, the cost of restarting, and the need for a ready result.
Stopping the upstream and clearing retained values are separate decisions. `WhileSubscribed` first waits for `stopTimeoutMillis`; after the upstream stops, `replayExpirationMillis` begins.

blocks.code:
subscriber count:
1 -------- 0 -------------------------------- 1
           |<--- stopTimeoutMillis --->|
upstream:
running ------- still running ------- stopped ------ restarted

upstream stopped
       |<--- replayExpirationMillis --->|
                                       retained value is reset

blocks.text:
The default `replayExpirationMillis` is `Long.MAX_VALUE`, meaning retained values are kept indefinitely. With plain `WhileSubscribed()`, the upstream stops as soon as the last subscriber leaves, but its last value remains available.

In the reported run with a 200-millisecond expiration, the state still held the upstream value 150 milliseconds after stopping and had reset to `initialValue` by 750 milliseconds. For `shareIn`, expiration instead empties the replay cache. These observations illustrate the separate expiration timer.

By default, stopping the upstream does not reset `stateIn` to its initial value. The retained value remains available until an update replaces it. A returning subscriber may observe it before fresh values arrive, but a fast restarted upstream can update the state before that subscriber collects the retained value.

In the reported JVM run, the retained value arrived within a few milliseconds and the restarted upstream produced its first value 250 milliseconds later. This can support showing cached data while confirming it, but can mislead if stale data appears current. In the corresponding `shareIn(..., replay = 0)` run, the subscriber received nothing during that 250-millisecond gap because no value was retained.

Normal upstream completion does not complete the shared result. In the reported JVM run, an upstream emitted once and finished, while its subscriber stayed active and the state retained that value.

An upstream failure terminates the sharing coroutine and is handled by its owning scope; it is not emitted as failure of the `StateFlow` or `SharedFlow`. If failure handling cancels that scope, subscriber coroutines in it can be cancelled too. Put recoverable `catch` or `retry` handling before `stateIn` or `shareIn`, where it can handle the upstream failure.

The suspending `stateIn(scope)` overload has no explicit initial value. It starts the upstream and waits for its first emission, throwing `NoSuchElementException` if the upstream completes without emitting. This is useful when no sensible initial value exists, but the caller must wait.

Once a `StateFlow` is returned, its operator-fusion rules apply: adding `flowOn`, `conflate` or `distinctUntilChanged` has no effect.

Explain how the supplied scope bounds the sharing coroutine’s lifetime. Distinguish the subscriber-gap timeout in `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` from the separate replay-expiration delay, and explain why five seconds is an application choice.

lessons.title: Choosing a Stream Abstraction by Delivery Guarantees
lessons.summary: Choose among a plain value, suspending function, cold `Flow`, `StateFlow`, `SharedFlow` and `Channel` by the required production and delivery semantics. Consider who produces values, who receives them, what late observers need, and whether completed handling must be guaranteed.

blocks.text: Choose the abstraction by the behaviour consumers need. The following questions narrow the choice: whether values arrive over time, whether production is shared, and what each consumer must receive. Consider the answers together before choosing a type.

First, distinguish one value from a series over time. A value available now can be returned directly; one asynchronous result can come from a suspending function. A series requires an abstraction that represents values over time.

blocks.code:
fun currentConfig(): Config                 // one value, available now
suspend fun loadConfig(): Config            // one value, computed asynchronously
fun observeConfig(): Flow<Config>           // values over time

blocks.text: Next, decide whether each consumer should run its own producer. A cold `Flow` fits independent queries or subscriptions per collector. If consumers should share one producer, use a hot stream; `shareIn` or `stateIn` can share a cold source (see **Sharing Cold Flows with `stateIn` and `shareIn`**).
Then decide whether a current value must always be available. If a new observer needs the current state immediately, `StateFlow` provides that guarantee.

For broadcast delivery, subscribers observe the same stream rather than divide its elements between them. `SharedFlow` supports this model. Configure it according to whether late subscribers need replay, whether slow subscribers may miss values, and whether a full buffer should suspend the emitter. Also decide what is needed when nobody is subscribed.
If each element should instead go to one receiver, such as a job taken by one worker, consider a `Channel`. That delivery model differs from broadcasting to all subscribers.

Decide whether you need one value or a series, independent or shared production, a guaranteed current value, and broadcast or single-receiver delivery. Use those requirements together to choose the abstraction and its configuration.

A `Channel` distributes elements among receivers. It resembles a `BlockingQueue`, but `send` and `receive` suspend instead of blocking. Several worker coroutines can receive from the same channel, with each element taken by one worker rather than broadcast to all of them.

A shared flow offers each value to all subscribers; a channel delivers each element to one receiver. For a queue of outgoing commands processed by a worker pool, a channel divides the work among workers. Replacing it with a shared flow would offer every command to every worker. The distinction concerns who receives the element; completed handling is a separate requirement.

Receiving an element removes it from the channel; the channel does not track whether the receiver finishes processing it.

In the reported JVM measurement, one worker received elements 1, 2 and 3 from a five-element queue. It finished 1 and 2, then was cancelled part-way through 3. A replacement worker received 4 and 5, but 3 was not redelivered. Single-receiver delivery did not guarantee completed work.
Channel capacities, pipelines, fan-in, `produce` and `select` support other arrangements of producers and receivers. They do not by themselves guarantee that received work is completed.

rows: A value that is simply available
A plain value or property
Nothing observes changes
One result, computed asynchronously
A suspending function
One value, and the caller waits for it
Repeated values, produced independently per consumer
Cold `Flow`
Production is per-collector
Repeated values, one production shared by several consumers
`shareIn` or `stateIn` over the cold source
Production moves to a supplied scope
A current value every observer needs, including late ones
`StateFlow`
There is always a current value
Values broadcast to whoever is subscribed, with chosen replay
`SharedFlow`
Each value is fanned out to current subscribers; what each one receives depends on the buffering configuration
Each element taken by exactly one receiver rather than by all of them
`Channel`
Queued delivery to a single receiver, not broadcast

blocks.text:
Use the table with explicit requirements: whether late observers need current state or history, whether each occurrence matters, and whether losing a value is acceptable. Multiple candidates may fit until those requirements are settled.

The table concerns delivery. None of these types alone guarantees that the work triggered by a received value finishes.

Current authentication state fits `StateFlow` when any screen may begin observing and needs the latest state immediately.

A "sync finished" notice intended only for currently open screens fits `SharedFlow` with `replay = 0`. If later subscribers should also receive recent notices, choose a replay size; those notices remain available only until displaced by newer emissions.

A cold database-query flow shared through `stateIn` fits two screens that need current rows from one shared collection.

"`StateFlow` for state, `SharedFlow` for events" can be a starting heuristic, but the event label does not determine a delivery guarantee. For each occurrence, decide whether late observers must receive it and whether someone must eventually finish handling it.

A `SharedFlow` with `replay = 0` drops values emitted without subscribers. Replay can retain them for later subscribers, provided newer emissions have not displaced them. Neither configuration records completed handling or guarantees it. If an occurrence must eventually be handled, the stream alone cannot satisfy that requirement.

A `Channel` also cannot guarantee completed handling: the worker cancelled during element 3 left that work unfinished. A must-be-handled occurrence needs application-level tracking. It may be durable state marked handled by acknowledgement, or work persisted in a queue with handling tracked separately. If missing a notice is harmless, accepting the loss may instead be appropriate. Choose from the required outcome.
For a UI occurrence, the delivery requirement also determines how the screen models and consumes its effect. **What Delivery Guarantee Does This Occurrence Need?** applies this reasoning to Compose.

Start with one result versus a series, then independent versus shared production. For a shared stream, choose retention and start policy separately. Whether every occurrence or only the latest state matters determines whether skipping values is acceptable.

Explain the requirement before naming the type: for example, "A late observer needs the current value, so use `StateFlow`." For a one-off occurrence, distinguish replay across a subscription gap from eventual handling. A `SharedFlow` with `replay = 0` drops values without subscribers; a must-be-handled occurrence needs acknowledgement and, where required, persistent state or queued work.

units.title: Architecture as Responsibilities and Boundaries
units.summary: Architecture assigns responsibilities, controls who may change data, and sets dependency directions and lifetimes. A changing requirement helps reveal those decisions: which components need to change, and which can remain as they are? This unit uses a borrowed-items feature to examine responsibilities, interfaces and layers, including the costs of introducing boundaries.

lessons.title: What Architecture Actually Decides
lessons.summary: Architecture assigns responsibilities, ownership, dependency direction and lifetimes. Tracing a requirement through the code shows how those decisions affect the cost of change. Folder names and library choices alone do not describe that arrangement.

blocks.text: The borrowed-items service introduces a three-day grace period: an item no longer counts as overdue immediately after its due date. The calculation is small, but implementing it may require changes in several places. Which components should own this rule, and which should be able to continue unchanged?

The answer depends on decisions already present in the code: where the overdue rule lives, which components use it, and what they expect from it. These are architectural decisions. Five related concerns help explain how the arrangement works:

items: **Responsibility** — which component decides, formats, stores or coordinates a particular behaviour. *Who owns this decision?*
**Ownership** — which component may change a value rather than merely read it. *Who is allowed to write this, and through what path?*
**Dependency direction** — which component may refer to another in its code. *Who needs to know about whom, and which details should remain hidden?*
**Lifetime** — how long a responsibility and its data must exist, and what ends them. *How long does this need to live?*
**Change propagation** — which components a given requirement reaches and which it leaves alone. *What should have to change when this requirement changes?*

blocks.text: A directory listing can suggest where these responsibilities belong, but it does not show whether the code respects them. A library list says which tools the team uses, but not who owns a rule or a value. Tracing a requirement through the code reveals those relationships more clearly.

Architecture includes decisions about responsibility, ownership, dependency direction, lifetime and change propagation. Folder names and dependencies can express parts of that design, but they do not establish who owns a decision. To examine the arrangement, choose a plausible requirement change and trace the components it would affect.

Two teams are handed the same feature — a list of borrowed items showing a due date, an overdue banner and a way to renew — and both ship the same five types with the same calls between them. They arrange the files differently.

blocks.code:
Team A                          Team B
loans/                          ui/
  LoanListScreen.kt               LoanListScreen.kt
  LoanRenderer.kt                 LoanRenderer.kt
  OverduePolicy.kt              domain/
  LoanStore.kt                    OverduePolicy.kt
  DueDateFormatter.kt           data/
                                  LoanStore.kt
                                util/
                                  DueDateFormatter.kt

blocks.text:
The screen asks the policy, the renderer calls the formatter, only the store writes, and none of those components depends on the screen. Both teams have the same responsibilities and dependencies despite their different folder trees. Organizing the files differently can help readers find them without changing those relationships.

Extracting `data/` into a Gradle module adds a build boundary. That can restrict access and enforce a chosen dependency direction, but the module still needs a clear responsibility and an appropriate public API. Creating it does not by itself decide which behaviour belongs there.
Folder names can also suggest a separation that the code does not follow:

Suppose this code sits in a project with `ui`, `domain` and `data` packages. The screen still takes `LoanDatabase`, constructs `LoanStore` and decides whether an item is overdue. Changes to the database API or the overdue rule can therefore require screen edits; the `domain` package does not mediate either dependency.

Android’s recommendations advise UI components to access data through repositories rather than interact directly with data sources. Package names can help express that arrangement, but the types the screen uses and the decisions it makes show whether the arrangement is actually present.
Library choices leave similar questions open:

rows: "We use Koin, so our architecture is dependency injection"
How objects are declared and resolved at run time, and where construction happens rather than being hard-coded
Which component owns each responsibility and which components may depend on it. Koin can wire a screen directly to a database or to a repository; the team chooses that relationship.
"We use Compose, so our architecture is MVVM"
How UI is described from state and updated as that state changes
Who owns the state, how long it lives, and where the rules that produce it run

blocks.text: Frameworks and libraries support design decisions and constrain some choices, but they do not assign every responsibility for you. Clean Architecture, for example, treats frameworks as tools that the application’s rules should not depend on. Whether or not you adopt that approach, the design still needs to say which component owns each decision.

A stack such as Compose, Koin, Room and Retrofit describes the tools in use. To describe the architecture, explain the main components’ responsibilities and dependency directions, then trace a requirement change through them.

One way to assess an architecture is to examine the cost of change. Two codebases can have similar classes and call graphs while placing the overdue decision in different components. Their diagrams may look alike even though a new grace-period rule requires very different edits.
Return the grace-period requirement to two such codebases.

rows: One policy answers the question; the renderer asks it, and storage keeps dates and nothing derived from them
One function and its tests
Screen, renderer, formatter, storage, and every test that does not concern the rule
The renderer compares dates while formatting, storage writes a precomputed `is_overdue` column, and a nightly job recomputes it
The renderer, the storage write path, a migration for the stored flag, the job, and every test that fixed a date near the boundary
Very little — and the three copies of the rule can now disagree with each other

blocks.text:
The first arrangement keeps the rule in one policy; the second spreads it across rendering, storage and a nightly job. Introducing the grace period requires those copies to agree.

The second arrangement may have grown through reasonable local decisions: a precomputed flag helps performance, comparing dates while formatting is convenient, and the nightly job repairs stale values. The maintenance cost appears when a later requirement changes the rule they all implement.

A file count alone does not measure design quality. Some requirements must reach several components: a new field that users need to see, store and sync may affect every component that handles it. An arrangement that makes one change easy may make another harder. The useful question is which changes you expect and where their costs will fall.

When asked to describe an app’s architecture, explain the main components’ responsibilities and the direction of their dependencies. Explain what the opposite direction would expose each component to. Then choose a requirement that changed during the project and trace the edits it required.

lessons.title: Responsibility, Cohesion and What Changes Together
lessons.summary: Responsibilities become clearer when you identify why code would need to change. Behaviours driven by different requirements may belong in separate components; behaviours that change together may be easier to understand and maintain together.
