blocks.text: To decide what belongs in a component, consider why its behaviour might need to change. Describing a class as “managing loans” is less useful than identifying the requirements it serves: displaying due dates, applying lending rules or saving renewals.

The **single-responsibility principle (SRP)** recommends giving a module one reason to change. This is a guideline about responsibility, not class size. Robert C. Martin explains it in terms of people and the requirements they own: keep together behaviour that changes for the same reasons, and separate behaviour that changes for different reasons.

A designer may request different wording, the lending team may change a business rule, and the infrastructure team may replace storage. Labels such as “formatting” or “database work” help describe the code, but the requirement and its owner explain why it changes.

**Cohesion** describes how closely the behaviour inside a component belongs together. **Coupling** describes how much components rely on each other’s contracts or details. In this lesson, use those terms to ask whether a particular requirement can be changed in one place or needs coordinated edits elsewhere.

A useful design question is: **under which plausible requirement would these two behaviours need to change independently?** A concrete answer gives a reason to consider a boundary. If you cannot name one, keeping the behaviour together may avoid an extra contract and more navigation between files.
`LoanEntry` contains three public functions for the borrowed-items feature:

“How many things does this class do?” depends on the level of description: all three methods manage loans, but each serves a different requirement. Tracing possible changes makes that difference more concrete.

headers: What should be able to ignore it
rows: Due dates are shown as "12 March" instead of "Due in 4 days", and translated
`dueLabel`, and anything else that turns a date into text
The overdue rule and the write path
An item counts as overdue only after a three-day grace period, and never on a weekend
`isOverdue`, and every other place that compares a due date with today
The label’s wording requirements and the write path; a label that reports overdue status may need to use the revised policy
Loans move from a local table to a store with a different write path
`renew`, and everything that names the database
The label and the overdue rule

blocks.text:
The three requirements affect date presentation, lending policy and storage. A formatter, an overdue policy and a write gateway can give each a clear owner. Class size did not reveal that distinction; the possible changes did.

Separating them also makes their relationship explicit. If the label reports whether an item is overdue, it should use the lending policy’s answer rather than silently keep its own rule. The wording can change independently while the displayed status remains consistent with the policy.
Splitting code into small classes can also separate parts of the same responsibility. In this version, one class calculates the day difference and another turns it into text:

`DueDateFormatter` calculates a day difference and immediately delegates to `DueDateTextBuilder`. The additional class introduces a contract and another file to visit while following the formatting logic.

Some changes, such as different wording in `Strings`, need not touch both classes. A change from relative wording to a full calendar date, however, could require changing the value passed between them. The question is whether callers need these as separately usable responsibilities. If they do not, keeping the formatting together may be clearer; small class size alone does not justify the split.
The opposite failure is a container whose members share nothing except where they are stored.

blocks.code:
internal object Utils {
    fun formatDueDate(date: LocalDate, today: LocalDate): String =
        "Due in ${today.daysUntil(date)} days"

    fun isValidEmail(value: String): Boolean = value.matches(EmailPattern)

    fun toDatabaseTimestamp(date: LocalDate): Long =
        date.atStartOfDayIn(TimeZone.UTC).toEpochMilliseconds()

    fun shortTitle(title: String): String = title.take(40)
}

blocks.text: `Utils` groups date wording, email validation, storage conversion and title shortening under one name. These behaviours serve different requirements, so the object does little to explain their ownership. Readers looking for a lending rule or a storage conversion must first know that it lives in a general utility file. Giving the functions appropriate owners makes those responsibilities easier to find and keeps storage-specific details out of a general-purpose API.

Ownership also matters when a component can change data. State hoisting in Compose places a value according to its readers, writers and required lifetime (see **State Hoisting and the Lowest Sensible Owner**). At a larger scale, components that can write the same value need an agreed update path and consistent rules. Otherwise a requirement about that value may need to be implemented independently in both places.

Before splitting a class, identify a requirement that should change one part while leaving the others alone. Public method count and class size can guide readability decisions, but they do not establish separate responsibilities. If the proposed classes still serve one requirement together, weigh the extra contract and navigation against the readability benefit.

A broad description such as “handles loans” can make several responsibilities sound like one. Identifying the possible requests for change gives that description more substance. When lending rules and presentation requirements are owned and changed independently, code serving both needs a way to keep those changes from interfering with each other.

A boundary reflects an expectation about future changes. Separating overdue policy from date wording assumes that those requirements can change independently. Evidence from the feature helps assess that expectation: if both have changed separately several times, there is a stronger reason to separate them than there is for a storage abstraction whose only motivation is a hypothetical future replacement.

Both choices have costs. A missing boundary can require coordinated edits and may become harder to introduce as more consumers depend on the existing code. An unnecessary boundary adds contracts and navigation each time someone reads or changes the feature. Consider both costs rather than introducing every separation you can imagine; known change patterns give you a useful starting point.

SRP is the S in SOLID. The remaining principles are easier to apply through the design problems they address. For example, deciding which side of a boundary declares an abstraction is part of dependency inversion (see **Who Defines the Abstraction?**).

When explaining why you split a class, name the requirements: “The label wording changed three times last quarter, while another team owned the lending rules, so we gave those responsibilities separate places to change.” A case where you kept two functions together because they changed together can explain the same reasoning.

lessons.title: Which Way May This Dependency Point?
lessons.summary: A source dependency exists when one component refers to another in its code. The depending component relies on the other’s exposed types and behaviour. Distinguishing source dependencies from calls and data flow helps you decide which changes should cross a boundary.

blocks.text:
If `LoanRenderer` uses `LoanStore` as a parameter type, return type or constructor, it has a source dependency on `LoanStore`. Compiling that code requires the type, and understanding the renderer requires knowing the parts of the store’s contract it uses.

That does not imply a dependency in the other direction. The store may refer to a renderer, or it may know nothing about rendering. Deciding which references are permitted helps determine which components can be changed or reused independently.
Keep three directions separate when examining this relationship:

rows: Source dependency
Which component refers to the other’s types or declarations in its source code
The imports and the signatures
Call direction
Which component invokes the other while the program runs
The call stack
Data flow
Which way values actually travel
The arguments and return values, which frequently travel back along a call

blocks.text: A call and its source dependency often point the same way, but callbacks can separate them. The source dependency determines which declarations a component relies on; call direction and data flow describe how that relationship is used at runtime.

A component that depends on another is exposed to changes in the contract it uses. Private implementation changes can remain hidden, while a changed parameter type, result type or promised behaviour may require caller edits. Dependency direction matters when those contracts change for reasons the caller does not share. Frequent internal changes alone do not mean every caller will change too.

Clean Architecture describes source dependencies as pointing inward, towards application policies. That direction makes sense within its particular arrangement of layers. For a codebase without those layers, ask the more general question: which component should refer to the other, and what changes would that reference expose it to?
The borrowed-items screen reads data from a sync service. This version shares the service’s payload type directly with the renderer:

Sharing the type avoids a second model and a mapper. Any field declared in `LoanPayload` is directly available to code using it.

Now the service changes `due` to `dueAt` with time-zone information and replaces `renewals` with a nested object. Presentation requirements may be unchanged, but the renderer must adapt to the new date field. Other payload consumers and tests that construct the type may also need edits.

The renderer depends on the sync service’s representation, so a wire-format change reaches presentation code. One alternative is for the renderer to use a presentation-owned type, with translation at the sync boundary.

That adds a type and a mapper, and fields needed on both sides must be represented in both. The tradeoff is whether maintaining that translation costs less than adapting presentation whenever the service’s representation changes.
A shared helper can obscure ownership in a similar way. Both storage and presentation use dates, so their functions are placed together:

The functions share a date type but serve different requirements: one controls display wording, the other controls storage representation. A package called `common` or `util` does not explain who owns either decision. Keeping them together means readers must sort through both responsibilities even when they need only one; separating their owners can make that distinction clearer.

Shared code is useful when both callers need the same concept. A business-day rule, for example, may legitimately serve both a renderer and a lending policy; naming that rule gives each caller a deliberate dependency.

If the two functions instead serve independently changing requirements, keeping each with its owner may be clearer. Similar code does not always mean a shared responsibility: compare the reasons it would change before merging it.
A callback shows how calls and data can move against a source dependency. This loader reports each batch to a function supplied by its caller:

Trace the three directions separately. The **source dependency** points one way only: the screen names the loader, and the loader names nothing about screens. **Control** crosses in both directions — the screen calls `load`, and the loader then calls back into code the screen supplied. **Data** travels from the loader to the screen, against the source dependency. Replace the screen with something else entirely and the loader does not notice, because it never knew what was on the other end of `onBatch`.

The callback allows control and data to travel from the loader to screen code without the loader referring to a screen type. Clean Architecture uses the same distinction between runtime control and source dependencies. Choosing which side defines a contract can direct those source dependencies even when calls go the other way; that is the subject of dependency inversion (see **Who Defines the Abstraction?**).

A callback into code supplied by the screen does not necessarily create a source dependency on the screen. Here the loader accepts a function type and can compile without `LoanListScreen`. To identify a source dependency cycle, inspect the referenced types and declarations rather than infer it from calls crossing in both directions.

A source dependency cycle occurs when components refer to each other, directly or through other components. Inside one compilation module, such references can be legal, but they make it harder to move or reuse either component on its own. A cycle across build-module dependencies can also prevent the build from having a valid dependency order.

The cycle does not mean every edit to one component must change the other. The maintenance risk is that their contracts are intertwined, so changes to those contracts can require coordinated edits. Examine which responsibilities created the references before deciding how to break the cycle.

Prefer depending on contracts that remain stable for the kinds of change your component needs to absorb. A lending rule unchanged for three years may be more predictable than a partner’s JSON format that changes quarterly. That history helps explain why presentation might use an application-facing contract rather than the wire format directly; calling one side “low-level” does not settle the choice.

For each pair of components, identify the changes a direct dependency would expose the caller to and the cost of avoiding that exposure. In the payload example, a presentation-owned type and mapper isolate wire-format changes, but both must be maintained. Sharing the payload avoids the mapper and leaves the renderer responsible for adapting to relevant format changes. Which cost is preferable depends on how the two sides change.

A build module can enforce part of a dependency rule. If screen types are unavailable on the sync module’s compile classpath, sync code cannot refer to them directly. Within a shared module, package organization alone does not enforce that separation; code review and access restrictions must help protect it. A module is one way to enforce a chosen direction, with build costs of its own.

For two components, explain which one refers to the other, which contract changes could affect its caller, and what reversing or removing that dependency would cost. For example, keeping database details out of the UI can isolate schema changes, but may require an application-facing type and a mapper that someone must maintain.

lessons.title: When an Interface Is a Boundary, and When It Is Only Indirection
lessons.summary: An interface separates a consumer from a concrete implementation. Its usefulness as a design boundary depends on the contract: does it express the consumer’s needs, hide implementation details, and allow the two sides to change independently? Weigh that benefit against the added contract and navigation.

blocks.text: `LoanListScreen` constructs `LoanStore` directly. The team introduces a `LoanStore` interface, renames the concrete class `FileLoanStore`, and passes the interface to the screen. The screen now depends on a contract rather than that concrete class. To assess the change, examine what the contract still requires the screen to know about storage.

If the interface exposes the file store’s rows and transaction methods, the screen still needs to understand those storage details. If it instead describes the operations the screen needs, `FileLoanStore` may change its internal format without requiring screen edits.

A useful boundary depends on that contract: who defines it, which requirements it serves, and which implementation changes it can hide. The `interface` declaration makes substitution possible, but those decisions determine what the substitution is useful for.

Martin Fowler recommends designing interfaces around their clients’ needs rather than copying an implementation. An interface copied from a single concrete class can add a second contract to maintain without establishing a useful separation between responsibilities.

Before extracting an interface, identify which implementation changes it should hide from the consumer. Also consider which changes to the consumer’s needs would require revisiting the contract. If both sides would still move together for the changes you expect, weigh the benefit of substitution against the extra API and navigation.
Here is the interface that team extracted.

`LoanStore` exposes rows and a transaction pair. Those choices describe storage operations rather than the screen’s lending requirements, so the screen must know how to use that storage-oriented contract.

If writes become suspending, both the interface and its implementation must change, and callers may need to adapt. A new column may instead change `LoanRow` without adding a method. The relevant question is which details the consumer still shares with storage, not whether every storage edit touches both files.

The interface allows another implementation to be supplied, but it still exposes a storage-oriented API. If that API changes for file-store reasons, the screen may need to adapt. The additional contract also has maintenance costs:

items: Another name in the codebase, which every reader has to learn and keep distinct from the implementation's name.
Another file and another step when following a call to its implementation.
A contract to document and maintain alongside the implementation when its API changes.
An abstraction whose intended role readers need to understand, especially if only one implementation exists.

blocks.text: Now the product needs loans to come from either on-device history or an exported archive, without the screen choosing the source. The sources have different failure behaviour and refresh rules. A lending-oriented contract can describe what callers need while leaving those source decisions behind it:

`LoanSource` describes loans, a due-date window and a renewal outcome. Callers no longer need row or transaction operations. Defining the contract from those lending needs allows an archive format or on-device schema to change while the operations offered to the screen remain the same.

Multiple implementations make that separation useful here, but their count is not the deciding factor. One implementation can also hide storage details if its contract remains appropriate for its consumers.

An interface can also make tests easier by letting a test supply a controlled substitute. That is a real benefit, even when only one production implementation exists. The contract determines how much setup and storage knowledge the test still needs.

A fake with rows and transaction methods leaves the consumer test coupled to a storage-oriented API. A lending-oriented contract can let the test exercise screen behaviour without a file or database. Consider both the testing benefit and the contract’s maintenance cost rather than treating an interface as sufficient evidence of a well-placed boundary.

An interface removes a consumer’s direct reference to a concrete implementation, but may leave it dependent on that implementation’s concepts. If the contract simply mirrors storage methods, relevant API changes can still reach the screen. Assess the changes it hides and the substitution it enables, then weigh those benefits against the extra contract.

When one implementation already meets the consumer’s needs and no independent contract is needed, delaying the abstraction may be reasonable. Compare the costs of introducing it now with the risks of extracting it later:

headers: Add it when a concrete need appears
rows: When the cost is paid
An extra contract now, with maintenance and navigation costs while it remains in use
Extraction work when a concrete need appears; subsequent contract maintenance still applies
What the contract is designed from
Current consumer needs and one known implementation; the contract may mirror that implementation
Additional real requirements that help distinguish the common contract from implementation details
The risk
The abstraction remains unused as a boundary but continues to require upkeep
"Later" arrives with several consumers already coupled to the concrete type, making the extraction wider than it would have been

blocks.text: Earlier agreement can be valuable when another team is building the implementation or different platforms need to provide it. Both sides can then work against the same contract. Published libraries also have consumers who cannot immediately coordinate an interface extraction with their maintainers; Fowler identifies this as a reason to design public contracts earlier. These are concrete needs to weigh against maintenance cost, rather than a general possibility that an interface may someday be useful.

A single implementation can still provide a useful boundary. `LoanHistoryRepository` may have only `LocalLoanHistoryRepository`, yet offer lending operations such as recording a return, checking whether an item was borrowed and reading loans in a defined order.

If the contract exposes no database-specific types or behaviour, storage can change while consumers continue using those operations. The contract’s vocabulary and the changes it hides matter more than the implementation count.

Whether an abstraction is a boundary at all is a separate question from *where* it should live and which side should declare it so the dependency arrow points the way you intended; that second question is dependency inversion (see **Who Defines the Abstraction?**).

When explaining why you would keep a concrete dependency, describe the condition: the proposed contract would copy the implementation, anticipated changes would still require coordinated edits, and no consumer needs an independently defined API. Then identify what could justify an abstraction later, such as another source, different platform implementations, a separately developed implementation or a shared consumer contract.

lessons.title: Layers as One Answer, and What They Cost
lessons.summary: Layers group responsibilities under dependency rules. Each added layer introduces costs such as contracts, mapping and navigation, so evaluate what it isolates and whether that benefit is useful for the feature. A layer count alone does not establish design quality.

blocks.text: A **layer** groups components with related responsibilities and defines how they may depend on other layers. In a UI-and-data arrangement, for example, UI code can use data-layer APIs while data code remains independent of presentation. A shared dependency rule makes the arrangement easier to describe and check.

Layering is one way to organize boundaries. A useful design can have two layers or a different arrangement of responsibilities; a strict-looking stack can still have code that crosses its intended boundaries. Each additional layer needs a purpose that justifies its contracts and other maintenance costs.

Adding a layer is useful when it isolates a responsibility that needs to change independently. If it merely forwards calls and copies the same data, it may add maintenance work without reducing the changes reaching its neighbours.

Android’s guide recommends UI and data layers and treats a domain layer as optional. Its recommendations describe use cases as helpful in larger apps when business logic is reused across ViewModels or a particular ViewModel becomes too complex. The guidance also asks teams to adapt recommendations to their apps. Those conditions help decide whether an additional layer has work to own.
An additional layer can introduce concrete maintenance costs:

items: a second representation of the same concept, and the mapping code that translates between them;
forwarding methods that exist only to pass a call through;
another name for something the codebase already had, and a vocabulary a new engineer must learn before reading one screen;
more files to open to follow one feature end to end, and more places a single change lands;
a contract that has to be agreed, documented and kept accurate.

blocks.text: This version adds a forwarding gateway between the borrowed-items screen and its source, together with a separate presentation model:

The card now needs to show how many renewals remain, and the service provides a renewal limit. `Loan` gains a field, `LoanSummary` gains the corresponding field, `toSummary` copies it, and the card reads it.

For this change, the separate model does not isolate presentation from the new data: the field must pass through both types and the mapper. The gateway also only forwards the call shown here. These additions need a benefit beyond duplicating the data and call path.

The tradeoff changes when storage and presentation need different representations. Storage may keep a row version, soft-delete flag, server ID and epoch-millisecond due date for sync. The card instead needs a due state that accounts for the grace period and a remaining-renewals value derived from stored fields.

blocks.code:
internal data class StoredLoan(
    val id: String,
    val serverId: String?,
    val title: String,
    val dueAtMillis: Long,
    val renewals: Int,
    val renewalLimit: Int,
    val rowVersion: Long,
    val deleted: Boolean,
)

internal data class LoanSummary(
    val id: String,
    val title: String,
    val due: DueState,          // Upcoming, DueToday or Overdue(days)
    val renewalsRemaining: Int,
)

blocks.text:
A mapper between these representations can keep sync bookkeeping out of the card. Adding a storage-only field need not change `LoanSummary`, while changing the grace period can change how `DueState` is computed without changing stored data. Filtering deleted loans can also happen before the screen receives them.

The number of layers has not changed. Their value here comes from translating between storage and presentation needs, rather than copying an identical representation.

headers: When the two representations are the same
rows: What the boundary isolates
Nothing — every field is transcribed unchanged
Storage bookkeeping and representation from the fields the card needs
What it costs
A type, a mapper, a forwarding class, a navigation hop
The same type, mapper and hop
What a new field costs
Two declarations and a mapping line, for no isolation
One declaration for a field used only on its own side; shared needs can still require mapping edits
Verdict
Mapping cost without isolation for the change shown
Mapping that isolates distinct storage and presentation needs

blocks.text:
A well-placed boundary can improve testability by reducing the unrelated details needed to exercise one side. The due-state rules, for example, can be tested without a database or sync protocol if their inputs and results do not expose those details.

An extra layer does not guarantee that isolation. If its contract still requires the same storage setup, tests may gain another call to pass through without becoming simpler. Evaluate what the boundary lets a test supply or omit, alongside its other benefits and costs.

A layer count does not show whether responsibilities are well separated. A forwarding layer adds a contract and another step through the code; inspect what it isolates or otherwise enables before keeping it. Judge each layer by its purpose and cost, rather than assuming that a taller stack is better.

A layer describes logical responsibilities and dependency rules. A Gradle module is a build unit with its own configuration and dependencies; it can also enforce visibility restrictions. Aligning modules with layers can help enforce the intended separation, but a layer may span modules and a module may contain more than one layer. Module granularity also affects build performance and maintenance.

A lending feature can use `LoanHistoryRepository` while `LocalLoanHistoryRepository` keeps database details under `data/local`, all within one module. The contract can separate their responsibilities even without a separate compilation boundary.

Android’s recommendations allow small apps to organize data-layer types in a package or module. The modularization guide also notes that modules add build complexity and boilerplate, and that small projects may not gain enough scalability or build-time benefit to justify them. Choose a module when its enforcement or build role is useful, rather than requiring one for every logical boundary.

The familiar concentric Clean Architecture diagram illustrates dependency direction rather than prescribing exactly four layers. Its author describes the circles as schematic and allows other counts. The dependency rule is the subject of **Clean Architecture: the Dependency Rule, Not the Diagram**.

The transfer, storage and display split used above is an example of mapping cost, not a prescription. Deciding which representations a real feature should have, where the translation belongs, and how failure crosses those boundaries is a design problem of its own; **Model and Error Boundaries: What May Cross** works through it.

To justify adding a layer, name the responsibility it will own, the independent change it should isolate, and its dependency direction. Then describe the types, mapping and navigation it adds, and explain why the benefit is worth those costs. The same reasoning can justify keeping the current arrangement when the proposed layer has too little to own.

units.title: Screen State Holders, ViewModel and UI State
units.summary: A screen-level state holder produces the state the screen renders and handles the intentions the UI reports. Choose its implementation and lifetime from those responsibilities: in-memory retention does not provide persistence, and work that must outlive the holder needs another owner. UI state can take several shapes; the right model depends on which combinations the screen needs to show.

lessons.title: What a Screen State Holder Is Responsible For
lessons.summary: A screen-level state holder owns the screen’s current state, accepts user intentions, and turns application results into state the UI can render. ViewModel is one implementation of that responsibility; choose it when the lifetime provided by its owner fits the screen’s needs.

blocks.text: A borrowed-items screen lists loans with their due dates, marks the overdue ones, lets the reader narrow the list to the overdue ones only, and offers a renewal control on each row. The rendering composable receives one immutable value describing all of that and reports what the reader did; something outside the Composition has to supply that value and receive those reports.
Before choosing `ViewModel` or another holder type, identify what the component will own and how long it needs to live. For this screen, its responsibilities are:

items: **Own the state the screen renders.** There is one current value describing what the reader is looking at, and this component is the only one that may produce it.

**Accept the intentions the UI reports.** The reader renewed a loan, chose a filter, asked for a retry. Those arrive as reports of what happened, not as instructions about what the state should become.
**Obtain the application results the screen needs.** Loans come from somewhere — a store, a service, a cache. Getting hold of them, and reacting when they change, belongs here.

**Turn those results into current screen state.** A loan record is not a row. Deciding that a loan four days past its due date renders as overdue, and what the renewal control says when renewal is not allowed, is work this component does.
**Own the state transitions.** Changes from one current screen value to the next happen here, so a wrong value has a clear starting point for investigation.

blocks.text: Together, these responsibilities define a **screen-level state holder**. They describe what the component does without requiring a particular base class or library. The implementation still needs a lifetime that matches the state it owns.

`ViewModel` is one implementation. A host can retain it when the UI is recreated, making it useful for screen state that must survive those events. A state holder can also be a plain object retained by a longer-lived owner, or an object remembered by a composable when its state only needs to last as long as that composable. The responsibility remains the same; the owner determines how long the object is retained.

A screen-level state holder owns the screen’s current state, handles user intentions, obtains application results, and turns them into state the UI can render. `ViewModel` is one implementation. Choose the implementation and owner whose lifetime matches the state’s requirements.
For each value on the loans screen, ask who reads it, who changes it, and how long it needs to live. Those requirements lead to different owners:

rows: Whether the "how renewals work" help panel is expanded
One composable draws it, the same composable's toggle writes it, nothing else looks at it
Local, remembered inside the composable that draws it
Nothing outside the panel reads it, and it is no longer needed after the panel is gone. Moving it to the screen holder would add a field and a transition without satisfying another requirement.
The text in the search box, before the reader submits it
The field draws it and writes it; on this screen nobody else reacts until submission
Local, unless the requirement changes
Ownership follows readers and writers. Add a requirement — the count in the header must update as the reader types — and the readers change, so the answer changes with them
The chosen filter and the loan rows currently being rendered
Several sibling composables read them; only one component may change them; they must survive the screen being re-created
The screen-level state holder
Several readers share one current value, with one writer and a lifetime longer than any individual composable’s.
How many items the reader currently has borrowed, shown as a badge on several destinations
Read by this screen and by two others; updated when a borrowing or return changes the count
A longer-lived holder shared by those destinations
The count must remain available when this screen is gone. A holder shared by the destinations gives them one current value instead of separate copies that can disagree.

blocks.text:
The help panel and search draft can remain local because, under these requirements, no other component needs them. If another part of the screen begins reacting to the draft, its owner may need to move higher.

The badge has the opposite requirement: several destinations need the same count even when the loans screen is gone. A holder scoped only to that screen would have too short a lifetime.

The borrowed-items badge can use a plain state holder shared by the destinations. It publishes the current count, updates it in one place, and reads results from a store. Its owner retains it after an individual destination is destroyed.

No framework base class is required for that responsibility. What matters is that the chosen owner lives long enough for every destination that uses the count.
These two implementations expose the same screen contract. The plain class relies on its caller to retain it and supply a scope; the `ViewModel` is retained by a host-provided owner.

How either object is actually constructed and handed to the screen — by a factory, by a container, by the caller — is a separate decision with its own trade-offs. An application may well supply both kinds through the same container; that is a fact about its wiring, not part of what a state holder is.
Keep references tied to a particular UI instance out of a screen holder that may outlive that instance. Rendering details also belong with the UI that uses them:

items: A composable, a `View`, or any other UI instance.
A rendering decision: a colour, a dimension, a layout choice, a scroll offset that only means something while a particular UI exists.
An `Activity`, a `Fragment` or any other host object it could outlive.
A framework `Context` retained so that the holder can format the text it puts in the state.

blocks.text: A ViewModel may survive the Activity or Fragment instance that originally used it. Retaining a reference to that instance, or to a `Context` or `Resources` tied to it, can keep obsolete UI objects alive. The holder would also be using dependencies associated with a UI that has been replaced.

A platform-backed abstraction, such as a text provider, clock, or permission checker, can still be a valid dependency. Check the implementation as well as the interface: wrapping an Activity reference in an abstraction does not change its lifetime. The dependency must remain valid for as long as the holder uses it.

Putting every UI value into a ViewModel can give unrelated state the same owner and lifetime. The help panel’s expansion can stay local, while a badge shared by several destinations needs an owner that outlives one screen. Choose from the state’s readers, writers, and lifetime requirements.
Separating the responsibility from the `ViewModel` class makes the design choice clearer: which implementation and owner should retain this state, and for how long?
Match the implementation to the lifetime the requirement needs:

items: an object a composable remembers, when the responsibility genuinely dies with that piece of UI;
a plain class owned by something else, when the lifetime should be that something else's and not a framework's;
a `ViewModel`, when the owner a host supplies for it is exactly the lifetime the screen needs;
an application-lifetime holder, when several screens share one truth and it must survive any of them being destroyed.

blocks.text: Longer-lived owners retain state and dependencies for longer. An application-lifetime holder is appropriate when several screens need the same current value after any one screen is destroyed, but it also keeps that state for the life of the process. Choose the shortest lifetime that satisfies the requirement; **Choosing an Owner From the Lifetime the Requirement Needs** works through the options.

The holder owns *presentation state*. It consumes application results and derives the current screen value from them. Data sourcing, caching policy, conflict resolution, and reusable business rules belong in the data layer or, where needed, a domain layer.

Keeping these responsibilities separate lets a change to storage policy remain independent of a change to what the screen displays.

When explaining what a ViewModel is for, start with its responsibility: produce current screen state, handle intentions, and own the transitions. Then explain why its owner’s lifetime fits the screen. A local help-panel flag or a badge shared across destinations can illustrate why some state belongs elsewhere.

lessons.title: The ViewModel Owner: Lifetime Is Not Persistence
lessons.summary: A ViewModel is retained in a ViewModelStore belonging to an owner, such as an Activity, Fragment, or scoped navigation entry. The store’s retention and clearing determine its lifetime. Following the loans screen through seven events separates ownership, lifetime, and persistence: who changes a value, when it is lost from memory, and how it can be restored.

blocks.text: The loans screen’s state is held in memory by a `ViewModel`. To know which events it survives, identify the owner that retains the ViewModel’s store. The class name alone does not tell you whether a navigation event removes that owner or leaves it in place.
The retention relationship is:

blocks.code:
LoansViewModel
      is stored in ->  ViewModelStore          (a map of ViewModels, keyed)
      which belongs to ->  ViewModelStoreOwner (an Activity, a Fragment, a back-stack entry)
      whose lifetime decides ->  when the store is cleared

ViewModelStore.clear()  ->  every stored ViewModel is cleared  ->  its state is gone

blocks.text: The owner retains the `ViewModelStore` across configuration changes and clears it when the owner is permanently removed. For example, a recreated Activity reconnects to its previous store, while a finishing Activity clears it. Clearing the store clears its ViewModels and invokes their cleanup, including `onCleared()`.

Ask two questions: **which owner holds this ViewModel, and does the event retain or clear its store?** If the store is retained, the same ViewModel and its in-memory state remain available. If the store is cleared, that ViewModel is no longer retained there. Leaving the Composition alone does not decide either outcome.

A ViewModel is retained in a `ViewModelStore` belonging to a `ViewModelStoreOwner`. Retaining the store preserves its ViewModels; clearing it ends their retention. Identify the owner and what happens to its store before deciding whether an event preserves screen state.

The loans screen can encounter these seven events. For navigation rows, assume it has a destination-scoped owner; the later example shows how Navigation 3 installs that scope. In each case, check whether the ViewModel’s store is retained.

headers: Which owner is being asked about
Is it still holding its store?
rows: The screen recomposes, possibly many times
Unchanged — recomposition never touches the owner
Yes; nothing asked it to clear
Survives. Recomposition does not clear this owner’s store.
The composable that reads the state leaves the Composition while its destination stays on the back stack
Still the destination's owner
Yes; a composable leaving is not its owner being destroyed
Survives, and is there again when the destination composes again
Android re-creates the UI for a configuration change
The Activity or Fragment, re-created for the new configuration
Yes — the owner is required to hand the new instance the previous store
Survives because the recreated owner reconnects to the retained store.
The reader navigates forward and this destination stays on the back stack
This destination's entry, still on the stack
Yes; nothing removed it
Survives. The retained holder still has its current state when the screen is shown again.
The destination is popped and its entry removed
That entry, now being destroyed permanently
No — it clears its store
Is no longer retained, and the cleared ViewModel receives `onCleared()`.
The system kills the process while the app is in the background, and Android later restores the task
A new owner, created when the destination is re-created in a new process
No — the old store died with the process; the new owner starts with an empty one
Is gone. The re-created screen can read back small values it recorded in saved state, such as `SavedStateHandle` entries, because Android restored this task; everything else has to be reloaded
The task itself is gone — the user swiped it away from Recents, the app was force-stopped, or the device rebooted — and the app starts fresh
A new owner in a new task
No — a new, empty store, and no saved state from the old task to restore
Is gone, and so is the old task's saved state. Only durable storage, such as a database, brings anything back

blocks.text: The same ViewModel class can have different lifetimes depending on the owner used to obtain it. A destination being popped clears an entry-scoped store, but does not by itself finish the Activity that could own a different instance.

**Which owner holds the store is decided where the ViewModel is obtained, not by the class.** The same `LoansViewModel` class can be stored by three different Android owners, and each gives it a different lifetime:

items: **Activity.** An Activity retains its store across configuration recreation and clears it when it finishes. An Activity-scoped ViewModel therefore remains available while that Activity’s retained scope exists.

**Fragment.** A Fragment has its own `ViewModelStore`. The store is retained across configuration recreation and cleared when the Fragment is permanently destroyed; destroying only its view does not clear that store.

**Navigation back-stack entry.** With Navigation 3 entry scoping installed, each entry has an owner whose store remains while that entry is retained on the back stack. Removing the entry clears its store.

blocks.text:
In Navigation 3, pass `rememberSaveableStateHolderNavEntryDecorator()` followed by `rememberViewModelStoreNavEntryDecorator()` to `NavDisplay`. The latter provides a `ViewModelStoreOwner` for each entry; ViewModels obtained inside that entry’s content are scoped to it.

Navigating forward retains the earlier entry and its store. Popping that entry clears the store. Without the ViewModel decorator, a ViewModel obtained in the content uses the available surrounding owner rather than gaining this entry scope.

“Survives configuration changes” does not specify the complete lifetime. Activity-, Fragment-, and entry-scoped ViewModels can all survive configuration recreation, yet be cleared by different events. Name the owner before explaining what navigation or finishing an Activity will do.
Ownership, lifetime, and persistence answer different questions about the same state value:

rows: Ownership
Who may change this value, and through what path?
The screen-level holder, through its named intention functions, and nothing else
Lifetime
When does that owner disappear?
When the back-stack entry is removed and its store is cleared
Persistence
How does the value come back after the owner is gone?
It does not, unless something else recorded enough to rebuild it

blocks.text:
Moving state into a ViewModel can extend its in-memory lifetime across UI recreation. A half-filled renewal form can remain available after rotation because the recreated UI uses the retained ViewModel.

That value still lives inside the process. If the system kills the process, the old owner, store, and ViewModel are lost. Retention across configuration changes does not by itself provide process-death restoration.

Moving state out of the Composition changes its owner and may change its lifetime. It does not make that state durable. If the reader must recover it after process death, another mechanism must record enough to restore or reload it.

Saved state records a small amount of transient UI state. `SavedStateHandle` serves a ViewModel, while `rememberSaveable` serves state in the Composition. When Android restores a task after system-initiated process death, the recreated screen can use those saved values to reconstruct its UI.

Saved state is tied to the task. Removing the task from Recents, force-stopping the app, or rebooting the device removes that restoration path. For data that must remain available on a fresh launch, use durable application storage, such as a database. A state holder’s in-memory lifetime does not replace either mechanism.

For “Does a ViewModel survive this event?”, identify its owner, explain whether the store is retained, and distinguish retention from restoration. Configuration recreation can keep the same ViewModel; process death loses it and requires saved state or durable storage to reconstruct what the screen needs.

lessons.title: Modelling the Current UI State
lessons.summary: The screen renders one current immutable value, but its shape depends on the screen’s requirements. A data class can describe independent facts that coexist; a sealed hierarchy can enforce mutually exclusive modes. Modelling the loans screen both ways shows how each affects invalid combinations and partial updates.

blocks.text: The screen renders one current immutable value, and the holder produces it. Immutability is what lets the renderer treat each new value as a complete description of what to draw rather than as a set of changes to apply.

The loans screen needs to represent an initial load, a loan list, a selected filter, a failure with no content, and a failed refresh while useful loans remain visible. Several models can describe those situations, but they make different combinations and updates easy to express.

Ask **which combinations the screen needs to represent, and which combinations the product forbids.** A settings form and a payment confirmation can have different answers. Choose the state shape from those requirements rather than applying one Kotlin construct to every screen.

A model that allows invalid combinations leaves the holder and renderer responsible for preventing or handling them. A model with mutually exclusive variants can prevent those combinations, but updates must account for the current variant and what data belongs in the next one.

Choose the shape of the current immutable UI state from the combinations the screen requires. Independent fields make partial updates straightforward but may allow invalid combinations. Exclusive variants can rule out those combinations, while requiring updates to handle the current mode explicitly.
A data class can represent the loans screen as independent fields:

blocks.code:
internal data class LoansUiState(
    val loans: List<LoanRow>,
    val filter: LoanFilter,
    val isLoading: Boolean,
    val errorMessage: String?,
)

blocks.text: And the same screen, the same requirements, as a hierarchy of mutually exclusive states.

In the sealed version, a failed refresh is represented by `refreshFailed` inside `Content`. Using top-level `Error` would hide the loans, even though the requirement says to keep them visible. The table shows how that distinction affects the two models.

rows: First load, nothing to show yet
`isLoading = true`, empty list, no error — three fields have to agree
`Loading`. One value, nothing to coordinate
Loans on screen
Populated list with the flags off
`Content`, and the renderer knows the list is there without checking
Load failed with nothing to show
Error set, list empty, loading off — and the renderer has to work out that this means a full-screen failure
`Error`. The renderer branches once and is done
A refresh fails while loans are on screen
Natural: set the error, leave the list alone. The fields are independent, which is exactly what this requirement needs
Keep `Content` and update `refreshFailed`. The failure needs its own field because it can coexist with the loans; switching to top-level `Error` would hide them.
The filter changes while a refresh is running
One field copied; everything else untouched
While content remains visible during a refresh, copy the filter in `Content`. `Loading` has no filter field, so preserving a filter during the initial load would require changing this model.
How much the renderer must branch
Reads several fields and reconstructs the screen's mode from their combination, on every render and in every consumer
Branches on the type once; each branch then has exactly the data that branch needs

blocks.text:
A sealed hierarchy fits modes that genuinely exclude each other. A data class fits facts that can be true and editable at the same time. A codebase may use both because its screens have different requirements.

For example, `ReminderSettingsUiState` can be a data class containing reminder time, days of notice, delivery channel, and quiet hours. The reader can configure all of these together; selecting one does not put the screen into a mode that excludes the others.
The data class also permits combinations that may conflict with the product’s rules:

blocks.code:
LoansUiState(
    loans = listOf(overdueLoan, dueSoonLoan),  // there is content
    filter = LoanFilter.Overdue,
    isLoading = true,                          // and it is loading
    errorMessage = "Could not reach the library",  // and it failed
)

blocks.text:
If the product forbids content, loading, and an error from appearing together, this value violates that rule. The compiler accepts it because the fields are independent.

A header might use `isLoading` to show a spinner while the list uses `loans` to show rows, leaving the UI inconsistent with the intended mode. A failure handler can produce this accidentally by setting `errorMessage` and forgetting to clear `isLoading`. The holder must enforce the invariant if the type does not.

The sealed version prevents that exact combination: `Loading` cannot also contain loans and an error. Updates must then account for which variant is current. A refresh failure can be copied into an existing `Content`, but an update outside `Content` needs a separate decision.

Adding another top-level mode can require changes wherever the renderer branches on the state. These checks are useful when the modes really are exclusive; they add work when the screen mostly needs independent partial updates.

Use a top-level `Error` when failure leaves the screen with nothing useful to show. If only one region fails, keep the useful content visible and model the failure in that region. Otherwise, a missing badge can unnecessarily become a blank screen.

Some screens contain regions that load and fail independently. The loans screen also shows membership status from another source. If that read fails, the membership line can show the failure while the loan list remains usable.
Represent that independent region with its own state nested inside the screen state:

Model a failure at the level of the part that failed. Here, an unreadable membership record affects the membership line; the loans remain listed and renewable. A screen-level `Error` would hide content that is still useful. The field’s comment records why membership has its own state.

“Make illegal states unrepresentable” means using the type to prevent combinations the product forbids. It can remove checks that would otherwise be repeated by each consumer.

The cost depends on the model. An elaborate hierarchy can require more branches and more decisions about which data to carry between variants. A nested data class or region state may preserve the necessary invariant while keeping ordinary partial updates straightforward.

For each screen, explain what its chosen shape represents well. Exclusive modes suit requirements where overlapping states would produce an incoherent UI. Independent fields suit simultaneous facts, such as the settings in a form. A dashboard may combine both by giving each independently loading region its own state.

How a failure is represented as it crosses out of the data layer — whether a load returns a result type, throws, or is modelled in the application's own vocabulary — is a different decision made at a different boundary (see **Model and Error Boundaries: What May Cross**). The UI state only models the error the screen has to render. What Compose can conclude from an immutable type is covered in **Immutability in Kotlin vs. What Compose Needs**.

When comparing sealed and data-class UI state, use a particular screen. Identify required and forbidden combinations, and any region that fails independently. Explain one cost of the chosen model: an invalid combination the holder must prevent, or an update that must account for several possible variants.

lessons.title: State Out, Intentions In
lessons.summary: The holder exposes current state read-only and receives intentions through named functions. It decides how those intentions change the screen. Exposing the mutable container gives callers another write path, allowing them to bypass transition rules and making incorrect state harder to trace.

blocks.text: The loans holder controls state changes only if its API keeps writes inside it. If callers can also assign the state, they can bypass its transition rules and become additional writers.
The contract keeps state and intentions moving in these directions:

blocks.code:
current screen state
        |
        v
       UI                      (read-only: the UI renders it and cannot change it)

reader's intention
        |
        v
screen state holder            (one named path in)
        |
        v
state transition, work
        |
        v
new current screen state

blocks.text:
Within the composable tree, state travels down and callbacks report interactions to the owner. The same direction applies between the screen UI and its state holder. Here, handling an interaction can start work, read application data, and produce new screen state.

If the UI also writes that state directly, it can bypass those decisions. The result is another place where transitions are defined, rather than one owner that coordinates them.

An intention describes what the reader did: “the reader chose the overdue filter.” The holder then decides what that means for current state and any related work. A contract phrased only as “set this field” emphasizes the current assignment rather than the interaction’s meaning.

State leaves the holder read-only; intentions enter through named functions; the holder decides what they mean and produces the next state. This keeps the rendering UI from bypassing the holder’s transition rules.
Exposing a `MutableStateFlow` lets UI callers assign state directly, even when the class is internal to one module:
That additional write path creates three problems:

items: **Updates can overwrite each other.** The holder may publish a refresh result while the UI assigns state from a click. If these changes are not coordinated, the later assignment can discard the earlier one. The resulting bug depends on the order in which the updates arrive.

**Callers can bypass transition rules.** The holder may require a supported filter, or allow `Loading` only when there is no content. The public mutable flow does not enforce those rules. The caller above can publish an empty `Content` while loading is still in progress, whether or not that transition is allowed.

**Incorrect state has more possible sources.** With writes kept inside the holder, investigation starts with its transitions. If callers can also assign state, finding the cause requires locating those assignments and checking the order in which they ran.

blocks.text: Keep the mutable flow private and expose a read-only view, with functions for the interactions the UI can report:

The holder updates its private `MutableStateFlow`; callers receive a `StateFlow` view. They can read current state and report interactions through functions, but cannot assign a new value through that public flow.
Function names can make the distinction between an interaction and an assignment clearer:

rows: `onFilterSelected(filter: LoanFilter)`
The reader picked this filter
The holder
`setFilter(filter: LoanFilter)`
Put this value in that field
The holder implements the assignment; the name does not describe any wider interaction

blocks.text:
Suppose selecting a filter must also clear the search box and remember the choice for the next visit. `onFilterSelected` can coordinate all three actions inside the holder without changing callers.

If the UI instead coordinates separate calls to `setFilter`, `setSearchText("")`, and `rememberFilterChoice(filter)`, every caller must preserve their relationship and order. A setter could also encapsulate those actions; the benefit of the intention-based name is that it describes the interaction whose meaning the holder owns.

A setter is appropriate when the interaction really is assigning one value and the holder has no wider decision to make. When an interaction coordinates state or work, name the function for that interaction so its contract can remain useful as the implementation changes.

Module visibility limits which callers can reach mutable state; it does not remove their ability to write it. Two uncoordinated writers inside one feature can still overwrite each other’s updates. Keep transition control with the holder even when its callers are nearby.

A form makes the ownership decision concrete. Reporting every keystroke in the loans search box to the holder requires a function for reporting edits and a state transition for each edit. That is useful when the holder or another part of the screen needs the draft before submission.
Ask **who needs to react to the draft before it is submitted.**

rows: A renewal note that is validated against the loan's remaining renewals, with the Renew control enabled or disabled as the reader types
Validation the holder owns, and a control elsewhere on the screen
The holder, because validation and the Renew control depend on the draft before submission
A search box whose text only matters when the reader presses Search, and which nothing else on the screen reads
Nobody
Local to the field. One intention — the submission — crosses the boundary, and the draft never does

blocks.text: If only the field reads and edits the draft, it can keep that state locally. On submission, it reports the completed value to the screen holder. This preserves unidirectional flow for the state the holder owns without routing every local edit through it. The help panel’s expansion follows the same ownership test.

Intentions can also be modelled as values in a closed set, with one function receiving them and a reducer producing the next state from current state and intent. **MVI: Intent, Reduction and One Current State** develops that design. Named functions per intention can already centralize transition decisions; the boundary described here does not require an intent hierarchy.

To explain unidirectional data flow, describe the contract: state is read-only to the UI, intentions enter through functions, and the holder controls transitions. Then give a concrete reason for that boundary, such as preventing an uncoordinated UI assignment from overwriting a refresh result.

lessons.title: Work Whose Lifetime Is the Owner's
lessons.summary: Work launched in a scope owned by the screen holder is cancelled when that holder is cleared. Use that lifetime for work that is no longer needed after the holder is gone. If an operation must finish afterwards, its owner or persistence mechanism needs to outlive the screen.

blocks.text: The loans holder starts work as well as holding state: loading loans, refreshing them, or requesting a renewal. Each operation needs an owner that determines how long it should continue.
For asynchronous work, identify the scope’s owner and the event that cancels it. A screen holder therefore needs to answer:
**Is this owner the right owner for this work?**

Work launched in a scope owned by the screen holder receives cancellation when that holder is cleared. Use this arrangement when the work is no longer needed once the holder is gone. If the operation must still finish, such as a confirmed return submission, it needs a longer-lived owner.

Decide what should happen if the screen’s owner is cleared mid-operation. A read whose result is only needed by that screen can be cancelled. An operation the reader expects to complete after leaving needs another owner. Navigating away is relevant when it actually clears the holder; an entry retained on the back stack may keep its ViewModel alive.

Choose the work’s owner from its required lifetime. A screen-holder scope fits work that may be cancelled when the holder is cleared. Work that must finish afterwards needs a longer-lived owner or a mechanism that survives process death.

`viewModelScope` provides owner-scoped work for a `ViewModel`. With the default setup, the extension property creates a scope on first access, registers it as a closeable resource, and returns that same scope on later accesses. Its default setup has three relevant properties:

items: It contains a `SupervisorJob`, allowing direct child operations to fail independently without cancelling sibling jobs.

Its default dispatcher is `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`. On Android, work starts on the main thread without an extra dispatch when already there. Blocking or CPU-heavy work still needs an appropriate dispatcher, for example through `withContext`.

Local JVM tests can replace Main with `Dispatchers.setMain`. A custom scope can also be supplied through the ViewModel constructor rather than using this default.
The scope is registered as a closeable resource. Clearing the ViewModel closes it and cancels its coroutine context.

blocks.text: The scope’s key lifetime property is cancellation when its ViewModel is cleared. Supervision controls how sibling failures interact, while the dispatcher determines where work runs. Check all three separately when choosing how to launch an operation.
Two operations on the loans screen need different lifetimes:

headers: If the screen’s holder is cleared mid-operation
rows: Refreshing the loan list after a pull-to-refresh
This screen, and nothing else
No completion is required by this requirement; the result was only for this screen.
The screen holder fits this lifetime; cancellation is allowed.
Submitting a return: the reader confirmed they are returning an item
The library, the reader's borrowed-items badge, every other screen showing their loans
The return must still be submitted because the reader expects the confirmed operation to complete.
A longer-lived owner is needed so clearing the screen holder does not cancel submission.

blocks.text:
In this example, the comment about leaving assumes that the destination is removed and its ViewModel is cleared. Navigating forward while retaining its back-stack entry would not cancel the refresh for that reason.

The return submission needs an owner that outlives this screen holder. Choose its lifetime from the completion requirement (see **Choosing an Owner From the Lifetime the Requirement Needs**). If it must survive process death, an in-memory scope is insufficient; use a mechanism for persistent work, such as WorkManager.

Launching every operation in `viewModelScope` gives it the ViewModel’s lifetime. A quick test may miss the problem because the operation finishes before the holder is cleared. Check what happens when the holder is cleared during the operation, especially for work the reader expects to complete.
A scope can be tied to the holder itself or supplied from a longer-lived owner. These arrangements assign the work different lifetimes:

rows: The owner creates its own scope, or uses the one its base class gives it
From the holder’s own lifetime
Clearing the holder cancels work in this scope. This fits operations that need not outlive it.
A longer-lived scope is supplied to the owner from outside
From the longer-lived owner that supplies the scope
The supplied scope can keep work alive after this holder is cleared, provided that clearing this holder does not cancel that scope.

blocks.text: A supplied scope makes the lifetime dependency visible in the constructor. It still needs a clear owner and cancellation policy. Confirm that the holder uses the longer-lived scope without cancelling it when the holder is cleared.

An application might define `ApplicationScope`, a distinct wrapper around a scope with a `SupervisorJob`, so injection identifies it unambiguously. Shared caches or the borrowed-items badge can use that scope because they remain needed after one destination is destroyed.

The shared-state requirement justifies the longer lifetime. The scope and its wrapper make that lifetime available to the components that need it.

An application scope fits state and work that genuinely need the process’s lifetime. It also retains their resources for that long, so use it for a stated requirement rather than as a default for every operation.

It still ends with the process. Work that must survive process death needs persistence and a mechanism that can resume or retry it afterwards.

When explaining where a ViewModel launches work, describe the required lifetime first. A screen-only refresh may use `viewModelScope`; a confirmed return that must finish after clearing the screen needs a longer-lived owner. Then distinguish the default scope’s supervision and dispatching: `SupervisorJob` isolates direct sibling failures, and `Dispatchers.Main.immediate` selects main-thread execution without making blocking work safe there.

sources.title: Use Kotlin coroutines with lifecycle-aware components

units.title: Repositories, Data Ownership and Single Source of Truth
units.summary: Repositories own the policies for reading and changing application data: which source answers, when to refresh, and where a write lands first. This unit explains how to choose an authoritative owner when copies disagree, when consumers need streams or one-shot reads, and which models and failures should cross the data boundary.

lessons.title: What a Repository Is Responsible For
lessons.summary: A repository is the data layer's entry point. It can own source selection, refresh policy, conflict resolution, and the contract consumers use. Even a repository that only forwards calls can provide a consistent entry point; additional responsibilities should follow from the feature's needs.

blocks.text: A borrowed-items screen needs to read the reader's loans. A repository gives the screen an entry point into the data layer and can decide which source to read, when to refresh, and what data to expose. Describing it only as an interface around an API or a DAO leaves these responsibilities unspecified.
To identify its responsibilities, ask: **what data decision should this component own so its callers do not have to?** A repository can take responsibility for any of the following:

items: **Exposing application data through a contract written for its consumers**, rather than one shaped by whatever produced the data.
**Centralising changes to that data**, so a write has one path rather than several.
**Coordinating more than one source** — deciding which one answers, and how their answers combine.
**Deciding freshness**: when a refresh is attempted, and whether what is currently held may still be shown.
**Resolving conflicts** when two sources disagree about the same fact.
**Hiding origin**, so nothing above the data layer knows which store or transport produced a value.

blocks.text: Android's data-layer guidance describes repositories as exposing data, centralising writes, resolving conflicts, hiding data sources, and containing business logic. A particular repository need not implement all of these. Choose the responsibilities the feature needs rather than adding forwarding code to fill out the list.

A **data source** works with one source of data, such as a file, a network service, or a local database. A Room DAO, an HTTP service, a file reader, or a platform key-value store supplies operations for that source. The repository defines the contract consumers use above those operations.

In Android's recommended architecture, other layers access data through repositories. If a screen reads a DAO directly, it can bypass the repository's decisions about source selection or freshness. Keeping that access behind the repository lets callers share the same policy.

A repository is the data layer's entry point. It exposes the contract consumers use and owns the source selection, refresh, conflict, or write policies the feature needs. A data source works with one source. A forwarding repository may provide a consistent entry point without owning additional policy yet.

Suppose the library runs a service, so the reader's loans exist both on the device and in the library's records. `LoanRepository` coordinates two sources, each of which handles its own storage or service operations:

blocks.code:
LoanRepository
    ├── LocalLoanSource    // knows the device's store, and nothing else
    └── RemoteLoanSource   // knows the library service, and nothing else

rows: Which source answers a read
`LoanRepository`
Each source knows only itself. If the screen chose between them, it would take on the source policy that belongs inside the data layer.
Whether the copy currently held may still be shown
`LoanRepository`
The local store can report what it holds. The repository applies the application's freshness policy to decide whether that copy is acceptable to show.
Where a renewal lands first, and what happens if the other side rejects it
`LoanRepository`
The write path crosses both sources, so only the component that can see both can define it
What consumers see, and in what vocabulary
`LoanRepository`
The contract is written for callers. Both sources speak their own language — rows and columns on one side, a wire format on the other
How a row is read out of the device's store
`LocalLoanSource`
Reading the row depends on the local store's mechanism; it does not require knowledge of the remote source.
How a list of loans is requested from the library service
`RemoteLoanSource`
Requesting loans depends on the library service's API; it does not require knowledge of the local copy.

blocks.text: These responsibilities do not depend on a class-name suffix. A `LoanRepository` may only forward calls to a DAO, while a `LoanStore` may own source selection, freshness, and conflicts. Describe what each component does to apply the same reasoning in codebases that use different names.
A simpler feature has fewer decisions. The reader chooses a time of day for reminders about loans coming due. The value has one source, with no second copy, refresh policy, translation, or conflict:

This class forwards both operations unchanged. It gives callers a repository entry point, but it does not yet introduce source policy or translation. Adding a field would require changing both the repository and the source together. The extra class also adds a name, a file, and forwarding functions to maintain.

Android recommends repositories even for a single source, keeping the UI from accessing that source directly. This gives the codebase a consistent entry point. If reminder times later gain a refresh policy or a second source, the repository can handle that change without each caller doing so.

For this small feature, the benefit is consistency and room for later change. It is worth weighing that benefit against the forwarding code to maintain; the guidance allows adaptation to the application's requirements.
The pass-through repository provides a consistent entry point. These requirements would give it additional decisions to own:

items: the reminder time also lives in the reader's account on the service, and the two copies can disagree;
the value must be readable instantly even when the store is slow, so something has to decide what is shown meanwhile;
a second screen starts reading the same value, and both must be guaranteed to see one answer;
the stored representation stops matching what the application wants — minutes past midnight on disk, a time of day in the app.

blocks.text: With any of these requirements, the repository can own a decision that would otherwise be repeated in its callers.

A repository does not automatically need an interface. As discussed in **When an Interface Is a Boundary, and When It Is Only Indirection**, an interface is useful when its contract can stay stable while implementations change. For a repository, look for requirements such as these:

items: More than one implementation genuinely exists or is imminent — a device-only implementation beside a synchronised one, or a demo implementation the product ships.
The source policy is expected to move while the contract stays still.
The implementation is volatile in a way its callers should not inherit.
Several consumers depend on one stable data contract while the implementation changes underneath them.

blocks.text: Without a need for an independently stable contract, an interface may add another file that changes alongside its only implementation. Whether that cost is useful depends on the feature. **Who Defines the Abstraction?** addresses the separate question of which side should define an interface so dependencies point in the intended direction.

Defining a repository only by the API or DAO it wraps does not explain its responsibilities. Identify the source selection, freshness, conflicts, writes, or consumer contract it owns. If it only forwards calls, describe that accurately: it may provide a consistent entry point without adding source policy.

Hiding a DAO is useful when it lets callers depend on a contract that can stay stable as storage changes. If the repository also chooses sources or coordinates writes, those decisions explain what the boundary protects. A repository that only forwards calls has a smaller role; assess that role against its maintenance cost.

A codebase may call this component a store, gateway, client, or provider. A `LoanStore` that exposes application data and owns the relevant source policy has the responsibilities described here, whatever its name. In an interview, explaining those responsibilities lets you discuss the design even when the team's terminology differs.

Consider a loan-history feature that works entirely on the device. `LoanHistoryRepository` exposes a contract in the feature's vocabulary and translates database rows into those types. The feature never depends on the database directly, so storage can change without changing its callers.

With one source, this repository has no sources to coordinate, refreshes to schedule, or conflicts to resolve. If the history later gains a synchronised server copy, those responsibilities can be added. Describe the responsibilities it has now rather than assigning it every role a repository could have.

When explaining a repository, name its role as the data layer's entry point and the decisions the feature needs it to own. Use an example with source selection, freshness, or conflict resolution, then contrast it with a single-source repository that only forwards calls. Explain the benefit and cost of each arrangement.

lessons.title: Coordinating Local and Remote Sources
lessons.summary: With local and remote copies, the repository decides which source answers reads, when to refresh, where writes land first, and how failures affect the data shown. Consumers may need freshness, refresh, or confirmation status without depending on the storage and transport used to obtain a value.

blocks.text: The library records the reader's loans on its service, and the device keeps a local copy. The local copy can answer quickly but may be out of date. The service has the library's records but may be unreachable.
The repository now has four coordination decisions to make. Neither source knows the other, so neither can choose the policy for both:

items: **Which source answers a read**, and what happens when the chosen one cannot.
**When a refresh is attempted**, what triggers it, and whether the consumer waits for it.
**Where a write lands first**, and what has to accept it before the reader is told it worked.
**What a failure of either side means** for the data the consumer is looking at.

blocks.text: The consumer asks for the application's current loans through the repository contract. Choosing whether to read the device or the service belongs inside the data layer, so the consumer does not have to repeat that policy.

A repository coordinating multiple sources decides which source answers reads, when to refresh, where writes land first, and what failures mean for consumers. These policies follow from product requirements. Callers use the resulting data contract without choosing the underlying store or service themselves.

Suppose the loans list must appear immediately, even without connectivity, and avoid a loading spinner when the device already has data.
