While connectivity permits refreshes, it should stay within a few minutes of the library's records while visible. During an outage, that freshness bound cannot be guaranteed. These requirements suggest starting with the local copy and then refreshing:

blocks.code:
a consumer asks for the current loans
        ↓
the local source answers immediately with what it holds
        ↓
the repository exposes that value
        ↓
a refresh from the service is attempted
        ↓
on success, the local copy is updated
        ↓
the consumer sees the updated loans without having asked again

blocks.text:
This diagram refreshes when the list is opened. It does not by itself keep the list fresh for as long as it remains visible: after an hour, the single refresh could be an hour old.

Meeting the ongoing freshness requirement needs another trigger, such as refreshing while the screen is visible or receiving notice that the library's records changed. The choice depends on the product and available infrastructure. Scheduling, sockets, or push delivery implement that choice; the repository still needs an explicit policy for when to refresh.

Changing the requirement can change the read path. If a fine balance must never be presented from an unconfirmed local copy, displaying that copy as current would violate the requirement. Local-first reads are suitable for these loans-list requirements, rather than a policy every repository should use.
Writes also depend on what the reader must be promised. Two renewal requirements produce different write paths and different visible outcomes:

rows: Renewing must work with no connectivity, and the library reconciles afterwards
Local first: the device's copy changes and is marked as not yet sent; the service is told at the next opportunity
The new due date appears at once, with whatever indication the product chooses for "not yet confirmed"
The local write may succeed without confirmation from the library. The library can later refuse the renewal, so the application must decide how to represent that refusal.
A renewal is only real once the library has accepted it
Remote-confirmed: the service must accept the renewal before the local copy changes
A pending control until the service answers, and then the new due date
Either the library refused it and nothing changed anywhere, or the answer never arrived and the outcome is unknown — a third case the design has to represent rather than guess at

blocks.text:
Waiting for remote confirmation does not guarantee that the two copies always agree. If the library commits the renewal but its response is lost, the write happened remotely while the local copy remains unchanged. From the failed request alone, the application cannot tell whether the renewal succeeded.

Ordering the remote and local writes does not make them one atomic operation. The contract must therefore represent an unknown outcome as well as acceptance and refusal.

The screen needs to represent that the renewal's outcome is not yet known. Resolving it requires checking with the library. If resolution involves retrying the renewal, repeating it must not produce an unintended second renewal.

The remote-confirmed path avoids intentionally showing a new due date before the library accepts it. It can still leave the local copy behind when a response is lost.

Local-first renewal allows the device and library to disagree temporarily so the reader can act offline. Remote-confirmed renewal makes the reader wait and still needs to represent an unknown outcome. Choose and document the behaviour the product needs.

Retries, backoff, and scheduling work that survives the app closing are mechanisms for carrying out that write policy.
Keeping storage and transport details inside the data layer does not mean returning only a list of loans. The screen may also need information that affects how it presents those loans:

items: That what is shown is older than the policy allows, so the screen can say when it was last confirmed.
That a refresh is currently running, so the screen does not offer an action that assumes fresh data.
That the last refresh failed, so the screen can say so and offer a retry.
That a local change has not yet reached the library, so the reader is not told something is final when it is not.

blocks.text: The distinction is between **application meaning** and **implementation origin**. The screen may need to know that the loans were last confirmed forty minutes ago. It need not know whether a database query or a network call supplied them. A contract can express the first without exposing the second:

blocks.code:
internal data class LoansSnapshot(
    val loans: List<Loan>,
    val lastConfirmedAt: Instant?,
    val refresh: RefreshState,      // Idle, InProgress, or Failed with an app-level reason
    val hasUnsentChanges: Boolean,
)

blocks.text: Nothing in that type names a transport library, a client's response class, a stored row or an exception from either side. A caller can render "updated forty minutes ago", show a retry, and decide whether an action is safe to offer — and still not know whether the loans arrived from a database, a file or an in-memory cache. How that failure reason is represented, and which types must never appear inside it, is the subject of **Model and Error Boundaries: What May Cross**.

Local-first reads with background refresh are useful when the product needs offline access and tolerates some staleness. A balance that must be confirmed before display, or a write that must be accepted before it is shown as final, needs a different policy. Specify which source answers, how fresh its answer must be, where writes land first, and what consumers see when either source fails.

**A freshness policy needs information beyond the loan values themselves.** A list of loans does not say when it was confirmed. To decide whether a copy can still be shown, record what the policy needs: a confirmation timestamp, a service-issued version, or a marker for an unsent local change.

The offline-first guidance also describes recording change metadata for conflict resolution. A cache that does not record the information a freshness policy needs cannot apply that policy to existing entries reliably. Adding the metadata later may require a migration or treating old entries as unconfirmed until they are refreshed.

The decision and its mechanisms are separate. How a store keeps that timestamp, when entries are evicted, how a synchronisation job is scheduled, and what algorithm merges two divergent copies are all mechanisms. The repository's decision is what those mechanisms implement: this repository holds a copy, this is what makes the copy acceptable to show, this is when it is replaced, and this is what the consumer is told while it is not.

A second source is useful when the product needs it, but it brings coordination work. A feature with one source may need only a repository contract, without refresh or conflict policies. There is no need to introduce those responsibilities before there is another source to coordinate.

To explain local and remote coordination, start with a requirement and derive the read and write paths from it. Describe when copies may disagree and what consumers learn about stale data, pending writes, and failures. Include the metadata the freshness policy needs, and explain which choices would change under different requirements.

lessons.title: Which Source Is Authoritative?
lessons.summary: A single source of truth identifies the owner whose value takes precedence when copies of a fact disagree. Different facts can have different owners: the library service for a fine, a local store for a draft, or an in-memory holder for a session choice. In an offline-first design, the local source can be the repository's consistent read source while synchronisation still respects server authority for particular facts.

blocks.text: A **single source of truth** identifies which owner supplies the authoritative value for a fact. A database can fill that role, but so can a service or an in-memory component. To choose one, name the fact and the requirement that determines whose value takes precedence.

For the conflict examples in this lesson, the source of truth is **the owner whose value takes precedence for a particular fact when copies disagree**. The decision is per fact, so one application can have several owners. Each owner may store its value on disk, provide it through a service, or hold it in memory.

Android's data-layer guidance asks each repository to define a source of truth and expose data from it consistently. That source can be a database or an in-memory store, and different repositories can use different kinds of sources.

A **cache** keeps a copy for speed or availability. It need not be authoritative for the underlying business fact: a cached fine may differ from the amount the library currently records. The app can still use that cache as its consistent read source, provided the contract identifies the value as last confirmed rather than necessarily current. The same Room database can own a draft locally and hold a cached fine whose business authority remains with the library.

Choose an authoritative owner for each fact from the product's requirements. It may be a service, a local store, or an in-memory component with a deliberately short lifetime. Other copies must follow the chosen conflict policy. The storage technology alone does not determine which value takes precedence.
Three facts in the borrowed-items application have different requirements and therefore different authoritative owners:

headers: Why the other candidates do not meet this requirement
rows: The review the reader is drafting for a book
It must be editable with no connectivity and must survive the app being closed; the service receives it when the reader submits it
The local store on the device
The service does not have the draft at all until submission, so a server copy treated as authoritative would let a synchronisation overwrite what the reader typed
The fine currently owed on overdue loans
It must never be presented as current when it may have changed, and payments can be made at the library desk
The library service
The device cannot know about a payment made at the desk. The local copy is a cache, and showing it as truth misinforms the reader about money
The sort order the reader chose for this visit to the loans list
It applies while the reader is using the app and is meant to be gone next time
An in-memory holder that lives as long as the session
Persisting it would make a deliberate default sticky, and asking the service would give a private, momentary choice a lifetime nobody asked for

blocks.text: The sort order lives only in memory and disappears at the end of the session, as intended. It still has an authoritative owner: other components read the current order from that holder. Choosing an owner determines whose value takes precedence; choosing its lifetime determines how long that value exists.
Now make a disagreement concrete. Two copies of the fine, at the same moment:

blocks.code:
the device's copy says:   fine = 80
the library service says: fine = 100

blocks.text:
For this fine, the library service is authoritative because payments can occur at the desk without the device knowing. The fine is therefore 100, and the local 80 is a stale copy to replace.

Choosing the newest value would be appropriate only if the product had chosen a last-write-wins rule. Other facts may need different conflict policies:

items: the service wins and the local copy is a cache, as above;
the local copy wins until it is submitted, which is the rule for the reader's own draft;
the disagreement is surfaced to the reader to resolve, which fits when both versions represent real human intent;
an application-level rule reconciles them — per field, or by preferring whichever change the reader made themselves.

blocks.text: Choose a conflict rule from the fact's requirements and make its owner explicit. Automatic reconciliation has its own algorithms; the architectural decision here is which rule the application will apply when copies disagree.

Suppose the loans list and account screen each keep a copy of the fine. One refreshes and the other does not, so they display different amounts. Keeping copies is normal; the problem is that these screens have no shared policy for bringing their copies into agreement with the authoritative value. A common owner and update policy give them one place to resolve the discrepancy.

The service is authoritative for the fine. The repository owns the policy for obtaining and exposing it, and the state holder owns how this screen presents it. These are separate responsibilities.

A repository that chooses the wording of a zero-fine label takes on presentation work that may differ between screens. A state holder that independently decides when the cached fine is too old takes on source policy that other screens may implement differently.

Android recommends a local source of truth for offline-first reads. In that arrangement, repositories update the local source and higher layers read from it consistently, rather than alternating between local and network results. This defines the app's read source; it does not make the device authoritative for every business fact.

The reader's draft can be locally authoritative until submission. The library remains authoritative for the fine, even if the repository stores its last confirmed value locally and exposes it from there. The fine's contract must still prevent an unconfirmed value from being presented as current. Choosing a consistent read source and choosing which copy wins a conflict are related decisions, but they need not select the same store.

Calling the database the source of truth is incomplete until you state which data and which responsibility it owns. Name the fact, its consistent read source, and the rule for resolving disagreement. A database may supply the app's reads while a service remains authoritative for changes to that fact.

The case worth being able to handle is the one where neither source can simply be declared authoritative. The reader edits their review offline; meanwhile a librarian corrects the same record because of a complaint. Both changes are real, both are intended, and neither store contains a rule that settles which one the application should keep.

The application needs a reconciliation owner that applies a rule to the two versions and produces the value consumers use. Both stores supply inputs to that decision.

That owner needs rules for fields that can diverge and a defined outcome when a rule cannot choose. If the reader must resolve the conflict, the UI needs to represent it rather than silently discard one change.

The architectural question is who owns reconciliation and what rules that owner applies. An interview answer can establish those responsibilities before moving on to merge algorithms or synchronisation mechanisms, if the discussion requires them.

A shared state holder can publish a projection of repository data without becoming an independent authority. For example, it can expose the loan list several screens observe and re-read it after every change.

The repository remains authoritative for that data; the holder stores only the projection and does not introduce another write path. The projection has a UI purpose, while disagreements between underlying sources remain the repository's responsibility.

Explain the authoritative owner of a fact with examples that have different requirements: a local draft, a service-owned fine, or a session-only sort order. When discussing offline-first guidance, distinguish the local source used for consistent reads from the owner that resolves conflicting values. For conflicting edits, identify the reconciliation rule and the component responsible for applying it.

lessons.title: An Observable API, or a One-Shot Read?
lessons.summary: Choose a stream when a consumer needs notifications of changes over time, and a suspending read when it needs one result. Streams require a collection lifetime and handling of later values. A one-shot result does not update itself. Observable UI state can also be built above a one-shot repository if another component coordinates all relevant changes.

blocks.text: Android's data-layer and coroutines guidance recommends suspending functions for one-shot operations and `Flow` for notifications of changes over time. The choice depends on what the consumer needs to observe.

Almost any data can change. What matters for this API is whether **this consumer needs to be notified when it changes**. That requirement determines whether the data layer should expose updates or one result.
These facts alone do not establish that a repository needs a stream:

items: **The data can change.** A consumer may still need only a value captured for one operation.
**Streams are common in current APIs.** The guidance also recommends suspending functions when the operation needs one result.
**The state holder exposes `StateFlow`.** That describes how the UI observes state; the holder may build that state from one-shot repository calls.

blocks.text: Choose the API from what the consumer needs to observe. A stream can notify it of changes made elsewhere. A suspending read can return one snapshot for an operation that needs a fixed value. That snapshot does not update automatically; its acceptable freshness is part of the contract.
The same loan data can support two consumers with different needs:

**The first requirement is observation.** The loans list must reflect renewals and returns made elsewhere in the application while the reader is looking at it — a renewal triggered from a notification, a return processed on the account screen. The consumer cannot know when those happen, so it cannot know when to ask again:

blocks.code: fun observeLoans(): Flow<List<Loan>>

blocks.text: **The second requirement is a deliberately frozen snapshot.** Tapping Renew shows the new due date and any fee for that renewal, quoted at that moment and held still while the reader reads it and confirms:

blocks.code: suspend fun quoteRenewal(id: LoanId): RenewalQuote

blocks.text: The library may reprice a renewal after the call returns, but this requirement keeps the quoted terms fixed while the reader confirms. The one-shot result fits that snapshot. Using a stream would require the caller to stop collecting or ignore later quotes so the dialog does not change underneath the reader.

The one-shot contract says that this call returns one quote and does not keep it updated. For this confirmation dialog, that is deliberate: the reader needs the terms captured for this operation. A later change at the service does not by itself create a need to observe updates here.
A stream also needs a contract for how callers receive and handle updates. A collecting consumer must manage:

items: a collection lifetime — when collection starts and stops, so updates continue for as long as they are needed and work is not kept alive unnecessarily;
the handling of every later value, including ones that arrive while the consumer is in the middle of something else;
a policy for values it no longer cares about — ignoring them, conflating them, or cancelling the collection.

blocks.text: An observable API places these obligations on consumers that collect it. Choose it when updates are useful to them. The collection, sharing, and conflation contracts are covered in **One Value or Many: Why `Flow` Exists** and **`StateFlow`: One Current Value**.
Whichever read API is chosen, callers should not be able to bypass repository operations by mutating its exposed state:

A public `MutableStateFlow` lets callers assign loans directly. That can bypass the repository's write coordination, freshness policy, and conflict rules. Expose observation read-only and provide named operations for changes, so the repository can apply those policies.

A repository can expose suspending functions for one-shot operations and flows for changes over time. Choose from the consumer's requirements. A one-shot snapshot can be the right result, while a stream adds collection and update handling that should serve a real need.
A repository may legitimately offer both a stream and a suspending read for the same data, and that does not create two sources of truth by itself:
For these methods to expose the same underlying authority, keep these conditions true:

items: both reads follow a declared contract for the same underlying authority; they may use different read paths, such as cached observation and a service-confirmed snapshot;
each read makes its freshness and source policy explicit; any deliberate difference between them must remain consistent with that authority;
neither creates an independently mutable copy that can drift from the other.

blocks.text: With these conditions, the stream and suspending read are two ways to query the same owner. Separate return types do not create separate authority; independently mutable data or incompatible source policies would.

**Consider repositories that expose only one-shot suspending reads.** The UI can still be observable: after the reader renews a loan, the loans list, due-soon badge, and account summary can all update.

It obtains that one level up. A state holder shared by those screens reads from the loan repository, publishes a `StateFlow` of the resulting projection, and re-reads from the repository after every write. The repository stays one-shot; the observation and the projection belong to a holder that outlives any one navigation entry.

rows: Repositories keep a small one-shot contract, and the projection several screens share is assembled in one place — which that application needed anyway, because the state has to survive any single destination being destroyed

Every writer must go through the same coordination path, because the published projection is only current if the holder re-reads after the write. A write that reached the database by another route would leave the visible state stale with nothing to notice
The data layer makes no commitment about collection lifetimes, so each consumer decides what it needs to observe and for how long
A consumer that wanted its own observation of this data cannot have one from the repository; it would have to ask the holder, or the repository's contract would have to change

blocks.text:
An observable repository can coordinate updates for independent consumers in the data layer. With a one-shot-only repository, another component must keep their projections current.

In this example, the screens already need one shared projection, so its holder also coordinates re-reads after writes. The design is suitable only if that holder sees every relevant change. Choose where observation belongs from the consumers and writers the application actually has.

When discussing whether a repository should return `Flow`, describe what the consumer needs to observe. Contrast a loans list that follows changes with a fixed renewal quote. Explain collection lifetime and handling of later values, and keep mutation behind repository operations rather than exposing a mutable stream.

sources.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

lessons.title: Model and Error Boundaries: What May Cross
lessons.summary: Whether a concept needs a transfer, a storage and an application representation — or one type for all three — is a trade-off between mapping cost and coupling rather than a rule. When one type crosses every boundary, a wire-format change can reach a screen. Failure raises the same question: how much should a caller have to know about how the data layer is built in order to handle an error?

blocks.text: A feature may use separate transfer, storage, application, and UI models, or share a type across some of those roles. Separate types allow the representations to change independently; a shared type avoids mapping code. The feature's needs determine which trade-off is useful.

Ask whether **these representations need to change independently enough to justify mapping between them**. Mapping can protect callers from changes in storage or transport, but it adds code to maintain. Errors raise a similar question: how much of the data layer's implementation should callers need to know to handle a failure?

Android recommends exposing the data other layers need and creating separate models when a source's representation does not match the rest of the app. When the representations already align, weigh the benefit of independent change against the extra classes and mappings.

Separate transfer, storage, and application models allow independent changes but add mapping code, repeated fields, and more places to maintain. A shared type avoids that mapping but couples its consumers to the same representation. Decide for the feature; different features may reasonably make different choices.
Take the loan concept and split it, with a library service supplying the transport side:

blocks.code:
@Serializable
internal data class LoanPayload(        // wire format
    val id: String,
    val title: String,
    val due: String,                    // ISO-8601, exactly as the service sends it
    val renewals: Int,
)

@Entity(tableName = "loans")
internal data class LoanEntity(         // stored representation
    @PrimaryKey val id: String,
    val title: String,
    val dueAtMillis: Long,
    val renewals: Int,
    val pendingSync: Boolean,
)

internal data class Loan(              // application model
    val id: LoanId,
    val title: String,
    val dueOn: LocalDate,
    val renewalsRemaining: Int,
)

blocks.text:
The three types serve different constraints. `LoanPayload` carries the service's date string. `LoanEntity` stores epoch milliseconds and tracks pending synchronisation. `Loan` uses `LoanId` and `LocalDate`, and expresses the application's remaining renewal allowance rather than the raw count.

Mapping connects these representations. Their differences give the application a reason to keep them separate.

rows: The service can rename or restructure a field and the change stops at one mapping function
Mapping functions to write and maintain; adding a field across all three representations requires updating their mappings.
Storage concerns — annotations, a synchronisation flag, a column type — stay below the boundary
The same field is named in three places, so a reader tracing one value opens three files
The application type says what the application means rather than what a store happens to hold
Translations need explicit decisions; defaults and computed values can contain application policy that must remain correct.
Changing transport or storage becomes a data-layer change rather than a codebase-wide one
More names to learn for one concept, which may be unnecessary when the representations do not need to change independently.

blocks.text: Alternatively, the same concept can use one type for serialization, database storage, and the screen:

One type avoids mapping and gives the reader one definition to follow. It also connects the screen to the service's date encoding: `dueLabel` parses the same `due` string received over the network.

If the library changes that encoding to epoch milliseconds and the shared type follows it, the screen's parser must change too. The product still means the same thing by a due date, but the transport change now reaches presentation code.

A wire-field rename alone need not change the application property: a serialization annotation can map the new wire name onto the existing one when the representations otherwise align. The example's coupling comes from the date encoding itself. Because the screen parses that encoding, changing it affects rendering code as well as serialization.

For the reminder-time preference, a shared type may be sufficient. There is one value, one store, no transport representation, and no storage annotation that callers need to handle. If both sides use the same representation and change together, separate models would add a field-copying mapping without isolating a meaningful difference.

A small mapping can still be useful. `LocalLoanHistoryRepository` maps a two-field `ReturnedLoanEntity` into `ReturnedLoan`, so the feature's types have no Room annotations and do not expose the stored representation. The cost is a few mapping lines; the benefit is the freedom to change persistence without changing the feature. That does not require the reminder-time preference to make the same choice.
The error contract also determines what a caller must know about the data layer. Consider a state holder that catches a transport-specific exception:

The state holder now depends on the HTTP client's exception type. Replacing the client or changing the source used for this operation can require changes in callers that catch that exception. An application-level error contract can instead report that loans could not be refreshed, the session expired, or the library refused a renewal, with a reason the consumer can use.
Android's guidance describes custom exceptions and result types as ways to expose failures. The existing contract can also carry status alongside data. These options serve different needs:

items: a sealed result whose branches are exactly the failures the caller must distinguish;
an application-owned exception type, which keeps the ordinary path free of wrapping;

an outcome carried inside the data the repository already returns — a snapshot whose refresh state records that the last refresh failed, as in **Coordinating Local and Remote Sources**, is this option.

blocks.text: Each mechanism has trade-offs. Whichever is chosen, expose failures callers can interpret in application terms. A screen should not need to name a transport library or storage type merely to handle an expected failure.

Before adding separate models or choosing one shared type, ask which changes should remain independent and what mapping would cost. A preference whose stored form already matches the application may need no translation. A service-controlled representation that the screen must parse creates a stronger reason for a separate application model.

Models and errors both determine what callers know about the data layer. Mapping is useful when it lets storage or transport change without requiring caller changes. Where the representations already fit and change together, a shared type may be sufficient. Apply the trade-off to each contract rather than uniformly to the whole codebase.

Maintaining a mapping also means maintaining its translation decisions. Omitting a returned loan, replacing null with a default, or converting a renewal limit and count into an allowance can change application behaviour. Treat those choices as policy to review, rather than assuming every mapping is field-copying boilerplate.

The data error contract and the screen's error state have different jobs. The data layer describes what went wrong in application terms. The state holder decides how the screen represents it: as a state field, a sealed variant, or a failure in one region. **Modelling the Current UI State** covers that presentation choice. Keeping the contracts separate lets the screen handle a failure without depending on an HTTP client's types.

Kotlin's sealed types can express a closed set of failure cases in the contract. Storage and serialization annotations serve a different purpose: they identify how a representation is persisted or transferred. Separate application models keep those concerns off the types the screen reads when that separation is useful.

When discussing DTOs, entities, and application models, use a stated feature to weigh independent change against mapping and maintenance costs. Include a case where one type is sufficient. For errors, explain what callers need to learn about the failure and how the contract avoids making them depend on the data layer's implementation.

units.title: Domain Logic, Use Cases and Dependency Direction
units.summary: A domain layer can provide one home for shared operations, coordination across repositories, or business rules with their own reasons to change. Decide whether a layer or an individual use case is useful by identifying what it would own. Separate business policy from framework and infrastructure details, then trace source dependencies to see which side defines the contracts. Clean Architecture’s dependency rule concerns that direction; it does not prescribe a particular layer count.

lessons.title: When Does Another Layer Earn Its Existence?
lessons.summary: A domain layer is optional. It is useful when it gives shared operations, coordination across repositories, independent business policy, or complex decision-making a clear home. Apply those criteria to the feature’s current requirements, and identify what would change a decision to keep the existing arrangement.

blocks.text: In the borrowed-items feature, `LoanRepository` decides which source answers a read, when to refresh, and what contract its callers see. The screen’s state owner reads from that repository. These responsibilities are already separated; adding a layer between them needs a reason.

A **domain layer** can hold application operations and rules that belong neither to presentation nor to storage. It sits between the UI and data layers and is optional. Android’s guidance recommends using it when needed, for example to manage complexity or reuse behaviour.

For this feature, the question is what the additional layer would own that does not already belong to `LoanRepository` or the screen’s state owner. If there is no such responsibility, the existing arrangement may be sufficient.

**A boundary is useful when it separates responsibilities that need their own home.** For a domain layer, look for operations or rules that do not fit the screen’s state owner or the data layer. Four kinds of responsibility can justify that separation.

items: **Reuse across callers.** More than one screen, feature or background owner needs the same operation or the same rule, and there is currently no single place that owns it.

**Orchestration.** One application operation coordinates several repositories or several responsibilities, and somebody has to decide the order, what a partial failure means, and what the operation amounts to as a whole.

**Business policy worth isolating.** A rule belongs to the application rather than to what a screen is currently rendering or to how a source stores rows, and it changes for its own reasons and on its own schedule.
**Meaningful complexity.** The behaviour contains enough decision-making that it deserves one authoritative home instead of being re-derived correctly, or incorrectly, wherever it is needed.

blocks.text:
One of these conditions can be sufficient. A lending rule may need its own home even if only one screen currently uses it, and an operation that coordinates repositories may also apply that rule.

A domain layer is therefore not required in every production application. Clean Architecture specifies a dependency direction rather than a mandatory Android domain layer, as **Clean Architecture: the Dependency Rule, Not the Diagram** explains. Logic concerned only with one screen, and changing with that screen’s requirements, can remain with its state owner.

A domain layer is optional. Look for a responsibility it can own: behaviour shared across callers, coordination across repositories, business policy with independent reasons to change, or substantial decision-making. One condition can justify it; the presence of logic alone does not tell you where that logic belongs.

Consider a reminder-time preference. One screen lets the reader choose a time for reminders about loans coming due. A state holder reads and writes the value through one repository over a simple source. There are no additional rules, repositories to coordinate, or other callers. Adding a domain layer produces this arrangement.

blocks.code:
reminder/
  ReminderSettingsViewModel     the screen owner
  domain/
    GetReminderTime             calls the repository, returns what it returned
    SetReminderTime             calls the repository, returns what it returned
  ReminderPreferenceRepository  the data boundary

blocks.text: `GetReminderTime` and `SetReminderTime` forward calls without adding a rule or coordinating work. Under these requirements, they separate no additional responsibility. They still add maintenance and reading costs:

items: two more types, and two more files to open when reading the feature end to end;
two more names to invent, keep distinct from the repository's, and keep accurate when the repository's change;
one more navigation hop between the screen owner and the implementation when reading the feature;
one more boundary that has to stay consistent, so a signature change now lands in three places rather than two;
a domain directory whose name suggests rules or operations that its forwarding types do not contain.

blocks.text: A directory labelled `domain` but containing only forwarding types can also make responsibilities harder to find: its name suggests policy that is not there. For this feature, the added boundary currently costs more than it contributes. That assessment can change when the requirements change.

Now consider loan renewal. The operation needs the loan and its current term, the borrower’s standing and unpaid fines, and rules about renewal limits and the new due date. It then performs a write consistent with those decisions.

Three callers perform renewals: the borrowed-items list, the loan detail screen, and the action attached to the due-soon reminder. A fourth caller only checks eligibility so it can enable or disable a control.

blocks.code:
renewals/
  RenewLoan              orchestrates the operation, applies the policy, performs the write
  RenewalEligibility     the rule: may this loan be renewed, and until when
  RenewalOutcome         what the operation can result in, in the application's own terms
        │
        ├── LoanRepository       the loan and its term
        └── BorrowerRepository   standing and outstanding fines

blocks.text:
All four criteria are present here. Three callers reuse the renewal operation; it coordinates two repositories; eligibility belongs to the library’s lending policy; and term, standing, fines, and renewal count need one consistent decision.

If that behaviour lived in the borrowed-items state holder, the loan detail screen would need to call another screen’s owner or duplicate the rule. In this design, `LoanRepository` owns loan data, so giving it the cross-repository renewal policy would combine responsibilities that change for different reasons.

rows: What the middle layer would own
Nothing the repository does not already own
An eligibility rule, the orchestration of two repositories, and the meaning of the operation
How many callers need it
One screen
Three that perform it and one that only asks whether it is possible
What changes it independently
No independent middle-layer responsibility under these requirements
Lending-policy changes that need no storage or presentation change
What the layer costs
Two forwarding types, two names, one hop, a third place a change lands
Additional operation, policy and outcome types, justified by the responsibilities they separate
Verdict
Not yet. The repository is already the boundary this feature needs
Yes. There is responsibility here that belongs to neither neighbour

blocks.text: Renewal justifies a separate home because the operation and its eligibility rule do not fit the screen’s presentation responsibilities or either repository’s data responsibilities. File count and feature size do not establish that separation.

A less clear case is the ordering of the borrowed-items list. It shows overdue loans first, then loans inside the grace period, then loans whose renewal window is about to close. An unpaid fine raises an item’s priority because it blocks renewal.

Only this screen needs the moderately complex rule today. A weekly summary notification might eventually need it too, but that notification is not currently a requirement.
Decide what current evidence would justify extracting the ordering rule. For example:

items: a second caller genuinely appears, and the choice becomes one home or two copies;
the state holder's own code becomes mostly this rule, so reading the screen's logic means reading the library's policy;
the rule starts changing for reasons the screen never changes for — a lending-policy change with no visual consequence;
the rule needs to hold in a context the screen cannot reach, such as work that runs while no screen is open.

blocks.text: Until there is evidence for a separate responsibility, keeping the rule with its single consumer is a reasonable choice. Revisit it when complexity, reuse, or independent policy changes appear. Possible future flexibility needs a concrete benefit to justify the additional boundary.

The presence of business logic does not by itself require a domain layer. Ask what the logic is about, what changes it, and whether reuse, coordination, independent policy, or complexity calls for a separate home. Screen-specific decisions can remain with the screen’s state owner.

Explain a domain-layer decision using the feature’s requirements and what would change your assessment. The same criteria support either outcome.

For the reminder preference: “One caller, one repository, and no additional policy or coordination. A middle layer would only forward calls. Shared rules or another caller could change that decision.”

For renewals: “The eligibility rule changes with lending policy, three callers perform the operation, and it coordinates two repositories. A separate operation keeps the sequence and rule consistent across those callers.”

A domain layer is a **logical** separation of responsibilities; a Gradle module is a **physical** build unit. A domain layer can live in packages within one module, while a `:domain` module can contain only forwarding functions. Creating one does not establish the other.

Here, “domain” refers to application operations and business policy. Domain-Driven Design includes further concepts, such as aggregates, value objects, and bounded contexts; those are separate from deciding whether this feature needs an additional layer.

Deciding whether a feature needs another layer is separate from deciding whether one operation needs its own type. One useful operation may need little surrounding structure, while several policy types can form a domain layer as responsibilities emerge. **Use Cases That Earn Their Place, and Pass-Through Cost** examines the per-operation decision.

When asked whether an app should have a domain layer, explain the conditions rather than giving a universal answer. Apply reuse, coordination, independent policy, and complexity to a concrete feature. Explain why the reminder preference can use its repository directly, why renewal needs a shared operation and rule, and what would make you revisit either decision.

lessons.title: Use Cases That Earn Their Place, and Pass-Through Cost
lessons.summary: A use case represents one application operation. A separate type can give a rule, a coordinated sequence, or shared behaviour one home. A type that only forwards a repository call adds indirection without separating those responsibilities. A team may still choose to route every data call through use cases for consistency, provided it weighs the maintenance cost.

blocks.text: Whether a feature earns a domain layer is one decision. The question that actually produces code is narrower: does *this operation* deserve a type of its own?

A **use case** represents one application operation, such as renewing a loan, submitting a return, or signing the reader out. It may coordinate repositories, apply a rule, compose other operations, or provide behaviour shared by several callers.

In Android’s guidance, use cases do not have their own lifecycle: they are scoped to the class that uses them. A state holder, service, or another use case can hold the ordinary object and call its operation.

This curriculum uses **interactor** as another name for a use case. Terminology varies between sources and codebases, so check what a team means by the term before treating the names as different responsibilities.
Naming and implementation conventions can make use cases consistent, but they do not establish what an operation owns.

items: A `UseCase` suffix identifies a convention. `RenewLoanUseCase` may only forward a call, while `RenewLoan` or `RenewalService` may coordinate two repositories and apply a rule. Read the behaviour to identify the responsibility.
It is not `operator fun invoke`. Making an instance callable is a Kotlin convenience the guidance itself offers as an option, and it changes nothing about what the type is responsible for.
It is not inheritance from a `UseCase` base class or a shared `Result` wrapper. A base class is a decision about consistency and cross-cutting behaviour, not about whether this operation exists.
A `domain/` folder locates code; the behaviour inside determines its responsibility.

blocks.text: So the test is the ownership question, asked of a single type: what does this operation own that its caller should not own itself? Two types deliberately given the same structure show both answers.

A use case is one application operation, identified by the responsibility it owns rather than by a suffix, an `invoke` operator, a base class or a directory. “Use case” and “interactor” name the same idea. The question that decides whether one should exist is what it owns that its caller should not — orchestration, a rule, or a behaviour more than one caller needs.
The borrowed-items screen needs the reader’s loans. This use case fetches them through the repository:

`GetLoansUseCase` has one caller and forwards the repository result unchanged. It adds no rule, coordination, or translation, and has no independent reason to change under these requirements. Its maintenance costs are concrete:

items: One more type, one more file, and one more name that has to stay meaningful and stay in step with the repository method behind it.
One more hop between the screen owner and the repository implementation when reading the feature.
One more abstraction to explain in review and in documentation, whose explanation is that it forwards.
A precedent priced per operation: applied consistently, it is one class for every repository method, so a repository with six functions becomes six more types.
A domain directory whose forwarding functions do not contain the business responsibility its name suggests.

blocks.text: `RenewLoan` also has constructor dependencies and one callable operation, but it coordinates two repositories and applies a lending rule.

Both types are classes with constructor dependencies and one function. `RenewLoan`, however, loads inputs from two repositories, applies eligibility policy, represents refusal as an outcome, and writes the new due date only when renewal is allowed.

Removing `RenewLoan` means placing that sequence elsewhere. Removing `GetLoansUseCase` lets its caller make the same repository call directly. The difference is the responsibility the type separates, rather than its size or shape.

rows: What does it own?
Nothing — one call, forwarded unchanged
The order of two reads, a policy decision, the write, and the operation's outcome vocabulary
What makes it change?
Only a change to the repository method behind it
A change to lending policy, or to what the operation must mean when it is refused
What happens if it is deleted?
One caller calls the repository directly, and nothing else moves
The coordinated sequence must move elsewhere; copying it into callers creates multiple homes for the rule
Who needs it?
One state holder
Three callers perform renewal; a fourth needs the shared eligibility rule without performing a write

blocks.text:
Reuse is one reason to extract an operation, rather than a minimum caller count. One caller can justify a separate type when the operation owns substantial policy or coordinates work that does not belong in its state holder. Conversely, two callers may share a small function without needing a separate layer.

Ask what the operation owns and what changes it. Caller count helps answer those questions; repetition alone does not settle them.

A team can choose to route **all** data access through use cases, including forwarding calls. This prevents UI callers from bypassing domain behaviour, but it adds types even where there is no additional logic.

Android’s guidance recommends adding use cases when required, while allowing a uniform path when the UI already uses them almost exclusively. The decision depends on the codebase’s need for consistency and the cost of extra indirection.

rows: The claim being made
This operation owns responsibility its callers should not
Every operation is reached the same way, whatever it owns
What it is derived from
This feature's requirements and reasons to change
A decision about consistency across the whole codebase
What it buys
One home for a rule, an orchestration or a shared behaviour
Predictable placement, one convention, and fewer case-by-case arguments
What it costs
The ordinary cost of one type
Forwarding types priced per repository method, and a layer whose name overstates what is in it

blocks.text:
A uniform path gives each call an obvious location, a place to add behaviour without changing call sites, and one convention for new engineers to learn. These benefits can reduce recurring placement decisions.

The trade-off is more forwarding classes as the data API grows, an extra navigation hop, and boundaries that may separate no independent responsibility. A team can choose that cost deliberately. Recording the benefit and cost makes the convention easier to reassess when the codebase changes.

A matching use case for every repository method is a team convention, rather than a universal architectural requirement. A forwarded call adds a type, file, name, and navigation hop without separating a rule or coordinated operation. If the team chooses that uniform path, document what consistency provides and what the extra types cost.
A `UseCase` convention is not the only way to give an operation a home. Types can instead be named for the responsibility each one owns, so the name tells a reader what is inside without opening it.

items: **A service that orchestrates.** The renewal operation above could as well be a `RenewalService`: it loads a loan and the borrower's standing from two repositories, applies the eligibility rule, and performs the write for every caller that renews.

**A policy that decides and nothing else.** A `RenewalEligibility` answers whether a loan may be renewed, and until when, from the loan and the borrower's standing passed to it — no repository, no clock of its own, no platform type. A rule with one caller can still deserve its own home when it changes on the library's schedule rather than the screen's.

**A derivation that computes.** An `OverdueSummary` calculation turns a list of loans and today's date into the counts and totals a screen displays, and owns nothing beyond that transformation — no reads, no writes.

blocks.text: **Responsibility determines whether a separate type is useful; the name communicates that responsibility.** A service, policy, or calculation does not need a `UseCase` suffix, an `invoke` operator, or a base class. A consistent `UseCase` convention is also reasonable. In either style, judge a forwarding type or a coordinated operation by what it contributes.

A state holder owns what its screen renders and how user intentions change that state. A use case owns an application operation that still makes sense without that screen.

If the renewal rule lives in one screen’s state holder, a second caller must reach into that owner or duplicate the rule. Separate copies can diverge when lending policy changes. A shared policy gives the callers one rule to use.

Define a use case as one application operation that may coordinate repositories, apply policy, or serve several callers. Explain why `RenewLoan` benefits from a shared home and why `GetLoansUseCase` only adds forwarding under the stated requirements. Naming, callable syntax, and folders are conventions. A team may still choose a uniform use-case path if its consistency benefits justify the extra types.

lessons.title: Policy, Framework and Detail
lessons.summary: Policy expresses rules the application would still need if its UI toolkit, storage, or transport changed. Detail is how the current program implements those rules. Separate them according to their reasons to change, and examine signatures as well as bodies: framework types in a policy contract can couple it to infrastructure, while a shared rule inside one screen owner can lead other callers to duplicate it.

blocks.text: An operation’s responsibility helps determine its dependencies. To decide which types and APIs it should use, distinguish application policy from implementation detail.

**Policy** is a rule the application or business would still need if this program were rewritten. The library allows two renewals per title unless a fine is outstanding; a loan inside its grace period is not yet overdue; and a reader may not renew a title somebody else has reserved. These rules are independent of the screen, database, or network used to implement them.

**Detail** is how this program implements behaviour: its platform APIs, HTTP client, database, object mapper, serialization format, or UI toolkit.

Separate policy and detail by their **reasons to change**. Lending policy changes when the library changes its rules. Implementation detail changes when the team replaces a client, upgrades storage, adds a platform, or redesigns a screen.

Keeping those responsibilities separate lets a detail change without rewriting the policy it serves. Clean Architecture expresses this through its dependency rule: source dependencies point inward toward policy, and inner code does not name outer implementation details.

Purity and responsibility are different questions. A renewal rule that reads today’s date is policy with a dependency. A side-effect-free function that formats a date for a particular wire protocol is detail, because its purpose comes from that protocol.

Likewise, plain Kotlin can avoid framework coupling without establishing a business responsibility. A class that only forwards a call remains a forwarding class even if it imports no framework types.

Policy describes application or business rules; detail implements them with particular tools. Ask what would cause the code to change: new lending rules, or a change in transport, storage, platform, or presentation? Purity and plain Kotlin alone do not answer that responsibility question.
The library lets readers return a book by photographing a drop-box receipt. This version of the application operation exposes infrastructure types in its signature:

The signature states the return operation in Android and HTTP-client types. That may work in an Android feature, but it couples an operation intended as application policy to those components. The consequences are specific:

items: **A transport change reaches callers of the operation.** `Response` is the HTTP client’s type. Replacing that client, or answering behind a cache with a different result contract, can require changes to callers of `submitReceipt` for reasons unrelated to the meaning of a return.

**A platform type restricts where the operation can run.** `android.net.Uri` requires Android API types, so a plain Kotlin/JVM module needs an Android dependency to compile this signature, and tests need suitable support for that type. The rule itself—a return needs a receipt and a loan identifier—has no inherent Android requirement.

**The rule is now written in somebody else's words.** A caller reading the signature learns about URIs and HTTP responses, and learns nothing about what outcomes a return can have. The application has no vocabulary of its own for one of its own operations.

blocks.text: Use application-owned types in the policy contract, and translate to infrastructure types in an adapter outside that boundary.

`ReceiptImage` and `ReturnOutcome` express the application’s inputs and outcomes. `RemoteReturnRepository` adapts them to the image loader and transport. The client can then change behind that repository without changing the operation’s contract, provided the new implementation can still fulfil it.

Keeping those application types free of platform dependencies also lets the policy run without Android. The translation has a maintenance cost, so place it where representations have different reasons to change. **Model and Error Boundaries: What May Cross** examines that trade-off.

Framework-independent signatures do not solve a responsibility placed in the wrong component. Here, renewal eligibility lives inside the borrowed-items state holder because that screen needed it first.

When the loan detail screen also needs eligibility, putting the rule in the first screen’s owner makes sharing awkward. If the second screen copies it, a later reservation-policy change may update one copy and leave the other unchanged.

The rule belongs to the library’s lending policy, which must hold regardless of which screen is open. The screen owner instead controls its presentation and the user intentions that change it. A shared policy separates those responsibilities and gives both screens one decision.

A ViewModel still needs presentation logic. Disabling a control while a request runs, dismissing an error banner after a successful load, and choosing an empty state instead of a spinner are decisions about the screen. Distinguish those from lending rules by asking what the decision is about and which other callers need it to hold.

headers: Belongs to policy with its own home
rows: What is it about?
What this screen is currently showing
The rules of an application or business operation
Who else needs it?
Nobody — another screen showing the same data would legitimately decide differently
Any caller performing the same operation, screen or not
What changes it?
A design or interaction change to this screen
A lending-policy change that need not require a presentation change
Example
Disable the renew control while a request is in flight
Whether this loan may be renewed at all, and until when

blocks.text: Plain Kotlin avoids some framework coupling, but does not identify domain logic. A forwarding class still only forwards; a lending rule still needs an owner broader than one screen when other callers rely on it. Ask what the code is about and what changes it, then check whether its signature exposes types belonging to infrastructure.

**Policy that does not depend on Android, a database, or an HTTP client can be exercised without those implementations.** If it needs their behaviour through contracts, tests can supply substitutes. The dependency boundary enables that isolation.

Layer count does not establish it. Five layers can still leave policy coupled to framework classes, while two layers can separate the dependencies well enough to test the policy independently.

Separating policy from framework detail can make it usable by another screen, feature module, background worker, or test. Each caller still has to provide the policy’s actual dependencies. Being in a domain layer does not by itself make code usable everywhere; inspect what that code depends on.

A pure `RenewalEligibility` rule receives the loan’s due date and renewal count, the borrower’s standing, and today’s date as values. It does not read a clock, call a repository, or use Android APIs, database entities, or HTTP models.

For the same inputs, it produces the same decision. That makes the rule straightforward to reason about and exercise without infrastructure. Its framework-independent types also allow it to run in contexts that do not provide those frameworks.

A type’s dependencies determine this separation, rather than its package name. Two operations in the same package can have different dependencies; moving a file alone changes neither its vocabulary nor its reasons to change. When policy needs a contract for external behaviour, **Who Defines the Abstraction?** explains how to place that contract so the source dependency points inward.

To identify infrastructure coupling in policy, inspect parameter and return types as well as the body. Explain which platform, transport, or storage dependency a type introduces, how changes can reach callers, and where the operation can run. Application-owned types with an outer adapter can separate those changes. Tie testability to the dependencies that tests can replace, rather than the number of layers.

lessons.title: Who Defines the Abstraction?
lessons.summary: An interface can allow substitution without reversing a source dependency. For dependency inversion, define the contract according to the consumer’s needs and have the implementation depend on it. Trace named types and imports to check the direction. This is separate from dependency injection, which concerns how dependencies are supplied to objects.

blocks.text: Extracting an interface can make implementations interchangeable. To see whether it also reverses the source dependency, check which side defines the contract and which side depends on it.

An interface specifies a contract. It can be defined around the implementation’s capabilities or around the consumer’s requirements. **Who defines the abstraction?** is the question that determines which responsibility drives that contract.

In dependency inversion, the consumer’s side defines the contract it needs, in its own vocabulary. The implementation depends on that contract to fulfil it. Source dependencies therefore point from detail toward policy, even though the runtime call goes from the consumer to the implementation.

blocks.code:
consumer / policy          declares what it needs
        ↑
  abstraction              the contract, owned by the consumer's side
        ↑
implementation / detail    depends on the contract in order to satisfy it

blocks.text: Contract ownership is a responsibility, rather than a package or module name. Physical placement should express that ownership. How the implementation is supplied to the consumer at runtime is a separate construction decision: dependency injection.

Inspect imports and references to types or functions to trace source dependencies. Then check whether the contract expresses the consumer’s requirements or exposes the implementation’s representation.

An interface enables a contract, but its existence alone does not establish dependency inversion. The consumer’s side defines what it needs, and the implementation depends on that declaration. Check source references for the direction and the contract’s vocabulary for whose requirements it serves.

Take the same three conceptual types twice: the renewal operation, a loan repository contract, and a local implementation of it. Nothing is added or removed between the two arrangements — only who owns the middle one.

**Arrangement A — the abstraction lives with the implementation.** The data side declares the interface, because the data side is where the loans actually are, and the renewal operation takes it as a constructor parameter.

`renewals` imports `data.loans`, so the renewal operation depends on the data-side contract. The interface now allows another implementation to be substituted, but this source dependency still points outward.

The contract exposes rows, string identifiers, and epoch milliseconds. A storage change that alters those exposed representations can therefore change the contract and its policy callers. It does not isolate the renewal operation from those details.
**Arrangement B — the abstraction is owned by the consumer.** The renewal side declares what it needs, in the vocabulary of renewals, and the local implementation depends on that declaration.

rows: Which side names the other
`renewals` imports `data.loans`
`data.loans` imports `renewals`
Who the contract was designed for
The store — rows, identifiers as strings, epoch milliseconds
The operation — loans, `LoanId`, a due date
What a storage change costs
A change to exposed storage types or semantics can change the contract and policy callers
The implementation absorbs changes that preserve the loan contract’s meaning
What a policy change costs
A new policy requirement may need a contract change, depending on what it already exposes
A new requirement can change the consumer-owned contract; the implementation then follows
Who can vary without the other
Only the implementation, behind a contract it also owns
The implementation can change behind the contract; policy requirements determine any contract changes
Was anything inverted?
No. Substitution improved; ownership did not move
Yes. The detail now depends on the requirement

blocks.text: The storage-change row shows the practical difference. Arrangement A exposes storage representations to renewal code. Arrangement B expresses loans and renewal dates, so storage changes can remain in the implementation while that contract still holds. Source references show the dependency direction; the contract shows which details it isolates.

Arrangement B can live in one module. `com.example.renewals` declares `LoanRepository` in the vocabulary of renewals, while `LocalLoanRepository` in `com.example.data.loans` imports it to provide an implementation. The renewal policy needs no data-package reference.

A composition root names the concrete implementation, constructs it, and passes it to the consumer. That wiring is outside the policy. Separate Gradle modules can enforce the direction through allowed build dependencies; they are not required to create it.

An interface can improve substitution while leaving the source dependency unchanged. In arrangement A, the consumer still imports a data-side contract written in storage terms. In arrangement B, the implementation depends on the renewal-side contract. Inspect both the source references and the contract’s vocabulary to distinguish them.

Consumer ownership means that the contract is defined by the consumer’s requirements. File placement should make that responsibility visible. Fowler’s **Separated Interface** pattern puts the interface in a different package from its implementation, letting the client use the contract without naming the implementation.

A shared contracts package can also remove a direct dependency between consumer and implementation. It still needs clear responsibility for the contract: a neutral location alone does not decide whether consumer requirements or implementation details shape it.

**Dependency inversion** concerns source dependencies: policy defines its required contract and detail depends on it. **Dependency injection** concerns supplying dependencies to an object rather than having that object construct or locate them itself.

Separating assembly from use, as Fowler describes, complements separating a contract from its implementation. These are related decisions with different purposes.

rows: The question it answers
Which side defines the contract, and which way does the source dependency point
Which implementation does this consumer get, and who constructs it
When it is settled
At compile time, by what the code names
At assembly or run time, by whoever wires the application
Where you can see it
In the imports and in who the contract was written for
In the wiring — a container, a factory, or a constructor call in a main function
Can you have it without the other?
Yes — inversion concerns source dependencies, regardless of how the consumer obtains the runtime implementation
Yes — a container can supply a concrete type nobody abstracted

blocks.text:
Using an injection framework does not by itself invert source dependencies. A container can supply concrete implementation types that policy still names. Conversely, arrangement B keeps its inward dependency when the objects are assembled by hand.

The constructor parameters here make dependencies visible; they do not prescribe a container or assembly method. **Dependency Injection as Object Construction** examines how those objects are supplied.

Dependency inversion is the D in SOLID. Use the name to identify the principle, then explain it by tracing the contract and the source references: which side states the requirement, which side fulfils it, and which changes can remain inside the implementation?

First decide whether a separate contract provides a useful boundary. Then decide whose requirements should define it. An interface that merely repeats an implementation’s methods may add indirection without isolating an independent responsibility, as **When an Interface Is a Boundary, and When It Is Only Indirection** explains. Ownership is worth considering once that boundary has a purpose.

Explain dependency inversion by showing which side defines the contract and tracing the source references. Compare a storage-shaped contract with one defined for renewal requirements, and explain how package or module placement expresses that ownership. Then distinguish injection: supplying an object’s dependencies does not determine whether its source references point toward policy.

lessons.title: Clean Architecture: the Dependency Rule, Not the Diagram
lessons.summary: Clean Architecture’s dependency rule directs source dependencies inward toward policy: inner code does not name outer details. Its diagram illustrates responsibilities rather than prescribing a fixed number of layers. Two-layer and larger designs can satisfy the rule. A presentation–domain–data template, a use case for each repository method, and a Gradle module per layer are separate structural choices.

blocks.text: Clean Architecture's central claim is the **Dependency Rule**: "source code dependencies can only point inwards", inward meaning toward policy, and nothing declared in an outer circle may be named by code in an inner one.

The circles illustrate that dependency rule. Their names and number help describe responsibilities; the original article calls the circles schematic and explicitly allows a different number. Copying the diagram alone does not establish whether a design’s source dependencies follow the rule.
The diagram’s orientation and layer count need separate checks:

items: **The rule is about direction, not about count.** Any number of concentric groupings can satisfy it, including two. Any number can violate it, including four.

**Inward means toward policy, not toward the bottom of a diagram.** As you move inward, detail gives way to rules — policy being what the application would still need if the program were rewritten, and detail how this program happens to implement it.

blocks.text:
Presentation, domain, and data are one possible Android structure. They do not define Clean Architecture’s dependency rule. Neither a fixed layer count nor a use case for every repository method follows from that rule. Decide whether an operation needs its own type by what it owns, as **Use Cases That Earn Their Place, and Pass-Through Cost** explains.

Gradle modules are another separate decision: they are build units that can enforce architectural dependencies. The rule concerns the direction of source dependencies, regardless of how many modules express them.

The dependency rule directs source dependencies inward toward policy. Inner code does not name outer implementation details. Check that direction in the code; layer count, one use case per repository method, and one module per layer do not establish it.
Consider a common UI–domain–data diagram. Before using it to assess dependency direction, establish what its arrows mean.

blocks.code:
UI
 ↓
Domain
 ↓
Data

blocks.text:
The boxes show a possible application structure. If the arrows show runtime calls, a domain operation can call a data implementation through an interface. If they show source dependencies, a domain-to-data dependency points outward. To keep that boundary inward, the policy side defines the contract and the data implementation depends on it, so the source arrow runs from data toward policy. The boxes alone leave that distinction unresolved.

Android’s architecture guidance recommends UI and data layers with an optional domain layer when complexity or reuse calls for one. That guidance describes a possible arrangement of responsibilities, rather than prescribing the number of circles in Clean Architecture.
A reminder-time feature can express the dependency rule with two logical layers: the consumer-side contract and its implementation.

blocks.code:
ReminderSettingsViewModel  ── owns the screen's state, and declares what it needs
        ↑                     ReminderPreferenceRepository (the contract)
        │
LocalReminderPreferences  ─── implements the contract; names the store, the platform, the types

blocks.text:
The state holder refers to its contract, while the implementation refers to that contract and the storage library. Within this boundary, source dependencies point from storage detail toward the consumer’s requirement.

These reminder requirements add no independent domain operation or rule, so the feature needs no separate domain layer, use case, or mapping. The size of the arrangement does not determine whether this dependency follows the rule.
Renewal adds an application operation and lending policy, giving four conceptual groupings:

blocks.code:
RenewalEligibility       the lending rule; names only its own types
                            ↑
                        RenewLoan            the operation; names the rule and the
                        ↗       ↖                  contracts it declares for itself
   BorrowedItemsViewModel     LocalLoanRepository
   screen state; names        detail; names RenewLoan's contract
   the operation              in order to satisfy it

blocks.text:
The illustrated dependencies point toward policy. `RenewalEligibility` holds the lending rule; `RenewLoan` coordinates it with the contracts it needs. The screen owner calls the operation, and the repository implementation fulfils its contract.

The screen owner and repository implementation are both outside the operation. Neither has to name the other, so these dependencies form branches rather than one downward stack.

rows: Does every source dependency point toward policy?
Yes
Yes
Layers
Two
Four
Is there a domain layer?
No — nothing earns one
Yes — an operation and a rule with their own reasons to change
Mapping between representations
None; one type, because both sides change together
At the data boundary only, where the stored representation and the application model diverge
Compliant with the dependency rule?
Yes
Yes

blocks.text:
Clean Architecture names its circles entities, use cases, interface adapters, and frameworks-and-drivers. Entities hold enterprise-wide business rules; use cases hold application-specific rules. Android’s guidance instead names UI, domain, and data layers and uses “use case” for types in its optional middle layer.

Other sources and codebases may use interactor, application layer, or infrastructure differently. Compare the responsibilities and dependencies rather than assuming equivalent labels. In an interview or a new codebase, clarify what “domain” means in that context.

A three-layer template does not by itself satisfy the dependency rule, and the rule does not require one use case per repository method. Trace what inner code names. A small design can keep detail outside policy; a larger design can still couple its policy to framework types.

When policy does not depend on outer implementation details, an HTTP client, storage implementation, or UI toolkit can be replaced without rewriting the policy, as long as the new implementation fulfils the required contracts. The same independence can let other callers reuse the policy without bringing those details along.

Dependency direction does not guarantee fewer files, faster builds, simpler code, fewer modules, or better runtime performance. Separating representations may add mappings, and consumer-owned contracts add types to maintain.

Assess those costs against the independence each boundary provides. The dependency rule tells you how to keep policy separate from detail; the feature’s responsibilities determine where that separation is useful.

Policy can be tested without outer implementations when its dependencies allow tests to supply the required inputs or contract substitutes. Source dependency direction makes that separation possible. Merely adding layers does not remove a framework dependency from policy, while a small design can establish the needed boundary.

Architectural boundaries can exist within one Gradle module or across several. In one module, conventions and review can keep policy from naming implementations. Separate modules can enforce permitted dependencies through build configuration, at the cost of additional configuration and build complexity.

Organising modules by feature or by layer is a separate build decision. Either arrangement still needs source dependencies that follow the intended direction.

Explain the dependency rule: source dependencies point inward toward policy, and inner code does not name outer details. Apply it by tracing concrete types and contracts, showing how a small design can preserve the direction and a larger one can violate it. Then describe the trade-off: independence from frameworks, storage, and transport can require contracts and translations; it does not guarantee build speed, file count, or fewer mappings.

units.title: MVP, MVVM and MVI Responsibility Models
units.summary: MVP, MVVM and MVI describe ways to organise a screen's state and behaviour. Compare them by asking where state lives, who may change it, whether its owner references the UI, and how input and output travel. Teams use these names differently, so describing the responsibilities helps establish what a label means in a particular codebase.

lessons.title: One Screen, Five Questions
lessons.summary: Five questions help describe a screen: where state lives, who may change it, whether the behaviour owner knows the UI, how input arrives, and how output returns. These choices affect the lifetime coordination the screen needs. The questions provide a common basis for comparing MVP, MVVM and MVI when sources use the names differently.

blocks.text: MVC, MVP, MVVM and MVI describe arrangements of state, behaviour and UI responsibilities. To understand a screen using one of these names, look at who owns its state, who may change it, which components reference each other, and how their lifetimes are managed.

These names have been used across different UI toolkits for decades, and their meanings vary between sources and teams. Fowler's account of GUI architectures documents substantial differences among designs called MVC. When discussing a pattern, establish which arrangement the speaker means.

The following five questions make that arrangement concrete. They focus on the relationship between the UI and the component that owns its behaviour: ownership, the mutation path, dependency direction, and the paths for input and output.

items: **Where does the screen's state live?** Which component holds the values the screen renders — a widget, a composable, a screen-scoped owner, something longer-lived.
