**Who is allowed to mutate that state?** One component through one path, or anything that can reach it. Ownership here means who may write a value, not who reads it.
**Does the behaviour owner know the UI instance?** Does it hold a reference it can call, or publish values the UI observes? This dependency affects how output and view lifetime are managed.
**How does user input reach the behaviour owner?** A method call on a contract, a named function on a holder, a value representing what the user did — and who decides what that input means.
**How does output or state reach the UI?** A sequence of imperative calls into the UI, or one current value the UI observes and renders.

blocks.text:
After answering these questions, ask **what lifetime coordination the arrangement requires**. If the behaviour owner holds a UI reference and can outlive that UI instance, something must track when the reference is usable. Without that reference, there is no view attachment to manage. The owner's lifetime and the lifetime of its observers still need to be decided.

MVP, MVVM and MVI differ especially in how the owner relates to the UI and how input and output travel. Those choices help explain their different coordination needs.

Compare screens by asking where state lives, who may change it, whether the owner references the UI, how input reaches the owner, and how output reaches the UI. Then check the lifetime coordination that follows, including whether a held UI reference must be attached and detached.
Take one concrete screen: a **practice-configuration screen** in a quiz application, with these requirements:

items: It loads the practice options that are available — which topics can be practised, and which difficulty levels exist.
It holds several selections the user makes: a topic, a difficulty, and how many questions the session should contain.
It validates those selections against each other, because not every combination has questions behind it.
It enables a Start control only when the current configuration is valid.
It can be loading, and it can fail while loading.
After a failure it offers a retry.

blocks.text: Here is one possible design for the practice-configuration screen. It assigns ownership and communication paths explicitly, then identifies the lifetime coordination those choices require.

blocks.code:
1. Where does the state live?      One screen-scoped owner holds the loaded options,
                                   the current selections, and whether Start is allowed.

2. Who may mutate it?              Only that owner. The UI never assigns to it.

3. Does the owner know the UI?     No. It holds no reference to any UI instance and
                                   cannot call one.

4. How does input reach it?        The UI reports what the user did — chose a topic,
                                   chose a difficulty, asked to retry. The owner decides
                                   what each of those means for the configuration.

5. How does output reach the UI?   The owner publishes one current value describing the
                                   whole screen. The UI observes it and renders it.

6. What bookkeeping follows?       No owner-to-UI reference exists, so nothing has to
                                   track whether the UI is attached. The owner's own
                                   lifetime, and the lifetime of whoever is observing,
                                   are still real and still have to be decided.

blocks.text:
In this design, the UI reports choices to one state owner and renders the state it publishes. Because the owner holds no UI reference, a replacement UI can observe the same owner without being attached to it. The owner and observation still need appropriate lifetimes.

This description leaves other decisions open: whether a repository exists, which data source is authoritative, whether domain logic needs its own layer, and how dependencies are supplied. A pattern name provides shorthand for the presentation arrangement once the team agrees on its meaning.
Teams might use the following labels for this general arrangement. One also changes how input is represented, while keeping the same ownership and dependency direction.

rows: A
MVVM
A screen-scoped state holder that publishes observable state and holds no reference to the UI.
Nothing. This is the arrangement described above.
B
MVI-ish MVVM
The same holder, but user input is represented as values of a closed set of types rather than as separate functions.
How input is modelled (question 4). Ownership, mutation path and view knowledge are identical.
C
UDF, or state-holder architecture
State flows out, intentions flow in, and one owner writes.
The same responsibilities, described as UDF rather than with a presentation-pattern label.

blocks.text: All three designs share the same ownership and dependency direction; Team B makes input values explicit. Describing those similarities and differences is more informative than comparing the labels alone. Within a team that shares a definition, a label such as MVVM is useful shorthand. Across teams, confirm the responsibilities it refers to.

MVC originated in Smalltalk and separates Model, View and Controller. The controller role has since acquired different meanings; some designs use controller where another source would use presenter. When asked about MVC, clarify what the controller owns and how it communicates with the model and view.

A name such as “MVVM with Clean Architecture” leaves important details open. Follow it with a description of where state lives, who may change it, whether the owner references the UI, and how input is modelled. That gives the listener a concrete design to discuss.

UI toolkits help explain why these patterns evolved. Smalltalk MVC let views observe the model directly. Other frameworks relied more on a presenter updating widgets. Presentation Model separated presentation state and behaviour from the controls themselves. As toolkits changed, teams adapted the arrangements while retaining familiar names.

Even early accounts differed. Fowler records differences between descriptions of MVP and distinguishes later Passive View usage from the original accounts. This history is another reason to describe the responsibilities you mean when using a pattern name.

A held UI reference creates a lifetime obligation when the owner can outlive the UI: the owner must avoid calling an instance that is no longer usable. Removing the reference removes that particular obligation.

Other lifetime responsibilities remain. Something owns the state holder, observers must start and stop observing, and work needs an appropriate cancellation boundary. Check these separately from view attachment.

A shared pattern name helps a team coordinate, but leaves implementation choices open. “We use MVVM” does not establish whether state is published as one value or several, whether input uses methods or action values, or whether transitions have an explicit function. Ask about those choices when they matter to the design.

Describe a screen's state ownership, mutation path, UI dependencies, input and output, then give the label your team uses. If the question is about MVC, clarify the controller's responsibility. Explain the lifetime coordination needed by the actual arrangement.

lessons.title: MVP: an Explicit View Contract
lessons.summary: In the MVP arrangement examined here, a presenter holds a view abstraction and calls its methods to update the UI. The contract lists those updates, and their sequence determines what the widgets display. If the presenter can outlive the view, attachment and detachment must keep the reference usable. The arrangement has useful strengths as well as coordination costs.

blocks.text:
The practice-configuration screen loads topics and difficulty levels, holds the user's choices, validates them, and enables Start when the combination is valid. It also handles loading failures and retry.

In the MVP arrangement used here, the behaviour owner receives **a reference to a view abstraction**: an interface it can call to update the screen, rather than a concrete widget class.

That owner is the **presenter**. It receives user actions, decides what they mean, obtains the data it needs, and updates the screen by calling the view interface. The view renders those updates and reports user actions. This differs from a state-based arrangement in which the owner publishes values for the UI to observe.

blocks.code:
1. Where does the state live?      In the presenter, and — importantly — partly in the
                                   widgets themselves, which hold whatever the last call
                                   left them displaying.

2. Who may mutate it?              The presenter mutates its own state; the widgets are
                                   mutated by the presenter's calls.

3. Does the owner know the UI?     YES. The presenter holds a view abstraction and can
                                   invoke it. This is the pattern's defining property.

4. How does input reach it?        The view calls the presenter directly: onTopicChosen,
                                   onRetryClicked. The presenter decides what each means.

5. How does output reach the UI?   As a sequence of imperative calls into the view.

6. What bookkeeping follows?       Because of (3): something must know whether the view
                                   the presenter holds is still there.

blocks.text: MVP has variants with different divisions of view logic. In **Passive View**, the presenter directs widget updates; in **Supervising Controller**, simple model-to-view mapping stays in the view while the controller handles input and more complex view logic. Some sources call the presenter a controller. The example here uses a presenter that calls a view abstraction.

In this MVP design, the presenter receives user actions and calls a view abstraction to update the screen. Passive View and Supervising Controller differ in how much logic remains in the view. If the presenter outlives a UI instance, its view reference needs lifetime coordination.
`PracticeConfigView` lists the updates the presenter can request: loading, options, selection, Start availability and failure feedback.

blocks.code:
interface PracticeConfigView {
    fun showLoading()
    fun showOptions(options: PracticeOptions)
    fun showSelection(selection: PracticeSelection)
    fun setStartEnabled(enabled: Boolean)
    fun showFailure(message: String)
}

blocks.text: And the presenter holds one, receives the user's actions, and decides what each of them means.

This sketch omits the loading implementation, but shows the communication path: **the presenter updates the UI through a sequence of calls**. Loading options and choosing a valid difficulty might produce the following sequence:

blocks.code:
showLoading()
showOptions(...)
setStartEnabled(false)
showSelection(...)
setStartEnabled(true)

blocks.text:
The widgets display the accumulated result of the calls they receive. After a selection change, the presenter must update both the selection and Start availability. If it forgets the second call, the widgets can show a combination the presenter did not intend. A presenter that updates all affected controls in the right order can keep them consistent.

Publishing one immutable state value changes what the consumer observes: selection and `canStart` arrive together in each published value. The owner must still construct that value correctly. Updating the selection while leaving a stored `canStart` stale would publish an inconsistent value. Deriving the flag from the selection, or using a state model that prevents disagreement, protects that invariant before rendering. A presenter can also maintain this invariant internally, while still needing to keep its view calls consistent.

The presenter holds `view`, but a UI instance may be destroyed while the presenter survives, for example during navigation or host recreation. The reference can still point to an object even though its widgets are no longer usable. Calling it may update an invisible UI or access resources that have been torn down.

`attach` supplies the current view; `detach` clears it when that instance should no longer receive calls. The host decides which callbacks perform this coordination and how the presenter is retained. The need arises when the presenter and view have different lifetimes.
This arrangement offers several useful properties:

items: **The contract lists the updates available to the presenter.** Reading `PracticeConfigView` shows what this owner may ask the UI to do.
**Presentation logic leaves the view class.** Loading, selection and validation can be tested separately from widget wiring and host lifecycle callbacks.
**The view can stay simple.** In the passive variant it renders the supplied updates and reports user actions.
**The presenter defines the view contract it needs.** A rendering implementation depends on that abstraction, allowing a different renderer to supply the same methods.

blocks.text: Its costs are concrete as well:

items: **Contract changes for new UI capabilities.** New failure feedback, validation messages or progress indicators may require interface changes, view implementations and presenter call sites.
**A view relationship to manage.** The presenter holds a nullable reference and every call site has to cope with its absence.
**Attach and detach bookkeeping**, which has to be right for every path out of and back into the screen, not just the common one.
**Update ordering as a correctness concern**, because output is a sequence and the sequence has to leave the widgets in a coherent combined state.
**Contract growth.** More distinct UI updates can mean more methods and more coordination between presenter and renderer.

**Screen state can be distributed.** In this example, the presenter holds selection while widgets retain the results of previous calls. There is no single output value describing the whole screen for logging or restoration.

blocks.text: MVP separates presentation logic from view classes and makes the available view updates explicit. Understanding that arrangement helps you compare it with observed-state designs, including the contract you gain and the update coordination you must manage.

An explicit view contract makes the updates the presenter may request easy to enumerate: calls outside that interface do not compile. A state-based design instead publishes a complete value for the UI to render. Related fields can travel together, although the owner must still keep the value valid.

These are different ways to express output. Compare the contract and update sequence with the state type and its transitions when deciding which arrangement suits a screen. Neither guarantees a correct implementation by itself.

MVP leaves threading, presenter lifetime and the data layer open. A presenter can use repositories, use cases, both or neither. Whether it survives a configuration change depends on its owner; if it does, it must handle changes in the attached view.

View contract granularity is also a choice. One contract per screen is common, while contracts for separate screen sections trade one longer interface for several shorter ones.

The host affects the cost of holding a view reference. On Android, a UI instance may be destroyed and recreated while its presenter survives, so that relationship needs coordination. If their lifetimes match, less coordination may be necessary. When evaluating a pattern's cost, consider both its dependencies and the environment that manages them.

Explain how the presenter uses a view abstraction, and when that reference needs attachment and detachment. Name strengths such as an explicit contract and presentation logic outside view classes, alongside costs such as contract growth, update ordering and lifetime coordination. Distinguish Passive View from Supervising Controller where relevant.

lessons.title: MVVM: a UI That Observes State
lessons.summary: In the MVVM arrangement examined here, the behaviour owner publishes state and the UI observes it. The UI reports user intentions, and the owner holds no reference to a UI instance. This removes view attachment from the owner's responsibilities, while leaving owner and observer lifetimes to be managed. Class names, folders and state-stream counts do not establish those relationships.

blocks.text: In the MVP example, the presenter holds a view interface and calls `showOptions` or `setStartEnabled`. An alternative is to remove that reference and **publish state for the UI to observe**. The UI then renders the current state instead of receiving instructions to update individual controls.

blocks.code:
UI reports an intention
        │
        ▼
   state owner  ──── decides what the intention means,
        │              produces the next current state
        ▼
  current UI state
        │
        ▼
   UI observes it and renders whatever it currently says

blocks.text: This observed-state arrangement is commonly called MVVM. **The owner holds no reference to the UI instance.** It publishes state through an observation mechanism, and the UI decides when to observe it. The following answers show how that changes ownership and communication compared with the MVP example.

blocks.code:
1. Where does the state live?      In the screen's state owner, as one or more
                                   observable values. Nothing authoritative lives
                                   in the widgets.

2. Who may mutate it?              Only the owner, through one write path.

3. Does the owner know the UI?     NO. This is the change, and the rest follows.

4. How does input reach it?        The UI reports what the user intended; the owner
                                   decides what that means. (Unchanged from MVP.)

5. How does output reach the UI?   As current state the UI observes, not as calls.

6. What bookkeeping follows?       No presenter-to-view reference exists, so nothing
                                   has to track whether the view is attached.

blocks.text:
Removing the UI reference removes the owner's need to attach and detach a view or call its update methods. The owner publishes state instead, and the UI observes it.

Lifetimes still matter: something owns the state holder, observers must start and stop, and work must have an appropriate cancellation boundary. Also, published state must remain valid; removing the view reference alone does not prevent inconsistent updates.

In this MVVM arrangement, the owner publishes state, the UI observes it, and user intentions travel inward. The owner holds no UI reference, so it has no view attachment to manage. Owner, observer and work lifetimes still need to be defined.

A screen state holder owns the values the screen renders, accepts user intentions, updates its state, and exposes that state read-only. It holds no UI reference. **What a Screen State Holder Is Responsible For** examines these responsibilities in more detail.

There is no `PracticeConfigView` interface, nothing to attach, and nothing to detach. The observable value is shown here as a `StateFlow`, a Kotlin stream that always holds one current value, but **the choice of carrier is not part of the pattern**: an observing UI can read a `StateFlow`, a Compose snapshot state object, a platform observable, or a callback registration, and the responsibility arrangement is unchanged.

**A class named `ViewModel` does not establish an MVVM arrangement.** Android's `ViewModel` supplies a lifetime through its store owner; you still need to examine its state, mutation path and UI dependencies. A subclass that holds a view interface and calls it has a presenter-style relationship.

A plain class can instead publish state for the UI to observe without holding a view reference. Android's guidance distinguishes business-logic state holders, typically implemented with `ViewModel`, from UI-logic holders, typically implemented as plain classes. Choose the implementation according to the responsibility and lifetime it needs.
The second: **a folder layout does not make an architecture MVVM.**

blocks.code:
model/          ← says nothing about who owns data or who may write it
view/           ← says nothing about what the view is allowed to decide
viewmodel/      ← says nothing about whether anything in here holds a view reference

blocks.text: Two projects can have identical folder trees but different mutation paths and dependency directions. To understand the arrangement, inspect what the state owners reference and how the UI receives their output. A reference to a UI instance is particularly relevant to the distinction between the MVP and MVVM examples here.

**The number of observable values does not define MVVM.** A state owner can publish one combined UI state or several separate observables without holding a view reference in either case.

A combined value lets related fields arrive together in one emission, provided the owner updates them together. Separate observables can expose intermediate combinations during a multi-field change unless their updates are coordinated. That is a state-modelling decision within the observed-state arrangement.

Android's UI-layer guidance describes immutable UI state and unidirectional data flow: state travels from its owner to the UI, and events travel back. These responsibilities describe the arrangement directly, even without choosing between the MVVM and MVI labels.

Check what a `ViewModel` does before classifying it. Its superclass supplies lifecycle ownership, while its implementation determines the mutation path, UI dependencies and output contract. A plain class can publish observed state too; the framework type is a separate choice.

With no held UI reference, the owner exposes output through something the UI can observe. Current state is the main output in this arrangement, but the owner may also publish one-off instructions. Their delivery guarantees need a separate decision.

The owner can run while the UI is absent without calling a destroyed instance, and its behaviour can be tested without constructing a UI. The observation mechanism may still react to subscriber presence, and work still needs a lifetime. Publishing state while also retaining a view reference would not remove the need to manage that reference.

MVVM is related to **Presentation Model**, which separates presentation state and behaviour from GUI controls. Fowler's account allows different reference directions for synchronisation. MVVM developed in a setting with declarative data binding, but modern implementations use several observation mechanisms. That history helps explain variation around binding, class names and output delivery. For the arrangement examined here, the important relationship is that the UI observes the owner and the owner holds no UI reference.

Whether a state owner outlives a UI instance depends on what holds the owner. Removing the UI reference changes their dependency relationship; it does not choose either lifetime. Examine ownership separately when reasoning about recreation or navigation.

MVVM describes a *presentation* arrangement. It leaves data-layer contracts, repositories, optional domain logic, dependency provision and modularisation open. A team may combine the presentation pattern with conventions for those decisions, but the pattern name alone does not establish them.

Explain how the UI observes published state and why the owner has no view attachment to manage. Distinguish that from owner and observer lifetimes. Use a concrete implementation to show why class names, folder names and observable counts do not identify the arrangement by themselves.

lessons.title: MVI: Intent, Reduction and One Current State
lessons.summary: The MVI arrangement examined here represents input as explicit values, keeps one current screen state, and makes state transitions explicit. These choices make inputs and transitions easier to inspect. They also require input types, transition logic and a delivery decision for outputs that are not represented as state.

blocks.text: The practice-configuration screen can keep the observed-state arrangement from the MVVM example: its owner publishes state and holds no UI reference. The MVI design examined here adds two modelling choices: it represents input explicitly and makes the transition from one state to the next explicit. Those choices help you follow how a topic or difficulty selection changes Start availability.

First, **represent user input as a value**. Instead of calling `onTopicChosen(topic)`, the UI passes a value saying that a topic was chosen. A sealed type lists the input variants handled through this path in one place.

The second idea is **one current state and an explicit transition between states**. There is one value describing the whole screen, and moving from one to the next is a named, readable step rather than a set of assignments spread across handler functions.

blocks.code:
current state  +  intent
        │
        ▼
   transition
        │
        ▼
   next state

blocks.text:
**Reduction** is the step that produces a next state from the current state and an input. The function or component performing it is usually called a **reducer**.

Android MVI implementations differ in how they organise this step. Some require a pure function; some use a store abstraction or a dedicated transition class. Here, the key property is that the transition is explicit enough to inspect. Check an implementation's contract rather than assuming the word reducer establishes purity or a particular library structure.

In the MVI design used here, input is represented by explicit values, one current state describes the screen, and reduction produces the next state. The owner publishes state without holding a view reference, as in the MVVM example. Purity, stores and supporting machinery depend on the implementation.
The clearest way to see what this buys is to write one transition out in full. The user has chosen a topic and no difficulty yet, so Start is not allowed. Then they choose a difficulty.

blocks.code:
current:
  options    = loaded
  topic      = Coroutines
  difficulty = null
  canStart   = false

intent:
  SelectDifficulty(Advanced)

next:
  options    = loaded
  topic      = Coroutines
  difficulty = Advanced
  canStart   = true

blocks.text:
During this transition, `canStart` is decided from the topic and difficulty in the next state. The UI renders that decision rather than setting it. If every write passes through transitions that preserve this invariant, downstream consumers receive consistent state.

The reducer gives that validation a visible place. In the example below, choosing a topic or difficulty calls `revalidated()` before returning the new state.

blocks.code:
fun reduce(state: PracticeConfigState, intent: PracticeIntent): PracticeConfigState =
    when (intent) {
        is PracticeIntent.SelectTopic ->
            state.copy(topic = intent.topic).revalidated()
        is PracticeIntent.SelectDifficulty ->
            state.copy(difficulty = intent.difficulty).revalidated()
        PracticeIntent.Retry -> state.copy(failure = null, isLoading = true)
        PracticeIntent.Start -> state
    }

blocks.text: This arrangement makes several parts of the screen easier to inspect:

items: **The screen's state has one explicit representation.** There is a single value you can print, log, compare or reconstruct that says what the screen currently is.
**The input variants are enumerable.** The closed intent type lists the inputs handled through that path, with compiler checks for exhaustive handling.
**The transitions are discoverable.** Asking what `SelectDifficulty` does is answered by reading one branch, not by finding every handler that touches the difficulty field.
**The mutation path can be explicit and singular.** When every state change passes through the transition, the write path is visible in one place.

blocks.text: Explicit inputs and transitions make behaviour easier to inspect, but the transition rules still need to be correct. Thread safety depends on how state is held and updated. In-memory state still needs persistence if it must outlive its owner, and output delivery still needs a guarantee if an action must happen once. Rendering performance depends on the resulting state reads and UI structure.
These choices also add code and concepts:

items: **A type per kind of input.** Choosing a topic goes from one function signature to one declared type plus one branch that handles it.
**A transition for changes that were previously one assignment.** Toggling a switch is a type, a branch and a state copy where it used to be a line.
**One state model that grows with the screen.** Every field any part of the screen needs lives in the same value, and keeping it coherent is a design task that gets harder as the screen does.

**A delivery decision for outputs beyond current state.** Navigation requests or transient feedback may use a separate output mechanism, or pending state with acknowledgement, depending on the required guarantee.

**More concepts to learn before reading the screen.** Depending on the implementation, a newcomer meets an intent type, a state type, a transition function and possibly a store or a dispatch mechanism before they can follow one button press.

blocks.text:
Some implementations deliver navigation requests or transient messages as outputs separate from the current UI state. MVI material often calls them **effects**. Other implementations represent a pending request in state and acknowledge it after handling; the representation must fit the required delivery guarantee.

In Compose, `LaunchedEffect`, `DisposableEffect` and `SideEffect` name APIs for work associated with composition. They are distinct from an MVI output. Make the meaning clear when both uses appear in the same codebase.

For a separate output, decide what happens when no consumer is listening, whether a late consumer should handle it, and how handling is recorded. **Lost, Repeated or Acknowledged: Stating an Occurrence's Guarantee** examines those choices.

A sealed input type makes the input variants explicit, but does not by itself define how state changes. If handler branches still perform separate updates, check whether validation is applied consistently and whether intermediate values can be observed. The input model and transition discipline are separate decisions.

**Observable count alone does not distinguish MVVM from MVI.** An owner can publish one combined immutable value without explicit input types or a reducer. Conversely, explicit transitions need not use `StateFlow` as their carrier. Examine state modelling, input representation and transition logic separately. **Classifying What a Real Codebase Actually Does** compares concrete designs.

**MVI does not guarantee fewer recompositions.** Compose invalidation depends on state reads and update behaviour, while UI structure and stability affect what re-executes. A pattern name does not establish those properties.

For example, a composable observing one large state value may be invalidated when a field it does not display changes. Narrow observables can let it observe only the value it renders. The performance consequence depends on the actual implementation; **Stability and Skipping** explains the relevant Compose behaviour.

André Staltz describes MVI in **Cycle.js** as a composition of stream transformations: Intent turns user events into actions, Model turns actions into state, and View turns state into output. Android adaptations use these ideas in different ways, including different reducer, store and side-output contracts. A library's conventions describe that implementation; check them before assuming what its MVI label guarantees.

Explicit transitions are especially useful when inputs interact, invalid combinations are possible, or debugging requires tracing how the screen reached a state. A screen with a few independent fields and simple rules may need less machinery. Weigh the inspection and validation benefits against the extra input types, transition code and delivery concepts the screen requires.

Describe the input values, current state and transition in the implementation you use. Work through a transition such as choosing a difficulty, including where Start availability is decided. Explain the added types and mechanisms, and distinguish their benefits from guarantees they do not provide, such as reduced recomposition. Clarify whether effect means an MVI output or a Compose API.

lessons.title: Classifying What a Real Codebase Actually Does
lessons.summary: Production screens can combine a lifecycle-owned state holder, immutable state, callbacks or action values, and explicit transitions. Classify such a design by its responsibilities, then relate those choices to MVP, MVVM and MVI. Concrete examples show why stream counts, sealed inputs, recomposition claims and folder names are insufficient to identify the arrangement.

blocks.text: A production screen may combine decisions made at different times: a lifecycle-owned state holder, a combined immutable state, callback functions or action values, and explicit transitions where they help. Examine each responsibility before deciding which pattern the arrangement resembles.
A useful order is to describe the responsibilities, relate them to familiar patterns, and then give the team's label.

items: **Answer the five questions.** Where the state lives, who may mutate it, whether the behaviour owner knows the UI instance, how input reaches it, how output reaches the UI — plus the bookkeeping that follows.

**Name what each answer resembles.** A held view abstraction and pushed updates resemble MVP. Published state and no view reference resemble MVVM. Input as values from a closed set, one current state and an explicit transition resemble MVI.
**Describe the design in a sentence.** For example: “A screen-scoped owner publishes immutable state, accepts callbacks, holds no view reference, and has no central transition function.”
**Then offer the label the team would use**, and note that the term varies if it matters.

blocks.text: Describing the responsibilities makes disagreements easier to locate. Two engineers may use different labels while agreeing on ownership, mutation and communication paths. They may also share a label while imagining different write paths. Comparing the concrete arrangement reveals whether the difference is terminology or behaviour.

Describe ownership, mutation, dependencies, input and output before choosing a pattern label. A screen can combine techniques associated with different patterns. Explain which choices it makes; it does not need a new name for that combination.
The following three designs share some responsibilities and differ in others. Compare the state, input and transition models alongside the labels a team might use.

headers: What a team might call it
rows: A
A lifecycle-owned `ViewModel`; one immutable UI state value; named callback functions for input; no transition function anywhere; no reference to any UI instance.
State in the owner, one write path, no view knowledge, input as calls, output as observed state. Transitions are distributed across the callback bodies.
MVVM. Another team would say MVI-lite, or UDF, on the strength of the single state value.
B
A lifecycle-owned `ViewModel`; one state value; a closed set of action values; an explicit reducer; a separate mechanism for one-off outputs that are not state.
Same ownership and view knowledge as A. Input is modelled as values and the transition is explicit and in one place.
MVI, using the platform's ViewModel lifetime ownership alongside explicit transitions.
C
A screen-scoped state owner; several observable values rather than one; named callbacks for input; no reference to any UI instance.
The same ownership and UI dependency as A. State is split, so separate updates may expose an intermediate combination unless coordinated.
MVVM; the observable count differs from A, while the dependency relationship remains the same.

blocks.text: A and C differ in whether state is combined or split. A and B differ in input representation and whether transitions are centralised. All three put state in an owner that holds no UI reference. The following examples show why a label alone does not settle those differences.

**Stream count does not identify the transition model.** Design A publishes one state value, while C publishes several observables. Both use callback handlers rather than an explicit reducer. Combining C's state would change what consumers observe, but would not add input values or centralised transitions. A combined value can be useful in either arrangement.
**"MVI is MVVM plus sealed intent classes."** Take design A and add an action type, then dispatch to it:

The action type makes input explicit, but the state changes still happen in separate steps. Each selection update is followed by `recheckStartEnabled()`. If a branch omits that call, validation can become stale; between the calls, a consumer may observe an intermediate state.

A transition that computes the selection and Start availability together before publishing would address that concern. The useful distinction is what the write path guarantees, rather than whether the input has a sealed type.

**A pattern label does not determine recomposition.** In design C, a composable may observe only the value it renders. In A, a composable observing the whole state value may be invalidated when an unrelated field changes. Actual re-execution also depends on update behaviour, UI structure and stability. Compare those properties before attributing a performance change to the architecture.

**Folder names do not establish the communication path.** Designs A, B and C could all use `model/`, `view/` and `viewmodel/` folders. A class under `viewmodel/` might even hold a view interface and call `setStartEnabled`, giving it the presenter-style relationship from the MVP example. Read the dependencies and write paths to understand the arrangement.

When MVVM and MVI labels overlap, describe the state owner, mutation path, view dependencies, input representation and transition logic. Those facts let another engineer compare implementations even if the teams use different names.

A reducer can be useful without defining the whole screen architecture. For example, `ToolbarScrollReducer` turns scroll offsets into `ToolbarUiState` describing whether a feed's top bar should be visible. If it accumulates distance in its own fields, it is stateful rather than a pure function of explicit state and input.

That is a local transition technique. Inspecting how the rest of the screen owns state and handles input is still necessary to classify its presentation arrangement.

Consider `CheckoutViewModel`: it holds one immutable `CheckoutUiState`, exposes it read-only, and accepts callbacks for choosing a delivery slot, applying a voucher or retrying. It holds no UI reference and derives Place Order availability from its state.

In this example, a request to open confirmation is delivered through a separate channel, whose delivery guarantee must be chosen separately. There is no action type or reducer. These details describe the design regardless of which label the team uses.

MVP, MVVM and MVI describe **presentation responsibilities**. They leave repositories, authoritative data sources, data-layer APIs, optional domain logic, dependency provision, navigation and modularisation open. A team may use conventions for those choices alongside a presentation pattern.

They can also coexist with **Clean Architecture**. Its dependency rule concerns source dependencies between policy and detail; the presentation patterns concern a screen's relationship with its behaviour owner. A codebase can use inward-pointing dependencies, observed state, and explicit transitions in selected state holders without needing a separate name for the combination.

An interview answer can describe the arrangement before giving its name: *Our screen-scoped owners publish immutable state without holding view references. The UI reports intentions and observes state. Screens with interacting inputs use action values and a reducer; simpler screens use callback functions. The team calls this MVVM, with MVI-style transitions where useful.*

Adapt the description to the codebase you worked on. Its value is that each responsibility can be examined and discussed even when the interviewer uses the labels differently.

Describe an unfamiliar screen's state location, mutation path, UI dependencies, input, output and transition logic before naming the arrangement. Use concrete examples to explain why observable counts, input types and folder names leave questions open. Distinguish presentation choices from data, domain, navigation and rendering decisions.

units.title: State, Events, Lifetime and Architecture Selection
units.summary: Designing a feature starts with what the application must represent: a current fact, or an occurrence that calls for an action. Then establish the required delivery guarantees and lifetime before choosing an owner and a mechanism. Some obligations need a durable record of what remains pending; a transient in-memory signal cannot establish that they were handled. Finally, choose enough structure to give each responsibility a clear owner, using the feature’s complexity and the team’s needs to justify each addition.

lessons.title: Is This State, or Is It Something That Happened?
lessons.summary: A scored practice session can appear as current screen state, a durable result, or a reason to celebrate briefly. The requirement determines the representation. Distinguish what is currently true from what happened, then decide how long the current truth must remain reconstructable. A fact can be both state and durable; a celebration needs a separate rule for whether it may be lost or repeated.

blocks.text: Before choosing a type or owner for a new feature, establish what the application must represent.

**Is this something that is currently true, or an occurrence that calls for an action?** A screen renders current state: it reads a value and draws it, and rendering that value again need not repeat an action. An occurrence may instead call for an animation, navigation or another effect whose repetition matters to the user. **Rendering State and Running a Transient Effect** draws this distinction for a single screen.

For current state, ask **how long must this truth remain reconstructable?** It may be needed only while one component is on screen, while a destination exists, or after the process has been killed and restarted. These are lifetime requirements placed on state. The three cases below therefore describe different requirements, rather than three mutually exclusive runtime types.

items: **Representation: current truth or an occurrence to act on.** Does the screen need to *show* a fact, or does the application need to *do* something in response? Choose from the requirement, before choosing the code mechanism.

**Retention of current state.** How long must the truth remain reconstructable? Identify what may end that obligation: a composable leaving, a destination being removed, the process ending, or a later change to the stored fact.
**Durability is a retention requirement.** A fact can be both current state and durable, such as a saved score or an account setting.

blocks.text: The first question determines what to model: a published current value or an occurrence that needs a response. The retention question helps determine which owner can hold the current value; **Choosing an Owner From the Lifetime the Requirement Needs** develops that choice. Keeping these decisions separate helps avoid retaining a celebration that should expire, or carrying a result that must survive in a transient signal.

Distinguish a current truth from an occurrence that calls for an action. For current truth, decide how long it must remain reconstructable. Durability describes the required retention of state; the same real-world fact can need different representations under different requirements.

Consider one fact: **the practice session was scored.** The user answered the last question, the answers were marked, and a result exists. The application’s representation depends on what the product needs to do with that result.

**Requirement A — the result screen must render the finished session.** The user is looking at the score, the pass or fail verdict, their answers and the actions available next. What the application must represent here is a current truth: *this session currently has a completed result, and the result is this one.* A screen that arrives at this session later must immediately see the correct current result rather than waiting for something to be re-announced. That is current state with current-value semantics: an observer arriving at any time reads the latest value immediately, as a `StateFlow` collector does.

**Requirement B — the application must still know the score after the user leaves.** The user closes the result screen and returns tomorrow to a restarted process. The session must still show a score of eight out of ten.

This remains current state, with a longer retention requirement: it must survive the destruction of every in-memory owner. Record it somewhere that outlives those owners and reconstruct it from that record. Choosing which record is authoritative is a source-of-truth decision; **Which Source Is Authoritative?** covers that choice.

**Requirement C — immediately after scoring, celebrate.** On the active result screen, play a short animation, give one haptic confirmation and show a brief congratulatory message. The requirement calls for a brief response to scoring.

If the user closes the app before it runs, this requirement allows the celebration to be dropped. Playing it tomorrow would celebrate a session whose result the user has already seen.

headers: What a consumer arriving later should get
rows: A — render the finished session
Current state: this session has a completed result
The current result, immediately and correctly
A defect: the screen would show a session with no outcome
B — still know it tomorrow, after a restart
The same current state, with a retention requirement: it must be reconstructable after every in-memory owner is gone
The same current result, read back from wherever it was recorded
A defect: the application would lose a result it promised to retain
C — celebrate on the active result screen
A transient occurrence: something performed once, while somebody is watching
Nothing. There is no later consumer for this
Nothing. The requirement was about the moment, and the moment has passed

blocks.text: **Loss is a defect when it violates the requirement.** Requirement C permits doing nothing when the result screen is absent. A haptic response to a button press or a request to scroll the visible list to a newly added item can have the same condition: the effect is useful only while its UI is present. Giving these effects durable records and acknowledgements would add retention and handling rules that this requirement does not need.

For a transient occurrence, ask whether losing it would violate the requirement. An effect intended only for the visible UI may expire when that UI disappears; a confirmation the user must see later needs a different design.

A fact can become true at a particular moment and still need to be represented as state. Examples include an unfinished practice session, a failed submission attempt, a result awaiting review, or an account awaiting confirmation before another session can start. In each case, a screen opening later needs to know the current situation, not merely that something happened earlier.

The useful representation is the **current consequence**. “There is an unfinished practice session” remains true until the user resumes or abandons it. A screen opening six days later must be able to read that fact and offer to resume. An announcement sent only when the user stopped answering gives a later screen nothing to read; retaining the announcement also needs a rule for when that unfinished-session fact ceases to apply.
A transient response represented as persistent state can also repeat unintentionally. Suppose the result screen uses a boolean set when the score is computed:

If `showCongratulations` stays true, a new observer can trigger the celebration again. This can happen after a configuration change, when the user returns to a destination on the back stack, or after the flag is restored from durable storage. The consumer sees a request to celebrate but has no indication that the celebration already happened.

The missing part is **a rule for what “already handled” means**. A boolean can represent a pending response, but this one says only that a celebration is warranted. It does not distinguish a celebration still waiting to run from one already performed.

The repair depends on the required guarantee. The design might retain the state and add a handling rule, or use a transient response that may expire. **Lost, Repeated or Acknowledged: Stating an Occurrence’s Guarantee** explains that choice. Changing to an occurrence wrapper alone does not define the guarantee.

When a celebration, navigation or snackbar repeats, inspect the handling rule before changing its type. Does the requirement permit repetition, and what distinguishes a pending action from one already handled? A replacement type helps only if its contract answers those questions.
**Current state usually retains less information than the history that produced it.** The result screen may hold one value:

blocks.code: score = 8 / 10

blocks.text: This value can be enough to render the result, but it does not show which answer changed first, how long the user spent on question six, or whether the score was recomputed after a correction. Those details cannot be reconstructed from the final score because the application did not keep them.

A late observer can render `score = 8 / 10` correctly without knowing whether the session was answered in one pass or corrected later. Retaining that score does not restore the missing answer history. If the product needs that distinction, it needs additional recorded facts.

**When the product requires history, decide which historical facts to record.** “Show the last five practice sessions and their scores” requires records for those sessions, rather than just the latest score. Those records need a retention policy and a way to identify each session.

Keeping this history does not require recording every change and deriving all current state from a log. That approach, event sourcing, is a separate architectural choice with additional costs.

A scored session can be a durable database fact and current state projected in memory for screens to render. A saved draft or account setting can have the same arrangement. The design must identify which representation is authoritative and keep the projection consistent with it. Requirements A and B differ in retention, while both require the current result.

When asked whether something should be state or an event, explain what the requirement needs: a current truth or a response to an occurrence. For current truth, establish the required retention, including whether it must survive the process. Use the scored-session example to show why a past occurrence can have a current consequence, and why a pending celebration needs a rule that distinguishes it from one already handled.

lessons.title: Lost, Repeated or Acknowledged: Stating an Occurrence's Guarantee
lessons.summary: Before choosing a mechanism for an occurrence, establish whether it may be lost, whether a later consumer must act, whether repetition is safe, and whether handling must be recorded. Then decide whether the obligation must survive the process. A pending-or-handled record gives later consumers something to read; replay or a queue alone does not prove that the action was performed.

blocks.text: When an occurrence calls for an action, establish **what the product guarantees about that action**. An in-memory mechanism may deliver a value without establishing that a consumer handled it. Requirements for later handling, acknowledgement or persistence therefore need an owner that retains the outstanding obligation for the required lifetime.
Four questions help specify the guarantee. Answer each one: retention alone, for example, does not establish whether repeated handling is safe.

items: **May the occurrence be lost if nobody is listening?** If doing nothing in the absence of a consumer is acceptable, later handling may be unnecessary. Still establish whether repetition while the UI is present is safe.
**Must a consumer arriving later still act on it?** This is the question about absence: not whether something can be retained, but whether the product owes a later consumer an action.
**Is repeated handling safe?** Repeating a visual message and repeating a charge or borrowing request have different consequences. State what the product permits.
**Must the application record that it was handled?** If a later consumer must act and repetition is unsafe, the design needs an authoritative distinction between outstanding and handled.

blocks.text: If a later consumer must act, also ask **must that obligation survive the process ending?** Coroutine scopes, hot streams, state holders and ViewModels are in memory. When the process ends, those instances disappear. An obligation that must remain pending across that boundary needs a record with a durability contract.
Use these answers to choose the owner and its lifetime, then a mechanism that meets the guarantees:

blocks.code:
requirement
    ↓
guarantees          (may it be lost, must a later consumer act,
                     is repetition safe, must handling be recorded,
                     must the obligation survive the process)
    ↓
owner / lifetime    (who holds the fact, and what ends that owner)
    ↓
mechanism           (whatever satisfies all of the above)

rather than:

something called an event
    ↓
a stream type

blocks.text: Choose a mechanism after specifying the guarantees: permitted loss, required later handling, safe repetition, recorded acknowledgement and survival across process death. Establish who owns any pending obligation and for how long. A stream’s delivery contract must support those requirements; its name alone cannot establish them.

Consider a borrowing request for a title currently on hold. The library confirms it a minute or two after submission, when the reader has left the screen and backgrounded the app. The product requires the reader to see that confirmation when they next open the app, and requires an acknowledgement to be recorded. Compare that obligation with a request to scroll the visible list when a new loan appears:

headers: Scroll the visible list to the new loan
rows: May it be lost if nobody is listening?
No. The reader was told the request was submitted and is owed the outcome
Yes. If no list is on screen there is nothing to scroll, and nothing should happen
Must a later consumer act on it?
Yes. The next screen that opens must show it
No. A later screen has its own scroll position and its own reasons for it
Is repeated handling safe?
Repeated display may be untidy. Acknowledgement needs a rule that makes repeated handling safe or prevents it; re-submission is a separate action that must not create another borrowing request.
Repeated scrolling may be harmless if the list has not moved; after the user scrolls elsewhere, it could interrupt them
Must the application record that it was handled?
Yes. "Confirmed and seen" has to be distinguishable from "confirmed"
No. There is nothing whose handling anybody needs to know about
Must the obligation survive the process ending?
Yes. The confirmation may arrive while the app is not running at all
No. The obligation does not outlive the composition that has the list

blocks.text:
For the scroll request, act while the list is visible and discard the request otherwise. **What Delivery Guarantee Does This Occurrence Need?** covers such UI effects. A durable record and acknowledgement would add machinery without serving this requirement.

The borrowing confirmation needs more: it must remain available after the screen and process disappear, with a recorded distinction between pending and acknowledged.

**Replay retains values, not proof of handling.** A `SharedFlow` replay cache or a `StateFlow` current value lets a new subscriber recover retained data. Neither records whether an intended consumer acted, whether the action happened once, or whether the value survived process death. A collector created after a configuration change is a new subscriber and may receive the same retained value.

**Emission is not acknowledgement.** On a default unbuffered `MutableSharedFlow` with no subscribers, `emit` returns immediately and the value is lost; `tryEmit` can also succeed in that situation. A successful emission therefore does not establish that the reader saw the confirmation. It reports the result of the transport operation under its current configuration.

**Acknowledgement is state that somebody owns.** For the borrowing confirmation, a future consumer needs to read whether the acknowledgement remains outstanding. Represent that distinction with a value and identify the owner responsible for updating it:

Accepting or retaining a value does not establish whether its obligation is outstanding. The design must identify **who owns the pending-or-handled fact** and how long that fact survives. **Choosing an Owner From the Lifetime the Requirement Needs** develops that choice.

Android’s UI-event guidance recommends reducing ViewModel-originated actions to UI state when the producer outlives the consumer. Its message example stores an outstanding message in `userMessage`. After showing the message, the UI notifies the ViewModel, which clears that property with another state update. The consumer can read what remains to be shown rather than relying on a past emission.

A retained current value lets a later consumer read whether work remains. A transient emission that was discarded leaves no such record. Reducing the confirmation to pending state therefore supports later handling and acknowledgement. The scroll request has a different requirement: retaining it would add a lifetime and clearing protocol it does not need.

When an event is lost, check whether the requirement calls for later handling before adding replay. Replay may make a confirmation available to a later subscriber, but it may also replay it to a replacement subscriber after handling. Specify how pending and handled are distinguished, and whether repetition is acceptable.

An “exactly once” claim can refer to three different things: **recorded handling state**, **transport delivery**, or **side-effect execution**. A pending-or-acknowledged record lets the application read whether an obligation remains. A stream or network call delivers data. Neither alone establishes that an external action happened once.

Suppose the process ends after an external action succeeds but before its acknowledgement is recorded. The action happened, yet the record still says pending. Retrying from that record can repeat the action. The owner’s lifetime alone cannot close this gap.

Prefer a claim the design can support: “A consumer can read whether this obligation is still pending.” Claiming that the action executes exactly once requires more. An external system might recognise a stable request identity and treat retries as the same operation. That guarantee depends on the data and integration contract, beyond the state holder’s arrangement.

A `StateFlow`, `SharedFlow`, `Channel`, state holder or ViewModel instance disappears with the process. A ViewModel retains state according to its `ViewModelStoreOwner`; saved-state restoration is a separate mechanism.

If the borrowing obligation must survive process death, store it under a suitable durability contract, such as a local database. Retaining an object across configuration changes does not provide that durability.

A recorded obligation may lead to additional infrastructure: an event bus, a durable queue, retries, dead-letter handling, or an outbox that records outgoing work alongside a local data change. Each has its own guarantees and costs. First establish which guarantee is missing, which fact must be recorded, and who owns it; then decide whether that additional machinery is justified.

Delivery and handling need separate guarantees. If the obligation must survive process death, an in-memory stream cannot retain it alone. If it only needs in-memory retention, choose according to the remaining requirements: later subscribers, one receiver or multiple consumers, acceptable loss and acceptable repetition.

Replay, buffering, conflation and single-receiver or broadcast delivery have different contracts; **Choosing a Stream Abstraction by Delivery Guarantees** compares them. Those contracts determine what can be delivered. A handling rule is still needed when delivery must lead to a recorded action.

For a one-off-event question, establish permitted loss, required later handling, safe repetition, recorded acknowledgement and survival across process death. Name the owner and lifetime before choosing the mechanism. Explain why pending state helps a later consumer read what remains, and where its guarantee stops: recording acknowledgement alone does not prove exactly-once side-effect execution.

lessons.title: Choosing an Owner From the Lifetime the Requirement Needs
lessons.summary: Choose an owner by how long its state or work must survive and what may end it. The borrowed-items feature illustrates component, destination, application and durable-work lifetimes. A screen owner is too long-lived for a filter-sheet value that should reset, and too short-lived for a submission that must survive process death. Longer-lived owners also require explicit retention, freshness and reset policies.

blocks.text: Choose an owner for state, work or a pending obligation by asking **how long must this survive, and what event may end it?** Match that requirement to the owner’s lifetime. A conveniently available scope may or may not have the required lifetime.
Common lifetimes differ in what ends them. The final row is shorthand for durable work: it can also end through cancellation or a terminal failure under its work policy.

blocks.code:
a single UI element's own owner        ends when that element leaves the UI
        ↓
a screen or destination owner          ends when that destination is permanently gone
        ↓
an application-lifetime owner          ends when the process ends
        ↓
something that outlives the process    ends when the work is actually done

blocks.text: A longer lifetime keeps state or work alive across more changes, but also retains it longer and makes reset less automatic. Application-scoped state, for example, needs explicit rules for invalidation and sign-out. Choose that lifetime because the requirement needs it, rather than because the data seems important.
Prefer the shortest lifetime that satisfies the requirement. Start with the UI element’s owner and consider longer lifetimes only when the state or work must outlive it.

Match the owner’s ending event to the requirement. A UI element, destination, application process and durable work record provide different lifetimes. Prefer the shortest sufficient one, and account for the retention and reset rules required by a longer-lived owner.

The borrowed-items screen lists loans, supports filtering and refresh, and lets the reader submit a borrowing request. These responsibilities need different lifetimes. A destination-scoped owner works for some of them, but is too long-lived for one UI detail and too short-lived for durable submission work.

**One — whether the filter sheet is expanded.** In this feature, expansion is meaningful only while the sheet is present and should reset when it is reopened. Keep that state with the UI component.

Putting it in the screen’s state holder would retain it after the sheet disappears unless the holder explicitly resets it. It would also add a field and update function to the holder’s public surface, giving other screen code access to a UI detail it does not need.

**Two — the loaded loans, filter selection and in-flight refresh.** These belong to the destination. They must survive configuration changes while that destination remains, but may end when it is permanently removed. A destination-scoped state holder, such as a ViewModel, fits that lifetime. The refresh can run in its scope and be cancelled when that owner is cleared.

**Three — the loan count and overdue status shown on several screens.** A change made on one destination must appear on another when the reader navigates back. Shared data alone does not require an application-scoped projection: destination owners can observe the same data source and derive their own state.

If the source offers only one-shot reads, the design needs a way to refresh those projections after changes. A shared owner spanning the destinations is one option.

Suppose each repository read returns once and exposes no `Flow`. A renewal on the loan-detail screen updates the database, while the borrowed-items screen on the back stack still holds its previously loaded count.

One design gives the shared projection an owner above those destinations. It reads back after each relevant mutation and republishes the result, while the database remains authoritative. Choose a lifetime that spans the destinations that need it. If the projection is required throughout the process, a dedicated application scope, for example one using a `SupervisorJob`, can run that work. A destination-scoped `viewModelScope` would end too soon for that requirement.

Application scope is one design choice here. Observable repository reads or a shorter-lived owner shared by a navigation flow may be sufficient under different requirements.
Application-lifetime state remains eligible to live until the process ends. Its owner must decide what to retain, when to invalidate it and when to reset it:

items: **Retention.** A large projection built for a screen visited once may remain for the rest of the process unless the owner releases it.
**Freshness.** The owner needs invalidation or update rules; leaving a screen no longer resets the projection automatically.
**Coupling.** Screens that read the same projection are connected through it. A change for one can affect the others even without a direct call between them.
**Access control.** A shared owner needs a deliberate API so that broader reach does not become unrestricted global mutation.
**Reset semantics.** Sign-out, cache clearing or profile switching need explicit reset behaviour; leaving one destination will not clear the application owner.

blocks.text: When work is cancelled with a screen owner, first check whether that cancellation matches the requirement. If the work must continue after the screen disappears, choose a longer-lived owner deliberately. If it must also survive process death, an application scope alone is insufficient.

**Four — the submitted borrowing request.** The product promises completion even if the reader leaves the screen, backgrounds the app or the process ends before the network returns. An application scope can outlive the screen and foreground UI, but still disappears with the process.

This requirement needs durable work scheduling in addition to an in-process coroutine scope. On Android, WorkManager is designed for persistent work that remains scheduled across process exit and device restart. Its constraints and retry policy determine when attempts run. Those scheduling guarantees do not, by themselves, establish that the external borrowing request succeeds exactly once.

rows: One UI element's own owner
The element leaving the UI
The value is meaningful only while that element is present, and should reset when it returns
Local ownership; other components that need the value may require it to be hoisted
A screen or destination owner
The destination being permanently destroyed
The state is produced for this screen and stops mattering when the reader leaves for good
A lifetime longer than a single element's, and a public surface that everything on the screen can reach
An application-lifetime owner
The process ending
A process-wide shared projection must remain available after an individual navigation entry is destroyed
Retention, staleness, hidden coupling between screens, and reset that has to be written
Something outliving the process
Completion, cancellation or a terminal outcome under the work policy
The product promised the operation finishes regardless of the app being closed or killed
A scheduler such as WorkManager, with its constraints, deferral and retry policy

blocks.text: For these requirements, a screen holder is too long-lived for filter-sheet expansion and too short-lived for the borrowing submission. The expansion should reset when the sheet disappears; the submission must remain pending beyond process death. Either mismatch can be missed during a brief demo, where the sheet is opened once and the request finishes before navigation.

A ViewModel’s lifetime depends on its `ViewModelStoreOwner`. An activity, navigation entry or suitably scoped composable can have different clearing conditions. “The ViewModel survives the screen” is therefore incomplete without naming the owner. **The ViewModel Owner: Lifetime Is Not Persistence** explains those conditions owner by owner.

The same discipline applies to groups of destinations. A destination owns a lifetime, and so can a group of destinations: a multi-step flow can share one owner across its steps and lose it when the flow is popped, which is a genuinely different lifetime from either a single screen or the application. That is a real rung between the two, and how it is expressed depends on the navigation library in use.

Choose the lifetime from an ending condition such as “until the sheet closes”, “until the destination is removed”, “until the process ends” or “until this work reaches its terminal outcome”. A class location, available scope or convenient constructor does not establish that condition. Passing a deliberately chosen scope as a dependency can make the lifetime decision visible to the next engineer.

When asked where state or work belongs, identify what may end it and name an owner with the matching lifetime. Use the filter sheet and borrowing request to explain how a screen owner can be too long-lived for one responsibility and too short-lived for another. Account for retention and reset in an application owner, and for durable scheduling when work must survive the process.

lessons.title: How Much Architecture Does This Feature Need?
lessons.summary: Match structure to the responsibilities a feature must handle. A reminder-time setting can use a state holder and one data contract. A borrowing checkout needs shared eligibility logic, separate data responsibilities, explicit transitions and durable submission handling. Compare the cost of each addition with the requirement it serves, while allowing for the value of a consistent team structure.

blocks.text: Choose architecture by identifying the feature’s responsibilities and the boundaries, owners and lifetimes they need. A simple setting and a borrowing checkout can require different structures even within the same application.

**Justify each structural element by the problem it solves.** Use the feature’s actual complexity and the team’s needs to decide where boundaries belong. If a component has no current purpose, leave it out and identify what future requirement would justify adding it.

A screen state holder and one small data contract can fully serve a simple feature. A domain layer, use case, reducer or separate repository interface is useful when it addresses additional complexity. The smaller arrangement can be complete when it meets the feature’s requirements.
Use enough structure to give every responsibility a clear owner. A small architecture can be complete; add components when you can explain the feature or team requirement they serve.

Consider a reminder-time setting in a library application. The reader picks a time of day for reminders about loans due soon. This example covers the preference itself: load the current time, let the reader change it and store it through one source. It has one caller, one value and no coordination across sources.

blocks.code:
reminder/
  ReminderSettingsViewModel     owns the screen's current state and the one write path
  ReminderPreferenceRepository  the data contract the screen owner depends on
    LocalReminderPreferences    the implementation; names the store and the platform

blocks.text:
`ReminderSettingsViewModel` owns the screen state and its write path. `ReminderPreferenceRepository` keeps storage details out of the screen owner; `LocalReminderPreferences` implements that data contract.

A domain layer or forwarding use case adds little here: there is no shared application rule, cross-source orchestration or second caller. One assignment does not require a reducer and action type. There is no separate occurrence-delivery requirement, and both sides can use the same time-of-day representation.

The write still needs an appropriate lifetime. If the UI shows the new value as saved, the write must not be cancelled merely because the screen closes. Choosing an owner that can finish that write addresses this requirement without necessarily adding another type.
The borrowing checkout has more responsibilities. The reader assembles a basket, the app checks eligibility, and the request is submitted to the library:

items: Eligibility depends on loan limits by title and reader, unpaid fines, holds for other readers and membership expiry.
Answering it needs several data responsibilities — the reader's current loans and standing, the catalogue's availability and holds — each with its own source and its own freshness question.
Three surfaces perform the check: the checkout screen, the title detail screen, and a re-check at submission time.
The flow has one current workflow state with transitions that must hold invariants: nothing may be submitted from an unvalidated basket, and a confirmed request may not be edited.

The submitted request is a fact the reader was told about, so it must survive the screen, the app being backgrounded and the process ending, and it must be acknowledged once when the library confirms it.

blocks.text:
The eligibility rule is shared by three callers and combines several data responsibilities, so a domain operation gives it one owner. Repository boundaries separate loans and reader standing from catalogue availability, each with its own source and freshness policy.

An explicit transition function can enforce the workflow invariants across changes. A durable record distinguishes a pending submission or acknowledgement from one completed. Because submission must survive process death, persistent scheduling is also needed. Each addition serves a specific responsibility; none is justified merely by the feature’s size.

headers: The requirement that earns it in the checkout
Why it is absent from the setting
rows: A domain operation with its own home
One eligibility rule, three callers, and orchestration across two data responsibilities
One caller, no rule, nothing to orchestrate — the class would forward and nothing else
More than one repository boundary
Loans and standing change for different reasons and from different sources than catalogue availability
One fact, one source, one reason to change: a second boundary would isolate nothing
An explicit transition function
Invariants that must hold across every change, including "not submittable until validated"
One transition, and it is an assignment — a reducer would name the assignment and add nothing
A durable submitted-or-confirmed fact
The reader was told the request was submitted, and the confirmation may arrive with the app closed
Nothing here must reach anybody; the stored preference is the whole of what survives
An owner whose lifetime exceeds the screen
The submission must complete whether or not the reader stays, and survive the process
The preference write must commit after the screen closes, but the requirement does not call for ongoing submission work or durable scheduling

blocks.text: Suppose the reminder setting is given the checkout’s structure: `GetReminderTime` and `SetReminderTime` classes in `domain`, `ReminderAction` values passed through a reducer, another representation mapped at the repository boundary, and an occurrence mechanism for changes. Without requirements for those pieces, the team takes on additional costs:

items: Two classes and two files that forward a call and return what they were given.
A mapping function between two representations that change together, so every field added lands in three places instead of one.
An action type and a transition for a single assignment, and one more indirection between what the reader tapped and the value being written.
A delivery mechanism with no delivery requirement, which now has a configuration somebody has to defend in review.
A domain directory containing only forwarding classes can suggest that application policy is already represented there, making the responsibility harder to locate when it is later introduced.

blocks.text: Misleading structure also affects later maintenance. Engineers use the organisation of a codebase to find responsibilities, so a boundary or directory that suggests the wrong owner can repeatedly send readers to the wrong place.

Now suppose the checkout uses only the setting’s state holder and data contract, without distinct owners for its additional responsibilities. The gaps may not appear in a short demo.

Eligibility rules duplicated across three screen owners need coordinated updates. If source selection and freshness decisions move into those holders, data policy leaks upward. Invariants spread across callbacks can be enforced on some paths and missed on others.

A transient confirmation cannot satisfy the promise of later acknowledgement, and submission work tied to the screen may be cancelled when the reader leaves. These are missing responsibilities and lifetime guarantees, rather than simply too few classes.

Assess responsibilities and boundaries rather than class counts. Missing owners can leave a rule duplicated, an invariant inconsistently enforced or a submission promise unsupported. Unnecessary boundaries add indirection without separating useful responsibilities. Both problems can occur in the same feature.

Decide where state lives, who may update it, how transitions work, which lifetime each owner needs, what must be durable and which way dependencies point. Pattern names can then describe the arrangement. The checkout’s explicit transitions over one workflow state may resemble MVI; that description does not resolve its delivery or lifetime requirements.

**Uniformity has value too.** A team can use a common structure so that engineers know where to look in an unfamiliar feature, reviewers have a familiar shape to check, and tools and templates can assume consistent conventions. Those benefits may justify some additional indirection in smaller features.
