State that tradeoff explicitly. “We use a domain layer in every feature for consistency, accepting two forwarding classes in the small ones” explains the reason and the cost. It gives the team something concrete to revisit if the convention becomes less useful. “Every feature needs a domain layer” leaves that reasoning unstated.

A checklist can support this judgement without mechanically choosing the architecture. No fixed repository count requires a reducer, and no single complexity score establishes the need for a domain layer. Ask what each element would own and what it would cost; the answers require the feature’s context.
Use five questions to compare the setting and the checkout:

items: **What responsibilities exist?** The setting renders and stores one preference. The checkout assembles a basket, checks eligibility, manages a workflow and retains a submission obligation.
**Who owns them?** The setting has one state holder and data contract. The checkout separates owners for its additional data, policy, workflow and submission responsibilities.
**What may depend on what?** The same rule in both: the screen owner depends on a contract it needs, and the implementation depends inward on that contract.

**What lifetime does each part require?** The setting has screen state and a preference write that must commit; its stored value outlives the screen. The checkout also needs submission work and records that survive process death.

**What does each boundary cost?** The setting needs little indirection. The checkout’s additional boundaries separate responsibilities with their own sources, rules and lifetimes. Explain what each addition provides.

blocks.text: Choose an arrangement in which each responsibility has an owner, dependencies have a clear direction, lifetimes meet the requirements and boundaries provide enough value to justify their costs. The setting and checkout can both meet those conditions while using different amounts of structure.

When asked to architect a feature, establish the requirements and build from a small sufficient structure. Explain what each addition owns. Use concrete costs to discuss unnecessary boundaries, and concrete failures to discuss missing owners. If team consistency justifies extra structure, name that benefit and its cost explicitly.

units.title: Dependency Injection as Object Construction
units.summary: A class can construct a collaborator, fetch it from somewhere else, or receive it from outside. Receiving it is dependency injection. This makes construction a separate responsibility from using the collaborator, whether the objects are assembled by hand or with Dagger, Hilt or Koin. Who supplies an object and which side owns its contract are separate design decisions.

lessons.title: Who Constructs This Object?
lessons.summary: A class can construct a collaborator, fetch it from somewhere it can reach, or receive it from outside. These choices affect who selects and builds the collaborator, how instances are shared, and which requirements callers can see. Receiving it is dependency injection; no library is required.

blocks.text: A `StudySessionController` runs one study session. It needs questions to ask and a clock to record when the session began. The question repository and clock are **dependencies**: collaborators the controller uses to do its work.

A dependency is an ordinary object viewed from the class that uses it. `SystemClock`, for example, is a dependency of `StudySessionController` because the controller uses it to obtain the time. The construction question is where that clock comes from.

blocks.code:
StudySessionController
    ├── QuestionRepository
    └── SystemClock

blocks.text: Android’s dependency-injection guide describes three ways a class can obtain a collaborator:

items: **Construct it.** The class creates the collaborator itself, in its own body.
**Fetch it.** The class asks something else for the collaborator — a global registry, a static accessor, an ambient context object.
**Receive it.** Whoever constructs the class supplies the collaborator, as a constructor parameter or as an argument to the function that needs it.

blocks.text: Receiving the collaborator from outside is **dependency injection**. A class that accepts what it needs as a constructor parameter is using DI, even if the project has no container, annotations or generated code. The collaborator can be a concrete class; an interface is not required.

*Injection* describes who supplies the collaborator: outside code passes it in, rather than the consuming object obtaining it for itself. Bindings, modules, scopes and generated factories help arrange that supply as the graph grows.

A dependency is a collaborator a class uses to do its work. Receiving that collaborator from outside is dependency injection. This describes who supplies it, regardless of the library or the collaborator’s type.
These three versions of the controller use the same two collaborators. What changes is how those collaborators arrive and who makes the construction decisions.
**Version A — construct it.** The controller builds what it needs.

This controller chooses **which implementation** to use by naming its concrete type. It also knows **how to construct it**: if `QuestionRepository` gains a required constructor argument, this file must change.

It creates **one repository per controller** and keeps a reference to that instance. The caller cannot supply a different repository or share one across controllers through this constructor.
**Version B — fetch it.** The collaborators move out of the class into something the class can reach.

The controller no longer knows how to build the repository; other code fills the registry. A different instance can be installed without editing the controller.

Its constructor still reads `StudySessionController()`, so callers cannot see that the repository and clock must already be registered. If either `lateinit` property is unset, construction fails when the controller reads it. The controller obtains its own collaborators instead of receiving them from its caller. This is a **service locator**, discussed further in **Asking For It, or Being Given It**.
**Version C — receive it.**

The repository and clock are now constructor parameters. Whoever constructs the controller supplies their instances and decides how to build and share them. The signature makes both requirements visible to callers.

rows: Who chooses the implementation
The class itself
Whoever filled the registry
The caller
Who knows how it is built
The class itself
Whoever filled the registry
The caller
Who decides lifetime and sharing
The class itself, by implication
Whoever filled the registry
The caller
What `StudySessionController(…)` tells a reader
No collaborators are declared
No collaborators are declared
That both collaborators are required
Can one caller supply something different
No, not without editing the class
Only by changing state every caller shares
Yes, by passing it
When a missing collaborator is noticed
There is no collaborator argument to omit; construction runs inside the class
At run time, when the lookup executes
At compile time, at the construction site
Is this dependency injection
No
No
Yes

blocks.text: A project can use dependency injection without adding a library. Version C already does so. A DI framework automates supplying collaborators; it does not introduce the underlying design.
Dagger, Hilt and Koin each offer a way to automate and organise exactly these construction decisions. None of them is needed to make the decisions themselves.

Version C gives the assembling code control over construction. If each consuming class constructs its own repository, changing the implementation means finding and editing those construction sites. Supplying the repository from outside lets assembly code make that choice. Callers can then configure objects and provide suitable dependencies for tests without changing the consuming class.

Fowler describes the principle as separating service configuration from service use. Version A combines them: the controller both builds its collaborator and uses it. Version C leaves construction to outside code and keeps the controller focused on the study session.

For objects the application constructs, constructor injection makes required collaborators visible at the construction site. **A Dependency Should Be Visible** examines its guarantees.

A framework may own construction, leaving the application no ordinary constructor call to supply arguments through. If the framework assigns a collaborator to a field, that is still injection: the collaborator comes from outside. Field injection has different mechanics and fewer construction-time guarantees.

Explain dependency injection in terms of construction: a class can construct a collaborator, fetch it, or receive it from outside. Receiving it moves construction and sharing decisions to the supplying code. A framework automates that supply for a larger graph; constructor parameters already express the technique.

lessons.title: A Dependency Should Be Visible
lessons.summary: For a class the application constructs, required constructor parameters make collaborators visible and prevent callers from omitting them. Holding those parameters in `val` properties also prevents later replacement. Concrete collaborators can be injected without interfaces. A long parameter list makes responsibilities visible and gives you a reason to examine them.

blocks.text: Receiving a collaborator from outside is dependency injection, whether it arrives through a constructor or a property. When the application constructs the class itself, a **required constructor parameter** provides several useful guarantees.
A required constructor parameter has four distinct consequences:

items: **The requirement is visible.** It appears in the constructor signature, so callers can see what the class needs without reading its body.
**The requirement cannot be skipped.** Every constructor call must provide the required argument, or the code will not compile.
**The collaborator is supplied before the object is used.** There is no separate assignment or initialise-me call for the caller to remember.
**The reference can be immutable.** A constructor parameter can be held in a `val`, so no later code can swap the collaborator underneath an object that is already running.

blocks.text: These guarantees come from the constructor and, for the immutable reference, the `val` property. A DI framework arranges the arguments at the construction site; it is not needed for the language to enforce them.

For a required collaborator in a class the application constructs, constructor injection makes the requirement visible and mandatory, and supplies the reference before first use. Store it in a `val` if the reference should remain unchanged. These guarantees do not require a DI framework.
**A concrete dependency, injected.** The controller needs to know the time. Here is the collaborator that tells it:
`SystemClock` is a concrete class that reads the platform clock. The controller can receive it directly:

The controller receives a concrete `SystemClock`, so it is using dependency injection without an interface. Its caller supplies the instance. The constructor makes the requirement visible and mandatory, and the `val` keeps that reference unchanged after construction.

Dependency injection does not require an interface for every collaborator. Injection concerns who supplies the object. An interface lets a consumer state a requirement independently of the implementation. A concrete object can be supplied from outside just as an interface implementation can.

An interface is useful when a consumer needs to state a contract independently of its implementation, when the two sides change independently, or when someone else supplies the implementation. It also adds a type and contract to maintain. This example keeps `SystemClock` concrete because it does not yet need that boundary. **When an Interface Is a Boundary, and When It Is Only Indirection** develops the decision.
**What the alternative costs.** Compare the same controller with its collaborators assigned after construction instead of taken at it:

With these `lateinit var` properties, callers must assign the collaborators after constructing the controller. Calling `start()` before both assignments throws `UninitializedPropertyAccessException`. The missing dependency is found on the execution path that uses it, rather than checked at the constructor call.

The references can also be reassigned. Any code with access to the controller can replace its repository, so determining which repository a session used may require following those assignments.

Field injection can be useful when Android owns construction, as **When Android Owns Construction** explains. When the application can supply constructor arguments, the constructor avoids this separate initialization step.
**A constructor that has grown.** Suppose the same controller accumulates work over a few releases:

A long constructor is a reason to examine the class’s responsibilities, not a failure at a fixed parameter count. This signature makes nine requirements visible. Moving them into registry lookups would leave the controller needing the same objects while hiding those needs from callers.
The list supports several design questions:

items: **Does this class own too much behaviour?** It coordinates recording attempts, calculating scores and scheduling reminders. Some of that work may belong to a collaborator the controller calls.

**Do several parameters describe one responsibility?** If collaborators are always used together, an object that owns that work may be missing. The controller could then receive that object instead of coordinating the group.

**Is a parameter known only at run time?** `sessionId` is known when a session starts, rather than when the application graph is assembled. Supply it to the start operation or to a controller factory. **A Value the Graph Cannot Know** develops this distinction.

**Would an abstraction help a particular collaborator?** Apply the boundary test to each one: does a consumer need to state a requirement independently of its implementation? Parameter count alone cannot answer that.

blocks.text: Fetching collaborators from a container shortens the constructor without reducing what the class needs. If the list reveals too many responsibilities, address those responsibilities rather than hiding the list.

Some collaborators are optional: a build might omit analytics reporting, for example. Keep that choice explicit with a constructor default or a supplied implementation that does nothing.

A required collaborator should remain required. Making it nullable or assigning it through a setter to shorten the list moves responsibility from a checked constructor argument to runtime checks and initialization order.

Because the caller supplies collaborators, another caller can supply different instances compatible with the declared types. That gives tests control over construction, but does not make every concrete class replaceable by a fake. Kotlin classes are final by default; the concrete `SystemClock` shown here still reads the real clock. A compatible abstraction or other supported substitution mechanism is needed when a test must change that behaviour.

Constructor parameters make the choice explicit. Interfaces fetched from a global registry may support different implementations, but a caller must change registry state rather than pass its choices directly.

Constructor injection is a way of declaring a class’s requirements. Fowler describes it alongside setter and interface injection, independently of any DI library. A framework can generate or perform the construction and provide a configuration language. Constructors that do not depend on that framework can often stay the same when the wiring tool changes.

A constructor signature gives callers a place to discover required collaborators, and the compiler checks those arguments at each construction site. This makes omissions easier to find than requirements stated only in comments or buried in the class body. A long signature can also reveal responsibilities that deserve closer examination.

Explain constructor injection through its guarantees: required collaborators appear in the signature, callers must supply them, and there is no later assignment to remember. A `val` prevents replacing the stored reference. If the parameter list is long, examine the responsibilities it exposes before changing how dependencies arrive.

lessons.title: Injected, Inverted, or Both?
lessons.summary: Injection asks who supplies a collaborator. Dependency inversion asks which side owns the contract and which way the source dependency points. A constructor-injected database can still couple a consumer to a storage implementation. A consumer-owned repository interface can reverse that dependency while its implementation is supplied by hand, with no DI container.

blocks.text: These two statements concern the same repository, but describe different decisions:

items: "The repository is injected into the controller."
"The controller's dependency on the repository is inverted."

blocks.text: They answer different questions, and an arrangement can satisfy either one without the other.

rows: Dependency **injection**
Who supplies this object to the class that needs it?
The construction site — a constructor call, a factory, a container
Whoever assembles the objects
Dependency **inversion**
Which side declares the contract, and therefore which way does the source dependency point?
The import list — which file names which
Whoever designs the boundary

blocks.text: To check dependency inversion, locate the contract and inspect which side refers to it. In Clean Architecture, source dependencies point toward the inner policies: an inner layer does not name an outer implementation. That is separate from how objects are constructed. **Who Defines the Abstraction?** examines inversion in more detail.

Injection is about supply; inversion is about which side owns the contract in source. Injection is visible at the construction site, inversion in the import list. Neither implies the other, and all four combinations occur in real code.
**Arrangement one: injected, and not inverted.** An operation loads the questions a session needs. The class that stores them is a SQL-backed store belonging to the data implementation.

`LoadQuestions` receives its database through the constructor. The required argument is visible, and the compiler checks that a caller supplies it. Different callers can pass different `SqlQuestionDatabase` instances without the operation constructing them itself.

The source dependency still points from `session` to `data.sql`: `LoadQuestions` imports `SqlQuestionDatabase`. The operation therefore depends on the storage implementation’s type and cannot be compiled independently of it. Changes to that type’s contract can require changes in the operation.

Injection moved construction outside `LoadQuestions`; it did not change which type the operation names.

A DI framework can supply collaborators while the consuming classes still name concrete infrastructure types. To assess dependency inversion, inspect the contracts and source dependencies as well as the wiring.

**Arrangement two: inverted and injected by hand.** The session side needs a contract in its own vocabulary, while the storage implementation should be able to change independently. The session side declares that contract:
The application supplies the implementation in `main`:

`data.local` now imports the contract in `session`, while `session` no longer names the storage implementation. Declaring the interface on the consumer side changed the source dependency. The code in `main` separately chooses, constructs and supplies an implementation. It performs dependency injection by hand.

The interface separates the session requirement from the storage implementation. Without that boundary, the repository could remain concrete and still be injected, as `SystemClock` is here. Injection decides how the object arrives; the boundary decides whether a separate contract is useful.

rows: No
No
The class constructs a concrete collaborator itself
The class calls its collaborator's constructor in its own body, so it owns the implementation choice, the construction and the import
Yes
No
The collaborator is supplied from outside, and the consumer's source still names the implementation
Arrangement one above — real injection, unchanged source direction
Yes
Yes
The collaborator is supplied from outside, behind a contract the consumer owns
Arrangement two above: `main` supplies the implementation of a consumer-owned contract
No
Yes
The consumer owns the contract and fetches an implementation of it from a registry instead of receiving one

The consumer names its own contract and an accessible registry, without naming `data.local`. Assembly code registers the implementation. Source dependencies can remain inverted, while the consumer’s lookup hides the requirement from its constructor and defers a missing-registration failure to execution. See **Asking For It, or Being Given It**.

blocks.text: Arrangement two belongs in the *injected and inverted* row. Passing the repository in `main` is injection even without a framework. The *inverted but not injected* row instead describes a consumer that owns a contract and obtains its implementation through a registry. The distinction is between receiving and fetching, not between manual wiring and framework use.

Centralised wiring does not by itself show that source dependencies are inverted. A domain package may receive all collaborators through constructors while importing a networking client or a database row type. The wiring makes construction explicit, but the imports still couple policy to infrastructure. Inspect both relationships.

The decisions meet when a consumer-owned contract needs an implementation. Some assembling code must choose and supply that implementation without putting the concrete choice back into the consumer. Fowler discusses separation of configuration from use alongside separation of interfaces from implementation: they support each other while addressing different responsibilities.

Injection makes supply explicit through parameters and construction sites. It applies to concrete collaborators as well as interfaces. Inversion adds a contract that both sides must maintain and that must express the consumer’s needs. Decide whether that boundary is useful separately from deciding how to supply the object; otherwise every injection point may acquire an unnecessary interface.

Distinguish the concepts with two examples. A constructor-injected concrete database is injected without changing the source dependency toward storage. A consumer-owned repository interface, implemented by storage and supplied in `main`, is both inverted and injected by hand. Inspect the construction site for injection and the contract’s ownership and references for inversion.

lessons.title: One Place That Knows How to Build
lessons.summary: When consumers receive their collaborators, assembly code must choose and build the object graph elsewhere. A composition root places that responsibility near the application’s entry or integration point. Keeping application wiring there makes implementation choices reviewable and keeps feature code from rebuilding collaborators. A container can help perform the assembly, but is not itself the composition root.

blocks.text: When `StudySessionController` receives its collaborators, other code must choose their implementations, construct them and decide how instances are shared. That code knows the repository is `LocalQuestionRepository`, which data source it uses and which catalogue configuration the source needs. This assembly work belongs in a deliberate location.

A **composition root** is the location where the application’s object graph is assembled, as close as possible to its entry point. It describes a responsibility and a place, not a required class name. A `main` function that constructs the graph can be the composition root.

The composition root brings implementation choices together. It can refer to every concrete type needed to build the graph, while consumers receive their collaborators without knowing how they were assembled. This concentrates wiring in a place that can be reviewed as a whole. Consumers may still name concrete collaborator types when no abstraction is needed.

A composition root assembles the application graph near an entry point. Keeping wiring there lets consumers receive collaborators without rebuilding them. It can be a function or other integration code; a DI library is one possible assembly mechanism.
This `main` function assembles the study-session graph by hand:

The function constructs four objects linked by three dependencies. It builds the clock and data source first, then the repository, then the controller, because each constructor needs objects already available. `main` passes only the controller to `startStudyApplication`; the other objects are its collaborators.
Suppose the bundled data source now needs a catalogue path and expected schema version. The composition root can supply a configuration object:

blocks.code:
fun main() {
    val clock = SystemClock()
    val config = QuestionCatalogConfig(
        catalogPath = "questions/android-core.json",
        schemaVersion = 3,
    )
    val dataSource = BundledQuestionDataSource(config)
    val repository = LocalQuestionRepository(dataSource)
    val controller = StudySessionController(
        repository = repository,
        clock = clock,
    )

    startStudyApplication(controller)
}

blocks.text: The data source now receives a configuration, and `main` chooses its values. The controller and repository declarations stay the same: neither needs to know which catalogue this build reads. The additional construction work remains visible in the assembly code. **When Wiring It Yourself Is the Right Answer** considers how that work grows.
**Construction knowledge that leaks.** Now a feature class in the middle of the program does this:

`ReviewScreenPresenter` now has two responsibilities: presenting the review screen and assembling its repository. It names the repository implementation, data source and configuration, so changes in their construction can require presenter edits.

It also repeats the catalogue values chosen in the composition root. Those two copies can drift apart, and callers cannot choose a different repository for this presenter because construction is fixed in its body.
The design issue is that the presenter owns both screen behaviour and part of application assembly. Supplying its repository from outside separates those responsibilities.

The name `AppContainer` does not identify a composition root. Look for where the graph is assembled. A `main` function can perform that work, while an `AppContainer` accessed throughout feature code can also act as a service locator and hide consumers’ requirements.

**More than one entry point.** An application launch, background entry point and test harness may each need to initiate assembly. Shared construction can be factored into a helper instead of copied at each entry point:

Keep graph assembly at entry and integration points, with shared builders where useful. A second entry point may legitimately initiate construction. A presenter that rebuilds its repository has instead mixed feature behaviour with assembly. The important distinction is the responsibility of the code that performs the construction.

Locating assembly near an entry point makes the supply of collaborators explicit before feature work begins. Feature code can use the objects it receives, while implementation and configuration choices stay in assembly code. This reduces the need for feature classes to make their own construction choices, but does not enforce that separation.

A composition root gives readers a place to inspect the graph’s implementation choices and connections. In this example, that place is one function. If classes construct collaborators throughout the program, understanding the graph requires following those classes as well. Centralised assembly makes that review easier.

Centralised assembly can still hide requirements if feature classes start fetching collaborators from an `AppComponents` object. Construction remains in one place, but callers no longer see which dependencies each feature needs. These lookups introduce the service-locator costs discussed in **Asking For It, or Being Given It**.

A composition root identifies where graph assembly happens. A container is a tool that can hold definitions, manage reuse and produce objects. The `main` function above is a composition root without a container. It could also configure and use a container there, as **The Container, and the Modules That Fill It** shows for Koin. Keeping the terms separate helps you assess which assembly work the tool removes.

Describe a composition root as the location that assembles the graph near an entry point. An application may have several entry or integration points, with shared construction factored into builders. Keep this assembly responsibility separate from feature behaviour. A container can implement part of the assembly; a function with ordinary constructor calls can implement it too.

lessons.title: Asking For It, or Being Given It
lessons.summary: With a service locator, the consuming class obtains its own collaborators; with constructor injection, callers supply them. Both can produce a working object, but they differ in visible requirements and resolution responsibility. A framework-owned integration point may need a lookup to obtain an assembled object. Keeping that lookup at the boundary limits its visibility cost.

blocks.text: A **service locator** provides collaborators that consuming classes look up for themselves. This can produce the same working controller as injection. The difference lies in who obtains the collaborators and what the controller declares to its caller.
Compared with the constructor-injected controller, this version changes four things:

items: **The constructor no longer reveals the collaborators.** `StudySessionController()` takes no arguments, so the repository and clock requirements are absent from its signature.
**The caller must rely on prior registration.** The compiler allows the constructor call, but success depends on registry state established elsewhere.
**Missing registration is found when lookup executes.** Here, lookup runs during construction. If moved into a method, the failure occurs only when execution reaches that lookup.

**The class now knows that a resolution mechanism exists.** It depends on `ServiceRegistry` in addition to its two real collaborators, so the mechanism has become part of what this class needs in order to compile and run.

blocks.text: Fowler contrasts the visible requirements of an injected constructor with dependencies found by searching for locator calls. Android’s guide likewise describes service-locator dependencies as part of the implementation rather than the public API. In this example, finding the controller’s requirements means reading its body.

With constructor injection, the controller declares its collaborators and the caller supplies them. With this service locator, the controller looks them up and omits them from its constructor. That affects how callers discover requirements and when missing dependencies are detected.
The two controller designs have these differences:

rows: What the constructor declares it needs
No collaborators
A `QuestionRepository` and a `SystemClock`
Who performs the resolution
The controller itself
Whoever constructs the controller
Where to look to find its collaborators
Every line of its body, including lines added later
Its constructor
What a caller can vary
Nothing, without changing shared registry state
Either collaborator, per construction site
When a missing collaborator surfaces
When the lookup executes
At compile time, at the construction site
What the class depends on besides its collaborators
The registry, and the fact that somebody filled it first
Nothing

blocks.text:
Failure timing depends on the lookup design. This registry checks for a service when `resolve` runs. Startup validation could catch missing registrations earlier, while a lookup inside a rarely used method could fail much later.

The constructor signature does not give the compiler the information needed to check these requirements at the call site. A separate validation mechanism must supply that check.

A lookup can also serve as integration with a framework that constructs a screen itself. The application cannot pass ordinary constructor arguments to this screen, so it obtains an already-assembled controller when the framework attaches it:

`ReviewScreen` connects a framework-owned lifecycle to the application graph. It obtains a **complete** controller that assembly code has already constructed, and that controller’s collaborators remain visible in its own constructor.

The screen’s lookup still introduces an implicit dependency on `applicationComponents` and initialization order. Keeping that lookup in boundary code limits its spread instead of making ordinary feature objects resolve their own collaborators.
To assess a lookup, consider the responsibility of the code performing it:

items: A business, domain or feature object that fetches its own collaborators from a registry hides those requirements from its constructor callers. It takes on the lookup and registration costs described above.

Integration code at a framework-owned boundary may obtain a finished object whose collaborators are declared elsewhere. Keep that access confined to the boundary and pass explicit dependencies onward.

blocks.text:
Android creates framework objects such as activities, so an application may obtain its graph at that integration point and pass collaborators onward. A `ViewModel` is obtained through a `ViewModelProvider` and created by its factory when the owner’s store needs a new instance. The ViewModel can still declare required collaborators in its constructor.

These boundary operations differ from a domain class looking up each of its own dependencies. **When Android Owns Construction** and **Resolving a ViewModel at the Boundary** examine the Hilt and Koin arrangements.

A framework’s resolution API does not determine the architecture by itself. Check where resolution occurs, what object it obtains, and whether feature objects still declare their collaborators. The same library may support explicit injection and lookups; evaluate how it is used instead of treating its name as the design.

Framework-owned construction can make boundary lookup practical. If the framework cannot accept application-supplied constructor arguments, integration code needs another way to reach the graph. A registry or application component object can provide that access without requiring every feature class to use it.

A boundary lookup is easier to manage when it obtains a complete object, that object’s collaborators remain explicit, and only a small amount of integration code performs the access. Keep the boundary’s initialization requirements clear as well. These conditions limit the visibility cost; placing lookups throughout domain code spreads it.

Inspect the consuming code, not just the `resolve(...)` call. A registry, static accessor or framework API can hide collaborators inside a feature class, or provide access to the graph at an integration boundary. In either case, check which requirements readers can discover, what callers can supply and how registration failures are found.

Compare service locator and constructor injection through visibility and resolution responsibility. With injection, the constructor declares collaborators and the caller supplies them. With a locator, the consumer obtains them through lookup, and missing registration is found when that lookup or separate validation runs. A framework-owned boundary may justify limited graph access; ordinary feature objects can still receive explicit dependencies.

lessons.title: When Wiring It Yourself Is the Right Answer
lessons.summary: Manual dependency injection uses ordinary constructor calls to assemble the graph. It can express abstraction bindings, shared instances and fresh instances without a DI framework. As the graph changes, maintaining wiring, factories and lifetimes can become costly. Android recommends Hilt when possible; deciding whether to add a framework requires comparing the work it removes with its configuration and tooling costs.

blocks.text: **Manual dependency injection** means writing the constructor calls that supply collaborators yourself. It is a production technique: the resulting objects receive their dependencies whether or not a container arranged the calls.
A hand-written composition root can express these arrangements:

items: **Constructor injection**, which is the technique itself and needs nothing but a constructor call.
**Binding an abstraction to an implementation**, which is one line choosing which type to construct for a declared contract.
**A shared instance**, which is one `val` constructed once and passed to several consumers.
**A fresh instance per use**, which is construction at the point of use, or a function that constructs one on request.
**Explicit assembly order**, which the graph fixes: a node cannot be built before the nodes it needs.

blocks.text: The graph now has a question browser and a summary builder as well as the session controller. They show two different construction policies:

`controller` and `browser` receive the same repository instance. Each call to `newSummaryBuilder` constructs a fresh builder. A product requirement determines which policy is appropriate: shared state, required identity or construction cost may matter, as **One Instance, or a New One Each Time?** explains.

Both policies can be expressed with ordinary Kotlin. A larger graph adds work to maintain the choices and constructor calls.

Manual wiring can express bindings, shared objects and per-use construction. A framework can automate parts of that assembly, but the application still has to choose implementations and lifetimes. Compare the maintenance work saved with the tool’s own costs.
Maintaining a hand-written graph can introduce several kinds of work:

items: A new dependency can require edits to construction sites and intermediate factories that must now supply it. Centralised builders can limit how many callers need to change.
A long assembly must keep dependencies in construction order, since an instance has to exist before it can be passed to a consumer.
Reuse decisions require checking which instance is passed to each consumer.
If entry points duplicate assembly, shared construction changes must be applied consistently. A shared builder can reduce that duplication.
Frequent graph changes create mechanical wiring edits, which still need checking for incorrect arguments and unintended sharing.

blocks.text: Suppose `BundledQuestionDataSource` gains a cache dependency and three entry points each construct it directly. Its constructor changes, and all three assembly sites must supply a cache. If a helper instead constructs the data source, that helper needs the argument or a way to obtain it; callers change only if its public requirements change. These are wiring edits introduced by the graph’s new dependency.

Android’s manual DI guide describes two growing costs: maintaining factories and wiring can be error-prone, and the application must manage its containers’ scopes and lifetimes. It recommends Hilt “when possible.”

That recommendation is an Android default, not a claim that manual wiring is invalid. For this program, assess the work a framework would remove: repeated construction, factory maintenance and lifetime management. Compare it with the added configuration and tooling, rather than treating the recommendation as a measurement of this particular graph.

Manual wiring is not limited to prototypes or beginner projects. It can construct the same graph as a container, including shared and scoped objects. Adding a framework may save maintenance work; sharing and lifetime decisions already exist in the manual arrangement.

In this example, construction fits in one short function. There is one entry point and one shared repository, and the reuse decision is visible in the arguments passed to the controller and browser. The wiring is still straightforward to inspect. A framework would remove relatively little assembly code while adding a dependency, configuration vocabulary and failures to understand.
Keeping manual wiring is reasonable for this graph. Reconsider that choice if the maintenance work changes in one of these ways:

items: The graph grows substantially in depth, so that new dependencies are threaded through several construction sites rather than appearing at one.
Lifetime-specific scopes proliferate — several kinds of bounded lifetime, each with objects that must be created and released with it, tracked by hand.
Many contributors add bindings, making a central wiring file a frequent source of overlapping edits.
The same configuration is repeated across several entry points often enough that keeping them consistent becomes recurring work.

Several values of the same type circulate in the assembly — two repositories, two clients, two configurations — so passing the wrong one type-checks and is wrong. A missing argument is still a compile error, which is the guarantee hand-written wiring keeps; what it cannot check is that the argument you passed is the one you meant.

blocks.text: Dependency count alone does not provide a useful threshold. Ten independent objects assembled once may be easy to maintain; four objects with several lifetimes and entry points may require more work. Assess the construction and lifetime complexity, not just the number of types.

Compare two sets of costs. Manual assembly requires maintaining constructor calls, factories, sharing and lifetimes as the graph changes. A framework adds its own configuration, constraints and failure modes, and may require build tooling.

The balance depends on graph depth, rate of change, entry points and contributors. A small graph assembled once may gain little from automation; a frequently changing modular graph may gain much more. Reassess that balance as the program changes.

For a useful comparison, name the work each option leaves with the team. A framework may remove repeated constructor calls and factory maintenance while still requiring implementation and lifetime choices in its configuration. Manual wiring may make those choices easy to inspect but expensive to update. **The Smallest Sufficient Strategy** compares those costs across approaches.

Choose an assembly strategy that fits the program’s requirements and maintenance costs. Keeping manual wiring is defensible when its explicit construction remains easy to understand and change. Adding a framework is defensible when its automation removes enough recurring work to justify the tool’s costs. More than one strategy may be reasonable; explain the trade-off for the program in front of you.

Explain when manual DI is sufficient by describing the graph and its maintenance work. It already supports constructor injection, bindings, shared instances and per-use construction. Consider how often dependencies change, how many assembly sites repeat work and which lifetimes must be managed. Then explain what a framework would remove, while reporting Android’s Hilt recommendation with its “when possible” qualification.

sources.title: Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern

units.title: Object Graphs, Lifetimes and Scopes
units.summary: Requesting one object may require a whole graph of dependencies. Some instances need to be shared between consumers; others can be created for each request. These decisions come from the required behaviour. Distinguish the lifetime the behaviour needs, the owner retaining the instance, and the reuse rule applied within that owner. A dependency-injection scope describes reuse; a `CoroutineScope` manages coroutine work. These construction decisions can be made by hand or expressed through Dagger, Hilt or Koin.

lessons.title: From One Dependency to a Graph
lessons.summary: A dependency can have dependencies of its own, so constructing one object may require an entire graph. Each edge represents a requirement that construction code must satisfy. The graph root is the requested object; the composition root is where assembly happens. Shared nodes and cycles help reveal reuse decisions and problems in the design.

blocks.text: A controller may receive two collaborators from `main`, but each collaborator can need other objects. **A dependency can have dependencies of its own**, so construction extends beyond the arguments passed directly to the controller.

`StudySessionController` needs a `QuestionRepository`. The chosen implementation, `LocalQuestionRepository`, needs a `BundledQuestionDataSource`, which needs a `QuestionCatalogConfig`. Constructing the controller therefore requires all of these objects, even though its constructor does not name the catalogue configuration. The requirement is **transitive**: follow each dependency until you reach objects that need no further dependencies.
Five terms describe the structure:

items: **Node** — an object that has to exist.
**Edge** — the fact that one node cannot be constructed without another. It is directed, pointing from the object that needs to the object that is needed.
**Object graph** — the transitive closure of a node and every edge reachable from it: everything that must exist, directly and indirectly.
**Graph root** — the object that was actually requested, and from which the rest of the graph is reached.
**Graph assembly** — supplying each dependency before constructing the object that needs it. Independent branches may be assembled in either order.

blocks.text: The word *root* has two meanings in dependency injection:

blocks.code:
composition root   main()                    — a place in the program, where assembly happens
graph root         StudySessionController    — an object in a request, whose construction needs the rest

blocks.text:
The **composition root** is the place near a program entry point where construction knowledge is concentrated and objects are assembled. The **graph root** is the object requested from that assembly. Its dependencies determine what else must be available.

A program can have a small number of composition roots and many graph roots, such as the top-level objects requested by different entry points.

A framework may bring these ideas close together. A Dagger component declares a graph and provides entry points from which objects can be requested (see **Dagger: Compile-Time Object Graphs**). Distinguishing the place that configures construction from the object being requested helps explain both roles.

An object graph includes the objects a requested object needs, directly and indirectly. The requested object is the graph root. Assembly supplies each dependency before its consumer is constructed; the composition root is the place in the program responsible for that assembly.

The study application has a session controller and a browser that lists questions outside a session. The controller also records answered attempts, using an attempt store and a clock. Their dependencies form this graph:

blocks.code:
QuestionBrowser                          ← a second graph root
 └─ QuestionRepository

StudySessionController                   ← the graph root traced here
 ├─ QuestionRepository                     ← one object: a LocalQuestionRepository,
 │                                            requested as the interface
 │   └─ BundledQuestionDataSource
 │       └─ QuestionCatalogConfig
 ├─ AttemptRecorder
 │   ├─ AttemptStore
 │   └─ SystemClock
 └─ SystemClock

blocks.text:
`QuestionRepository` and `LocalQuestionRepository` name the contract and implementation of one repository object, not two separate objects. The controller requests the contract; the composition root chooses the implementation.

Following the controller’s repository dependency leads to the data source and then the catalogue configuration. Each constructor adds a requirement: the controller needs a repository, the repository needs a data source, and the data source needs configuration.
For each edge, identify the code that supplies the constructor argument and what it needs to know:

rows: `StudySessionController` → `QuestionRepository`
`repository`
Whoever constructs the controller — here, `main`
Which implementation satisfies the contract
`LocalQuestionRepository` → `BundledQuestionDataSource`
`dataSource`
Whoever constructs the repository — `main`
That this implementation reads bundled data
`BundledQuestionDataSource` → `QuestionCatalogConfig`
`config`
Whoever constructs the data source — `main`
Which catalogue this build reads
`StudySessionController` → `AttemptRecorder`
`attempts`
`main`
That attempts are recorded, and by what
`AttemptRecorder` → `AttemptStore`, `SystemClock`
`store`, `clock`
Whoever constructs the recorder — `main`
Nothing beyond the two class names
`StudySessionController` → `SystemClock`
`clock`
`main`
Nothing beyond the class name

blocks.text:
Here `main` supplies every dependency, concentrating construction knowledge in the composition root. The last column shows what it must know to do that.

The object graph differs from the import graph. `StudySessionController` does not name `BundledQuestionDataSource`, `QuestionCatalogConfig` or `AttemptStore` in its source, yet all three must be available to construct the objects it uses.
Assembly supplies dependencies before the objects that use them:

blocks.code:
fun main() {
    val clock = SystemClock()
    val dataSource = BundledQuestionDataSource(ProductionCatalogConfig)
    val repository: QuestionRepository = LocalQuestionRepository(dataSource)
    val recorder = AttemptRecorder(AttemptStore(), clock)

    val controller = StudySessionController(
        repository = repository,
        clock = clock,
        attempts = recorder,
    )
    val browser = QuestionBrowser(repository)
    val newSummaryBuilder = { SessionSummaryBuilder(SystemClock()) }

    startStudyApplication(controller, browser, newSummaryBuilder)
}

blocks.text:
The function builds dependencies before passing them to consumers. A line cannot move above the creation of an object it uses, although independent branches can be reordered.

`newSummaryBuilder` defers construction until a summary is requested. Each `SessionSummaryBuilder` is a small graph root of its own, separate from the controller’s graph. The `main` function acts as an **assembler**: it configures the objects and passes them to the code that uses them.

The controller and browser receive the same `QuestionRepository` because `main` passes the same `repository` value to both. Their constructors ask for a repository; the assembly code decides whether that means one shared instance or separate instances.

The required behaviour determines whether they need the same repository object or merely repositories configured alike. If the decoded catalogue should be read once and retained in the repository, sharing that repository supports the requirement. If behaviour does not depend on repository identity, the remaining difference may be construction cost. **One Instance, or a New One Each Time?** examines that decision.

An object graph describes construction requirements; an import graph describes source dependencies. The controller can need a data source, catalogue configuration and attempt store indirectly without naming them in its source. **Injected, Inverted, or Both?** examines this distinction.
A cycle can prevent ordinary constructor-based assembly:

blocks.code: AttemptRecorder ──► ScoreCalculator ──► StreakTracker ──► AttemptRecorder

blocks.text:
Each object takes the next as a constructor argument, and the last takes the first. There is no starting point for ordinary construction: whichever object is created first needs an argument that does not yet exist.

Review the responsibilities before changing the wiring. The recorder may be asking for streak state that another object should own, or the calculation may not need the recorder. The cycle identifies a relationship worth examining; it does not by itself identify the correct redesign.

A mechanism that defers a dependency can allow construction around a cycle. It still leaves a design question: are these mutual dependencies necessary and coherent? **Detecting or constructing a cycle does not establish that the responsibilities are well placed.**
A graph makes relationships across several objects easier to inspect than separate per-class dependency lists:

items: **Shared nodes.** A graph can show explicitly that two consumers receive the same object, exposing a reuse and lifetime decision.
**Several paths to one node.** The controller receives the clock directly, and also reaches it through the recorder. Showing both paths together makes the shared clock easier to recognise.
**Cycles.** Following edges across the graph reveals when a dependency path returns to an earlier object.
**Depth.** The catalogue configuration sits three edges below the controller. Tracing that path shows which construction sites may need to change when a leaf acquires a required argument.
**Ambiguity.** Two candidates of one type can both match a consumer’s request. Considering their relationships together reveals the need to distinguish them.

blocks.text: Node, edge, transitive closure, root and cycle give us enough vocabulary to discuss these construction relationships. The following decisions use that vocabulary without requiring a traversal algorithm or a proof of ordering.

The small composition root above is straightforward to write by hand. As assembly grows, inspect its shape as well as its length: dependency depth, shared nodes and the construction sites affected by a new parameter. These relationships can make wiring difficult to follow even when individual constructor calls remain simple.

To explain an object graph, include the dependencies reached indirectly from the requested object. Distinguish that graph root from the composition root, where assembly happens, and explain who supplies each constructor argument. Use shared nodes, repeated paths and cycles to show what the graph reveals about the design.

sources.title: Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern

lessons.title: One Instance, or a New One Each Time?
lessons.summary: When the graph is requested again, decide which consumers need the same instances and which can receive new ones. Shared state, required identity and measured construction cost can justify reuse. Sharing too widely can mix state that should be separate; sharing too little can reset state that should persist.

blocks.text: Take a study-session graph — a controller and a question browser over one repository, its data source and configuration, and a clock — and ask for it twice. A second study session starts; a second destination opens a browser. Which of the nodes beneath those requests must be **the same objects** as the first time, and which may simply be built again?

The dependency edges identify what each object needs. The required behaviour determines whether separate requests should share those objects. Decide what must remain the same before choosing how to reuse it.

For a small object with no shared-state, identity or significant construction-cost requirement, **creating a new instance per request is a useful baseline**. It avoids coordinating reuse and deciding how long a shared owner must retain it. Check the object’s requirements before departing from that baseline.
Three common reasons to reuse an instance are:

items: **State that must be one state.** The object holds something mutable that several consumers have to observe as the same value. Two instances would mean two answers to a question the product says has one.

**Identity something else depends on.** Another part of the system compares, registers, counts or keys by the object itself — a subscriber list, an open connection, a lock. A second instance is not an equivalent copy; it is a second thing.

**Construction cost that has been shown to matter.** Building it does measurable work: reading and parsing a file, opening a connection, warming a cache. The requirement here is a measurement, not an intuition.

blocks.text: If behaviour depends on neither shared state nor object identity, equivalent instances can behave the same whether reused or constructed separately. The remaining decision is usually about cost and how the assembly is organised. Reserve detailed lifetime reasoning for objects whose requirements make it consequential.

Reuse can be justified by shared state, required object identity or measured construction cost. For an object without those requirements, creating one per request may be sufficient. Decide which consumers must share before deciding how the instance is retained.
**The same graph, two different answers.** Nothing about the classes changes between the readings below. Only the requirement does:

rows: `QuestionCatalogConfig`
Every part of the build reads one catalogue, fixed at start-up
Reuse is convenient for one immutable configuration value. Equivalent copies would also satisfy this requirement if nothing depends on their identity.
`QuestionRepository`
The decoded catalogue is read once and kept, so opening the browser after a session does not re-read it
Reuse — decided by the caching requirement, not by the word "repository"
`QuestionRepository`, in a product with no cache
Every read goes to the data source anyway; nothing is retained between calls
Either. Behaviour is identical, so this one is a cost decision and should be defended as one
`SessionSummaryBuilder`
A summary accumulates one session's answers and is produced when that session ends
Fresh per use. A reused builder carries the previous session's answers into the next summary
`SystemClock`
It reads the platform clock and holds nothing
Either; it does not matter

blocks.text: The repository rows differ because the products have different caching requirements. The class name alone does not determine whether consumers need the same instance.
A reading app needs a signed-in reader shared across destinations and a separate draft note for each destination. Both objects hold mutable state, but their sharing requirements differ:

headers: What the requirement says must be true
rows: `ReaderSession` — who is signed in, and the credentials that prove it
Every destination observes one signed-in reader, and signing out ends it everywhere at once
One instance, shared by everything that asks
`DraftAnnotation` — the note being typed about the passage currently open
Each destination has its own note, and leaving the destination discards it
One per destination, discarded with it

blocks.text: The session needs to be shared across destinations; the draft needs to remain separate. These construction decisions follow from the behaviour each object supports.

**Sharing too widely.** Suppose the draft is treated like the session, and one instance is handed to every destination. Nothing crashes. The reader opens a passage, types half a note and navigates to a second passage — and the second screen opens with the first passage's half-written note already in it. Worse, typing there changes what the first screen shows when they navigate back. Two destinations that were never meant to be related now are: either can change what the other displays, and no line of code in either of them says so.

Sharing mutable state couples the consumers through that state: one destination can change what another displays even when neither directly references the other.

Reuse also needs an owner that retains the instance for the required sharing period. **A Scope Is a Rule; an Owner Is a Lifetime** examines that responsibility.
If each destination instead receives its own `ReaderSession`, signing in on the library destination does not update the session held by a passage destination:

items: The second destination has no signed-in reader, so it either asks the reader to sign in again or quietly shows the signed-out view.
Signing out on one destination ends a session no other destination was holding, so the rest stay signed in.
A catalogue or refreshed credential retained in one session may need to be obtained again in another, so duplicated sessions can repeat work intended to be shared.

blocks.text: Over-sharing makes state visible where separate state was required. Under-sharing loses continuity where shared state was required. Both can look like feature bugs, so check the construction decision when diagnosing the behaviour.

Sharing an object may reduce construction work, but it also requires an owner and a suitable lifetime. Shared mutable state can couple consumers. If cost is the reason for reuse, measure the work saved and weigh it against those responsibilities.

These choices can be implemented without a dependency-injection library. Android’s manual dependency-injection guide demonstrates application-wide dependencies alongside containers retained only for one flow, so state from an earlier flow is not reused accidentally. Dagger, Hilt and Koin provide different ways to express similar ownership and reuse decisions.

For an object with no mutable state, no relevant identity and no significant construction side effects, equivalent instances may behave the same whether shared or recreated. Choose an arrangement that is simple and consistent, and measure construction cost if it becomes relevant. If the decision affects behaviour, identify the state or identity requirement behind that difference.

**Reuse concerns identity, not just instance count.** Rebuilding one session whenever a destination opens may leave only one session alive at a time, but it does not preserve the same session across destinations. Conversely, two consumers may hold the same stateless object without depending on that shared identity. Ask which consumers, across which requests, require the same object.

Reusing an instance requires something to retain it for as long as consumers must be able to request that same instance. Releasing the owner ends retention through that owner. The instance becomes unreachable only when no other reachable object still holds it.

When discussing a shared dependency, identify the requirement: shared state, required identity or measured construction cost. Explain both failure directions—state leaking between consumers that need separate instances, and state restarting for consumers that need continuity. Then identify the owner that will retain the instance for the required period.

lessons.title: A Scope Is a Rule; an Owner Is a Lifetime
lessons.summary: Distinguish the lifetime the required behaviour needs, the owner that retains an instance, and the reuse rule applied within that owner. The same reuse rule can produce different lifetimes under different owners. A retained instance is not necessarily global or eagerly created, and retaining it in memory does not preserve it after process death.

blocks.text: When discussing dependency-injection scopes, distinguish three related ideas:

rows: **Lifetime requirement**
How long product behaviour needs a particular object identity, or the state inside it, to stay valid. Stated in product language, before any code
The product
**Owner**
The object or context that retains the instance and supplies it to consumers. An instance retained only through this owner becomes unreachable when the owner does.
The program's structure: what exists, and for how long
**Scope**
A rule about reuse and identity *inside* an owner: which requests served by that owner receive the same instance
Whoever writes the configuration

blocks.text: Choose the owner and reuse rule from the lifetime requirement:

blocks.code:
the lifetime the requirement needs
            ↓
an owner that exists for at least that long
            ↓
a reuse rule inside that owner

blocks.text: A reuse declaration needs an owning context that applies it. Giving the rule a name does not by itself establish how long that context will exist. Identify the owner and the events that create and release it.

A dependency-injection scope describes which requests within an owning context receive the same instance. To understand the intended reuse period, identify how long that owner retains the instance. A scope name alone does not tell you when the owner is created or released.

Start with the required lifetime, choose an owner that supports it, then define reuse within that owner. The scope describes which requests share an instance; the owner provides the retention needed to make that reuse possible.

`CoroutineScope` has a different meaning: it provides the context for coroutine work, normally including a `Job` hierarchy through which that work is cancelled. A dependency-injection scope describes object reuse within an owner. Qualify the word “scope” when both meanings could fit.
For the reading app, the session requirement is: *every destination observes the same signed-in reader until sign-out.* Use that requirement to answer four construction questions:

items: **What identity must stay the same?** The `ReaderSession` — the object holding who is signed in and the credentials that prove it.
**For how long, and what ends it?** From signing in until signing out. Signing out is the ending event; navigating between destinations is not.

**What can retain it for that period?** An owner that outlives individual destinations, such as the running application or a session container retained by it. Choose an owner that supports the required lifetime without retaining the session beyond sign-out.
**How should that owner hold it?** Construct one when the reader signs in, hand the same one to everything that asks it, and release it at sign-out.

blocks.text:
The first three answers identify the instance, its required lifetime and a suitable owner. The fourth defines reuse within that owner. This is the same lifetime reasoning used in **Choosing an Owner From the Lifetime the Requirement Needs**.

The owner also needs an owner: some reachable part of the program must retain the container for as long as it is expected to serve requests.
These two owners use the same reuse rule: each creates one draft and returns that instance whenever its property is read. Their intended lifetimes differ:

Each graph creates one `DraftAnnotation` and exposes it through a `val`. If one `ApplicationGraph` serves every destination, they receive the same draft and can see each other’s changes.

If each destination receives its own `DestinationGraph`, they receive separate drafts. Retain that graph while its back-stack entry exists and release it when the entry is removed. The classes do not implement these lifecycle decisions; the code holding the graphs must do so.

Android’s manual dependency-injection guide uses application-wide containers for shared dependencies and a separate container for a flow. The flow container is retained while needed and cleared when the flow ends. With hand-written containers, application code manages their creation and release.

A reuse declaration alone does not guarantee that later requests will find the same instance. Different owners applying the same rule can produce separate instances. Ask which owner serves the consumers that must share, and when it releases its retained instance. Consumers may also keep references after that release.
“Singleton” needs an owning context. In dependency-injection use, it commonly means one instance reused within that context. It does not automatically imply the following:

rows: One instance for the whole program, everywhere
Only when all relevant requests use the same owner. Separate owners can each retain their own instance.
It exists from start-up
Not necessarily. Construction may be eager or deferred until the first request; the reuse rule alone does not choose between them.
It lives forever
No. The owner retains it for a bounded period. After release, it remains reachable only if something else still holds it.
The value is saved
No. Reuse is about object identity in memory and says nothing at all about storage

blocks.text: **An instance held only in memory is lost when its process is destroyed.** This includes a ViewModel and objects retained by application-level containers. Reuse preserves an object within a running process; durable values require a separate persistence mechanism.
An owner that retains an object longer or more widely than required can cause two different problems:

First, an application owner can hand one `DraftAnnotation` to destinations that require separate drafts. The destinations then affect each other through shared state. This is a reuse error even if memory retention is otherwise intentional; a narrower owner can give each destination its own draft.

Second, an application-lived object may retain a reference to a destination’s state holder after that destination is gone. The state holder and objects reachable through it remain reachable, preventing collection while that reference persists.

This is unintended retention. Remove or clear the reference when its lifetime ends, or place the referencing object under an owner with a suitable lifetime. The fix must address the reference, not merely the reuse label.

Releasing and recreating an owner too early can reset identity that should be continuous. A session may restart for every destination, a cache may lose entries between requests, and expensive initialization may repeat. These symptoms appear in feature behaviour, so trace them back to the owner’s creation and release.

A graph or container is itself an object retained by another part of the program. Ask what holds it and what ends that retention. In hand-written assembly, this might be a local in `main` or a property associated with a destination. A configured container needs the same lifecycle decision, even when its construction is less visible.

Explain scope alongside the required lifetime and the owner that applies the reuse rule. The same rule under different owners can yield different reuse periods. Clarify that one instance per owner does not guarantee one instance globally, indefinite retention or persistence after process death.

lessons.title: A Value the Graph Cannot Know
lessons.summary: A `QuestionSession` needs a repository, a clock and the identifier of the question selected by the reader. Construction logic can supply the repository and clock; the request supplies the selected identifier. A factory combines them without sharing request-specific data globally or leaving the session incomplete after construction.

blocks.text: Construction logic can supply a repository and clock, but it cannot choose which question a reader will tap. An object may need both dependencies supplied by assembly and values supplied with a particular request.

A **graph dependency** is something construction logic knows how to supply: a repository, clock, data source, parser or startup configuration. It may already have an instance or know how to construct one when requested.

A **runtime input** is supplied by a particular event or request: the question identifier the reader tapped, a destination argument, text they entered or the attempt being reviewed. Construction logic alone cannot choose the correct value for that request.

The distinction depends on **when the correct value becomes known and who supplies it**, rather than whether it is an object or a primitive. A `QuestionCatalogConfig` containing a path and schema version can be fixed by the build and supplied through assembly. A selected `Question` is an object, but the selection comes from the reader’s action.

Ask whether construction logic can choose the correct value without knowing this particular request. If it can, supply it through assembly. If the value depends on the destination opened or item selected, pass it with the request. This is a useful heuristic: startup values can be obtained at runtime yet still belong in assembly, so also consider who is responsible for supplying the correct value.

Distinguish values supplied by construction logic from values supplied by a particular request. The selected question identifier comes from the caller; the repository and clock come from assembly. The distinction concerns origin and responsibility, not object versus primitive types.

**One object, both kinds.** A `QuestionSession` runs a single question: it loads the question, records when the reader started, and grades the answer. It needs a repository, a clock, and the identifier of the question that was tapped.

The repository and clock can be supplied before the reader selects a question. The correct `questionId` becomes known with the selection. The session’s constructor needs all three, but their values arrive from different sources.
One possible error is retaining the selected identifier in an application-wide holder that every session reads:

Suppose sessions keep reading this holder. The reader selects question 12, then opens question 30 while the first session remains on the back stack. Returning to the first session now shows question 30 under question 12’s timer.

A later screen can also read a selection left over from an earlier flow. In both cases, the shared holder supplies a value belonging to another request.

The holder shares one mutable selection between sessions that need independent identifiers. It also hides each session’s requirement: if `QuestionSession` receives only the holder, its constructor no longer requires the caller to supply the selected question identifier.
Another possible error is constructing the session before supplying its identifier:

blocks.code:
val session = QuestionSession(repository, clock)
session.questionId = selectedId   // only now is it usable

blocks.text: This alternative would require a different `QuestionSession` API from the constructor shown above. Between construction and assignment, the session lacks the identifier it needs. A writable identifier also allows the question to change after the session starts, and the constructor no longer enforces supplying it. **A Dependency Should Be Visible** discusses these costs.
Keep the runtime value as a required constructor argument. A factory can supply the other dependencies:

`QuestionSessionFactory` needs only the repository and clock, so assembly can construct and inject it in advance. The caller then provides `questionId` to `create`, and the factory supplies the retained dependencies to the session constructor.

The new session is the root of a small graph built for that request. All three arguments remain required, and the factory does not need a global “selected question” value. Android’s manual dependency-injection guide also uses factories that retain dependencies and create objects on request.

A function can serve the same purpose: a lambda captures the repository and clock, takes a question identifier and constructs a session. Choose a class or function according to the surrounding code. In either form, construction supplies its dependencies and the caller supplies the request-specific value.

Do not classify inputs by type alone. A catalogue path fixed by the build is a string supplied through assembly; a selected question is an object supplied with a request. Ask who knows the correct value and when it becomes known.

In an Android app, the question identifier may arrive as an argument of the destination the reader opened. That argument supplies the per-request value; the factory supplies the session’s repository and clock.

Construction describes how to supply an object’s dependencies; a request provides the data needed for that particular use. A shared selected-question holder mixes those responsibilities when independent sessions keep reading its changing value.

Frameworks offer ways to pass runtime values during construction. The requirement remains the same: give each session the identifier belonging to its request, under an owner whose lifetime supports that session.

`QuestionSessionFactory` belongs to the graph assembled in advance: its repository and clock can be supplied before a question is selected. A `QuestionSession` belongs to a small graph assembled for a particular request, when its identifier becomes known.

The factory connects those two construction moments. It retains the dependencies available from assembly and combines them with the argument supplied by the caller. This explains where to place an object that needs both kinds of input without treating “in the graph” as a single lifetime.

Retaining one changing selection across independent requests can produce the same error elsewhere: an old consumer reads the latest request’s value. A “current screen” or “last selected item” holder needs scrutiny when earlier consumers remain active. Check whether they should observe a shared current value or retain the value associated with their own request.

For a screen argument used alongside dependencies, explain which values assembly supplies and which belong to the request. A factory can take the request parameters and supply the other constructor arguments. Contrast this with a global changing selection shared by independent consumers, or an object that becomes usable only after a later assignment.

lessons.title: Two Dependencies of the Same Type
lessons.summary: Two differently configured instances of one type may both satisfy the same constructor parameter. The request needs to distinguish them. Use different types when they represent responsibilities the consumer must express, or extend the binding key when they are one concept configured in two ways. Selection order alone does not communicate the consumer’s requirement.

blocks.text: In a key-based dependency resolver, a request for `QuestionRepository` is matched to a **binding key**. A simple key is the type itself. If the configuration offers more than one candidate for that key, the request needs an additional distinction. In hand-written assembly, the code chooses the constructor argument directly.

Consider a reading application that talks to a server in two different ways. Browsing the public catalogue must work before anybody has signed in; everything about the reader's own library requires their credentials, and those credentials must never be sent anywhere else. Both are HTTP clients, configured differently:
Now a consumer declares what it needs:

Both clients have type `HttpClient`, but their configurations are not interchangeable. `LibraryRepository`’s parameter does not state which one it needs. A type-only resolver sees competing candidates; hand-written assembly can choose one, but the parameter type does not help catch the wrong choice.

When a request matches multiple differently configured instances, make the distinction explicit. A more specific type or an additional binding-key component can express which one the consumer needs. Consider what the distinction means before choosing the mechanism.
