Ask whether the consumer needs to express two different responsibilities, or distinguish two configurations of the same concept. That determines whether a separate type or an extended key is useful.

Here the clients support different responsibilities. The reader-library client can carry credentials; the public-catalogue client must not. Separate types let `LibraryRepository` state which kind of access it needs:
`LibraryRepository` now requires a `ReaderLibraryClient`. Passing a `PublicCatalogueClient` does not compile, so the parameter type catches this particular substitution.

The two types also expose different constructor requirements: `ReaderLibraryClient` accepts credentials, while `PublicCatalogueClient` does not. This prevents credentials being supplied through the public client’s shown constructor; its implementation must still preserve the no-credentials rule.

Thin wrappers around `HttpClient` provide a narrower guarantee. `PublicCatalogueClient(private val http: HttpClient)` makes the consumer’s request unambiguous, but assembly could still wrap a credentialed client. The wrapper distinguishes the roles without itself enforcing how the underlying client is configured.

Separate types add names and code to maintain. Use them when the consumer needs a requirement the existing type cannot express, especially a behavioural restriction such as the credentials rule. If the difference is configuration alone, such as a base URL, an extended binding key may be sufficient.

Suppose the application instead uses two caches with the same behaviour, one for images and one for parsed documents, configured with different size limits. If the existing type expresses their behaviour adequately, extend the key to distinguish the two instances:

blocks.code:
key = (type)                 → ambiguous: two candidates match
key = (type, distinction)    → two different keys, one candidate each

                                (Cache, "images")
                                (Cache, "documents")

blocks.text: A name, label or marker can add the distinction to the key. In Dagger, a key consists of a type and an optional qualifier; keys differ when their qualifiers differ. The two cache bindings can therefore have separate keys, and each request identifies the cache it needs.
Selection rules can choose a candidate without expressing the consumer’s requirement:

items: **Declaration order**, or the order in which groups of declarations were included — the meaning of a consumer's requirement would then depend on the order of unrelated lines in unrelated files.
**First or last registration** — changing registration order can change which client an existing consumer receives, even when the consumer has not changed.
**The most specific match** — two instances of the same type have no type-specificity distinction that identifies their intended roles.
**A tool’s default choice** — a documented precedence rule may resolve the key, but the consumer’s intended configuration still needs to be made clear.

blocks.text: A documented override or precedence rule tells you what a particular tool will select. It does not by itself tell you which client `LibraryRepository` intended to request. Express that requirement with a suitable type or key, then apply the tool’s resolution rules deliberately.

A qualifier can distinguish two configurations while leaving their shared type intact. A separate type can express a different responsibility. Check what the consumer needs to state before treating every same-type collision as a configuration problem or introducing a new type.
These two situations call for different design questions:

rows: Two implementations of one abstraction the consumer owns — a remote and a local source behind the same contract
A boundary question. The consumer declared a contract precisely so that more than one thing could satisfy it, and which one arrives is a composition decision
The interface-boundary test decides whether the abstraction exists at all; the composition root decides which implementation is supplied
Two configured instances of one technical type — two clients, two caches, two executors
A keying question. There is one concept and two configurations of it, and the consumer needs a way to say which
The construction contract, either by giving the configurations distinct types or by extending the key

blocks.text: If the consumer needs a behavioural boundary, attaching a label to a concrete technical type may leave that boundary unexpressed. If the difference is only configuration, a new interface may add little. Decide what contract the consumer needs before deciding how construction selects an implementation.

Two configured clients can be a valid arrangement. Ambiguity arises when the request does not distinguish their roles. Make that request more specific through a type or key. Removing a client or choosing a default helps only if doing so actually satisfies the consumer’s requirement.

Explain whether a same-type request identifies the required instance. Different responsibilities may call for different types; different configurations may call for qualifiers or another key component. State what each choice guarantees, and explain why selection order alone may leave the consumer’s intent unclear.

lessons.title: When Is a Broken Graph Detected?
lessons.summary: Missing dependencies and competing candidates are detected when the graph’s representation is checked. Explicit constructor calls are checked by the compiler; registered configurations may be checked during verification, startup or resolution; ahead-of-time graph analysis can reject invalid bindings before execution. A successful check establishes only the properties that mechanism checks, not the quality of the whole design.

blocks.text: Two construction faults to check for are:

items: **A missing edge.** Something needs a collaborator and nothing in the arrangement can supply it.
**An ambiguous edge.** Something needs a collaborator and two candidates match the request equally — two configured instances of one type, seen from the assembler's side.

blocks.text: These faults concern how a dependency requirement is satisfied. **When they are detected** depends on how construction is represented and what checks that representation. The labels “manual” and “framework” do not establish detection time by themselves.

headers: How the graph is written down
When a missing edge is reported
rows: Explicit construction in code — every object built at a call site
The compiler, because a constructor call missing a required argument is not a legal program
At compile time, at the construction site
A registered configuration resolved on request — declarations added to something that produces objects on demand
Whatever examines the registrations, and whenever that runs
It depends on the mechanism: at a verification step if one exists and is run, when the configuration is created if it validates then, otherwise the first time that path is resolved
A description checked before it is used — the graph is declared, and a tool analyses it ahead of execution
The tool, before the program runs
Before execution, as a failure of that check

blocks.text: Kotlin checks explicit constructor calls during compilation. Omitting a required argument is a compile error at that call site, so hand-written assembly already detects this kind of missing dependency. A container may add other checks, but this particular check does not require one.

Explicit constructor calls are checked at compilation. A registered configuration may be checked by a verification step, at startup or on first resolution, depending on the tool. Ahead-of-time graph analysis can reject invalid bindings before execution. Determine detection time from the mechanism and checks actually used.
Omit the catalogue configuration required by the study application’s data source. With explicit construction, the error is at the constructor call:

blocks.code:
val dataSource = BundledQuestionDataSource()          // does not compile
val repository = LocalQuestionRepository(dataSource)

blocks.text: Compilation fails at that line because the required configuration argument is missing. The program does not run.
Written as registrations — in a deliberately generic notation rather than any library's — the same fault looks like this:

blocks.code:
register QuestionRepository as LocalQuestionRepository(resolve QuestionDataSource)
register QuestionDataSource as BundledQuestionDataSource(resolve QuestionCatalogConfig)
                                                                ↑
                                        nothing registers QuestionCatalogConfig

blocks.text: For registered construction, detection depends on the checks provided and used. A verification step can report the missing registration before that path runs; Koin provides a configuration verification API for this purpose. A mechanism that validates registrations at startup can report it then. Otherwise it may appear only when a repository is first resolved, perhaps on a rarely opened screen.

A tool that analyses the declared graph before execution can reject the missing binding during its check. Dagger’s core model requires one binding for each required key. It also rejects cycles without a permitted deferred edge. If those requirements fail, it cannot generate the component implementation.

The build therefore stops before this graph is used, even though the programmer did not write each constructor call.
Now consider two candidates for one requested type:

rows: Explicit construction

The code chooses the argument explicitly. Passing the wrong configured `HttpClient` still type-checks because both instances have that type. More specific parameter types can help distinguish their roles.
Registered configuration

Reported by whatever examines the registrations: a duplicate key may be rejected when the configuration is created, at a verification step, or at resolution, and a mechanism may instead define an explicit override rule. The behaviour is defined by the tool, so it has to be read rather than guessed
Description checked ahead of execution
A key with more than one binding fails the check for the same reason a key with none does: the requirement is exactly one

blocks.text: For a registered configuration, read the tool’s duplicate-key and override rules. It may reject duplicate registrations, report them during verification or resolution, or apply a documented override. These choices differ between mechanisms.

Hand-written constructor calls detect missing required arguments at compile time. They do not catch choosing the wrong configured instance when both candidates satisfy the same parameter type. Keep these two faults separate when comparing construction mechanisms.

A successful ahead-of-time check establishes the conditions that checker enforces. In a simple constructor graph, this can include one binding for each required key and the absence of an unresolved construction cycle. It verifies construction relationships, rather than all runtime behaviour.
Structural validity alone does not establish these design properties:

items: **Dependency direction.** A domain class can receive a storage row type through a satisfiable constructor argument. The graph can be constructible while source dependencies cross the intended layer boundary (see **Injected, Inverted, or Both?**).
**Suitable lifetimes.** An application-lived owner can retain a destination state holder through an unambiguous binding. That does not establish that the selected owner has the right lifetime.
**Useful boundaries.** A consumer’s direct dependency on a concrete technical type can be satisfiable without being the right contract for that consumer.

**Required instance separation.** Two destinations can receive one shared instance even when the product needs a separate instance for each. Successful binding resolution alone does not establish that the sharing rule is correct.

blocks.text: A graph check is valuable evidence about the properties it examines. It does not substitute for reviewing source direction, ownership, boundaries and required behaviour. A graph can compile successfully while those design decisions still need work.

Ahead-of-time analysis requires construction information in a form the tool can inspect. That may involve declarations, annotations or code conventions, with limitations on what can be expressed or checked.

Weigh the work of maintaining that representation against the failures its checks detect. **When Should a Graph Error Surface?** compares the framework trade-offs; **Dagger: Compile-Time Object Graphs** examines one system that checks bindings during compilation.

Distinguish missing dependencies from competing candidates, then explain when each construction mechanism checks them. Explicit calls catch missing required arguments at compilation; registered configurations depend on the checks used; ahead-of-time analysis can reject invalid bindings before execution. State what a successful check establishes and what design decisions remain to be reviewed.

sources.title: Kotlin functions: default and named arguments

units.title: Dagger: Compile-Time Object Graphs
units.summary: Dagger turns dependency declarations into assembly code during the build. Those declarations specify how to construct objects, which implementations satisfy abstractions, which instances to share, and which dependency keys consumers request. A component defines the graph’s entry points and available bindings; its instance retains ordinary scoped objects. Dagger checks binding relationships before the program runs, but the application still determines appropriate lifetimes, dependency direction, and behaviour.

lessons.title: What Dagger Can Construct on Its Own
lessons.summary: Dagger generates assembly code from dependency declarations during the build. An `@Inject` constructor tells Dagger how to construct a type and which dependency keys to satisfy first. At runtime, the application executes that generated code rather than discovering the graph through reflection. Construction remains ordinary work: obtaining dependencies, allocating objects, and calling constructors.

blocks.text:
Assembling a dependency graph by hand involves both design and wiring. You choose which implementation satisfies an abstraction, which objects must be shared, and how long they should remain valid. You then write the constructor calls in an order that supplies every required argument.

As the graph grows, maintaining those calls takes more work. Dagger can generate the wiring, while the design decisions remain yours.

Dagger reads declarations in your source during the build and generates assembly code that is compiled alongside your own code. Its annotations describe construction, binding choices, and reuse rules. Each declaration answers a specific question about the graph.
Consider a study-session controller that receives its repository and clock through its constructor:

The constructor names two required collaborators and their types. Because the controller receives them rather than constructing them, its caller chooses what to supply. Annotating the constructor with `@Inject` makes this construction available to Dagger:

An `@Inject` constructor defines a **constructible binding**: Dagger can obtain a `StudySessionController` by calling this constructor. Its parameters identify the **dependency keys** to satisfy first. Here, Dagger needs a `QuestionRepository` and a `SystemClock` before it can create the controller. These dependencies are the outgoing edges of the controller’s node in the object graph.

The constructor already describes what the class requires. `@Inject` tells Dagger to use it when constructing the class and to obtain its arguments from the graph. The class can still be assembled by hand.

The annotated constructor does not choose which `QuestionRepository` implementation to supply or whether two consumers receive the same repository. Those binding and reuse decisions need additional declarations.
A hand-written composition root creates the dependencies and passes them into the controller:
Once the bindings are declared, Dagger generates the corresponding assembly. The generated controller construction performs calls like these:

Each provider obtains the value that satisfies its dependency key. That value may come from an annotated constructor or another binding declaration. The generated code performs the assembly you could write by hand, using the declarations to keep the calls consistent.

Dagger’s build step reads annotated declarations and emits source files. Generated per-binding factories can appear in stack traces and help you follow construction. Their names and contents are implementation details, so application code should not reference those factory types directly.
The annotation-processing mechanism, its configuration, and its incremental-build behaviour affect build cost. They do not choose the graph’s implementations or lifetimes.

A reflective container can inspect constructors and their parameter types while the program runs. Dagger performs that analysis during the build and records the result in generated code.

At runtime, construction calls those generated functions, which obtain arguments and invoke constructors. It does not discover the dependency graph through runtime reflection.

Dagger can therefore report a missing dependency binding during the build, before the application requests the object at runtime. **What the Dagger Compiler Checks** explains the scope and limits of this validation.

Avoiding reflection does not eliminate construction cost. Generated code allocates objects, calls constructors, and retains scoped results for reuse. Directly requested dependencies must still be obtained; `Provider` and `Lazy` can defer the work behind their requests.

This makes construction inspectable as ordinary code. Claims such as “zero overhead” or “faster than every other approach” need separate evidence about the graph and the alternative being compared.

You still decide which implementation satisfies `QuestionRepository`, whether consumers should share one repository, and how to supply a value that becomes available only after a user action. Dagger generates assembly from those decisions; it does not make them for you.
Generated assembly is ordinary code, which helps when you need to understand a construction path:

items: **In a stack trace.** Construction failures pass through ordinary generated frames with ordinary names, so the path from the request to the constructor that threw is readable. Nothing is hidden behind a reflective invoke.
**In a debugger.** The generated implementation is source compiled with the application, so it can be stepped into like any other code when the question is genuinely "what is this graph doing".
**In the error report.** A graph mistake is reported by the compiler against the declaration that caused it, rather than surfacing as a failure at the moment some screen first asks for something.

blocks.text: Read generated code when it helps answer a specific question about construction. Its structure and naming can change between Dagger versions, so understanding the graph’s declarations is more useful than memorising generator output.

You could write these construction calls by hand. Dagger reduces the wiring you maintain and moves detection of missing or ambiguous bindings to the build. In return, the project needs a processing step and generated source. Both the maintenance benefit and build cost matter when choosing the tool.

Explain instance creation from the constructor outward: it declares the dependencies, `@Inject` makes that construction available to Dagger, and the processor generates the binding’s construction code and component implementation during the build. At runtime, the application executes that code. Missing dependency bindings are build errors; object allocation and constructor execution still have runtime costs.

lessons.title: Declaring the Rest of the Graph
lessons.summary: An `@Inject` constructor is useful when you own the type and Dagger can construct it by obtaining its arguments. Other bindings may need a third-party builder, a choice of implementation, or computed configuration. `@Provides` supplies executable logic for obtaining a value. An ordinary one-parameter `@Binds` method delegates a key to an implementation binding. A module groups these declarations; the component determines which graph uses them and retains scoped results.

blocks.text: An `@Inject` constructor works when you can annotate the constructor and obtaining its arguments is enough to build the object. A reading application also needs bindings that cannot be expressed this way:

items: **A class you do not own.** The HTTP client comes from a library. You cannot add an annotation to its constructor, and it is usually not built by calling a constructor at all but by configuring a builder.
**An abstraction.** `LibraryRepository` is an interface, so it has no constructor to annotate. The graph needs a declaration that selects the implementation to supply.
**Computed configuration.** A configuration object may need values selected from the application’s environment. The graph needs a way to run that computation.

blocks.text: A **module** is a type annotated `@Module` that groups binding declarations. It can contain provider methods that obtain values and abstract binding methods that delegate to other bindings.
The two forms it can hold are these:

items: **`@Provides`** — a method with a body. Its return type, together with any qualifier, identifies the key it satisfies. Its parameters identify dependency keys Dagger obtains before calling the method. The body can build, configure, or compute the value.

**Ordinary one-parameter `@Binds`** — an abstract method without a body. Its return type identifies the requested type, and its parameter identifies the implementation binding to use. Any qualifier is also part of the corresponding key. Dagger uses the declaration to delegate the request rather than calling the abstract method.

blocks.text: Use `@Provides` when obtaining the value needs executable logic. Use an ordinary one-parameter `@Binds` method when the value can be supplied by delegating to an existing implementation binding.
The HTTP client comes from a third-party library and is configured through a builder. A provider method can run that builder with configuration obtained from the graph:

The return type `HttpClient` identifies the key this unqualified declaration satisfies. Before calling the method, Dagger obtains the `CatalogueConfig` argument. The provider method describes a graph node whose construction logic is written explicitly.

The application currently reads the reader’s library over the network and may later read it from a local cache. `LibraryRepository` lets callers use the same contract while the graph selects the implementation:

`NetworkLibraryRepository` has an `@Inject` constructor, so Dagger can construct it once its dependencies are available. A `LibraryRepository` request can delegate to that binding without additional construction logic:

The equivalent provider method would simply return its `impl` parameter. `@Binds` expresses that delegation without a method body. Dagger recommends it for this case because the module declaration is needed only during compilation, avoiding a runtime module call.
The preference for `@Binds` applies when a binding can delegate to an existing implementation binding. It does not replace provider methods that run a builder or compute configuration.
`CatalogueConfig` depends on the environment: the host changes for staging, and the page size may be overridden. A provider method can make those choices and construct the result:

Although `CatalogueConfig` is an application type with an ordinary constructor, this binding also needs a branch and a fallback. The provider method keeps that configuration logic in the graph declaration. Choosing between these forms depends on how the value is obtained, rather than only on who owns its type.
These cases suggest the following choice of declaration:

rows: You own the type and construction is just calling the constructor
`@Inject` constructor
The annotated constructor supplies the binding without an extra module method
The abstraction requested is satisfied by an implementation Dagger can already build
Ordinary one-parameter `@Binds`
The request delegates to an existing binding without a provider body or runtime module call
Construction needs logic, configuration, a builder, or a type you cannot annotate
`@Provides`
Something has to execute. An abstract declaration has no body and cannot branch, build or configure

blocks.text: In Kotlin, a module with abstract bindings can be an interface, and a module with provider methods can be an `object`. When one grouping needs both, an interface can hold the abstract methods while its companion object holds the providers:
This is one supported Kotlin layout. The important distinction remains the binding each method expresses: delegation or executable construction logic.

A Dagger `@Module` groups binding declarations in source code. A Gradle module defines a build and source-dependency boundary. One source file can contain several Dagger modules, and the same Dagger module can be installed in several components.
A module groups declarations; the component determines how they participate in a graph:

headers: A module is often assumed to…
rows: own the graph its bindings appear in
It declares bindings. Which graph they participate in is decided by the component that installs the module, and the same module can be installed in more than one
determine how long its objects live
It can carry a scope annotation on a binding, but the reuse that annotation describes belongs to a component instance, not to the module (see **A Scope Is a Promise the Component Keeps**)
be an architectural layer
A module can group bindings by layer or feature, but that grouping does not enforce architectural boundaries
correspond to a feature or a build module
A project may adopt that correspondence as a convention; Dagger does not require it

blocks.text: A module’s declarations can be valid but unusable in a particular component if their dependencies are unavailable there. Dagger checks the relationships between bindings where the component assembles the graph.

Current Dagger documentation also describes **parameterless `@Binds`**. It explicitly declares a binding for an eligible class with an `@Inject` constructor, rather than delegating an abstraction to an implementation. This is a separate form from the one-parameter binding above; the usual choice between delegated `@Binds` and executable `@Provides` remains the same.

Explain the choice in terms of how the value is obtained. An `@Inject` constructor describes construction Dagger can perform directly. An ordinary one-parameter `@Binds` delegates to an implementation binding without executable provider logic. `@Provides` runs the logic needed for a builder, configuration, or a computed value. A module groups these declarations; it does not establish a graph’s lifetime or a Gradle build boundary.

lessons.title: Which Graph Owns This Binding?
lessons.summary: A component defines a graph’s public entry points and the bindings available to satisfy them. Dagger generates its implementation, which the program instantiates and uses. Each entry point requires the dependencies beneath it to be satisfiable. The application’s composition root can create the component and request a root object from it.

blocks.text: Constructor and module declarations describe bindings. A **component** brings them together with the requests the graph must satisfy. It connects four aspects of dependency injection:

items: **A declaration of what may be requested.** The methods on the component interface are its public surface: the keys the rest of the program is allowed to ask for.
**A configuration of which declarations participate.** The `modules` it names, and everything reachable through them, decide what is available to satisfy those requests.
**A generated implementation.** Dagger writes a class implementing the interface, which is where the generated assembly code ends up.
**A concrete graph instance at run time.** The program creates one and holds it. That instance is the graph; two of them are two graphs.

blocks.text: Here is one, for the reading application:
To understand `readerHome()`, follow the dependency keys Dagger must satisfy to construct its result:

blocks.code:
readerHome(): ReaderHome            ← the requested key
  └─ ReaderHome                      @Inject constructor
      └─ LibraryRepository           @Binds  ← NetworkLibraryRepository
          └─ NetworkLibraryRepository @Inject constructor
              └─ ReaderLibraryClient  @Provides
                  ├─ HttpClient       @Provides
                  │   └─ CatalogueConfig  @Provides
                  │       └─ ReaderEnvironment  ← must come from somewhere
                  └─ ReaderSession    @Inject constructor

blocks.text: Every dependency in this trace must be satisfiable. `ReaderEnvironment` is required, but no binding for it is shown. If none is available to the component, Dagger reports a missing binding during the build. **What the Dagger Compiler Checks** follows that failure.
Read a component from its entry points through their dependencies. The entry points state what callers can request; the available bindings determine how those requests can be satisfied.
Adding an entry point adds another construction request. Suppose the application also needs the settings screen’s state owner:

The component must now satisfy the dependencies beneath `SettingsHome` as well. If it requires a `PreferenceStore` with no available binding, Dagger cannot generate this component. Each entry point therefore extends the graph’s construction contract.
A binding declaration in the source tree is not automatically available to every component. A component can use bindings from several sources:

items: Bindings declared by `@Provides` or `@Binds` methods in modules the component installs directly, or includes transitively through `@Module.includes`.
Any type with an `@Inject` constructor that is unscoped, or whose scope matches one this component declares.
**The component provision methods of the component's dependencies** — the published surface of another component, compared with nesting in **A Child Graph, or a Separate Graph?**
The component itself, builders for subcomponents it installs, and `Provider` or `Lazy` wrappers around any of the above.

blocks.text: A module that is not installed in a component contributes no bindings to that component. An installed binding that no entry point reaches need not be used in generated construction. It may still be subject to declaration and other compiler checks.

The component provides the entry point into generated assembly. `ReaderHome`, `LibraryRepository`, and `NetworkLibraryRepository` receive their collaborators through constructors and could also be assembled by hand.

The following snippet assumes all required bindings, including `ReaderEnvironment`, are available without caller-supplied component arguments, so Dagger can generate `create()`. The composition root creates the component and requests the root object:

One place creates the graph, asks it for a root object, and hands that object to the program. Everything downstream receives what it needs and asks the component for nothing: each class is handed its collaborators rather than fetching them.

The module list describes available binding declarations. The entry points describe the construction requests the component must satisfy. Two components can install identical modules while exposing different requests and therefore requiring different dependency paths.

The **composition root** is the application’s responsibility for assembling its objects near an entry point. With Dagger, your declarations express the wiring and generated code performs much of the assembly. The composition root can create and configure the component, then request the objects the application needs.

rows: What it is
A responsibility, and a location: assembling the graph near the entry point
A declared graph API and the generated implementation of it
Who provides it
You do, in whatever form suits the program
You declare the interface; the tool generates the implementation
Relationship
The composition root can create and hold the component, configure it, and ask it for an entry point
The component represents the graph the composition root is responsible for

blocks.text: In this arrangement, `main` performs the composition-root role by creating the component and passing its root object into the application. The component supplies the graph API and generated assembly used there.

Dagger validates individual declarations, then checks relationships between bindings at the component level. A module alone cannot establish whether its dependencies are available: that depends on the graph in which it is installed.

For example, `LibraryModule` delegates `LibraryRepository` to `NetworkLibraryRepository`, which requires a `ReaderLibraryClient`. If a component has no binding for that client, it cannot satisfy this dependency path even though the module declaration itself is valid.

The component’s public surface is also a design choice. A narrow set of root-object requests can keep assembly at a clear application boundary. If ordinary consumers instead use the component to fetch arbitrary collaborators, it serves as a service locator.

The number of methods alone does not establish that pattern; what matters is whether consumers receive their dependencies or look them up through the component.

Describe a component through its entry points, available bindings, and generated implementation. Each entry point requires its dependency path to be satisfiable, which is why binding relationships are checked at this level. Explain how the composition root uses it: application assembly code creates the component and requests a root object.

lessons.title: A Child Graph, or a Separate Graph?
lessons.summary: A subcomponent inherits bindings from its parent and ancestors and adds its own. A separate component using a component dependency gains access to the dependency’s published provision methods. Parent bindings cannot depend on child-only bindings, and sibling subcomponents cannot use one another’s bindings. These relationships define object-graph visibility; they do not themselves define Gradle build boundaries.

blocks.text: The reading application grows an annotation editor. It is entered from a book, it needs the reader's session and the library repository that the application graph already has, and it has objects of its own that exist only while the editor is open. The question is how its graph relates to the application's.
Dagger has two answers. Compare them by what the new graph can **see**.
**A subcomponent is a nested graph.**

items: It can use bindings from its parent and ancestors, as well as bindings declared in its own modules.
It may add bindings of its own, and a shorter-lived scope beneath the parent's.
Its parent cannot see into it, and neither can its siblings.

blocks.text: **A component dependency is a separate graph that names another as a dependency.**

items: It is an independent component. The other component is supplied to it as something it depends on.
It gains access only to the keys that component **publishes as provision methods on its interface** — its entry-point list, read as a public surface.
Everything else in the other graph, however many bindings it has, remains invisible.

blocks.text: Choose the relationship by the visibility the feature needs. A subcomponent can use its ancestors’ bindings. A component dependency exposes an explicitly published set of provision methods. This difference affects how much wiring you maintain and how deliberately shared dependencies are exposed.
For a nested editor graph, the parent exposes a method returning the subcomponent’s factory:

`AnnotationEditor` may now depend on `LibraryRepository`, on `ReaderSession`, on `HttpClient`, on `CatalogueConfig` — on anything the application graph binds — without any of it being declared again. It may also depend on `DraftAnnotation`, bound in its own module, which the application graph knows nothing about.
**The editor as a separate graph.** The relationship is declared the other way round:

`AnnotationEditor` can obtain `LibraryRepository` and `ReaderSession` through the published methods. This dependency relationship does not expose the parent graph’s `HttpClient` or `CatalogueConfig` bindings. To share those through `ReaderComponent`, add corresponding provision methods.

A component dependency exposes provision methods from the supplied component. It does not import that component’s internal binding declarations. To share another binding through this relationship, publish it on the dependency’s interface.

rows: What the new graph can use
Every binding in the parent and any ancestor, plus its own
Only the keys the other component publishes as provision methods, plus its own
What has to be declared to share one more type
Nothing — it is already visible
A provision method on the other component's interface
What happens when the other graph gains a binding
It becomes available here automatically
Nothing changes here until it is published
Relationship between the graphs
Nested: the child is created from the parent and cannot exist without it
Independent: each is its own component, one supplied to the other
Scopes
A child cannot declare the same scope as an ancestor; the application determines how long each component is retained
Each declares its scopes, subject to Dagger’s component-dependency rules

blocks.text: Bindings are visible downward through the subcomponent hierarchy. Parent objects cannot depend on child-only bindings, and objects in one subcomponent cannot depend on bindings that exist only in a sibling.

blocks.code:
ReaderComponent                    can see: its own bindings only
  │
  ├── AnnotationComponent          can see: its own + ReaderComponent's
  │        DraftAnnotation         ← invisible to the parent
  │                                ← invisible to the sibling
  └── SearchComponent              can see: its own + ReaderComponent's
           SearchQueryHistory      ← invisible to the parent
                                   ← invisible to the sibling

blocks.text:
The editor’s `DraftAnnotation` binding is available within its child graph, not to the parent or the search sibling. Nesting therefore permits broad access to shared ancestor bindings while keeping feature-local bindings out of other graphs.

That visibility rule prevents a parent binding from requiring an object supplied only by an editor subcomponent. Ordinary application code still determines which objects are retained or passed elsewhere.

A component boundary is an **object-graph** boundary: it decides which bindings are visible to which requests. A Gradle module boundary is a **build and source** boundary: it decides which code can be compiled against which other code. Some projects design the two together and many do not, and neither implies the other.

An explicit published surface makes shared dependencies visible in code review. If the editor needs another object from the application graph, a provision method must expose it. That can help enforce an agreed graph API, but it also means maintaining a declaration for each shared type.

A nested graph is a natural fit when the feature should use bindings already available in the surrounding graph. A separate component with a published dependency surface can suit a feature that should use only an agreed set of dependencies. Separate development or a deliberate boundary can justify maintaining that surface.

A subcomponent cannot declare a scope already used by an ancestor. Each scoped binding needs an unambiguous component instance to retain its result (see **A Scope Is a Promise the Component Keeps**). Siblings can use the same scope because neither is an ancestor of the other. Separate components define their scopes within Dagger’s component-dependency rules.

Compare these relationships through visibility. A subcomponent can use its own bindings and those of its parent and ancestors. A component dependency supplies the keys published by provision methods on another component. Parent bindings cannot depend on child-only bindings, and siblings cannot use one another’s bindings. Then explain why the feature needs inherited bindings or an explicit published surface. Neither arrangement alone defines a Gradle module boundary.

lessons.title: A Scope Is a Promise the Component Keeps
lessons.summary: A Dagger scope specifies reuse within a component instance. The application chooses how long to retain that component to match the required lifetime. Two component instances with `@Singleton` constructor bindings each retain their own results. Scope names do not choose a process-wide lifetime, and a subcomponent cannot repeat an ancestor’s scope.

blocks.text: The application needs its destinations to observe one signed-in reader: **one `ReaderSession` identity from sign-in until sign-out**. First choose a component owner retained for that period, then scope the binding so requests through that owner reuse the same session. The requirement determines the lifetime; the annotation expresses reuse.
Start with the question the notation has to answer:

blocks.code: Who actually retains this instance?

blocks.text: For an ordinary scoped binding, **the component instance** retains the result. A scope on the binding requests reuse, and a matching scope on the component declares where that result belongs.

The two annotations have related jobs. On `ReaderSession`, `@Singleton` requests reuse of the constructor binding’s result. On `ReaderComponent`, it declares the scope that component represents. Dagger requires an appropriate component scope for an ordinary scoped binding.
The lifetime decision becomes a component owner and a matching reuse declaration:

blocks.code:
the lifetime a requirement needs
        ↓   choose an owner whose lifetime matches
the component instance held for that long
        ↓   express reuse inside that owner
a matching scope annotation on the binding

blocks.text: A scope annotation specifies reuse rather than creating an application lifetime. The component instance retains the scoped result. The application decides how long to keep that component, and other references can keep its objects alive after the component is released.
Consider three requests for the `@Singleton ReaderSession` constructor binding:

blocks.code:
val first = DaggerReaderComponent.create()
val a1 = first.readerHome().session      // resolve from `first`
val a2 = first.settingsHome().session    // resolve from `first` again

val second = DaggerReaderComponent.create()
val b1 = second.readerHome().session     // resolve from a second component

blocks.text: How many distinct `ReaderSession` objects exist? Reason it out from ownership:

items: `a1` and `a2` are requests served by the **same component instance**, and the binding is scoped to a scope that component represents. The component holds one result and hands it to both. `a1 === a2`.
`b1` is served by a **different component instance**. It has its own storage for its own scoped bindings, and nothing connects the two. `b1` is a second object.

blocks.text: There are **two** `ReaderSession` objects. `a1` and `a2` share the result retained by `first`; `b1` comes from `second`’s separate constructor binding result. `@Singleton` requests reuse within each component instance, and this code creates two components.

`@Singleton` does not by itself select an application-wide or permanent lifetime. An ordinary scoped binding is reused within each component instance representing its scope. Application-wide sharing arises when the application creates one such component and retains it for the process.

Once the component and its scoped objects are no longer reachable, they can be garbage-collected. Dropping the component reference removes that owner’s retention, but an object passed elsewhere can remain alive through those other references.
A custom scope uses the same reuse mechanism as `@Singleton`:

Applying `@ReaderScope` to a component and a binding gives the same per-component reuse rule. The name communicates the intended owner to people reading the code. The application still has to retain the component for the intended reader lifetime.

A subcomponent cannot use a scope already declared by an ancestor. Otherwise the same scope would identify both parent and child owners, leaving scoped storage ambiguous.

Sibling subcomponents may share a scope name because each has a separate owner and neither is an ancestor of the other.

headers: What you want to be true
rows: One reader session observed by every destination until sign-out
A component held for exactly that long, representing a scope, with the binding scoped to it
A fresh draft annotation each time the editor opens
An unscoped request made for each opening, or a component created for that opening with the draft binding scoped to it
An object surviving the process
Nothing in this list. Nothing held in memory survives process death, and durability is a storage decision with storage tools

blocks.text:
Choosing a scope starts with the required identity lifetime. If a draft belongs to one editor opening, retaining it in an application-lived component shares it too broadly. Its text can appear in another book, and its memory can remain retained after the screen closes. Shared mutable state can also make tests depend on earlier tests.

**A Scope Is a Rule; an Owner Is a Lifetime** explains these ownership costs. Dagger expresses the selected reuse rule, so it cannot decide whether that lifetime matches the product requirement.

`@Reusable` permits allocation reuse when callers do not require a stable shared identity. Unlike an ordinary scope, it is not associated with one designated component, and it does not guarantee that the binding runs only once. Different components may receive different objects.

It suits immutable objects whose number of allocations does not affect correctness. A mutable object that consumers must share needs an identity guarantee this annotation does not provide.
Use `@Reusable` only when obtaining the value again is acceptable and reuse is an optimisation. It cannot satisfy a requirement that several consumers observe the same mutable state.

Describe scoped reuse through its owner: a component instance retains a binding’s result and serves it to requests within that scope. Two component instances resolving the `ReaderSession` constructor binding therefore produce two sessions. The application controls how long it retains the components; other references may retain their objects longer. Explain the ancestor-scope restriction in terms of choosing an unambiguous storage owner.

lessons.title: When the Type Is Not the Key
lessons.summary: A Dagger dependency key combines a type with an optional qualifier. Qualifiers distinguish bindings of the same type, and consumers request the qualified key they need. Multibindings solve a different problem: independently declared contributions satisfy one collection dependency. The consumer can depend on a shared abstraction without naming each contributor.

blocks.text: Consider a reading application that talks to its server two ways — the public catalogue, which must work before anybody signs in, and the reader's own library, which carries their credentials and must never send them anywhere else. Both are HTTP clients, configured differently. A consumer asks for one:

With two unqualified `HttpClient` bindings, this request is ambiguous: it identifies neither configuration. If the clients represent different responsibilities, distinct types can make that distinction explicit (see **Two Dependencies of the Same Type**). Qualifiers are another option when one type is appropriate but the graph must distinguish its configurations.
A Dagger key combines **a type and an optional qualifier**. A qualifier is an annotation marked with `@Qualifier`. Adding it changes the key Dagger resolves:

A qualifier is part of the dependency key. The declaration identifies the key it provides; the consumer’s parameter identifies the key it requests. If those qualifiers differ, that declaration does not satisfy that request. An unqualified request still needs an unqualified binding.
The qualifier annotation is declared once, and `javax.inject` supplies `@Qualifier` itself for the purpose:
Then it appears on the declarations, and on every request that means one of them:

`LibraryRepository` now explicitly requests the authenticated client. This disambiguates construction, but Dagger does not inspect whether a provider’s returned client has the intended credentials. A provider could still supply the wrong configuration under a qualified key. Distinct types can strengthen the contract when their APIs and construction enforce the difference.

An unqualified parameter requests the unqualified key. If both provider methods are qualified, neither satisfies that request, and Dagger reports a missing binding. Apply the intended qualifier to the consumer’s parameter as well as the provider.

The application also needs several independent features to contribute startup work: annotation editing, offline sync, and search indexing. A multibinding can supply these contributors as **one collection dependency**.
A coordinator that names each concrete contributor might begin like this:

This coordinator depends directly on every feature. Adding or removing one requires changing its constructor. A multibinding lets feature modules contribute implementations of a shared `StartupContributor` contract, while the coordinator receives the collection without naming those implementations:

`@IntoSet` contributes an element to `Set<StartupContributor>` rather than providing the entire set. Dagger combines contributions available in the component to satisfy the set dependency. Feature modules can declare their contributions separately, while `StartupRunner` receives one collection.

Adding or removing a contributor can change the installed feature modules without changing `StartupRunner`. Dagger also supports map multibindings, where each contribution has a key declared at compile time.

Multibindings let the coordinator depend on a shared contract instead of concrete contributors. The sketch below shows direct dependencies in the first arrangement and how contributions reach the coordinator in the second. The second set of arrows shows contribution flow, rather than source dependencies.

blocks.code:
without:   StartupRunner ──→ AnnotationStartup
                         ──→ OfflineSyncStartup
                         ──→ SearchIndexStartup

with:      AnnotationStartup ─┐
           OfflineSyncStartup ─┼──→ Set<StartupContributor> ──→ StartupRunner
           SearchIndexStartup ─┘

blocks.text: In the first arrangement, `StartupRunner` names concrete feature contributors. In the second, it requests a set of the shared `StartupContributor` abstraction, which each feature implements. When the coordinator owns that contract, the features depend on its abstraction rather than the coordinator depending on their concrete types. This applies dependency inversion to several contributors (see **Who Defines the Abstraction?**).

A multibinding alone does not make an architecture modular. Contributors still need appropriate boundaries, and placing them in separate build modules is a separate decision.

The injected aggregate is also a `Set`, which promises no execution order. If one contributor must run before another, this dependency does not express that requirement. `StartupRunner` still determines how to handle slow contributors or exceptions; changing its dependencies does not resolve those execution policies.

Qualifiers and multibindings both make dependency requests explicit. Qualifiers distinguish keys for differently configured values of one type. Multibindings combine separately declared contributions into a collection key. In either case, the consumer’s declared key determines what Dagger resolves, rather than registration or declaration order.

For same-type ambiguity, explain that a key is a type plus an optional qualifier, and show how the provider’s key matches the consumer’s request. For multibindings, describe the need first: several independent contributors must arrive as one dependency. `StartupRunner` requests the shared collection and does not name the implementations. Include the limit that a set supplies no execution order.

lessons.title: What the Dagger Compiler Checks
lessons.summary: Dagger checks binding relationships at the component level during the build. Missing or conflicting bindings for reachable requests are errors. A dependency cycle is permitted when it contains a `Provider` or `Lazy` edge. These checks do not establish whether the application chose appropriate lifetimes, dependency direction, or behaviour.

blocks.text: Dagger detects missing and conflicting dependency bindings during the build, before the application runs. **When Is a Broken Graph Detected?** compares this timing with other assembly approaches. Here, the question is which graph properties Dagger checks.

Dagger validates individual annotations and declarations, then checks the relationships between bindings at the component level. A module alone cannot establish whether its dependencies are satisfiable; that depends on the component’s available bindings and requests.
For an ordinary dependency request, the graph needs one unambiguous binding for its key. Dagger’s core semantics describes the two failures as missing and duplicate bindings:

items: **A missing binding** — a key contains zero bindings. Something reachable from an entry point requires it, and nothing declares it.
**A duplicate binding** — a key contains more than one binding. Two declarations satisfy the same key, and a request for it cannot be resolved.

blocks.text: The check establishes that ordinary reachable dependency keys have unambiguous bindings under Dagger’s graph rules. It catches missing and duplicate bindings before runtime, but it does not establish whether those objects should depend on one another or whether their construction logic will succeed.
For a missing binding, follow the dependency path from the entry point. Here it ends at `ReaderEnvironment`, for which the graph has no binding:

blocks.code:
ReaderComponent
  └─ readerHome(): ReaderHome         ← entry point: the graph must satisfy this
      └─ LibraryRepository            ← @Binds → NetworkLibraryRepository
          └─ ReaderLibraryClient      ← @Provides in LibraryModule
              └─ HttpClient           ← @Provides in NetworkModule
                  └─ CatalogueConfig  ← @Provides in NetworkModule
                      └─ ReaderEnvironment
                             ↑
                    no @Inject constructor, no @Provides,
                    no component dependency publishing it
                    → this key has zero bindings

blocks.text: The trace shows why construction cannot be generated: `readerHome()` requires a chain of dependencies that ends at an unsatisfied `ReaderEnvironment` key. Declare how that value is obtained or supply it when creating the component. If its binding already exists in a module, check that the component installs that module.
**An ambiguous binding, traced.** Two provider methods return `HttpClient`, and a consumer asks for `HttpClient`:

Dagger does not choose between these two bindings. If the clients have different responsibilities, different types may express that distinction. If the same type represents two configurations, qualifiers can distinguish the keys. The graph declaration must make the choice explicit.

Dagger does not resolve duplicate ordinary bindings by module order, declaration order, or a “most specific” match. Give each intended dependency an unambiguous key, then request that key from the consumer.

Dagger rejects dependency cycles unless the cycle contains an edge wrapped in `Provider` or `Lazy`. That wrapper permits indirection instead of requiring the whole cycle to be constructed through immediate calls. The exception is part of the graph rule; “Dagger rejects all circular dependencies” would be too broad.
Build-time generation and validation require processing work and tooling. Include that build cost when comparing Dagger with a container that resolves dependencies at runtime.
A successful build establishes specific structural properties of the graph:

items: Every dependency key reachable from the component's entry points is satisfiable under Dagger's graph rules.
An ordinary reachable key with no binding or conflicting bindings causes a build error.
The declarations, bindings and components satisfy Dagger's structural constraints, checked where the graph is assembled rather than per module.

blocks.text: It does not establish whether the graph meets the application’s design requirements:

items: whether the dependency direction and architectural boundaries are appropriate;
whether the consumer should depend on that abstraction;
whether the chosen component lifetime and reuse rule match the object’s required lifetime;
whether component boundaries match the product’s boundaries;
whether the program behaves correctly, or needs the dependency at all.

blocks.text: Consider a draft annotation that should belong to one editor opening. It holds the unfinished text a reader is writing about a particular book. Suppose its binding is scoped to an application-lived component:

Assuming the remaining dependencies are satisfied, the graph passes Dagger’s checks. `DraftAnnotation` has a constructor binding and a scope matching the component. There is no missing binding, duplicate binding, or prohibited cycle in that construction path.

If the application retains this component for the process, its editor requests share one `DraftAnnotation`. Open a book, type half a sentence, go back, and open a different book: unless application logic resets it, the same draft still holds the first book’s text.

The draft needed a lifetime tied to one editor opening, but its component owner retains and shares it much longer. **A Scope Is a Rule; an Owner Is a Lifetime** explains the distinction between the required lifetime, the owner, and the reuse rule. Dagger validates matching scope declarations, not whether that owner meets the product’s lifetime requirement.

A state owner can also depend directly on `NetworkLibraryRepository` instead of `LibraryRepository`. If the concrete type and its dependencies are available, Dagger can construct it. That does not establish whether bypassing the interface is appropriate for the architecture.

rows: Can every reachable key be satisfied unambiguously?
Yes, under Dagger’s binding rules
Are missing and conflicting dependency bindings detected before runtime?
Yes; constructor and provider behaviour can still fail at runtime
Is this object shared more widely than its requirement asked for?
No
Should this consumer be allowed to name this type?
No
Does the program do the right thing?
No

blocks.text:
Compile-time validation removes missing and conflicting binding failures from the application’s runtime paths. That is a useful guarantee about wiring. Constructor and provider logic can still throw, and a structurally valid graph can still have inappropriate dependencies or lifetimes.

Use the draft example to separate those questions: Dagger can validate its binding and matching scope while the application shares the draft across editor openings incorrectly.

Explain both the checked property and its boundary. Dagger validates binding relationships at the component level and reports missing or conflicting bindings during the build. It does not establish correct constructor behaviour, dependency direction, or product lifetimes. A draft scoped to an application-held component can pass the structural checks while sharing text between editor openings.

units.title: Hilt: Android Lifecycle-Aware Dagger
units.summary: Hilt uses Dagger's graph model and adds a predefined Android component hierarchy with generated lifecycle integration. Choose a component according to the Android owner and lifetime a dependency needs. A matching scope controls reuse within that component instance; `@InstallIn` controls where a module's bindings are available. Hilt manages the standard hierarchy, while the application still chooses its bindings and decides which objects need to be shared.

lessons.title: Hilt Is Dagger With the Decisions Already Made
lessons.summary: Hilt generates and uses Dagger components and bindings; what it adds is a standard Android component hierarchy and the generated integration that keeps component instances aligned with Android owners.

blocks.text: With Dagger alone, you declare components and their relationships, choose scopes, expose entry methods, and supply modules and bindings. **Hilt uses the same Dagger graph model.** Dagger still validates the reachable graph and generates the calls that construct its objects.

Hilt supplies several Android-specific decisions that an application using Dagger directly would otherwise make: which standard component types exist, how they relate, which Android owners create or retain their instances, and how framework-created classes receive dependencies. It provides a predefined hierarchy and generates the integration code for those owners.

blocks.code:
Raw Dagger
Application composition root
    ↓ creates
RootComponent
    ↓ creates or retains
ScreenComponent / other nested components
    ↓ application code connects them to
Android owners

Hilt
predefined generated Dagger hierarchy
    ↓ framework integration creates and retains
component instances at Android lifecycle boundaries
    ↓ generated entry integration connects
Android owners to the graph

blocks.text: An application using Dagger directly can also build lifecycle-aware Android graphs and construct the same objects. Hilt standardizes the component structure and generates Android integration code that the application would otherwise design and maintain.

items: Bindings, modules, constructor injection, scopes and compile-time graph validation are Dagger concepts Hilt continues to use.
The predefined Android component hierarchy, its standard scope names and generated owner integration are Hilt's conventions.
Hilt reduces handwritten integration code by standardizing component structure and lifecycle management.

blocks.text: Hilt uses Dagger components and bindings within a predefined Android component hierarchy. Its generated integration manages component instances according to the lifetimes of their Android owners.

In a reading application, `LibraryRepository` is supplied by a Dagger binding, and the signed-in reader's `ReaderSession` needs an owner. With Dagger directly, the application might define its own application and reader components:

Application code must also create `ReaderRootComponent`, decide when to create and retain `ReaderComponent`, reconnect it after configuration recreation if needed, and arrange Activity injection at the appropriate lifecycle point.

blocks.code:
SingletonComponent
    ├─ ActivityRetainedComponent
    │     ├─ ViewModelComponent
    │     └─ ActivityComponent
    └─ ServiceComponent

blocks.text: Hilt provides the hierarchy shown here and manages its component instances through Android integration. The application supplies Dagger bindings to those generated components. For a Compose UI hosted in a Hilt-enabled `ComponentActivity`, the Activity is the Android entry point; individual composables do not each receive a component or need `@AndroidEntryPoint`.

rows: Which component types exist?
The engineer defines them
A standard Android hierarchy is generated
How are components related?
The engineer declares subcomponents or dependencies
Standard parent-child relationships are predefined
Who creates and retains instances?
Application integration code
Generated Android lifecycle integration
What constructs objects?
Generated Dagger code
Generated Dagger code
Who chooses bindings and required reuse?
The engineer
The engineer

blocks.text: Hilt reduces boilerplate by standardizing component structure and generating Android lifecycle integration. Those conventions also limit how freely you can change the standard hierarchy, so the benefit depends on how well it fits the application.

Hilt's conventions fit common Android lifetimes: the application process, an Activity retained across configuration changes, a ViewModel, a concrete Activity instance, and a Service. A shared component structure gives teams consistent names and avoids rebuilding the same lifecycle integration.

A product lifetime may not fit that hierarchy. Hilt supports custom components and manual entry points, but using many adapters to express a core lifetime adds work. Compare that work with the cost of maintaining custom Dagger integration when deciding how well Hilt fits the project.

Explain the responsibilities of each layer. Dagger supplies bindings, components, scopes, generated construction and graph validation. Hilt supplies a predefined Android hierarchy and lifecycle integration for framework-created owners. The application writes less integration code in exchange for adopting that standard structure.

lessons.title: Which Android Component Owns This?
lessons.summary: A Hilt component is chosen by matching the required lifetime to the Android owner it follows; a scope then expresses reuse inside one instance of that component.

blocks.text: Start with how long the object must be shared. Match that requirement to an Android owner and its Hilt component, then choose the reuse rule:

blocks.code:
product lifetime requirement
        ↓
actual Android owner / generated component lifetime
        ↓
scope and reuse rule inside that component instance

blocks.text: Hilt manages generated component instances around Android owners. By default, a binding is unscoped: Dagger evaluates it for each request without caching its result for the component. A matching scope makes requests share one result within that component instance. **The component determines how long Hilt retains the scoped result; the scope determines reuse within that component.**

rows: SingletonComponent
The in-memory Application/process graph: created with Application startup and gone when the process is destroyed
@Singleton
ActivityRetainedComponent
One retained Activity identity: first Activity creation through final destruction, spanning configuration recreation
@ActivityRetainedScoped
ViewModelComponent
One ViewModel: created and destroyed with that ViewModel
@ViewModelScoped
ActivityComponent
One concrete Activity instance: created and destroyed with that instance
@ActivityScoped
ServiceComponent
One Service instance: created and destroyed with that Service
@ServiceScoped

blocks.text: `ActivityRetainedComponent` survives configuration recreation. Android can destroy the first Activity instance and replace it while the retained component continues. The component ends when that Activity is finally destroyed rather than recreated. It is distinct from both the concrete Activity instance and a ViewModel, and it does not survive process death.
Choose a Hilt component by matching the required lifetime to the Android owner Hilt follows. Only then decide whether repeated requests inside that component need the same identity.

A reading application's `ReaderSession` holds the currently open book. The reading Activity and objects beneath it must share that session, including after a configuration change recreates the Activity. The session should end when the reading Activity is permanently finished and should not be shared with unrelated Activities.

rows: ActivityComponent
A new component is created for the replacement Activity instance
Too short: the session identity is lost across configuration recreation
ActivityRetainedComponent
The same retained component spans the old and replacement Activity instances
Matches the requirement
SingletonComponent
The session can be shared across every Activity for the process
Too wide: unrelated owners can observe the same mutable session

blocks.text: `ActivityRetainedComponent` matches all three requirements: sharing beneath one Activity, surviving configuration recreation, and ending before process-wide ownership. `@ActivityRetainedScoped` makes requests within that component share the session. `@ActivityScoped` would retain a separate session only for each concrete Activity instance, losing that identity on recreation.

Now apply the same test to `@Singleton`. It requests reuse inside `SingletonComponent`, an in-memory graph attached to the Application/process lifetime. When the operating-system process disappears, the graph and every object retained in it disappear. **`@Singleton` does not mean durable across process death.** Restoring or persisting information is a separate responsibility (see **The ViewModel Owner: Lifetime Is Not Persistence**).

A longer-lived scope retains an object for longer and lets more consumers share it. Choosing one without a sharing requirement can expose owner-specific state to unrelated work, even if no Android object is leaked. Choose the scope that matches the required sharing and lifetime.

Scoping keeps a binding's result in memory for the lifetime of its component. Shared mutable state, coordination through one object, or a measured construction cost can justify that retention. An inexpensive stateless formatter usually does not need it: installing its binding high in the hierarchy makes it available to consumers without requiring them to share one formatter instance.

This lesson uses the application, retained-Activity, ViewModel, Activity and Service components. Hilt also provides Fragment and View components beneath the Activity branch. For any component you need, compare its documented creation and destruction points with the object's required lifetime.

For an object shared across configuration recreation but confined to one Activity, compare the three relevant owners. `ActivityComponent` ends with each concrete Activity instance; `SingletonComponent` permits process-wide sharing; `ActivityRetainedComponent` spans the Activity's first creation through its final destruction. Its matching scope reuses one result per retained component instance. Persistence across process death remains a separate responsibility.

lessons.title: When Android Owns Construction
lessons.summary: Field injection and Hilt entry points follow from construction ownership: Android constructs framework classes such as an Activity, so there is no application-owned constructor call at which to pass dependencies.

blocks.text: When application or graph code controls construction, required dependencies can be passed in the constructor. The caller supplies them before the constructor returns, and the signature makes those requirements visible. This remains the usual approach for ordinary classes in a Hilt application.

Android constructs an Activity. Application code does not call `ReaderActivity(repository, session)`, so it cannot pass graph dependencies at that constructor call. Hilt instead supplies them through generated lifecycle integration.

blocks.code:
application owns construction
        ↓
constructor injection

Android framework owns construction
        ↓
generated lifecycle integration and members/field injection

unsupported or unmanaged owner
        ↓
explicit Hilt entry point at the integration boundary

blocks.text: `@AndroidEntryPoint` connects a supported Android class to Hilt's generated component hierarchy. For an Activity, generated integration obtains the appropriate component and injects fields through the base-class lifecycle path when `super.onCreate()` runs. The annotation therefore connects framework-owned construction to Dagger injection at a defined lifecycle point.

Field injection appears at the Android boundary because the application does not own construction of the framework class. Ordinary classes that application or graph code constructs should still prefer constructor injection.

In this Activity, `readerController` has been injected when `super.onCreate()` returns, so the next line can use it. Injection occurs at different points for Fragments, Views, Services and BroadcastReceivers. Check the documented point for the Android type before using an injected field. ViewModels use the separate `@HiltViewModel` API.

Hilt-injected fields cannot be private because generated code must assign them. Unlike a constructor parameter, this `lateinit` property is unavailable during the Activity's initial construction; Hilt assigns it at the documented lifecycle point. Ordinary classes whose construction the application controls can avoid that gap by using constructor injection.

Field injection hides dependencies from the constructor signature and leaves a period when the object exists but the fields are not ready. Framework-owned construction can require that arrangement. For an ordinary class with too many responsibilities, hiding constructor parameters does not reduce those responsibilities.

A `ContentProvider` is created by Android but does not support `@AndroidEntryPoint`. It can obtain dependencies through an explicit Hilt entry point: a small interface exposing the bindings that this integration boundary needs.

`@EntryPoint` makes the generated component implement `CatalogProviderEntryPoint`. `@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)` places that interface in the application component, and `fromApplication` retrieves it from the matching holder. The provider performs this lookup because Android controls its construction. Ordinary domain objects can keep their dependencies explicit through constructor parameters.

An entry point couples boundary code to Hilt access APIs and makes graph lookup explicit there. This can be necessary for code Hilt cannot inject directly. If an ordinary feature or business class uses the same lookup, check whether its caller could supply the dependency through construction instead.

The location and purpose of the lookup determine its architectural effect. `CatalogProvider` accesses Hilt because Android creates it outside ordinary constructor injection. A reusable domain object that looks up its own dependencies instead hides requirements from its callers. **Asking For It, or Being Given It** explains the same distinction without Hilt.

Explain why construction ownership matters. Android creates the Activity, so Hilt supplies its fields through `@AndroidEntryPoint` integration at the documented lifecycle point. Classes that the graph can construct normally use constructor injection. Unsupported or unmanaged code can use an explicit `@EntryPoint`, which couples that integration boundary to Hilt access APIs.

lessons.title: ViewModels, Their Component, and the Values That Arrive Late
lessons.summary: Hilt constructs a ViewModel from graph dependencies; its ViewModelStore owner retains and clears it. Each dependency's own component and scope control reuse. Runtime input, such as a selected book ID, can arrive through a state channel or assisted creation.

blocks.text: Hilt can constructor-inject a ViewModel because its ViewModel factory participates in platform creation. The constructor receives dependencies supplied by the graph:

`@HiltViewModel` registers the ViewModel with Hilt's ViewModel factory, which uses Dagger bindings to construct it. Obtain the instance through ViewModel APIs so its `ViewModelStoreOwner` and store can retain and clear it. Direct Dagger injection would bypass that ownership and could create another instance, so Hilt rejects it at compile time.

Hilt supplies ViewModel dependencies from `ViewModelComponent` and its parent components. The component follows the ViewModel's lifetime. It also provides `SavedStateHandle` and `ViewModelLifecycle` as default bindings; `SavedStateHandle` is one route for state or navigation-derived values.

rows: ViewModel
A lifecycle-aware state holder obtained through a ViewModelStore owner; may expose UI state and behavior
The owner/store clears it according to ViewModel semantics
@ViewModelScoped dependency
A graph object reused inside one ViewModelComponent instance
Retained by its component until that ViewModel component ends
@ActivityRetainedScoped dependency
A graph object reused inside one retained Activity component and shareable across its ViewModels
Retained by its component until the retained Activity component ends

blocks.text: Hilt changes how a ViewModel is constructed and which graph can supply it. The ViewModelStore owner still determines the ViewModel's actual lifetime, and each injected dependency follows its own component and scope.

Suppose `ReaderViewModel` and `NotesViewModel` each need their own parser instance. A constructor-injected `BookParser` annotated with `@ViewModelScoped` is available in `ViewModelComponent` and shared within each ViewModel's graph:

Within one ViewModel graph, any dependency that requests `BookParser` receives the same scoped instance. If `ChapterIndexer` also requests it, it shares the parser supplied to `ReaderViewModel`. Another ViewModel has its own `ViewModelComponent` and receives a different parser.

If several ViewModels associated with one retained Activity must share a `ReaderSession`, use `ActivityRetainedComponent` with `@ActivityRetainedScoped`. `@Singleton` permits wider sharing and should correspond to a process-wide requirement.

A ViewModel and an ActivityRetained-scoped dependency can both survive configuration changes, but they have different roles. A ViewModel is a state holder retained and cleared through a ViewModelStore. The dependency is a graph object retained by Hilt's component; it does not automatically become UI state or gain the ViewModel retrieval contract.

`LibraryRepository` can be supplied by the graph, but the selected `bookId` arrives at navigation time. It need not be registered as an application-wide binding. If navigation supplies the key through saved state, the ViewModel can read it from the `SavedStateHandle` available in `ViewModelComponent`:

Here, navigation supplies the runtime value through `SavedStateHandle` rather than an application-wide binding. Whether the value can be restored depends on the saved-state contract; injection alone does not provide restoration.
If the caller supplies a creation-time value that does not naturally belong in `SavedStateHandle`, assisted ViewModel injection combines that value with dependencies from the graph:

Assisted input is tied to construction; it does not become durable merely because it entered a ViewModel. Hilt does not persist an assisted `bookId` to disk. Saved-state restoration and durable storage remain separate contracts, just as a ViewModel instance surviving configuration recreation is not the same as surviving process death.

A creation callback supplies initial values; it does not update an existing ViewModel. For the same owner and ViewModel key, ViewModel APIs return the stored instance, so another creation callback does not replace its assisted values.
