To change the selected book while that instance remains in use, expose an explicit state or event operation.

Distinguish construction, retention, dependency reuse and runtime input. Hilt/Dagger constructs the ViewModel, and its ViewModelStore owner retains and clears it. Dependencies are shared according to their own components and scopes. Runtime input can come from a state channel or assisted creation. Choose ViewModel or retained Activity scope according to which consumers need to share a dependency.

lessons.title: Which Graph Does This Binding Join?
lessons.summary: `@InstallIn` places a module's bindings in generated Hilt components and determines where they are available. Scope separately controls whether requests within one component instance share a result.

blocks.text: A Dagger module contributes binding declarations the graph cannot obtain from constructor injection alone. A Hilt module remains a standard Dagger module. The new question is where those declarations join Hilt's predefined hierarchy.

`@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)` places `LibraryModule` in the generated application component. Its `LibraryApi` binding is available there and in descendant components. This annotation neither creates the component nor scopes the API; reuse is a separate binding decision.

blocks.code:
SingletonComponent       LibraryApi visible here
    ↓                         and below
ActivityRetainedComponent   ← visible
    ├─ ViewModelComponent   ← visible
    └─ ActivityComponent    ← visible

A binding installed in ActivityComponent is visible there
but cannot be requested upward by ActivityRetainedComponent
or sideways by ViewModelComponent.

blocks.text: Bindings in a component can use bindings declared there or in its ancestors. A parent cannot request a binding declared only in a child, and sibling components cannot see one another's bindings. These rules determine availability; scoping separately determines reuse.
`@InstallIn` decides which generated graph receives a module and therefore where its bindings are visible. Scope decides whether requests within one matching component instance reuse the same result.
Place an unscoped parser binding in `ActivityRetainedComponent`. Both a ViewModel below it and an Activity below it can request the parser, but each request receives a new result:
Now add the component's matching scope to the same binding:

rows: Installed in ActivityRetainedComponent, unscoped
Retained component and its ViewModel/Activity children
A new result per request
Installed in ActivityRetainedComponent, @ActivityRetainedScoped
Exactly the same
One result per retained component instance

blocks.text: Adding `@ActivityRetainedScoped` keeps the parser available to the same consumers, but makes them share one result per retained component instance. Moving the unscoped module to `ActivityComponent` would instead change which consumers can request it, without adding scoped reuse. Installation and scope control different aspects of the binding.

Installing a binding in `SingletonComponent` makes it available across the hierarchy, but does not automatically make its result shared. Without a scope, Dagger evaluates the binding for each request rather than caching the result for the component. Choose visibility and reuse separately.

A scoped binding in an `@InstallIn` module must use a scope supported by the target component. For example, `@ActivityScoped` cannot scope a binding installed in `SingletonComponent`: it belongs to `ActivityComponent`. Hilt reports this mismatch at compile time.

A module's installation shows which consumers should be able to request its bindings. Scope annotations show which consumers should share a result within a component instance. Reading both declarations lets you compare those choices with the product's visibility and sharing requirements.

Explain `@InstallIn` as placement: it adds a Dagger module to one or more generated Hilt components, making its bindings available there and in descendants. Explain scope separately: a matching component scope caches one result per component instance, while an unscoped binding is evaluated for each request. A binding declared only in a child is unavailable to its parent.

lessons.title: Hilt, or Components You Write Yourself?
lessons.summary: Hilt and custom Dagger components use the same graph model. Choose between Hilt's standard Android hierarchy and a custom structure by comparing lifecycle fit, integration work and migration cost.

blocks.text: Hilt uses Dagger's bindings, scopes, modules, generated construction and compile-time validation. Choosing between Hilt and custom Dagger components primarily means deciding **who designs the component structure and its Android integration**.

blocks.code:
requirements fit standard Android owners
        ↓
Hilt hierarchy removes repeated structural decisions

requirements need materially different owners
        ↓
custom Dagger components preserve structural freedom

blocks.text: Compare how well Hilt's predefined hierarchy expresses the project's ownership and lifetime requirements, and how much work it saves relative to maintaining custom Dagger components. The following questions help assess that fit:

items: Lifecycle fit: do application, retained Activity, ViewModel, Activity and Service owners express the important lifetimes?
Integration gained: how much framework-created Android plumbing would otherwise be repeated?
Existing structure: is there already a substantial, understood custom Dagger hierarchy?
Customization cost: would the convention require many custom components, entry points or adapters?
Migration and team cost: what must be learned, rewritten and maintained?
Platform context: is the graph primarily Android-oriented, where Hilt's conventions carry their intended value?

blocks.text: Hilt provides standard Android component ownership and generated integration. Custom Dagger components provide control over boundaries and lifetimes. Compare their fit with the application's requirements and their total maintenance cost.

**Scenario A: the convention fits.** A new Android reading application needs process-level networking, one session across an Activity's configuration recreation, per-ViewModel parsers, per-Activity UI integrations and a background Service dependency. Android creates the framework owners, and the team would otherwise write the same component creation and retention plumbing around them.

These requirements map to `SingletonComponent`, `ActivityRetainedComponent`, `ViewModelComponent`, `ActivityComponent` and `ServiceComponent`. Hilt can remove repeated integration work while preserving the lifetimes this application needs.

**Scenario B: a custom structure fits.** A mature Android product has a Dagger graph organized around logged-in account sessions, concurrent document workspaces and hardware connections. These owners can outlive an Activity, and several instances can coexist. Their lifetimes do not map cleanly to one retained Activity or process component.

The team understands its factories and component relationships. Migrating would introduce adapters and manual access points without removing much existing integration work.

Custom Dagger components express this application's product owners directly. Hilt can coexist with custom components or be extended, but a migration would need to save enough work to justify the adapters and migration effort. Compare that cost with the ongoing work of maintaining the existing graph.

rows: Do lifetimes fit?
Most map directly to standard Android owners
Core product owners have lifetimes or concurrent instances outside the standard hierarchy
What integration is removed?
Repeated Android component creation and entry plumbing
Little, because mature integration already exists
What structure is surrendered?
The standard hierarchy preserves the boundaries the application needs
Well-understood boundaries that encode product semantics
What is migration buying?
Consistency and lower ongoing integration cost
Savings do not justify adapters, retraining and migration work

blocks.text: Generated integration saves work only if it fits the application's ownership requirements. Custom lifetimes may require extensions rather than rule out Hilt entirely. Describe the required owners, then compare how much ongoing work each arrangement needs.

Official Android guidance recommends Hilt for Android dependency injection. Its standard hierarchy and ecosystem integration address common Android ownership needs. When applying that recommendation, check whether those lifetimes match the project and identify any important requirements that need a different arrangement.

One custom lifetime may be handled by a Hilt extension or entry point without replacing the entire standard hierarchy. Compare the work of that exception with the work of a custom hierarchy. Record the expected owners, integration work saved, manual access or extensions required, and migration cost so the decision can be revisited when those conditions change.

Describe an Android project whose lifetimes fit Hilt's standard hierarchy and a mature graph where product lifetimes or migration cost favor custom Dagger components. Both use Dagger for construction and validation. Explain the choice through the required ownership structure and the integration work each option needs.

units.title: Koin: Containers, Definitions and Scopes
units.summary: Koin uses definitions written in Kotlin to describe how objects are constructed. Modules group those definitions; a running Koin container loads them and resolves requests. On Android, application startup normally configures the application-level graph. `single` and `factory` control instance reuse, while a scope lets an owner share instances for a bounded lifetime. ViewModels are resolved at a boundary where their platform owner is available.

lessons.title: The Koin Container and Its Modules
lessons.summary: On Android, application startup chooses the definitions to load into Koin. The container uses them to construct dependencies and retain instances according to their reuse rules. Modules group definitions, and the classic Kotlin DSL is one of several ways to declare them.

blocks.text: Dependency injection makes construction explicit: requirements become constructor parameters, the constructor calls form a graph, and the composition root is the place near an entry point that knows how to assemble it. Koin does not replace those decisions. It stores **definitions** that describe the construction, then resolves requests by following the same graph.

blocks.code:
dependency requirement
        ↓
construction decision
        ↓
object graph
        ↓
Koin definition

blocks.text: `startKoin { ... }` creates and configures a Koin application, registers its container in the global Koin context, and loads the supplied definitions. The code that chooses and loads those definitions is the composition root. On Android, it normally runs in `Application.onCreate`, before Activities and Services begin resolving dependencies.

A Koin **module** groups definitions. Here, `dataModule` groups repository construction, while `databaseModule` groups the Room database and its DAOs. The container loads their definitions and manages retained instances; declaring a module does not create an independent graph.

A Koin module is distinct from a Gradle module, an architecture layer, and an object's lifetime.

Application startup configures the graph at the composition root. `startKoin` creates the Koin application and container; modules supply grouped definitions. The container retains instances according to their reuse rules.

`androidContext(this@OrdersApp)` makes the application `Context` available to definitions that need it, including the Room database definition in `databaseModule`. Consumers receive the resulting dependencies: a repository declares `OrderDao` in its constructor, and a ViewModel declares the repository.

In this arrangement, consumers do not call `startKoin`, check whether Koin is running, or load modules. Keeping setup at startup gives them one configured graph. If repositories configured containers themselves, construction decisions would be scattered, and consumers could disagree about which definitions were available.

Koin's Android integration also supports AndroidX App Startup through `KoinStartup`. Whichever startup mechanism is used, initialize the graph before features resolve dependencies.

rows: Application startup
Chooses and starts the complete application graph
How every dependency should be designed
Koin application/container
Registers definitions, constructs instances, and retains them according to reuse rules
Product lifetime requirements
Koin module
Groups related definitions
Architecture layer, Gradle module or lifetime
Definition
Describes how one requested key is satisfied
Whether its choice is correct for the product

blocks.text:
Gradle modules and Koin modules organize different things. A Gradle module is a compilation and visibility boundary: `:feature:orders` is built separately and can hide its internals. A Koin module groups construction definitions.

A feature Gradle module often exposes a Koin module, but the relationship need not be one to one. One Gradle module can contribute several Koin modules, and definitions from several Gradle modules can be grouped into one Koin module. The application module assembles the features used by this app, so it can list their application-level definitions at startup.

Group definitions according to how they are owned and changed. A module with one definition can mark a useful ownership boundary; a larger module can group definitions that change together. Koin supports composing modules with `includes()`, and listing them directly at startup, as this example does. Changing the grouping alone does not change how objects are constructed or reused.

The examples use Koin 4.2's **classic Kotlin DSL**, including `module { single { ... }; viewModel { ... } }`. Koin also supports annotations and a Compiler Plugin DSL. Compiler-assisted forms can transform declarations and check configuration during compilation. They require build configuration that these examples do not include.

rows: Classic DSL
Explicit Kotlin lambdas and `get()` calls; the example above uses this
Annotations
A supported declaration form processed by Koin's compiler tooling
Compiler Plugin DSL
Compiler-assisted declarations and configuration verification

blocks.text: A comparison such as 'Dagger is compile-time and Koin is runtime' leaves out Koin's compiler-assisted declarations and verification. These examples use the classic DSL without the Compiler Plugin. When comparing error detection, specify the declaration mechanism and checks enabled in each project.

Koin centralizes assembly, but the application still determines which objects should be shared and for how long. A `single` definition records a reuse decision; module grouping records an organizational decision. Neither a global context nor either declaration makes in-memory state survive process termination.

For this classic-DSL graph, Kotlin compilation checks the lambda code and types. It does not, by itself, prove that the assembled configuration can satisfy every request. A missing definition may be found during resolution or by an explicit verification check.

Koin's Compiler Plugin adds graph and call-site checks during compilation. To explain when a project detects configuration errors, identify which declaration and verification mechanisms it enables.

Explain how the composition root chooses the graph, `startKoin` creates the Koin application and loads definitions, and modules organize those definitions. State which declaration and verification mechanisms are configured before describing when errors are detected.

lessons.title: Definitions and Instance Reuse
lessons.summary: `single` reuses one retained instance, while `factory` runs its construction lambda for each resolution. Choosing an implementation for an interface is a separate decision. In either case, consumers can declare their dependencies as constructor parameters.

blocks.text: Choose the reuse strategy according to whether callers need the same object or a separately constructed result. Koin's classic DSL records that decision in the definition. **One Instance, or a New One Each Time?** examines the shared-identity requirement in more detail.

rows: Every resolution from this container/context must share one retained identity
`single { ... }`
The definition retains and returns one constructed instance
Each resolution should receive a fresh result
`factory { ... }`
The definition runs its construction lambda for each resolution

blocks.text: `ReaderSession` remains an ordinary class. Koin retains and reuses the instance produced by this definition; it does not turn the class into a Kotlin `object`. The `single` rule describes reuse in the configured container; it does not promise one instance shared by independently started Koin applications.

The retained instance is still in memory: `single` does not write it to disk or preserve it across process termination. Nor does the keyword alone request creation before first use. In a globally started application container, retention usually lasts for that container's lifetime, so that lifetime needs to match the sharing requirement.

`factory` runs the construction lambda for each resolution, and Koin does not retain the instances it produces. The example creates a `SessionSummaryBuilder` each time; it does not require a class named `SessionSummaryBuilderFactory`. A dedicated factory class or function may still be useful for runtime inputs that arrive later, but that is a separate design choice.

Use `single` when callers need a shared instance and `factory` when each resolution should construct a separate result. These definitions control reuse; they do not provide persistence, turn classes into Kotlin `object`s, or require dedicated factory classes.
A data module often places a concrete definition beside an interface binding:

A request for `OrderImporter` uses the first definition. A request for the consumer-owned `OrderRepository` interface uses the second, which constructs a `LocalOrderRepository`.

The requested type identifies the binding; `single` controls reuse of the result. Choosing an implementation and choosing whether to share it are separate decisions.

`LocalOrderRepository` declares `OrderDatabase` as a constructor parameter and has no dependency on Koin. The module supplies that parameter with `get()` when it constructs the repository. Resolution stays in the assembly code, and the repository's requirement remains visible to callers.

Here, `LocalOrderRepository` fetches its own `OrderDatabase` from the global container. Its constructor no longer tells callers that it needs a database. The repository is using Koin as a service locator.

The distinction depends on where resolution happens: the module assembles an object with visible constructor parameters, while this repository hides a dependency inside its implementation. **Asking For It, or Being Given It** discusses the wider trade-off.

A `ThemeController` needs shared identity when it applies the theme above navigation and must outlive the settings screen that changes it. A `SyncStatusHolder` needs shared identity when several screens must display the same sync progress. These behaviors can justify `single`; being a state holder alone does not determine the reuse strategy.

Choose reuse for each definition rather than copying the strategy used by other repositories, services or state holders. Identify the behavior that needs a shared instance and the owner that bounds its lifetime.

Consider where a container lookup occurs. In a module, `get()` supplies constructor parameters while assembling the graph. A host can also resolve a data initializer immediately after startup: that integration code depends on Koin, while the initializer can still declare its collaborators explicitly.

If a domain class performs a lookup internally, its callers cannot see that dependency in the constructor. A missing definition is then discovered when the lookup executes rather than when the caller supplies the collaborator.

For a stateless object that is cheap to construct, either reuse strategy may be reasonable. Retaining one instance can simplify configuration or avoid repeated construction without affecting behavior. Shared identity, shared state, synchronization and construction cost provide stronger reasons to choose reuse. When none applies, explain the practical trade-off rather than treating `single` as a default requirement.

Explain how a definition associates a requested type with construction and how its reuse strategy controls instances. Compare a module supplying constructor parameters with a business class fetching a hidden dependency from the global container.

lessons.title: Koin Scopes and Their Owners
lessons.summary: A Koin scope lets several consumers share an instance for a bounded period, such as one interview flow. The owner creates the scope when that period begins and closes it when it ends.

blocks.text: Suppose an interview flow needs one mutable `InterviewSession` shared by its question, notes and result screens. Each new flow needs a fresh session, and completing or abandoning the flow should end that session's retention. The three screens need to share an instance within the flow, without sharing it across separate interviews.

rows: `single`
One retained identity in the application container
Too wide: a later interview can inherit the previous session
`factory`
A fresh identity on each resolution
Too narrow: the three screens do not share one session
bounded Koin scope + `scoped`
One identity reused inside one explicitly owned scope
Fits if the flow owner opens and closes the scope at the correct events

blocks.text: A Koin scope is a resolution context with its own identity. A `scoped` definition reuses one instance within that scope. For the interview flow, the owner creates a scope when the flow starts and closes it when the flow ends. The declaration supplies the reuse rule; the owner connects it to the required lifetime. **A Scope Is a Rule; an Owner Is a Lifetime** explains this distinction more generally.
This declaration tells Koin to reuse an `InterviewSession` within each scope instance. The integration code that knows when the flow starts and ends must create and close the scope at those events.
A Koin scope is a bounded resolution context. `scoped` means one reused instance within that context. The owner that creates and closes the scope supplies the actual lifetime.

Before declaring the scope, identify its owner, the event that starts it, the consumers that resolve through it, and the event that ends it. The owner must also ensure that `close()` runs on every exit path. These decisions connect `scoped` to the interview flow's actual lifetime.

blocks.code:
flow entered
    ↓ owner creates interview scope
question / notes / result resolve the same InterviewSession
    ↓ complete or cancel
owner closes interview scope
    ↓ scoped instances released; scope unusable

blocks.text: Closing a Koin scope releases the instances it retains, runs registered close callbacks, and prevents further resolution through that scope. A later lookup fails. Closing it while the flow is still active can therefore break consumers that need another resolution or depend on resources released by a callback. Leaving it open retains session state beyond the intended flow and can carry stale state into later work.

Platform helpers can associate Koin scopes with Activity, navigation, Compose or other lifecycle owners. They automate parts of scope ownership, but the selected owner's start and end events still need to match the lifetime the application requires.
A scope declaration alone does not determine when the flow ends. Identify the owner that creates the scope and ensures it is closed at the required end event.

A custom scope can fit a bounded sharing requirement that existing lifecycle owners do not match. It adds coordination work: consumers need access to the correct scope, concurrent flows need distinct scope identities, and every normal or exceptional exit must close the scope for that flow.

For the interview flow, explain why `single` shares the session too widely and `factory` creates separate sessions for its screens. Show how `scoped` allows sharing within one flow, and name the owner that creates and closes its scope. Explain what closing releases and why later lookups fail.

lessons.title: Resolving a ViewModel at the Boundary
lessons.summary: A Koin ViewModel definition is a construction recipe; the `ViewModelStoreOwner` decides which instance is retained and when it is cleared. Route values enter as runtime parameters, and whether a container lookup is service location depends on where it happens.

blocks.text: At a screen boundary, a Koin `viewModel { ... }` definition describes how to construct the ViewModel. `koinViewModel()` connects that definition to Compose's ViewModel support. The host-supplied `ViewModelStoreOwner` and its store determine which instance is retained and when it is cleared.

blocks.code:
Koin ViewModel definition
        ↓ construction recipe

koinViewModel(...) at destination
        ↓ integrated resolution

ViewModelStoreOwner / store
        ↓ retained identity and clearing

blocks.text: Koin constructs the ViewModel with dependencies from the graph. The platform owner provides the store that retains it and bounds its lifetime. **The ViewModel Owner: Lifetime Is Not Persistence** explains that ownership contract in more detail.
`OrderListViewModel` declares its collaborators as constructor parameters and does not access Koin. The screen resolves the completed ViewModel where a `ViewModelStoreOwner` is available.
Koin supplies ViewModel construction. The selected `ViewModelStoreOwner` retains the instance and determines when it is cleared.

An `orderId`, `customerId` or `itemId` identifies the destination being opened. These values arrive with the route, while repositories and services are resolved from definitions in the graph. Koin's runtime parameters pass the route values to the ViewModel's construction definition.

When this definition constructs `OrderDetailViewModel`, `orderId` comes from the route through `parameters`. The repositories and state holder come from the graph through `get()`. Using a container-wide binding for the current route ID would make destination-specific input shared configuration, which could be replaced by another destination.

Runtime parameters are used when the ViewModel is created. If the same store already holds an instance under the same key, `koinViewModel()` returns it; passing a different `orderId` does not update that instance.

Both identifiers are `String`, so type alone cannot distinguish them. The definition reads them by position: the destination must supply the order ID first and the item ID second. Swapping them still compiles, making their order part of this resolution contract.

**Two Dependencies of the Same Type** discusses this kind of ambiguity. Positional values are one way to handle this example, rather than a requirement for every pair of identifiers.

A destination composable can resolve the completed ViewModel using the lifecycle owner supplied by its host. The ViewModel itself continues to receive collaborators through its constructor.

A settings screen can use `koinInject()` as a default parameter for an application-scoped settings holder, while allowing callers to supply the holder explicitly. A theme wrapper can also treat a dependency as optional so that previews render without a started graph. These are integration choices at the UI or infrastructure boundary; they do not justify hiding dependency lookups inside repositories or use cases.

Evaluate a lookup by the caller's responsibility. A host, UI or infrastructure boundary can deliberately resolve a completed object. A business object that fetches its own dependency internally hides a requirement that could have been visible in its constructor.

In Koin 4.2, `koinViewModel()` accepts a `ViewModelStoreOwner`, defaulting to `LocalViewModelStoreOwner.current`. The surrounding host or navigation integration supplies that local owner, such as an Activity, Fragment or navigation back-stack entry.

Moving the call under another owner changes the store used to retain the ViewModel. Its lifetime then follows that owner; Koin still supplies construction and runtime parameters.

Requests for the same ViewModel type reuse an instance when they use the same store and key. A navigation destination's owner clears its ViewModel when that destination is removed from the back stack. An Activity owner retains its ViewModel across configuration changes and clears it when the Activity finishes.

To determine how long the ViewModel lives, inspect the selected owner and store, alongside the Koin definition that describes construction.

Trace a screen from route input to retained ViewModel: `parametersOf` supplies construction input, the definition combines it with graph dependencies, and `koinViewModel()` resolves through the current `ViewModelStoreOwner`. Explain how the owner retains and clears the instance, while the ViewModel's constructor keeps its collaborators visible.

units.title: Choosing a Dependency Injection Strategy
units.summary: Choose a dependency-construction strategy by comparing the work the project needs with the costs each strategy introduces. State why the choice fits today and what observable change would justify reconsidering it.

lessons.title: What a DI Framework Provides
lessons.summary: Manual DI, Dagger, Hilt and Koin can construct the same kinds of object graphs. They differ in the construction, ownership and checking work they automate, and in the configuration, tooling and maintenance they require.

blocks.text: Manual DI, Dagger, Hilt and Koin can all supply constructor dependencies, bind abstractions, reuse instances, create fresh instances and assemble graphs with defined boundaries. A framework is useful when automating or standardizing that work addresses a project requirement. Choosing one means comparing the work it removes with the configuration, conventions and tooling it introduces.

blocks.code:
project requirements
        |
        v
properties that matter
        |
        v
strategies that provide them
        |
        v
cost of each strategy
        |
        v
smallest sufficient choice
        |
        v
observable condition that would change the choice

blocks.text:
Manual DI uses ordinary construction code, with little setup and no container abstraction. Dagger generates construction code from bindings and components, manages scoped reuse, and validates component graphs. Hilt uses Dagger's model and adds a predefined Android component hierarchy and generated integration for Android objects created by the framework.

Koin's classic DSL uses Kotlin definitions and container-managed reuse without requiring code generation. Its Compiler Plugin can also generate constructor wiring and check supported graph properties during compilation. These strategies automate different parts of the work; the team still maintains the declarations, ownership rules and tooling it uses.

Graph size is only one input. A stable graph of eighty objects assembled through two entry points may change monthly, while a smaller graph may change daily across several features. A constructor change can require edits along multiple construction paths, depending on how those paths are organized.

Consider how often wiring changes, how many entry points assemble overlapping subgraphs, how far constructor changes propagate, and how much assembly the team maintains by hand. There is no dependency-count threshold at which manual DI stops being appropriate.
A DI framework automates or standardizes construction and graph management. Choose one when the work it removes is worth its configuration, conventions, tooling and migration cost.
The first comparison covers the assembly and ownership work each strategy leaves to the team:

rows: Assembly code the team writes
Every constructor call, owner and reuse rule
Bindings and components; generated code does the construction
Bindings; generated code constructs and integrates standard Android entry points
Kotlin definitions; the container constructs on request
A deep constructor change
May require edits to several explicit construction paths
Generated assembly absorbs most of the propagation
Same as Dagger
With hand-written DSL wiring, edit that class's definition; callers that resolve it by the same key can remain unchanged
Lifetimes and graph boundaries
Application code creates, retains and clears every owner; every boundary is visible code
Custom components and subcomponents encode owners and scopes, and the team designs them
Predefined Android components fit common lifetimes; other lifetimes may need custom components or explicit integration
Container and scopes retain instances; application code manages custom scope lifetimes, while supported Android integrations can manage lifecycle-bound scopes
Platform and lifecycle integration
The application wires its framework-created owners by hand
The application maintains its integration with framework-created objects
Generated integration for supported Android owners
Android, Compose and ViewModel integration libraries
Where it can be used
Any Kotlin or Java code; no framework is involved
Plain JVM and Android modules
An Android application whose `Application` class is annotated `@HiltAndroidApp`
Plain JVM and Android modules

blocks.text: The next comparison covers checking, tooling and maintenance costs:

rows: Graph-error detection
Kotlin compiler at each call site; type-correct miswiring needs review
The build validates reachable bindings before execution
Inherits Dagger's check; no second validation model
Classic DSL: verification or resolution. 4.2 Compiler Plugin: documented graph and call-site checks at compile time
Runtime composition flexibility
Ordinary control flow; every branch maintained by hand
Declared graph; variation through runtime inputs and component instances
Standard Android hierarchy, with extension or integration work for other owners
Definitions selectable at runtime; each selectable configuration must be exercised or compiler-checked
Build and generated work
Ordinary compilation only
Code generation and graph analysis in the build
Dagger generation plus generated Android integration
No generation required for the classic DSL; the Compiler Plugin adds analysis and can generate constructor wiring
Convention imposed
Naming, owner structure and entry-point design are project decisions
Explicit components and bindings; graph structure chosen by the project
Standard Android component ownership and entry paths
Standard container and definition vocabulary; module and scope organization chosen by the project
Observability and debugging
Direct source; ordinary stack traces
Inspectable generated factories and component code appear in traces
Generated Dagger code plus Hilt's component ownership in the trace
Definitions and resolution form the trace; compiler diagnostics if the plugin is enabled
Team familiarity
Little framework-specific knowledge needed
Existing skill lowers declaration and diagnosis cost
Existing experience reduces the work of adopting Android integration and the component hierarchy
Existing skill lowers definition, scope and resolution-diagnosis cost
Migration and reversibility
Adopting a framework changes roots and integration; constructor-injected consumers can often remain unchanged
Primarily bindings, components and build tooling; ordinary constructor-injected classes can often remain unchanged
Dagger bindings and components, plus Android entry integration and predefined component ownership
Definitions, startup and resolution boundaries; much wider if consumers call the container

blocks.text: Labels such as ‘scales better’, ‘easier’ or ‘lightweight’ need a concrete consequence to support them. Identify which edits disappear, which owners are predefined, where errors appear, which modules can use the strategy, and what build or migration work it adds.

The strategies incur costs at different stages. With manual assembly, the team writes and reviews composition roots. With generated validation, it maintains build tooling and waits for graph analysis. With runtime-configurable composition, it verifies, exercises and diagnoses the allowed configurations.

A predefined component structure reduces design work but constrains how owners fit into the graph. A custom structure gives the team more control and more maintenance responsibility. Migration work grows when framework APIs are used throughout consumers rather than kept near construction boundaries.

Android's guidance recommends Hilt for Android dependency injection and advises preferring it over manual DI when possible. Its manual-DI guidance also explains the boilerplate and owner-management costs that can grow with a graph.

Apply that advice by checking which needs the project shares: Android targets, framework-created objects, lifecycle-aligned components, frequent wiring changes, and a component convention the team can adopt. The recommendation is useful evidence for the decision; the project's requirements still determine how well it fits.

Framework documentation can establish construction mechanisms, component hierarchies, platform support and compiler checks. Whether a tool is easy to use or performs well in a project depends on the team's experience and the actual configuration. Claims about startup time, binary size or memory use need measurements against specific versions and configurations before they can support this decision.

The construction strategy is easier to change when consumers declare their dependencies. A class with `LibraryRepository` in its constructor can be constructed by hand, by Dagger or Hilt, or by a Koin definition without changing its business behaviour. A class that calls the container to obtain the repository also depends on that container API, so migration must change the consumer as well. Constructor injection keeps more of that work at the construction boundary.

To compare DI strategies, first establish the project's targets, graph change rate, entry points, lifetime boundaries, framework-created objects, checking requirements and runtime variation. Include build constraints, the current strategy, team experience and migration cost. Then explain which relevant properties each candidate provides and what work they remove or add.

lessons.title: When Should a Graph Error Surface?
lessons.summary: When a missing dependency surfaces depends on how the graph is represented and checked: explicit construction, a generated Dagger or Hilt component, Koin's classic DSL, or Koin's Compiler Plugin. A graph that passes every check can still encode the wrong ownership.

blocks.text: A missing dependency is detected by the checking mechanism a project uses: explicit constructor calls, a generated component, Koin configuration verification or the Koin Compiler Plugin. To compare detection timing, identify how the graph is represented, what checks it, and which configurations the check can see.

blocks.code:
ReaderViewModel
    |
    v
LibraryRepository
    |
    v
CredentialsProvider   MISSING

blocks.text: In this graph, `ReaderViewModel` needs `LibraryRepository`, and the repository requires a `CredentialsProvider` that has not been supplied. Keep that missing dependency the same while comparing the strategies. The difference is which mechanism checks the path and when it reports the failure.

In manual DI, this Kotlin call does not compile because a required constructor argument is absent. Passing the wrong type also fails at the call site. Other mistakes can still pass type checking: two `CredentialsProvider` values of the same type might be swapped, and separate construction paths are checked at their individual calls rather than as one declared component graph.

Detection timing depends on the representation and checking mechanism. Manual constructor calls, generated Dagger or Hilt components, Koin DSL verification and the Koin Compiler Plugin can check different properties of the same conceptual graph.

rows: Manual constructor wiring
The Kotlin compiler checks the explicit `LibraryRepository(...)` call
Compilation of each construction path fails when the required argument is absent or mistyped
The team maintains every call path, and type-correct semantic wiring still needs review
Dagger component
Dagger analyzes the reachable component binding graph and generates construction
A missing reachable binding prevents the component from compiling
Graph analysis and generated machinery are part of the build; the guarantee is bounded to Dagger's structural rules
Hilt generated component
Dagger checks the generated Hilt component graph
A missing reachable binding prevents compilation
Dagger's build-time graph analysis, plus Hilt's Android conventions and generated integration
Koin 4.2 classic DSL without Compiler Plugin
Kotlin checks the definition lambdas; Koin verification or resolution checks the configured dependency path
The problem can be found by pre-shipping verification/tests or when the unresolved path is requested
Runtime-selectable definitions remain possible, and the project must exercise the configurations it can choose
Koin 4.2 with Compiler Plugin
The plugin validates documented dependency-graph and injection call-site properties
Missing dependencies, qualifier mismatches and broken call sites can fail compilation
Compiler/plugin integration and build-time analysis are added; only the properties checked are guaranteed

blocks.text: Dagger rejects a missing reachable binding before execution by validating the component's binding graph. Hilt uses that checking mechanism because its generated hierarchy consists of Dagger components. Hilt adds Android component ownership and integration; it does not add an independent graph validator.

A classic Koin DSL graph can be checked during development through configuration verification and tests that resolve its dependencies. Compiling its definition lambdas alone does not check that every requested dependency exists in the configured container.

With the Compiler Plugin enabled, Koin 4.2 can check missing dependencies, qualifier mismatches and injection call sites during compilation, including supported classic DSL declarations. Those checks apply to the graph the plugin can assemble; definitions loaded later with `loadKoinModules` are outside that assembled graph.

A successful compiler check establishes that the graph properties covered by that check passed. It does not establish correct ownership, useful boundaries, business behaviour or appropriate platform lifetimes. Those require separate review or testing.

Earlier detection requires build-time work such as compiler integration, graph analysis or code generation. Runtime-selectable definitions allow the graph to vary with the environment or a later choice, but the project must verify or resolve the configurations it may select. Compare that work with when the project needs errors to be found.

When discussing Koin, state the version and declaration style, whether the Compiler Plugin is enabled, and whether classic configuration verification is part of delivery. These details determine which checks occur during compilation and which depend on verification or resolution. They are needed to make a useful comparison with other strategies.

A graph can pass structural checks and still retain an object for the wrong lifetime. Suppose `ReaderSession` should end with a reading session but is bound in an application-wide owner. Its dependencies are available and its keys are unambiguous, so graph verification can pass while the application keeps the session alive too long.

**What the Dagger Compiler Checks** explains the limits of structural validation. **A Scope Is a Rule; an Owner Is a Lifetime** explains how the owner determines the lifetime of retained instances.

Compile-time versus runtime checking remains a useful distinction, provided it refers to the mechanism rather than the framework name. Dagger performs build-time graph analysis, the Koin Compiler Plugin can also check graphs during compilation, and manual constructor calls fail compilation when required arguments are missing. Each check has its own coverage and tooling cost.

Earlier checking is valuable when incomplete configurations must be rejected before execution. Runtime composition is valuable when the environment or a later choice changes which definitions the application uses. A project can need both: selectable configurations checked as early and as completely as the chosen mechanism allows.

Given a graph error, ask four things: how the graph is represented, what mechanism checks it, which configurations that mechanism can see, and what the successful check actually proves. Then name the cost of moving that check earlier and the architectural properties it still cannot validate.

lessons.title: Three Projects, Three Answers
lessons.summary: The same decision process leads to different choices for a small stable graph, a growing Android graph with several lifetimes, and an Android application already using Koin. Each comparison connects requirements to costs and a concrete reason to reconsider the choice.

blocks.text: Begin with the requirements and identify which properties would help meet them. Compare the viable strategies, excluding those with incompatible capabilities or costs the project cannot justify. Choose a strategy, state the cost the team accepts, and name a changed requirement that would justify reconsidering it. The three projects below use this same process.

blocks.code:
requirements
  -> valuable properties
  -> viable strategies
  -> concrete mismatches and costs
  -> plausible choice
  -> cost accepted
  -> revisit trigger

blocks.text: A strategy may be capable of constructing the graph yet add configuration or tooling the project does not need. A framework may also require less work overall when it supplies ownership rules, checking or platform integration that would otherwise need to be maintained by hand. Compare the work needed to meet the requirements, rather than counting framework features.

Connect the choice to the project's requirements, explain the cost the team accepts, and state when to reconsider it. A change in requirements can justify a different strategy even when the earlier choice was appropriate.

**Project A: a small stable application.** It targets one desktop platform, has twelve straightforward objects, two entry points, one application-owned shared catalogue, fresh per-use report builders, no framework-created lifecycle owner, and a three-person team. The graph changes a few times per quarter. Constructor injection and one composition root already make requirements, sharing and fresh construction visible.

rows: Requirements
One platform; stable graph; two visible entry paths; application and per-use lifetimes; small team
Valuable properties
Direct visibility, low setup, ordinary compiler checking, explicit reuse
Viable strategies
Manual DI, Dagger and Koin can construct the desktop graph; Hilt's generated integration is Android-specific and cannot serve this target
Concrete eliminations
Hilt is excluded by target compatibility; Dagger generation and Koin container configuration add machinery for no stated requirement
Plausible choice
Manual constructor wiring in the composition root
Cost accepted
The team edits the two explicit construction paths when a deep dependency changes
Revisit trigger
Deep changes repeatedly touch many paths, lifecycle-specific owners are duplicated, independent features must contribute bindings, or whole-graph automated checking gains measurable review value

blocks.text: The composition root creates one catalogue and shares it between both consumers. It creates a fresh report builder for each request and keeps platform-specific construction in one place. Consumers receive their dependencies rather than looking them up in a global registry. These explicit rules meet the project's requirements without adding container configuration or tooling.

**Project B: a growing Android-only application.** Android creates Activities and Services, while the ViewModel machinery creates and retains ViewModels. The application needs dependencies with several lifecycle boundaries, and graph changes arrive weekly from several feature teams. The team wants consistent Android entry integration, Activity-retained and ViewModel ownership, and generated checks before execution. These requirements make Hilt's predefined hierarchy and generated integration useful.

rows: Requirements
Android only; framework-created owners; several matching Android lifetimes; ViewModels; frequent graph changes; multiple contributors
Valuable properties
Lifecycle-aligned conventions, generated owner integration, shared component structure and build-time graph checking
Viable strategies
Manual DI, raw Dagger, Hilt and Koin can all construct the graph; each leaves different integration work to the team
Concrete eliminations
Manual wiring leaves repeated owner integration to the team; raw Dagger requires a custom component structure; Koin offers Android integration but not Hilt's generated component convention
Plausible choice
Hilt, because the predefined Android ownership model matches the required lifetimes
Cost accepted
The team adopts Hilt's component hierarchy and generated integration; other owners require supported extensions or explicit integration
Revisit trigger
Custom non-Hilt lifetime boundaries become central, or the target/platform requirement changes

blocks.text: Raw Dagger can remain appropriate when mature account, workspace or device-session components already match the application's central owners, and migration would add adapters without removing comparable work. Koin can also fit an Android application whose requirements match its definitions and integration model. Project B favours Hilt because its required lifetimes match Hilt's hierarchy and the team wants generated Android integration.

**Project C: an Android application already running Koin.** Its working graph spans feature modules, each contributing a Koin module. Two optional features load definitions with `loadKoinModules` when enabled and unload them when disabled. The team has maintained this graph for years, and its existing scopes fit the required lifetimes. It estimates a framework migration at several months.

A recent release omitted a definition needed by an optional feature. The failure appeared only when a user enabled that feature. The team now needs checks that catch missing definitions before release, including configurations formed when optional modules are loaded.

rows: Requirements

Android only; a working Koin graph across feature modules; definitions loaded at runtime for optional features; strong team familiarity; high migration cost; a new requirement for earlier detection of missing definitions
Valuable properties
Keeping the working graph and its runtime-loaded features, plus configuration checks that run before release
Viable strategies
Keep Koin and add verification; migrate to Hilt or raw Dagger for build-time graph validation; migrate to manual DI
Concrete eliminations

Hilt or Dagger would require rewriting bindings and replacing runtime-loaded modules with another variation mechanism. Manual DI would restore hand assembly across the features. The new checking requirement does not yet justify these migrations.
Plausible choice

Keep Koin; use checks supported by the project's version and verify or resolve each optional-feature configuration. With Koin 4.2's Compiler Plugin, also check the startup graph visible to the plugin.
Cost accepted

Maintain verification and resolution tests for optional-feature configurations; if the Compiler Plugin is adopted, also maintain its build integration. A successful check covers only the graph and properties it can inspect.
Revisit trigger
Incidents keep escaping the adopted checks, the lifetime model converges on Hilt's predefined Android hierarchy, or migration cost falls far enough for Hilt's generated integration to repay it

blocks.text: For Project C, the new need is earlier detection of missing definitions. Verification or resolution tests can cover the optional-feature configurations while the team retains its working graph. The Compiler Plugin can add checks for the graph it sees at compilation, but it cannot establish that later module-loading sequences are correct. Given the estimated transition cost, improving these checks is a plausible first choice before migrating to another framework.

Projects B and C both target Android, but their integration needs, lifetime models and existing investment differ. The platform helps determine which strategies can be used and which integration work is needed. Include graph change rate, team experience, build constraints and migration cost before choosing among them.

Consider a mature Android application with hundreds of working raw-Dagger bindings, custom account and hardware-session component owners, and engineers familiar with the generated graph. Hilt's Android integration is available, but its predefined hierarchy would remove little of the work this application currently maintains. Migration would also touch critical integration boundaries.

Keeping raw Dagger is a plausible choice, with the cost of continuing to maintain custom Android integration. Reconsider it if the lifetime model comes to fit Hilt's hierarchy or if repeated integration work makes migration worthwhile.

Now consider an Android application with six stable objects, one construction entry point and infrequent graph changes. The team already uses Koin, but manual construction might require little work. Compare the ongoing container configuration, startup and diagnostic work with the cost of replacing those definitions with explicit construction. Existing familiarity matters, and so does whether the current mechanism still removes enough work to justify maintaining it.

Project C's migration estimate represents current risk and opportunity cost: rebuilding the graph would take months while the existing construction strategy meets most requirements. The balance could change if its hand-managed scopes became a recurring source of lifetime bugs and those owners matched Hilt's component hierarchy. The framework capabilities could remain the same while the project's needs changed.

In an interview, ask about targets, the existing graph, ownership boundaries, framework-created objects, change rate, checking needs, runtime variation, tooling limits and team experience. Use those answers to explain the choice and its migration cost. This gives the interviewer a decision they can assess against the stated requirements.

For each candidate, explain which stated requirement it meets, what construction or integration work it removes, what cost the team accepts, and what future change would justify reconsidering it. Ask for more project information when one of those connections is unclear.

lessons.title: The Smallest Sufficient Strategy
lessons.summary: Choose enough construction, checking and ownership support to meet the requirements at acceptable cost. Manual DI can be a complete solution, and explicit constructor dependencies make it easier to change the construction strategy later.

blocks.text: Each part of an architecture should address a requirement that justifies its cost (see **How Much Architecture Does This Feature Need?**). Dependency construction follows the same rule. The **smallest sufficient strategy** supplies the construction, ownership and checking support the project needs, with acceptable setup and maintenance costs. That comparison includes more than line count, library count or build time.

A framework can require less work overall. For an Android application with many framework-created objects, lifecycle-aligned graphs and component-level checking requirements, maintaining the equivalent integration by hand may cost more than adopting the framework. Manual DI can remain the long-term choice when explicit assembly costs less to maintain than container configuration, tooling and team adoption. Both can be complete solutions for the requirements they serve.

blocks.code:
requirements satisfied?
    no  -> strategy is insufficient
    yes -> compare accepted operating cost
             |
             v
        choose least mechanism
             |
             v
        record a revisit trigger

blocks.text:
Team familiarity affects how quickly engineers can review configuration, diagnose failures and maintain the build. It also needs to be considered alongside capability: knowing Hilt well does not make a custom session owner fit its predefined hierarchy. Supporting that owner may still require custom components or explicit integration.

Migration creates its own current costs. Changing hundreds of bindings and integration boundaries takes engineering time, introduces risk and displaces other work. Include those costs when comparing a working solution with an alternative.

Choose the strategy that meets the requirements with acceptable construction and maintenance work. Record a concrete change that would justify reconsidering it, such as repeated wiring changes across several paths or recurring ownership errors.

A desktop inventory utility imports a supplier catalogue, displays searchable items and exports a stock report. It targets one platform, has one application entry point, is maintained by four people and releases monthly. Its graph changes a few times per year.

Catalogue and cache objects live with the application; each export creates a fresh `ExportSession`. No platform framework constructs the feature owners, so the application can assemble both lifetimes directly.

blocks.code:
main
 |- InventoryController
 |   |- CatalogueRepository
 |   |   |- CatalogueFileStore
 |   |   `- SystemClock
 |   `- StockSearch
 |       `- CatalogueRepository  (same instance)
 `- exportSessionFactory
     `- ExportSession            (fresh per export)
         |- CatalogueRepository  (same application instance)
         `- CsvReportWriter

blocks.text:
The root passes the same repository to the controller, search and each export. Each call to `newExportSession` constructs a new session and writer, while reusing that repository. Required dependencies are supplied through constructors, and platform file access stays in the root and store implementation.

Kotlin checks the constructor calls. The creation and sharing rules are visible in this one place, without a global registry or consumers resolving their own collaborators.

Manual DI is sufficient here because the graph is stable, has one root and follows two simple ownership rules with little repeated assembly work. The team accepts maintaining the explicit constructor calls and reviewing which instances are shared or created afresh. If a dependency under the repository changes, the affected construction code in this root needs updating. That work currently costs less than adopting and maintaining a container and its tooling.

rows: Adding one deep dependency routinely changes five independent construction paths
Generated or container-managed assembly may remove repeated updates to construction paths
Several flows duplicate creation and cleanup of the same lifecycle-specific owner
A component or scope convention may reduce repeated owner integration
Independent features repeatedly edit one composition root to contribute implementations
Graph contribution mechanisms may reduce coordination at the shared file
Configuration mistakes escape review often enough to cause incidents
Earlier automated graph verification may earn its build/tooling cost
Composition-root maintenance becomes a recurring review and change burden
Recurring maintenance work provides a concrete reason to consider automation

blocks.text: These changes reopen the comparison; they do not determine the replacement on their own. Reassess requirements, available strategies and costs. Increasing object count matters when it increases maintenance, checking or ownership work, so describe that consequence before deciding to change strategies.

A manual-DI design can remain the chosen solution while it meets the requirements at acceptable cost. State its maintenance responsibilities and the changes that would justify another comparison, rather than assuming a framework will become necessary later.

Moving from manual DI to a framework may require changes to composition roots, build or container configuration, and Android or host integration. The team also adopts the framework's declarations and diagnostics.

Moving between frameworks, or back to manual construction, depends on where their APIs are used. Business classes with explicit constructor dependencies often need little change. Container lookups, framework base types and integration annotations in consumers increase the code that migration must touch.

Explicit constructor dependencies make the construction strategy easier to replace. An ordinary application class can receive the same dependencies through a Dagger `@Inject` constructor, Hilt's Dagger graph, a Koin definition or a manual root. Keep container resolution and integration for framework-created objects near composition boundaries so that migration mainly changes construction code rather than business behaviour.

Consider a mature Android application with a reliable custom Dagger graph. Hilt might remove future Android integration work, but migrating hundreds of bindings and custom components may cost more and introduce more risk than those savings justify. Compare that transition cost with the work of maintaining the existing graph. Repeated integration work or a changed lifetime model could later make the migration worthwhile.

Between compatible strategies, years of Dagger experience can reduce delivery and diagnosis costs compared with adopting Koin for the first time. A team already maintaining a working Koin graph has a similar advantage over migration. Familiarity can change the cost comparison, but the chosen strategy must still support the required owners and lifetimes.
Use this worksheet before naming a strategy:
