units.title: Shared ViewModels and Host Lifecycles
units.summary: Compose Multiplatform lets you write ViewModels, viewModelScope and lifecycle-aware collection in common code. Their behaviour still depends on the host: which owner stores and clears each ViewModel, what saved state can restore, which Main dispatcher is available, and how window, scene or page activity maps to lifecycle states.

lessons.title: Shared ViewModels, Host-Owned Lifetimes
lessons.summary: A shared ViewModel still needs an owner that stores it and decides when to clear it. Its saved-state behaviour and default viewModelScope dispatcher also depend on the host. When Main is unavailable, the default scope has no dispatcher; launch uses Dispatchers.Default unless a dispatcher is supplied.

blocks.text: A Kotlin Multiplatform project can put its ViewModels in shared code. The `androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-viewmodel` sources behind the `org.jetbrains.androidx.lifecycle` artifacts put `ViewModel`, `ViewModelStore`, `ViewModelStoreOwner` and `viewModelScope` in `commonMain` at **2.11.0-beta01**, so one `LoansViewModel` class can serve Android, desktop and iOS. Each instance still needs an owner that determines its lifetime.

A ViewModel is stored in a `ViewModelStore`, which belongs to a `ViewModelStoreOwner`. When that owner clears the store, the ViewModel is cleared too. Sharing `LoansViewModel` lets each host use the same class; it does not determine which owner stores an instance or when that owner clears it.

blocks.code:
commonMain   LoansViewModel, ViewModelStore, ViewModelStoreOwner, viewModelScope
                 (shared: the class and the clearing hook)
                        |
each host    which owner stores the ViewModel, and when that owner is cleared
                 (not shared: the lifetime)

rows: Android
The `Activity`, a `Fragment` or a navigation entry, exactly as in an Android-only app
The Android owner retains its store through configuration recreation; this is why its ViewModels can survive rotation.
Desktop
No Activity or Fragment exists; the owner is whatever the desktop host provides, or one the application or a navigation library installs
The owner determines when the store is cleared; Android’s configuration-recreation guarantees do not apply.
iOS
Shared Compose UI can use Compose Multiplatform’s common owner. Native SwiftUI integration needs an owner wired to the SwiftUI lifetime.
The Compose host or native UI integration determines when the store is cleared.

blocks.text: Sharing a ViewModel class shares its implementation. To work out how long an instance survives, identify the owner that stores it and the event that clears its store.

With Navigation 3 in common code, ViewModels are not automatically scoped to navigation entries. On Android, a ViewModel retrieved without entry scoping can remain tied to the `Activity` after the user navigates away. To give each entry its own owner, pass the saveable-state decorator followed by the ViewModel store decorator to the shared `NavDisplay`:

These decorators give each back-stack entry its own store on the hosts that run the shared `NavDisplay`. The host still determines what those stores survive beyond navigation. On Android, the entry stores are retained across configuration recreation along with the Activity’s store.

`rememberSaveable` is available in common code, but restoration depends on the host’s saved-state mechanism. On Android, saveable values are stored in a `Bundle` that can be restored after configuration or system-initiated process recreation.

The Compose Multiplatform lifecycle documentation describes states and events for desktop, iOS and web; those mappings alone do not specify equivalent restoration guarantees. Before relying on saved state after an event on another host, check what its saved-state integration supports.

The default `viewModelScope` in the same 2.11.0-beta01 sources combines a `SupervisorJob` with `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`. If Main is unavailable, scope construction uses `EmptyCoroutineContext` in its place. This leaves the scope without a dispatcher; `launch` then uses `Dispatchers.Default` unless you supply one. It does not inherit the context of the coroutine that calls it.

On desktop, `Dispatchers.Main.immediate` may be unavailable by default. Adding `kotlinx-coroutines-swing` supplies a Main dispatcher for the Swing event dispatch thread, allowing the default `viewModelScope` to run UI work there.

A ViewModel owned by an Android Activity can survive configuration recreation because that owner retains its store. For a shared ViewModel on desktop or iOS, check the owner supplied by the Compose host or native UI integration and when it clears the store.

`CoroutineDispatcher` is a common abstraction, but each target supplies its implementation. Declaring `Dispatchers.Main` in common code does not guarantee that a usable Main dispatcher is installed at runtime. Android, Desktop/JVM, iOS, JS and Wasm/JS can therefore use the same dispatcher names with different execution behaviour:

rows: Android
Main uses the Android main-thread dispatcher supplied by kotlinx-coroutines-android. Default and IO use the JVM coroutine dispatchers.
Desktop/JVM
Main needs a UI integration at runtime, such as kotlinx-coroutines-swing for the Swing event dispatch thread.
iOS / Darwin Native
Main uses Darwin's main queue. Default and IO exist, but Native IO has a different implementation; JVM thread-sharing and system-property claims are not Native guarantees.
JS and Wasm/JS browser

In kotlinx-coroutines 1.11.0 the shared implementation delegates Main to Default, with immediate support. These dispatchers schedule through the browser execution environment; choosing Default does not create parallel CPU workers. IO is not an API available across these targets.

blocks.text:
A shared function can accept a dispatcher, leaving platform assembly code to supply an appropriate implementation. This also lets tests control execution.

A JVM file-reading example that uses `Dispatchers.IO` cannot be copied unchanged into code shared with JS and Wasm/JS, where IO is not available. Supplying a dispatcher also does not create background CPU workers on a single browser thread.

To understand a shared ViewModel on a particular host, check three things: which owner stores it and when that store is cleared, what the saved-state integration can restore, and which dispatcher its scope uses. Reading the ViewModel class alone may not reveal the host configuration that supplies these behaviours.

Explain which `ViewModelStoreOwner` retains the shared ViewModel and when its store is cleared. On Android this may be an Activity, Fragment or navigation entry; on iOS it depends on whether the UI uses a Compose host or native SwiftUI integration. Then describe the host’s saved-state support and dispatcher setup. The default `viewModelScope` uses Main when available; without a dispatcher in the scope or launch argument, `launch` uses Default.

lessons.title: Lifecycle-Aware Collection on Each Host
lessons.summary: collectAsStateWithLifecycle can be called from common code, but the lifecycle that drives it is supplied by each Compose Multiplatform host, and the hosts map window, scene and page activity onto lifecycle states differently. The same STARTED threshold therefore stops collection on different user actions on Android, desktop, iOS and web.

blocks.text: Compose Multiplatform shares composables and their state model across platforms. Each platform supplies the host that runs them: an `Activity` on Android, a `UIViewController` created by `ComposeUIViewController` on iOS, a window on desktop, or a page in the browser. That host supplies lifecycle events used by lifecycle-aware APIs.

`collectAsStateWithLifecycle` collects while two conditions hold: the call remains in Composition, and its `LifecycleOwner` is at least `minActiveState`, which defaults to `STARTED`.

The API is available in common code through `org.jetbrains.androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-runtime-compose:2.11.0-beta01`, using the package `androidx.lifecycle.compose`. A shared destination composable can therefore call it on each target. The host supplies the lifecycle state that determines whether collection is active.
The `STARTED` threshold is shared across targets. Whether collection stays active after a user action depends on how the host maps that action to a lifecycle state.
The host mappings differ in exactly the places that matter for a `STARTED` threshold:

rows: Android
The relevant Activity, Fragment or navigation-entry LifecycleOwner supplies state
Collection is active at STARTED or RESUMED and stops when that owner falls below STARTED
Desktop
Visible and focused maps to RESUMED; visible but unfocused to STARTED; minimized or detached to CREATED; disposal to DESTROYED
Losing focus alone keeps collection active; minimizing stops it
iOS
Appeared, foreground and active maps to RESUMED; appeared and foreground but inactive to STARTED; background or not appeared to CREATED
An inactive foreground scene keeps collection active; backgrounding stops it
Web
Focus resumes, blur pauses to STARTED, and a hidden page stops; the documented normal host model skips CREATED and does not reach DESTROYED
A visible but blurred page keeps collection active; hiding the tab stops it

blocks.text: For a report such as “collection continues when the desktop window loses focus”, first check which lifecycle state follows that action. In the Compose Multiplatform 1.11.1 desktop host, focus loss sends `ON_PAUSE`, leaving a visible, unfocused window at `STARTED`, so collection continues. Minimizing sends `ON_STOP`, moving the lifecycle to `CREATED`, so collection stops.

For desktop, JetBrains notes that lifecycle coroutine scopes rely on `Dispatchers.Main.immediate`. Adding `kotlinx-coroutines-swing` supplies a Main dispatcher for the Swing event dispatch thread. Without a usable Main dispatcher, these lifecycle coroutine scopes cannot run as intended.

The same `STARTED` threshold can produce different results on different hosts. For example, losing desktop window focus leaves the lifecycle at `STARTED`, while minimizing moves it below that threshold. Check the host’s event mapping before predicting whether collection stops.

When the host lifecycle drops below the collection threshold, this collector stops and its subscription is removed. A shared upstream still follows its own scope and `SharingStarted` policy.

With `WhileSubscribed`, stopping upstream work depends on the remaining subscribers and any configured stop timeout. A desktop window that merely loses focus stays at `STARTED`, so this collector remains subscribed. Resource-use predictions must account for that host mapping as well as the sharing policy.

These mappings describe Compose Multiplatform 1.11.1 hosts used with lifecycle-runtime-compose 2.11.0-beta01. The lifecycle artifact is beta, and APIs or host mappings may change in later releases. Check the versions in your project before applying the table.

Given a target, current host state and collection API, answer in order: is the call still in Composition; which LifecycleOwner is relevant; what state does this host map the user action to; is that state at least the threshold; and who owns upstream production after this collector stops?

units.title: Koin and Dependency Injection in KMP
units.summary: A multiplatform dependency graph separates shared construction from bindings that need a platform API. Koin can express the shared definitions in common Kotlin code, while each host supplies its platform implementations. Whether to use a container depends on the graph's requirements and the cost of managing it.

lessons.title: One Graph, Several Platforms
lessons.summary: Construction that is identical on every target belongs in shared definitions, while implementations of platform APIs are bound by host modules. Each host assembles one complete graph from both.

blocks.text: A multiplatform graph starts with a construction question: **which decisions are identical on every target, and which require a platform API?** Shared definitions belong in common code when their constructors and contracts are platform-independent. Each host supplies the definitions that need Android, iOS, JVM desktop, or browser APIs.

blocks.code:
shared consumer graph
        ↓
shared abstraction
        ↓
host-specific implementation binding

shared modules + host modules
        ↓
complete graph for that host

blocks.text: Each host assembles the shared definitions with its own platform bindings. Together they form that host's complete application graph. The host composition root chooses the modules that make the shared definitions constructible on that target.

headers: Must be supplied by a host
rows: Repositories constructed from already-bound abstractions
Storage implemented with SharedPreferences, NSUserDefaults, JVM files or browser localStorage
Domain services and pure business rules
Database creation using the target's Room/SQLite environment
State holders and ViewModel construction recipes
Android Context where an Android implementation requires it

blocks.text: Put construction in shared code when it is genuinely platform-independent. Bind platform API implementations in platform modules, and let each host composition root assemble the shared and platform pieces into a complete graph.

Consider an application that stores user settings differently on each platform. Shared code owns a `SettingsStorage` abstraction, then builds `SettingsRepository` and `ThemeController` from it. The shared consumer graph names no platform storage API.

rows: `androidPlatformModule`
`SharedPreferencesSettingsStorage`
SharedPreferences
`iosPlatformModule`
`UserDefaultsSettingsStorage`
NSUserDefaults
`desktopPlatformModule`
`PropertiesFileSettingsStorage`
properties file
`webPlatformModule`
`LocalStorageSettingsStorage`
browser localStorage

blocks.text:
Each platform module binds `single<SettingsStorage> { ... }`, so the same `settingsModule` can construct `SettingsRepository` and `ThemeController` on every target.

This example uses an interface and a retained storage instance. Those choices, the division into modules, and the placement of the host module list depend on the application's requirements. The shared construction does not require Koin; the hosts could also supply their implementations through manual DI.

Database construction follows the same split. Each platform module also binds `OrderDatabase`, built by a host function that knows that platform's database driver and file location; only the Android one needs a `Context`. The shared `dataModule` then constructs `OrderRepository` and `OrderImporter` from the already-bound `OrderDatabase` without knowing which host built it.

Each host's startup function is its composition root. The shared module list is written once; each host adds its platform module and supplies any platform objects its definitions need. In this example, Android supplies an application context for its storage and database implementations.

Keeping the complete module list in each host's startup function is one workable arrangement. Koin's KMP guidance also shows a shared `initKoin` function that combines common modules with an `expect fun platformModule(): Module`. Each target provides the `actual` function, and each host calls `initKoin` from its entry point. Both arrangements locate the platform choice at assembly: one passes the platform module explicitly, and the other accesses it through `expect`/`actual`.

Common code cannot construct both `SharedPreferences` and `NSUserDefaults` implementations and choose one at runtime: those platform APIs are unavailable in code shared by Android and iOS. Put each construction in the corresponding platform source set.

The consumers can still be shared. `SettingsRepository` depends on `SettingsStorage`, so copying its construction into every platform module would duplicate code that does not use a platform API.

A screen's current route ID has a different role. It is input to that screen's operation, rather than shared or platform configuration. Registering one ID in the graph and replacing it on navigation would make per-screen input shared mutable state. Pass it when resolving the consumer with `parametersOf`, as on a single platform.

Keep platform API construction in the appropriate platform source set. Shared consumers can depend on the resulting abstractions, and each host combines the shared definitions with its platform bindings.

Koin's core APIs support common Kotlin targets, and a classic definition is a Kotlin lambda that calls a constructor. These definitions can be shared without reflection-based construction or generated target-specific code.

Koin 4.2 also provides compiler-assisted mechanisms. Multiplatform compatibility describes where the APIs can be used; compiler assistance describes how definitions are generated or checked. A DI library can provide both.

rows: Koin core lists Android, iOS, JVM, JS and Wasm support, plus macOS, Linux and Windows native targets
Core and multiplatform dependency-injection APIs
Koin Compose artifacts follow Compose Multiplatform's supported targets
Compose integration, not Koin core as a whole

blocks.text:
Hilt supplies Android-specific lifecycle integration, so it cannot construct the shared graph for iOS, JS or Wasm. Dagger generates Java code for JVM and Android use; that component cannot serve as the graph used by common Kotlin/Native, JS or Wasm code. Koin provides common multiplatform APIs.

Among the compatible strategies, the choice still depends on graph size, rate of change, verification needs, existing investment and team cost. **Choosing a Strategy for a Shared Graph** works through that decision.

Explain one concrete dependency path: shared `ThemeController` uses `SettingsRepository`, which depends on the shared `SettingsStorage` abstraction. Each host binds its storage implementation and combines that platform module with the shared modules. Explain why Koin's APIs can be used in common code, while keeping the choice of an interface, `expect`/`actual`, or a container tied to the project's requirements.

lessons.title: Choosing a Strategy for a Shared Graph
lessons.summary: A shared DI strategy must support every required target. Among compatible strategies, compare graph size, rate of change, verification needs, existing investment and team cost. These requirements determine whether manual construction or a multiplatform container is sufficient.

sources.title: Kotlin Multiplatform: project structure and source sets

blocks.text:
For a shared Kotlin Multiplatform graph, **the construction code must compile for every target the shared module builds for.** Code in `commonMain` is compiled for all declared targets, so the APIs it uses must be available on all of them. Any DI library it depends on must supply compatible artifacts for those targets.

The same restriction applies to other dependencies. An Android-only JSON or HTTP library can be used from `androidMain`, but cannot be called from code shared with iOS or web targets.

blocks.text: Compare four strategies against the required targets:

headers: Builds the graph in shared code?
rows: Manual DI
Yes
Constructor calls are ordinary Kotlin, which compiles wherever the shared code compiles; hosts pass in their platform implementations
Koin
Yes, within its documented targets
Koin core publishes multiplatform artifacts, and a classic definition is a Kotlin lambda that calls a constructor
Dagger
No
Dagger generates Java source during the build; that code compiles for the JVM and Android, not for Kotlin/Native, JS or Wasm
Hilt
No
Hilt is Dagger plus generated components attached to Android classes, starting from an `Application` annotated `@HiltAndroidApp`

blocks.text:
Both manual DI and Koin can support the shared graph. With manual DI, shared constructors take platform implementations as parameters, and each host calls a shared assembly function with its own implementations.

With Koin, shared modules describe the common construction, and each host adds its platform bindings. A container is useful when the assembly or management work it removes is worth its startup, configuration and diagnostic costs.
Check target compatibility first. Then compare manual construction and a multiplatform container against graph size, change rate, verification needs, existing investment and team cost.

Consider a shared module holding repositories, state holders and ViewModels for Android, iOS, JVM desktop and web hosts, each of which supplies its own storage and database implementations. The project requires one construction graph in shared code, and that graph has grown to about forty definitions that change most weeks.

rows: Requirements
One shared graph across Android, iOS, JVM desktop and web; shared ViewModels; per-host bindings; a large, frequently changing shared assembly
Capability filter
Hilt and Dagger cannot build a graph in shared code for iOS, JS or Wasm; manual DI and Koin can
Valuable properties
One declaration of shared construction, a small completion point per host, constructor-first consumers
Comparison of survivors
Manual DI works, but constructor changes may require updates through several levels of shared assembly; Koin definitions resolve registered dependencies with get(), reducing that wiring work
Plausible choice
Koin, with shared modules plus one platform module per host
Cost accepted
Container startup on every host, definition diagnostics, scope ownership, and a separate decision about how configuration errors are detected
Revisit trigger
The shared graph shrinks until explicit host wiring is cheaper, the required targets change, or verification needs outgrow what the chosen mechanism checks

blocks.text:
Now consider the same four hosts with six stable shared objects. Each host passes two platform implementations to one shared assembly function. Target compatibility leaves the same two candidates, but there is little repeated wiring to remove. Koin would add startup, a definition vocabulary and diagnostics without meeting an additional requirement in this scenario.

Manual DI is sufficient here. Reconsider it if the graph begins changing often enough that maintaining the assembly becomes costly.

Existing investment also affects the choice. Suppose a team knows its shared Koin graph well, but missing definitions have begun to cause incidents. The requirement is earlier detection, so first check whether the existing graph can be verified more effectively.

With Koin 4.2's Compiler Plugin applied and compile-time safety enabled, the build checks missing dependencies, qualifier mismatches and injection call sites in the graph it can analyze. Dynamic module lists and modules loaded later can fall outside that check. Koin's JVM-only `verify()` API can check constructor dependencies in a classic configuration from a test, but it does not check qualifiers or `get()` calls inside definition lambdas.

If these checks cover the incidents, changing DI strategies may add migration cost without solving another requirement. Hilt or Dagger alone would not replace a graph shared with iOS or web hosts, though Dagger can be used on JVM desktop.

A platform name alone does not determine the DI strategy. Check target support and platform integration requirements, then compare the compatible strategies against graph size, change rate, lifetime fit, verification needs, existing investment and migration cost.

Hilt cannot construct the graph shared with non-Android hosts because its generated components are attached to Android classes. It can still serve an Android-only graph. Dagger generates Java code for JVM and Android use; writing its consumers in Kotlin does not make that generated code available to Kotlin/Native, JS or Wasm.

An Android host could keep a Hilt or Dagger graph for Android-only bindings alongside the shared graph. That arrangement needs its own composition root and code that passes dependencies between the two graphs. Include that extra assembly work in the decision.

Check support for each artifact the shared graph uses, at the version in use. Koin core and its Compose integration have different target boundaries: Compose artifacts follow Compose Multiplatform's targets. Compiler-assisted mechanisms also have toolchain requirements; Koin's Compiler Plugin needs the K2 compiler. Compatibility therefore includes both the application's targets and its build tools.

Replacing a shared Koin graph with Hilt would still leave the non-Android hosts needing another mechanism. Dagger could serve JVM desktop as well as Android, but iOS, JS and Wasm would still need a compatible graph.

If the product later became Android-only and relied heavily on Android lifecycles, Hilt's integration could become more valuable. A change of targets can therefore be a reason to revisit the DI strategy even when the frameworks themselves have not changed.

Asked how to do dependency injection on a KMP project, state the capability filter first and apply it with a reason for each exclusion. Then choose between manual construction and a multiplatform container from graph size, change rate, verification needs, existing investment and team cost, name the cost accepted, and finish with the observable change, often a change of targets, that would reopen the decision.
